stories.Headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns and CFO Colette Kress becomes interim CEO
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as NVIDIA’s chief executive on November 12, 2026, after 33 years at the company he co-founded, following reports of personal misconduct and a board investigation. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. NVIDIA shares fell 4.34% to $166.19 that day, while AMD shares rose 5.86%. On Friday, AMD fell 8.75% to $534.06 and Broadcom fell 4.76% to $347.01. AMD CEO Lisa Su was named Yahoo Finance’s 2026 CEO of the Year on the same day Huang resigned.

AMD trades at a trailing P/E of 202, a forward P/E of 35 and 130.79 times free cash flow, with a free cash flow yield of 0.76%. Broadcom declared a $0.65 per share quarterly dividend on September 2, 2026, and produced $13.67 billion of free cash flow in a single quarter against a $1.656 trillion market cap. Broadcom’s fiscal Q3 free cash flow rose 94.5% and was 46% of revenue, with non-GAAP EPS of $3.32 extending its beat run to 9 consecutive quarters. AMD pays no dividend, and its Q3 free cash flow fell 70.9% to $554 million as capex jumped 151% and inventory rose to $11.46 billion, though it holds net cash and 28.2x interest coverage. AMD’s Data Center revenue reached $8.55 billion, up 97%, with segment operating margin expanding to 34% from 25%, and it guided Q4 revenue to about $17 billion, roughly 66% growth.

Lisa Su said “It is true that demand is higher than supply” and expects 2027 revenue to grow more than 80%. Broadcom management guided AI semiconductor revenue to $21.7 billion for the next quarter, after reaching $16.70 billion. Neil Shah, Co-founder and Vice President of Research at Counterpoint Research, said Huang’s role, presence, vision and execution had been central to NVIDIA and the AI ecosystem. Prabhu Ram, VP of Industry Research Group at CyberMedia Research, said the immediate challenge for interim leadership under Kress will be maintaining ecosystem trust, managing enterprise relationships, and proving NVIDIA’s innovation velocity can persist without its founder. Shah also said a slowdown in new, aggressive ecosystem-level investments and lucrative bilateral AI infrastructure deals from NVIDIA is likely without Huang at the helm.

One CNBC Fast Money guest said “AMD is the priciest of the three, but if you look at Broadcom and Micron, they’re still trading at a much lower multiple.” Gartner named Broadcom a leader in custom AI silicon, and its $8.75 billion quarterly infrastructure software business adds diversification AMD lacks. Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle are already running Helios racks, and Broadcom’s AI gains depend on just six XPU customers. AMD carries a 2.542 beta and a 52-week range of $188.22 to $658.52. NVIDIA helped finance many of its own customers, so a break there could slow AI spending across the industry, including at both companies.

Huang’s exit raises questions about whether NVIDIA can maintain its strategic direction and industry relationships. Hyperscaler hardware orders are locked in through at least Q3 and Q4 FY27, and NVIDIA’s near-term roadmap runs from Blackwell through Vera Rubin and Feynman generations. Huang had arbitrated GPU allocations and orchestrated multi-billion-dollar circular financing and compute-backed deals, and his relationships spanned TSMC, Foxconn and SoftBank. AMD shares have been up nearly 139% year-to-date, and Su acquired Fei-Fei Li’s spatial intelligence startup World Labs for $8.2 billion. AMD reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45% year-on-year.

In October last year AMD signed a multi-generation agreement with OpenAI to deploy up to 6 gigawatts of its GPUs, and earlier this year Meta signed another agreement for up to 6 GW of AMD Instinct GPUs, with first deployments for both expected in the second half of 2026 using custom MI450-based accelerators. Anthropic followed in July with a commitment to deploy up to 2 GW of AMD MI450 GPUs in its Helios rack-scale systems, with the first gigawatt scheduled for the first half of 2027. AMD also committed to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, including plans to buy $2.5 billion of its stock. NVIDIA’s stock has seen a 13.7% correction year-to-date, with shares down 32% from its all-time record on October 6, erasing roughly $1.86 trillion in valuation.

stories.Headline: Microsoft removes WordPad from Windows 11 as users restore it manually
stories.Summary:
The author copied WordPad from a fresh Windows 10 installation to a Windows 11 26H2 PC, as reported by Windows Latest on November 15, 2026. Microsoft had removed WordPad from Windows 11 version 24H2, and the app is still missing in 26H2. The author said he recently updated his father's PC to Windows 11 26H2, and his father asked whether it had WordPad. When told Microsoft had deprecated it, his father sighed and said it was enough for him. The author saw someone on X complain about the new Notepad a few days earlier, and most replies favored the post.

Microsoft deprecated WordPad in September 2023, saying it was no longer being updated and would be removed in a future release of Windows. In March 2024, the company confirmed WordPad would be gone from all editions of Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025. Three files were removed: wordpad.exe, wordpadfilter.dll and write.exe, and Windows no longer has a built-in RTF reader. Microsoft recommends Word for rich-text documents like .rtf and .doc, and Notepad for .txt files. WordPad arrived with Windows 95 in August 1995, replacing Microsoft Write, and the Windows 95 Reviewer's Guide admitted it was not a full-blown word processor.

Microsoft's developer documentation mentions the three removed files, and Microsoft's old Knowledge Base article Q135079 lists tables, borders, shading and columns among the Word formatting that disappears in WordPad, calling it a design limitation of WordPad. Microsoft's support page says Notepad's Writing Tools are powered by GPT, which means users must sign in with a Microsoft account to use them. Microsoft's old WordPad help page warned that headers, footers or comments opened in WordPad and saved would be lost. Microsoft did test Office banner ads inside WordPad in a January 2020 Windows 10 Insider build, but they were hidden behind a feature flag. Microsoft never formally announced a change of plans about the Ignite features, but they seem no longer under development.

The author said the Copilot branding is gone from Notepad, the Writing Tools can be switched off, and formatting or tables isn't hurting anyone. He said he doesn't mind the new features and sometimes uses them, but WordPad has no account prompt or AI button and won't get any updates. He said a missing spell check hurts the most, especially when the new Notepad has it, and that for a resume or a document with tracked changes, Word or the free Word for the web is still the right tool. Notepad got a Create a table option for everyone in January 2026, but those tables, along with bold, italics, headings and lists, are stored as Markdown in a plain-text file. PCMag's Chris Hoffman wrote that Microsoft unveiled several major Windows features at Ignite last year, such as a way for AI agents to access Windows desktop apps, but many never made it out of Insider builds.

WordPad sat between Notepad and Word for almost three decades, and its Office-style ribbon came with Windows 7. The Home tab has fonts and sizes, bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, subscript and superscript, text highlighting and font colors, plus alignment, indentation, line spacing and bulleted lists. The Insert group lets you add pictures, date and time, and objects from other apps, and a ruler lets you drag paragraph margins. WordPad documents save as RTF by default, but it can also save .docx, .odt and plain text files. At Build earlier this year, Microsoft announced experimental tools including Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) to safely sandbox OpenClaw agents, and at Ignite last year it debuted an on-device MCP server registry for Windows and a File Explorer MCP connector.

The author's archive has wordpad.exe, WordpadFilter.dll and an en-US folder with wordpad.exe.mui, and users copy them into C:\Program Files\Windows NT\Accessories and approve the administrator prompt. WordPad won't appear in Start menu search this way, so users pin it to the taskbar and set it as the default app for .rtf files from Open with > Choose another app. WordPad doesn't get security fixes anymore, so the author advises avoiding RTF or DOCX files from people you don't trust. Ignite runs from Nov. 17 to 20 at the Moscone Center in San Francisco, and CEO Satya Nadella will kick off the enterprise-focused event with a keynote.

The keynote starts at 10 p.m. in Dubai, 9 p.m. in Riyadh and 8 p.m. in Cairo, and the free digital pass is open to anyone, wherever they live.

stories.Headline: Bogdan Pătrăucean releases Wintoys 3.0 with an option to disable Windows 11 AI services
stories.Summary:
Wintoys 3.0, build 3.0.10.0, was released by developer Bogdan Pătrăucean and announced on Reddit, adding an AI components option under the Optimizations tab. The free tool is distributed through the Microsoft Store and runs on Windows 10 and Windows 11 through a WinUI 3 interface. The option disables background services such as WorkloadsSessionHost.exe, which hold machine-learning models in memory for features like Windows Recall and semantic search. Pătrăucean said those services can use 2GB to more than 8GB of RAM, including while the related features sit idle. On his 16GB Surface Pro 12, he reported that switching them off cut memory use from 11GB to about 5GB.

The option is limited to Copilot+ PCs with a neural processing unit, and on conventional desktops the entry is not expected to appear at all. Wintoys 3.0 also adds a separate Artificial Intelligence section for managing Recall, Click to Do, Notepad's writing tools and agentic search, with toggles depending on installed hardware and Windows features. Profiles exports and restores a Windows setup as a JSON file and requires the paid Wintoys+ add-on, a one-time purchase with lifetime access, while earlier functions remain free. A new Configuration mode applies settings as preferences or policies where the operating system supports it, improving synchronization with the Windows Group Policy Editor. The build also brings extra privacy controls, File Explorer preloading options, a reworked storage cleaner, clearer restart prompts and bug fixes.

Pătrăucean described the memory figures as individual observations rather than controlled benchmarks, and said actual savings will vary with hardware, software configuration and which AI workloads are active. He pointed to a Microsoft Q&A thread from July 2026 in which a different user described recovering about 5GB by halting the Windows AI Fabric service and its associated workload processes. He said the AI components option targets WorkloadsSessionHost.exe, which can run in multiple instances to keep models ready. He pitched Profiles at people setting up a fresh install or provisioning several machines. He said Configuration mode matters because policy refreshes can otherwise revert changes made by third-party tweakers.

The articles say disabling AI services can break the features that depend on them, and that users on work or organization-managed computers are advised to weigh the implications of each tweak because some changes may conflict with corporate configuration. The articles say Copilot+ machines ship with the AI stack enabled by default, and on 16GB configurations the resident models can consume a meaningful share of system memory. The articles say IT administrators may find the Group Policy synchronization the more consequential addition, since managed machines often have settings locked down by policy. The articles say the tool comes from an unverified third-party source rather than Microsoft's own settings app. The articles say Wintoys has been free since its launch and Profiles marks one of the first capabilities reserved for paying supporters.

The articles say Microsoft has worked to trim Windows 11's memory footprint, an effort the company has discussed publicly in recent months. The articles say Wintoys takes a more granular route by exposing individual components rather than waiting for Microsoft to retune them. The articles say the release lands as that Microsoft effort continues. The articles say Wintoys lets users manage system settings, uninstall applications, optimize performance and control privacy features. The articles say the update was detailed by the developer.

The articles say Wintoys 3.0 can be downloaded at no charge from the Microsoft Store. The articles say whether users who came for the memory savings will follow into the paid tier is an open question. The articles leave open the actual savings on other machines, since the figures are individual observations rather than controlled benchmarks. The articles leave open which toggles appear, since that depends on installed hardware and Windows features present on the system. The articles say users should review the implications of individual tweaks before applying them.

stories.Headline: Oakland City Council unanimously extends AI data center moratorium until October 2027
stories.Summary:
The Oakland City Council voted unanimously this week to extend the city's moratorium on AI data centers for 10 months, passing the extension at Tuesday's council meeting. The extension keeps the existing 45-day moratorium in place until Oct. 5, 2027, giving the city time to produce a policy protecting residents from public health and safety dangers posed by data centers. Councilmember Carroll Fife is leading the City Council's efforts to pass the moratorium. The original 45-day moratorium passed on Oct. 6 and was set to expire on Nov. 20. Mayor Barbara Lee backed the original moratorium in her recent State of the City address.

The extension runs until Oct. 5, 2027, and keeps the existing 45-day moratorium in place. The original 45-day moratorium passed on Oct. 6 and was set to expire on Nov. 20. Other California cities that already have passed data center moratoriums include San Francisco, Hayward, Oakley, Richmond, Monterey Park, Gilroy, South El Monte, Montebello, and Calexico. Thirty-five public speakers signed up to talk about the moratorium extension, and almost all of them supported it. A speaker for Care for Community Action said her organization surveyed more than 400 residents and found that 73% favor a permanent ban on all data centers being built in Oakland.

Fife said two of the giants in the tech industry have leased space in West Oakland, and another has shown interest in a downtown location. Fife said she felt it was imperative to take immediate action to protect Oakland residents from what has been seen in other parts of the country. Fife said the move is not a rejection of technology or economic growth but guardrails against an industry that has steamrolled individuals throughout the entire globe. Fife said it is important that staff have the ability to do the appropriate study and outreach to the community so the community has a voice. Mayor Lee said residents need to weigh in on any industry that is trying to come to Oakland.

Bill Gilchrist, director of the city's Planning and Building Department, said the city is committed to looking at areas that might be most severely impacted by land use and residential proximity. Gilchrist said the city wants to engage members of the community who may historically have not been able to participate or be invited to participate in this kind of discussion. Gilchrist said the idea for the city is to do no harm. Laney College professor Peter Brown said not to cast a vote based on the illusion of the old economy, where corporate investment in Oakland meant thousands of lasting, good-paying jobs and property, business, and income taxes flowing into city coffers. Brown said those days are long gone in this new economy, where every investment is just another asset to be exploited and used as collateral for more investment.

Nyah Tisdell, an East Oakland community organizer with Communities for a Better Environment, said community members say no to data centers that will go straight to East Oakland, which already has so much industry and pollution. Rev. Leslie Bowling-Dyer said data centers are part of the necessary infrastructure for the rise of an economically and politically untouchable class. Bowling-Dyer said people are not just being lunatics displaying an irrational fear of technology. Bowling-Dyer said technological innovation is not equivalent to social progress and technological advance is not the problem in itself, but the people who control it are. Some of the speakers urged the council to consider a permanent ban on data center development in the city.

Fife said she represents a district that many of these potential entities are interested in. Fife said there is an uprising across the country when it comes to how data centers are operating in regard to land use, impacts to the environment, excessive water use and pollution, air pollution, noise pollution, and a host of things negatively impacting communities. The city must ensure that it has adequate guardrails and that the community is actively involved in decision-making, Fife said. Some speakers praised Fife for her leadership on the issue. Protesters rallied against data centers outside Oakland city hall in September.

The articles do not state what the city's policy will contain or when the study and outreach will be completed. The articles do not state which tech companies have leased space in West Oakland or which company has shown interest in a downtown location. The articles do not state the outcome of the council's consideration of a permanent ban. The articles do not state what action, if any, the city will take after the moratorium ends on Oct. 5, 2027. stories.Headline: Punjab bans camera-equipped smart glasses for 30 days from October 2026
stories.Summary:
Pakistan's Punjab province imposed a 30-day ban on camera-equipped smart glasses with hidden recording ability, beginning in October 2026, according to a report by Husain Parvez published on November 15, 2026. The order also covered miniature cameras disguised as pens or keychains, and retailers could not evade it by selling the affected devices online. Punjab authorities said they had received complaints of spying devices being used for illegal surveillance, harassment and blackmail. The authorities did not mention which models were included, and the ban was limited only to Punjab. No country has a permanent, outright ban on AI glasses, the report said.

New York banned smart glasses with cameras, microphones or computers in all 1,240 state and local courts since July 20, 2026, requiring them to be turned over to uniformed court officers for safekeeping. Ray-Ban Meta glasses with prescription lenses are also prohibited in New York courts, and officials urged visitors to pack a traditional pair. Meta glasses are banned in courts and tribunals in England and Wales, where security personnel can hold them until visitors leave. Western Australia banned AI glasses from public schools since October 12, 2026, applying the policy to students, staff and visitors with exemptions for approved medical, accessibility and educational reasons. Victoria announced similar restrictions, which will not take effect until January 27, 2027.

Smart glasses are prohibited from SAT test sites, even during breaks, unless an accommodation is granted, and scores may be canceled for violating the testing rules. Marine Corps policy at Camp Lejeune and other bases does not allow the use of smart glasses. In Australia, Canterbury-Bankstown Council banned smart glasses at its leisure and aquatic centers. UK cinemas are rolling out measures to curb camera-enabled glasses, citing privacy and film piracy issues. Royal Caribbean permits smart glasses on board but prohibits their use in casinos, medical facilities or youth areas.

Norway's government is considering temporary restrictions that could cover parks, beaches, shopping centers and gyms, but those proposals have not been enacted. Norwegian officials have not settled on which types of smart glasses would be covered, a distinction that matters because the Even Realities G2 has no camera while Ray-Ban Meta and Oakley Meta glasses can take photos and videos. In September 2026, Paris prosecutors opened investigations following complaints about women being filmed without consent using smart glasses, with the footage posted online. Prosecutors did not identify which brands were involved. Meta claims the white recording LED on its glasses lights up when photos or videos are taken and that the camera is disabled if its system detects tampering with the light.

Ray-Ban's documentation states that some camera-based AI functions on newer models can work without the LED being activated, since they are not saving shareable photos or videos. Mark Zuckerberg's team showed up in Ray-Ban Meta glasses during his testimony in Los Angeles in February 2026. Judge Carolyn Kuhl warned, according to the Los Angeles Times, that if your glasses are recording, you must take them off, though no recording of the proceedings was confirmed. The report said AI glasses can look like a normal pair of glasses but are becoming more unwelcome in courthouses, schools and other public places for safety and privacy reasons. The report said the list of places banning AI glasses is expected to continue to grow.

The report was published by Engadget and republished by AOL, both dated November 15, 2026, with the Engadget version timed at 11:00 am EST. The report stated that in many other countries and states, AI glasses are banned in specific places. The report did not say what would happen when Punjab's 30-day ban expires. The report did not say whether Norway would adopt the temporary restrictions it is considering. The report did not identify the brands involved in the Paris complaints or confirm any recording during Zuckerberg's testimony.

stories.Headline: UT San Antonio wins 2026 WOW Award for its generative AI peer learning network
stories.Summary:
The UT San Antonio Generative AI Peer Learning Network received a 2026 Outstanding Work (WOW) Award from the WICHE Cooperative for Educational Technologies (WCET), the university announced on November 16, 2026. The award recognizes the university's approach to helping faculty, staff and students explore responsible use of artificial intelligence in teaching and learning. Academic Innovation launched the network in January 2023. The network has grown from a grassroots effort into a university-wide community of more than 150 faculty, staff, instructional designers, librarians, doctoral students and university partners. It meets monthly with participants from the university's academic colleges, Enterprise Technology Solutions, Student Affairs and Student Success.

The network supports AI adoption through collaborative experimentation, professional development, a self-paced faculty course, faculty and student AI resources, and the Student AI Partners program. Its work has informed course redesigns and authentic assessment strategies across disciplines. The group partnered with the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board to create "AI Essentials for Higher Ed Students," an open educational resource. The network has expanded collaboration with faculty at the Health Science Center. This is the second WOW Award for UT San Antonio's Academic Innovation team, which first received the honor in 2021 for its Faculty Champions program.

Melissa Vito, EdD, vice provost for academic innovation, said she saw energy, curiosity and willingness to experiment with AI in the curriculum every time the group meets. Vito said the group includes faculty from nearly every discipline, and what works in a writing program won't be the same as what works in a statistics course. She said the network's work is grounded in a shared belief that AI is a skill students will need in the workforce. Vito said the university was intentional about using AI to amplify creativity, not replace it, and to promote critical thinking. Claudia Arcolin, PhD, assistant vice provost for teaching, learning and strategic initiatives, said the network started as a grassroots project and became a community of practice across departments and colleges.

Arcolin said pedagogy is the foundation for every conversation around artificial intelligence. Chris Packham, PhD, professor of physics and astronomy, introduced AI-supported assignments in an introductory astronomy course in Fall 2023 and surveyed students. Research later published in a Springer Nature journal found that a majority of students surveyed reported improved understanding of course concepts and a more engaging learning experience. The course was enhanced in Spring 2026 with AI-generated podcasts, infographics and a course chatbot. Packham said having a group to share results and ideas and receive feedback has been invaluable.

Mary Dixson, PhD, a professor of instruction in communication, said she is in her 33rd year of teaching and the group helps her get out of her comfort zone. Dixson said if people are not sharing information, they will be left behind quickly. David Henzi, EdD, senior associate dean of the School of Health Professions, said the network has been a tremendous resource for Health Science Center faculty. Henzi said the community is building a shared understanding of the responsibilities, ethics and best practices surrounding AI. Rita Mitra, DMA, assistant department chair and professor of practice in the Department of Information Systems and Cybersecurity and an AI Faculty Fellow, said AI asks educators to revisit the purpose of education with transparency, urgency and shared responsibility.

WCET is the leader in the practice, policy and advocacy of digital learning in higher education and was founded by the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education (WICHE). WCET is a member-driven organization that brings together colleges, universities and educational organizations to improve the quality and reach of digital learning. WICHE is one of the nation's regional higher education compacts focused on expanding educational access, affordability and innovation through collaboration and public policy. According to WCET, the Outstanding Work Award recognizes initiatives that leverage innovative digital learning solutions, demonstrate measurable impact on learner success and offer models other institutions can adapt. The Faculty Champions program established faculty representatives within each college and department to support the university's rapid transition to online instruction during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The GenAI Peer Learning Network will remain focused on helping students develop the skills, critical thinking abilities and ethical understanding needed to succeed as AI reshapes higher education and the workforce. The university invites readers to learn more about the network and how to get involved and to explore its GenAI teaching resources. In a 2021 WCET guest blog, Melissa Vito and Claudia Arcolin reflected on how the Faculty Champions network helped sustain instructional excellence during the COVID-19 pandemic. The articles do not say when the 2026 WOW Award will be presented or what the award includes. The articles do not say how many institutions received the 2026 award or who else was recognized.

stories.Headline: Stanford AI Index reports global corporate AI investment tops $1 trillion in 2026
stories.Summary:
Global corporate investment in artificial intelligence has surpassed $1 trillion so far in 2026, already exceeding the entire 2025 total by 46 percent, according to new findings from the Stanford AI Index. The figures were released in a Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence article published on November 15, 2026, and written by AI Index editor Sha Sajadieh. The article says the money underscores an economic ambition of extraordinary scale, committed to a technology whose consequences are still being learned how to measure. The findings also describe effects unfolding in real time, from shifts in talent migration to emerging evidence in labor markets and expanding physical infrastructure that communities are being asked to accommodate.

The article reports that in every country surveyed, more people expect AI to eliminate jobs than to create them. In the United States, 60 percent of adults say they would feel uncomfortable with a new data center in their area, including majorities in both political parties, while globally a majority of survey respondents still believe AI's benefits outweigh its drawbacks. Data from the Stanford HAI Digital Economy Lab's AI Economic Indicators show that employment declines among younger workers in AI-exposed occupations have continued into 2026, particularly in customer service. A new finding broadens the concern, because declines have deepened even in occupations where AI supports rather than replaces human work, including roles such as marketing and IT managers. The article states that these patterns do not establish causality but raise important questions about how AI's economic effects may differ across the workforce.

Sajadieh is responsible for the article as the AI Index editor, and the Index describes its mission as providing unbiased, rigorously vetted, and globally sourced data for policymakers, researchers, journalists, executives, and the general public. The article says the findings come as the 2027 AI Index report is being prepared, with annual and year-to-date datasets refreshed periodically, and it recalls that last year's report documented a widening gap between capability, deployment, and readiness. It also asks whether the future being financed is the same future people expect, experience, or want for themselves, noting that public sentiment is turning out to be just as jagged as AI's technical frontier. The next AI Index will be released in April 2027.

stories.Summary:
AvePoint announced an expanded partnership with Microsoft to support AI deployment, governance, and security across tools such as Copilot, Agent 365, and Copilot Studio. The announcement came in a Simply Wall St article dated 2026-11-15T06:00:00Z. AvePoint also raised full year 2026 and Q4 revenue guidance and reported higher Q3 revenue, net income, and earnings per share versus the prior year. BlackLine announced an expanded AI roadmap with SAP SE, integrating Verity agentic AI tools with SAP Joule and SAP Business AI Platform. That announcement came in a Yahoo Finance article dated 2026-11-14T06:00:00Z.

The AvePoint partnership ties its Trust Platform and AgentPulse into Copilot, Agent 365, Copilot Studio, and Foundry. AvePoint is acting as Customer Zero for Microsoft AI technologies to feed real world deployment insights back into its product roadmap and customer playbooks. BlackLine's roadmap automates key record to report tasks such as reconciliations, high volume matching, and complex accruals across multi ERP environments. The partnership deepens BlackLine's role as an SAP Solution Extensions partner and ties its accounting controls and data integrity tools into SAP's Autonomous Finance vision. The AvePoint article says the business is positioning its AvePoint Trust Platform and AgentPulse as core infrastructure for AI governance. The article says the operational risk is that AvePoint leans even harder into one platform at the exact time analysts are watching for broader multi cloud traction. The BlackLine article says the partnership includes synchronized product development and unified support that can matter for enterprise adoption and platform stickiness. It says the expanded SAP AI roadmap directly touches the thesis and strengthens the story around deeper platform adoption, although it does not remove the risk of slower new logo additions.

The AvePoint article says the analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St still flags platform dependence and slower multi cloud expansion as pressure points. It says the most optimistic analysts were already pencilling in about US$878.0 million of revenue and US$128.4 million of earnings by 2029, compared with the consensus US$814.5 million and US$86.7 million. The BlackLine article says the analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St leans on a shift away from smaller accounts, despite slower forecast revenue growth of 9% per year and softer recent net revenue retention. It says BlackLine carries higher debt and lower margins than last year, as well as a P/E above the US Software industry average.

The AvePoint article says AvePoint's narrative projects US$814.5 million revenue and US$86.7 million earnings by 2029, assuming 20.4% yearly revenue growth and an earnings increase of about US$15.2 million from US$71.5 million today. It says the most optimistic views were set before this Microsoft partnership update, so estimates may change as different analyst camps refresh their forecasts. The BlackLine article says BlackLine's narrative projects US$1.0b revenue and US$168.4 million earnings by 2029, assuming 11.9% yearly revenue growth and an earnings increase of about US$133.6 million from US$34.8 million today. It says the most cautious analysts were only modeling around 9.4% yearly sales growth and about US$152.0 million earnings by 2029. It says the SAP focused AI roadmap sits alongside fresh Q3 2026 numbers.

The AvePoint article says the raised 2026 and Q4 revenue guidance, combined with higher Q3 net income, make near term execution on that thesis the key catalyst, particularly around AI related add ons. It says how well management balances those two forces now matters a lot for the medium term story. The BlackLine article says the earnings update gives a reference point for how much the Verity Prepare, Match and Accruals agents need to contribute over time to justify the heavier SAP alignment. It says to watch how remaining performance obligations, AI agent adoption and SAP led bookings trend relative to the guidance path. stories.Headline: Kenyan High Court Justice Andayi sets aside ODPC compensation award and questions commissioner's power to decide damages
stories.Summary:
Justice Francis Andayi of the High Court set aside a KSh1.25 million compensation award against a Nairobi healthcare business on a complaint by a patient identified as GW about CCTV cameras in a clinical examination room. The patient argued the cameras compromised her privacy, and the healthcare provider disputed the ODPC's findings and presented forensic evidence on the footage. The High Court did not decide whether the alleged privacy violation occurred, and instead examined whether the Commissioner had legal authority to order compensation. The judgment questioned whether the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner can independently determine damages payable to individuals under the Data Protection Act. The decision came after the ODPC built a record of financial enforcement, with more than KSh30 million paid to individuals during 2025.

The dispute centred on Section 65 of the Data Protection Act and Regulation 14(3)(e) of the subsidiary legislation, and Section 65 gives individuals a right to compensation for damage from a contravention of the Act. Justice Andayi observed that Section 65 does not expressly assign the Commissioner the job of deciding whether damage occurred or calculating compensation payable. He distinguished the regulator's powers to investigate complaints, impose administrative penalties and issue enforcement notices from the separate function of deciding monetary claims between parties. He questioned whether Regulation 14(3)(e) could introduce a substantive power Parliament had not expressly provided in the parent legislation. He relied on the principle that statutory agencies and tribunals can exercise only powers conferred on them by law.

Justice Andayi also questioned the procedure followed when the ODPC issued the award, after the regulator investigated the complaint, considered the provider's response and issued a monetary determination. He was concerned the process had not provided an adequate hearing at which both sides could contest the evidence and address the compensation claim. He questioned whether the same Commissioner could investigate an alleged violation, effectively prosecute the complaint and then determine the financial remedy without safeguards required by natural justice. He said: "Even if a hearing were to be conducted, I again doubt that it would be by the same Data Commissioner to be the one investigating, then prosecuting it and then deciding." He said that would be against all the rules of natural justice.

The patient and the Data Commissioner maintained that Section 65, read with Regulation 14, authorised the watchdog to issue compensation orders, and they relied on previous High Court decisions supporting the regulator's administrative remedies. Justice Andayi found the earlier authorities had not adequately addressed whether the compensation provision in the regulations exceeded the powers granted under the Act. He declined to strike down Regulation 14(3)(e) or declare all previous ODPC compensation awards unlawful, saying such a challenge required proceedings directed at the validity of the subsidiary legislation with the Attorney-General given an opportunity to participate. The judgment does not invalidate previous awards, and the underlying right of individuals to seek compensation under Section 65 remains. The ODPC's compensation decisions have affected financial services, healthcare, lending and digital commerce.

Standard Investment Bank was ordered to pay Andrew Endovo KSh50,000 after sending him an unsolicited promotional email without his consent, and Platinum Credit was ordered to compensate Philip Bolo KSh900,000 after continuing direct marketing despite his objection. Moja Expressway Company, which operates the 27-kilometre Nairobi Expressway, was ordered to pay former employee Cyrus Mwaniki Ndung'u KSh500,000 for using his photograph to promote electronic toll collection services without permission. Tech Limited faced a KSh2.6 million compensation order, which it subsequently challenged at the High Court. In April 2026 the regulator ordered St. Luke Orthopaedic & Trauma Hospital Eldoret to pay Merceline Akoth Odeyo KSh525,000 after she received medical test results belonging to another person on two occasions and her medical information was shared with an external laboratory without her knowledge or consent.

The hospital attributed the incident to human error and argued the information shared was limited to identification details, and the Commissioner found it had not demonstrated explicit and informed consent or adequately protected her personal information. TechTrendsKE reported in April 2025 that the ODPC issued 51 determinations in 2024, with average fines of approximately KSh522,308 per case, and those administrative fines serve a different purpose from compensation awarded to individuals. Immaculate Kassait, the country's first Data Commissioner, is preparing for a leadership transition after a six-year tenure, and a November 13, 2026 assessment listed more than 13,000 complaints handled, 459 determinations issued and 206 enforcement and penalty notice actions. The regulator had also registered approximately 28,000 data controllers and processors, and Kassait has called for amendments to the Data Protection Act on artificial intelligence, sensitive personal information, penalties and data governance.

President William Ruto nominated Lydia Sitienei Chelagat, formerly Director of Legal Services at the Communications Authority of Kenya, to succeed Kassait on November 10, 2026, and her nomination was forwarded to the National Assembly for consideration. In the EU, Ireland's Data Protection Commission found that Tinder's "Download My Data" tool omitted certain categories of personal information or provided only summaries without clearly informing users, and the EU fined Match Group, the owner of Tinder, €11 million. The investigation into Match Group was launched in 2020 and resulted in an order requiring the company to bring its data processing practices into compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation within three months. Match Group rejected the findings and announced plans to appeal, insisting that Tinder maintains strong privacy protections for its users.

The ODPC's ability to investigate complaints and enforce compliance remains intact, and the unresolved issue concerns the legal route through which it can determine compensation. The eventual determination of whether the Commissioner can independently award those damages will depend on a direct judicial examination of the regulation underpinning that authority. The judgment provides businesses grounds to scrutinise the statutory basis and procedures behind compensation orders, while Section 65 continues to recognise the right of individuals to seek compensation when personal information is mishandled. The incoming Commissioner will inherit an institution with a substantial enforcement record and an expanding regulatory mandate.

stories.Headline: Italy fines Meta 805 million euros for accessing Android photos without consent
stories.Summary:
Italy's data protection agency fined Meta 805 million euros on November 14, 2026. The agency says Meta accessed photos and videos from Android users without their consent. This action happened because Meta allegedly failed to inform users about this data access. The regulator claims the company used these files for its camera roll suggestions feature. This is the largest fine ever issued by the Italian data protection regulator.

The fine concerns the camera roll suggestions feature used when browsing Facebook on Android devices. Meta must now get separate and specific consent for this feature within 60 days. The company must clearly explain what the feature does and how users can disable it. This feature must be disabled by default, even for users who previously gave their authorization. The authority cited a violation of the Italian law implementing the EU's ePrivacy directive.

The Italian Data Protection Authority is responsible for this fine and the accompanying legal orders. They stated that a single permission for the entire app covers multiple features with different needs. The agency said a generic warning prevented users from understanding they authorized picture and video suggestions. They noted that full permission allows an app to read a device's entire photo archive permanently. The authority rejected Meta's claim that the Irish authority had jurisdiction over this specific matter.

Meta did not immediately respond to requests for comment regarding the fine or the findings. The company is affected by the ruling and now has the right to appeal. Android users in Italy are the ones whose photo and video privacy was allegedly violated. The regulator believes users could not verify which information the app was actually using. The agency claims the one-stop-shop mechanism does not apply to the ePrivacy regulation.

The investigation into Meta's data practices was launched by the Italian authorities in 2025. It focused on how the app requests access to the camera roll of Android phones. The agency found that the authorization request was preceded by a warning that was too generic. This process allegedly allowed the app to access the entire photo archive of the user. The regulator determined that this practice violated specific privacy laws within the country of Italy.

Meta must now implement the required changes to its consent process within the next 60 days. The company may choose to appeal the decision to the appropriate legal authorities. The articles do not state if Meta intends to challenge the 805 million euro fine. It remains open whether Meta will successfully argue for the jurisdiction of the Irish authority. The text does not say if other European regulators will take similar actions against Meta.

stories.Headline: Mars and Genpact open a Hyderabad capability centre to develop AI-assisted systems for Mars operations
stories.Summary:
Mars, Incorporated and Genpact inaugurated a Global Capability Centre in Hyderabad, according to announcements published in mid November 2026, with the facility spread across approximately 60,000 square feet and initially housing more than 400 Genpact colleagues. The centre will support Mars' operations across its global markets and will focus on digital innovation and AI-assisted business processes, with plans to scale to 1,000 Mars associates over time, although the announcements do not specify a timeline for reaching that workforce size. The launch builds on a relationship between the two companies that was established in 2018, and the companies plan to use Genpact's Agentic Operations model to redesign processes in order to improve operational speed, consistency and visibility. The Hyderabad centre will develop AI-assisted systems within a governance framework tailored to Mars' requirements, and human expertise and oversight will remain central to these operations, according to the announcement. The centre adds to Mars' presence in India, where the company has invested in seven local factories since 1995 and currently employs more than 2,400 associates across its Snacking, Food and Nutrition, and Pet Nutrition businesses, and its India operations also include a Royal Canin packaging centre.

Mars recently invested $55 million, or roughly ₹516 crore, to expand its Hyderabad Pet Nutrition factory, a move the company said would support domestic demand and exports, and it allocated an additional $12 million, or roughly ₹113 crore, for a Royal Canin distribution and packaging centre, which it said would strengthen localisation and supply resilience. The new GCC forms part of Mars' network of strategic hubs supporting business functions across its global markets. Tarun Chopra, Unit Leader for Consumer Goods at Genpact, said the centre would put the company's approach to work through Agentic-enabled Operations, designing AI-assisted systems that operate within a governance framework tailored to Mars and are meant to deliver measurable business outcomes, and he added that the approach would combine agentic AI capabilities with human expertise. Claus Aagaard, Chief Financial Officer of Mars, said India had remained an important market in the company's growth journey and noted that the Hyderabad centre would strengthen collaboration and advance digital capabilities.

D Sridhar Babu, Telangana's Minister for Information Technology, Electronics and Communications, Industries and Commerce, and Legislative Affairs, attended the inauguration and highlighted Hyderabad's technology ecosystem, skilled workforce and business environment, saying the city had established itself as a destination for global capability centres and that the new facility would connect Mars' established business in India with required technology capabilities and talent. Emilia B Smith, Acting Public Affairs Officer at the US Consulate General in Hyderabad, also attended the launch and highlighted the longstanding commercial relationship between the US and India. For Genpact, the partnership builds on nearly a decade of operational experience with Mars, and the companies intend to combine this process knowledge with agentic AI capabilities to support business functions. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the stated plans to scale the centre's workforce and the absence of a timeline for reaching 1,000 Mars associates.

stories.Headline: Anthropic buys 3.4 billion dollars of gas-fired engines from OnePWR Solutions for its AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Anthropic signed a contract for gas-fired engines on November 14, 2026, to power its AI data centers. The AI company behind Claude spent 3.4 billion dollars on this equipment. They purchased these power plants from OnePWR Solutions, which is an energy company based in Texas. This deal is the largest known single purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI lab. These engines will provide the data centers with an enormous amount of off-grid electricity.

The S-1 filing from Anthropic mentions natural gas five times in just one paragraph. The company notes that some planned data center facilities rely on dedicated on-site natural gas-fired generation. This exposes the company to fuel price volatility and supply disruptions that they bear on a pass-through basis. These facilities also face constraints on pipeline capacity and firm fuel transportation necessary to deliver gas. Failure to secure gas supply and transportation could cause a planned site to be delayed or abandoned.

Anthropic stated that natural gas is a cleaner fossil fuel but not a clean one. Their AI bot noted that gas plants emit 400 to 500 grams of CO2 per kilowatt hour. The bot explained that methane leaks during drilling and transport can erode the advantage gas has over coal. It mentioned that building new gas plants can lock in emissions for 30 to 40 years. The bot added that carbon capture could reduce emissions but remains costly and not widely deployed.

The Financial Times broke the news, while Futurism called the move a sign of turning away from the climate crisis. The Sierra Club estimated that upcoming AI data centers could release 2.1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by 2030. This amount of pollution could wipe out nearly 15 years of greenhouse gas reduction efforts. Voters showed they are fed up, as only one of 41 recent midterm ballot measures favored data centers. Researchers have found that the effects of AI on the environment are nothing short of devastating.

The articles note that 26.8 percent of U.S. businesses used AI in October 2026, compared with 3.7 percent in September 2023. Energy Transfer operates over 140,000 miles of pipelines across 44 states and has 68.8 billion dollars in long-term debt. Energy Transfer signed agreements to supply natural gas to Oracle and a Nexus Data Center hyperscale campus. They also have a 20-year binding agreement with Entergy Louisiana, which partners with Meta Platforms for a data center. Energy Transfer grew its adjusted EBITDA by 31 percent in the third quarter of 2026 to 5 billion dollars.

OpenAI may go public in 2027 and is currently burning through billions of dollars every quarter. Analysts covering Energy Transfer set a median one-year price target of 25 dollars for the stock. The articles leave open whether the AI industry will continue to favor gas over solar and wind power. It remains unclear if the debt of pipeline companies will lead to lower than expected returns. The future prognosis for the environment remains grim as AI companies race to secure necessary utilities.

stories.Headline: Velotic director Joe Gerstl leads webinar on building trusted data foundations for AI in manufacturing
stories.Summary:
A webinar titled Building the Data Foundation for AI-Powered Manufacturing is scheduled for 2 p.m. Eastern on November 19, according to Packaging Strategies, which published the announcement on November 15, 2026. The session will feature Joe Gerstl, Director of Manufacturing Execution Systems Software at Velotic, as the featured speaker. The webinar is described as thought leadership content for manufacturers, and registration is open through the publication. Artificial intelligence is transforming manufacturing, but the article says success depends on access to trusted, contextualized operational data.

The webinar will explore how leading consumer packaged goods manufacturers turn shop floor information into actionable intelligence through real-time data collection, manufacturing execution systems, analytics, and emerging AI technologies. Attendees will learn how to establish a scalable data foundation that supports predictive insights, operational visibility, and future AI initiatives without requiring a complete technology overhaul. The session will explain why trusted, contextualized manufacturing data is the critical foundation for successful AI initiatives and how MES enables real-time visibility by connecting equipment, process, quality, and production data. It will also cover practical AI and analytics use cases, including predictive maintenance, quality optimization, downtime reduction, and natural-language access to operational insights. A roadmap for advancing from data collection and analytics to scalable, AI-driven operational excellence in CPG manufacturing is also promised.

Gerstl is responsible for MES software at Velotic, and the article presents him as the expert leading the discussion on building the data foundation. stories.Headline: IT ministry opens consent manager registration portal for Indian companies
stories.Summary:
The IT ministry opened registration for consent managers under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 on November 16, 2026. This action allows eligible Indian companies to apply through a new online portal to operationalise data governance. IT secretary S Krishnan launched the portal, dpbi.gov.in, for applications to the Data Protection Board of India. The registration framework officially came into effect on November 13, allowing companies to seek this registration. Parliament passed the original Digital Personal Data Protection Act in August 2023 to establish a legal framework.

The Act regulates digital personal data and non-digital data that is subsequently digitised, with presidential assent given August 11, 2023. Eligible Indian companies must possess a minimum net worth of 2 crore rupees to qualify as consent managers. The DPDP Rules, 2025, were notified on November 13, 2025, to establish a phased timeline for implementation. Key provisions regarding data principals, data fiduciaries, and penalty processes will take effect on May 13, 2027. Financial penalties for specified contraventions under this legislation can reach up to 250 crore rupees.

MeitY stated that the new framework is an important step toward allowing data principals to exercise greater control over consent. The ministry requires data fiduciaries to obtain free, specific, informed, unconditional, and unambiguous consent before processing any personal data. Fiduciaries must inform individuals about the purpose of data collection and implement reasonable security safeguards for the information. They are also required to notify the Data Protection Board of India and affected individuals if a data breach occurs. The government received 6,915 inputs from citizens, startups, MSMEs, industry bodies, and civil society during the consultation process.

The Digital News Publishers Association, representing 21 news publishers, challenged the Act and the 2025 Rules before the Supreme Court. These publishers argue that the absence of a specific journalistic exemption could undermine investigations into corruption or misuse of office. Affected parties include data principals, who are individuals whose data is processed, and data fiduciaries, who determine processing means. The challenge specifically mentions Sections 7, 17, 18, 19, 27, 29, 36, 37, and 44(3), as well as certain provisions of the Rules. The publishers believe the law must distinguish legitimate public-interest journalism from the commercial exploitation of personal data.

The 2017 Supreme Court case Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India recognised privacy as a constitutionally protected fundamental right. The Act mandates verifiable parental consent for processing personal data of children below 18 years of age. It restricts tracking, behavioural monitoring, and targeted advertising directed at children, although some specified statutory exemptions still apply. The law grants data principals rights to access, correction, erasure, and the ability to withdraw their previously given consent. Section 44(3) of the Act amends Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, regarding personal information.

A Bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant issued notice to the Union Government on October 27, 2026. The Supreme Court has listed the matter for a further hearing on November 17, 2026, regarding the challenge. The court declined to grant interim relief to the publishers without first hearing the position of the Union Government. The articles leave open whether the law adequately safeguards citizens against excessive governmental access to their private personal information. It remains unclear how the court will reconcile the relationship between privacy, freedom of expression, and the public's right.

stories.Headline: Scott Wiener and Manny Rutinel seek to establish a federal law regulating artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Democratic congressmen-elect Scott Wiener and Manny Rutinel arrived in Washington this week for new lawmaker orientation. These two men previously created the first major state-level AI laws in California and Colorado. They now plan to work together to establish a federal law regulating artificial intelligence. Both legislators won tight congressional races last week to move their efforts to the national level. They have been phone friends for years while fighting tech industry lobbying and committee votes.

Wiener, 56, represented San Francisco and passed a limited AI safety law in 2025 after a 2024 veto. His law requires AI developers to report critical incidents and publicly disclose security and safety protocols. Rutinel, 31, passed Colorado legislation in 2024 and revised it in May 2026 to target AI discrimination. His rules focus on AI-powered discrimination within healthcare, finance, housing, and employment. They are now seeking spots on a potential House AI select committee for next year.

Scott Wiener said they fought this issue before it was popular and faced a brutal industry fight. He stated they are dogged in ensuring AI benefits humanity and does not cause any harm. Manny Rutinel called AI one of the most defining issues of our time for the world. He claimed large corporations put profits ahead of people and push reckless experiments risking families and kids. Both men are described as tenacious legislators who worry about the risk of AI losing control.

Democratic leaders in Ohio, Georgia, and Florida won races by demanding stronger regulation of data centers and AI. Public First super PAC spent 3.5 million dollars on Wiener and 2.6 million dollars on Rutinel. Nathan Calvin of Encode said Wiener first took an ambitious swing at regulating frontier AI risks. Scott Wisor of Secure AI Project said Rutinel is familiar with issues that day-to-day folks face. AI safety advocates and frontier AI labs provided thousands of dollars in donations to their campaigns.

Wiener studied AI safety in salons and is deeply enmeshed in the world of Bay Area tech workers. Rutinel is a former climate lawyer and Yale graduate who worked at McDonald's during his high school years. He began reading books on AI in 2018 and sold blood plasma to pay his bills. Former Assemblywoman Rebecca Bauer-Kahan said Wiener personally negotiated language and met every colleague to earn their support. Brad Carson said both candidates were heavily involved in AI politics before they decided to run.

Democratic plans for AI guardrails next year face a potential veto from President Donald Trump. Trump argues that limiting U.S. companies risks losing strategic ground to China on this pivotal technology. Markets are vulnerable after investors lost hundreds of billions following news about Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang. Huang was linked to a suspected Chinese spy, which impacted rosy expectations for industry profitability. The articles leave open whether the House will actually create the proposed AI select committee.

stories.Headline: Senator Elizabeth Warren urges Congress to restrict China's access to advanced AI technology
stories.Summary:
Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts used a post on X this past Sunday to call for new laws. She urged Congress to pass legislation that would restrict the access China has to advanced artificial intelligence technology. The Democratic senator argued that the financial interests of corporate executives could potentially undermine the national security of the United States. She questioned whether the leaders of major technology companies could be trusted to prioritize security over their own profits.

This legislative push comes as House Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana notes a growing bipartisan consensus for tighter restrictions on Chinese access to advanced AI chips. President Donald Trump recently urged senators to pass the American Affordability and Jobs Act, also known as S. 5653, to lower energy costs. This act would require data centers to pay for their own electricity while speeding up general development. Meanwhile, Microsoft Corp. and various industry groups recently asked the Trump administration to drop a proposed ban on certain Chinese data center technology. These groups warned that such restrictions could disrupt construction and weaken the overall competitiveness of the United States.

Senator Warren stated that the American people cannot rely on Big Tech billionaire CEOs to put national security above their bottom line. Palantir Technologies CEO Alex Karp also emphasized that American technological leadership is critical because China is a formidable competitor. He argued that advanced defense technology is necessary to deter potential adversaries and help prevent future wars. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt warned last month that China could overtake the U.S. because its companies offer cheaper AI products. He noted that China's access to AI model distillation and advanced chips puts the American lead at risk.

The debate has intensified following reports that link former Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang to a Chinese businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing. Because of this turmoil, Chinese AI firms are reportedly seeking Nvidia equipped data centers outside of China to secure computing resources. Scott Bessent has urged the U.S. and China to de-risk their relationship rather than decouple entirely amid these trade tensions. Beijing has warned of red lines regarding its national interests ahead of a meeting between President Trump and President Xi. More to follow.

stories.Headline: John Langford resigns from Microsoft after AI Frontiers restructuring
stories.Summary:
John Langford, a veteran machine learning researcher at Microsoft, has resigned from the company, and his departure follows the dissolution of the AI Frontiers research group, which was established in 2023. The 50-member team focused on exploring new approaches to artificial intelligence, working on projects like Microsoft's AutoGen multi-agent framework and Fara, a computer-use agent. A restructuring in September 2026 moved AI Frontiers from Microsoft Research into Microsoft AI, the company's commercial AI division. Langford stated that this change created differences over how AI development should progress within Microsoft.

The commercial division prioritised scaling existing models using larger datasets and computing resources, while AI Frontiers focused on developing alternative algorithms, optimisation techniques, and model architectures. Langford reported that the team's research was considered "aggressively not research" by the product organisation, which reportedly left several projects without a clear path towards adoption within Microsoft. The research group explored alternative AI technologies including Next Latent, Dion3, and Full Bandwidth Transformers, and these projects aimed to improve AI training and computational efficiency rather than relying on increasing model size. Langford's departure reportedly coincided with other senior researchers leaving the group, which highlights the differences between exploratory AI research and commercial product development.

stories.Headline: Nidus raises $30 million to develop AI for US defense manufacturing robots
stories.Summary:
Nidus raised thirty million dollars in pre-seed and seed funding to develop AI for defense manufacturing robots. The startup was founded in March by Justin Sealy and three other former Vannevar hardware team members. This funding was announced on November 10, 2026, to help the company build a robotics lab. The team aims to speed up production for defense industrial customers without rebuilding existing factory processes. They currently focus on automating the creation of wire harnesses for tanks, aircraft, and satellite receivers.

The pre-seed round was led by Costanoa, while Kleiner Perkins led the seed round for the New York company. Other participants included Ludlow Ventures, Absolute Partners, Hadrian CEO Chris Power, and Amca CEO Jai Malik. Nidus has already reached over one million dollars in bookings with unnamed defense industrial customers in four months. The company plans to use the money to hire aggressively at its headquarters in the Flatiron neighborhood. They intend to expand beyond wire harnesses into kitting, pre-assembly, and printed circuit boards.

CEO Justin Sealy stated that defense customers have different needs than those who fold towels at a Holiday Inn. He believes the United States must reindustrialize its supply chain to reduce dependence on China during geopolitical tension. Sealy noted that Silicon Valley often pursues easy commercial paths rather than urgent national security needs. Co-founder Harrison Nguyen added that the burgeoning need for reindustrialization is what excites the team most. They want to be the first world-class physical AI company based in New York City.

Investor Aatish Nayak said the proprietary data Nidus collects makes their specific industrial models tougher for rivals to replicate. He suggested other robotics labs might prefer partnering with Nidus due to its trust with defense customers. The company competes against general AI labs like Physical Intelligence, Skild AI, Figure AI, and Jeff Bezos's Prometheus project. The startup's technology affects highly skilled craftsmen who currently spend hours using hand tools for manual wire prep. Nayak argued that the mission-driven team is pragmatic and customer-first rather than being technology-first.

Justin Sealy grew up in a military family in Greenwood, South Carolina, where offshoring hurt the local textile industry. He studied at Clemson and later worked as a deployment strategist at Palantir in New York for three years. Sealy also worked at the safety startup Peregrine before joining the defense startup Vannevar to build an AI hardware team. At Vannevar, he met co-founders Harrison Nguyen, Charu Dwivedi, and Cane Punma, who provide expertise in operations, robotics, and AI. The idea for Nidus began after Sealy wrote an essay about accessible robotics capabilities last Christmas.

Nidus will now ramp up data collection and training for more secretive customers using its New York lab. The company is currently working to improve its fiber-optic cable connection to upload training data to a secure cloud. They plan to leverage frontier and open-source AI models to fine-tune custom models for specific industrial use cases. The articles leave open how Nidus will stay ahead of well-funded rivals in a fast-moving market. It remains unclear which specific defense industrial customers have already committed to the million dollars in bookings.

stories.Headline: US labor authorities launch PERM actions against Microsoft, Adobe and six IT firms
stories.Summary:
United States authorities in October initiated administrative action under the Permanent Labor Certification program against Microsoft, Adobe and six major technology outsourcing firms, including Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Cognizant and Capgemini, according to TechGig. The actions have disrupted the processing and acceptance of these firms' PERM applications, creating uncertainty for foreign professionals awaiting permanent residency. The federal inquiry centers on allegations that certain employers used immigration programs to replace American workers with lower-paid foreign personnel. Officials noted that the ongoing investigations and administrative actions do not constitute a final finding of guilt.

The PERM program is a critical step for US employers seeking to sponsor foreign workers for employment-based green cards, and employers must certify that insufficient qualified US workers are available and that hiring a foreign national will not adversely affect American employees. The Trump administration has introduced a requirement of $100,000 for certain new H-1B petitions while extending related visa restrictions through September 2027. The H-1B program allows US companies to temporarily employ foreign professionals in specialty occupations and has long been central to the Indian IT sector across software development, cloud services, cybersecurity and technical consulting. The administration has not formally announced a complete shutdown or overhaul of the H-1B program, focusing instead on audits, employer accountability and strict compliance.

US Department of Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito warned that temporary work visas cannot be treated as a permanent business strategy, stating that visas like the H-1B should only be used when qualified and willing American workers are unavailable for a given role. D'Esposito indicated that the probe is likely to widen and warned that similar actions could soon target additional companies and academic institutions. His office is coordinating closely with the White House Fraud Task Force, led by Vice President JD Vance, which aims to identify systemic irregularities and abuse within visa programs. The heightened scrutiny directly affects major Indian IT service providers whose US operations rely heavily on deploying specialized talent from abroad.

For Indian IT firms, the immediate challenge lies in balancing business continuity in their largest market with rigorous adherence to evolving immigration rules. If federal investigations expand and PERM restrictions persist, Indian service providers could face significant hurdles in talent deployment, foreign hiring and green card sponsorship for employees in the United States. The articles do not say what further steps, if any, the firms or the administration will take next.

stories.Headline: New York City Council passes bill banning surveillance pricing using personal data
stories.Summary:
The New York City Council passed a bill on November 12, 2026, that prohibits companies from using personal data and algorithms to set different prices for individual consumers. The legislation, known as Introduction 891-A, targets a practice called surveillance pricing, in which businesses use personal information to determine what each customer pays for identical goods or services. The bill would also restrict the collection, sale and sharing of personal information intended to facilitate such pricing. It is awaiting action from the mayor and would take effect one year after becoming law.

Surveillance pricing involves analysing personal information or consumer profiles to determine individual prices, and businesses may use browsing histories, geographical locations, shopping habits and demographic characteristics to estimate a customer's willingness to pay. Unlike conventional dynamic pricing, which responds to market conditions such as demand and availability, surveillance pricing relies on personal information to distinguish between consumers. In January 2025, the US Federal Trade Commission published initial findings indicating that pricing technologies could analyse detailed consumer behaviour, including mouse movements and products abandoned in online shopping carts. The intermediaries examined by FTC staff worked with at least 250 clients across industries including groceries and apparel.

The legislation preserves certain legitimate discounts, including qualifying loyalty and rewards programmes, and discounts offered to clearly defined groups such as veterans, senior citizens and teachers would also remain permissible, subject to specified conditions. These exceptions distinguish established discount arrangements from pricing systems that rely on detailed surveillance of individual consumers, so the bill targets the use of personal information rather than prohibiting every form of price variation. Personalised pricing does not necessarily mean every customer pays more, because some consumers may receive discounts while others could face higher charges based on estimated willingness to pay. The legislation seeks to address a lack of transparency by limiting the use of personal information in pricing decisions.

The collection of extensive personal information raises concerns extending beyond unequal pricing, because detailed consumer profiles can expose sensitive information and create risks of unauthorised disclosure. Consumers may also have little understanding of how companies assess their behaviour or determine the prices displayed to them. If enacted, the measure would establish restrictions on how businesses operating in New York City use consumer data when determining prices. Its implementation would begin one year after it becomes law, giving affected businesses time before the restrictions take effect.

stories.Headline: G20 Interfaith Forum closes AI webinar series with panel on whether AI threatens or benefits civilization
stories.Summary:
The G20 Interfaith Forum, in cooperation with the International Academy for Multicultural Cooperation, will close its eight-part AI Webinar Series on Thursday, August 20, 2026, with a session titled AI and the Future. The session asks whether artificial intelligence turns out to be a threat or a benefit, a question IF20 says is still a decision human beings get to make. The webinar will be held at 12:00 p.m. EDT, and Marianna Richardson, IF20's Director of Communications and head of its AI working group, will moderate. The panel brings together AI policy specialists, working technologists, and scholars of governance for the series' final conversation. The series has run since June and has taken up AI and faith, translation, benchmarks, the planet, peace, human flourishing, and education.

Richardson framed the stakes in stark terms, saying artificial intelligence is currently being described as both the destroyer and savior of civilization. She said that looking at the future of AI, the international community needs to decide which way the development of AI will go. IF20 argues that this decision is an ethical one before it is a technical one. The organization says AI will shape the future by amplifying human capabilities and transforming how people learn, work, and solve problems together. It says AI's impact will depend on whether societies guide it with strong ethical frameworks that protect dignity, fairness, and human agency, and that aligned with shared values, AI can help build a future that is more creative, connected, and compassionate.

The panel is deliberately unlike-minded, and their disagreements are the point. Clara Langevin is a Senior Manager on the Emerging Technologies team at the Federation of American Scientists, focusing on responsible AI adoption and policy guidance on AI and data ethics, transparency, and explainability. Josh Tan leads technology at Current AI and Public AI, runs Stanford AO at Stanford OpenLab, and co-founded Metagov, and his work focuses on AI as shared public infrastructure. Manisha Jain is an engineer and tech ethicist who has spent more than a decade in generative AI at Google, Meta, and Microsoft, including on Gmail SmartReply and Google Translate. David A. Wood is the Glenn D. Ardis Professor of Accounting at Brigham Young University and author of Rewiring Your Mind for AI.

Valerie Hudson is a University Distinguished Professor holding the George H.W. Bush Chair at Texas A&M University's Bush School of Government and Public Service, and she describes herself as an AI gloomer who has studied AI and politics since 1991. Langevin previously headed the AI and Machine Learning Platform at the Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution Brazil, a World Economic Forum affiliate, and holds an MPA from Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs. Wood has published more than 250 articles, books, monographs, and cases, and Accounting Today has named him one of the 100 most influential people in accounting. Jain's essay on Maslow's hierarchy, human dignity, and technology appeared in The Review of Faith & International Affairs. Hudson co-edited and contributed to the 2023 Oxford Handbook of AI Governance, following her 1991 edited volume Artificial Intelligence and International Politics.

IF20 describes itself as the world's leading organization focused on the intersection of faith and policy. Its AI work began in New Delhi in 2023 and has continued through convenings in Pune, Brasília, and South Africa. It has also created an AI Interfaith Task Force bringing technologists and religious leaders together to develop ethical guidelines and advocate for international standards. Richardson is an adjunct professor of management communication at Brigham Young University's Marriott School of Business and editor-in-chief of the Marriott Student Review. She has represented IF20 at international AI convenings, including the UN's first Global AI Dialogue in Geneva.

Expert speakers will present and discuss the topic, after which audience members may submit questions in the chat for further discussion by the panel. Registration for the free webinar is available at a Zoom link given in the announcement. Hudson's research has been funded by the National Science Foundation, the Department of Defense's Minerva Initiative, the Carnegie Foundation, and the Fulbright Commission, and Foreign Policy named her one of the Top 100 Most Influential Global Thinkers in 2009. Tan completed his PhD and postdoc at Oxford and has held fellowships at Stanford, Princeton, and MIT. The announcement does not say what the panel concluded or what, if anything, IF20 will do after the series ends.
