stories.Headline: Scott Loughlin says AI agents on personal devices test whether BYOD programs can survive
stories.Summary:
Employees who use personal devices for work are increasingly running artificial intelligence agents that can read work email, open files and act across applications without a person at the keyboard, and Scott Loughlin, a partner at Hogan Lovells Cadwalader in Washington, DC, wrote in a Bloomberg Law column published on November 16, 2026, that this raises the question of whether bring-your-own-device programs can survive agents in their current form. In a Gartner survey conducted in early 2026, 88% of employees with an enterprise AI tool also used personal AI tools for work, and those tools will likely increasingly include AI agents. Loughlin wrote that the core controls of a BYOD program, a company-managed container for work apps, monitoring of corporate systems and the ability to remotely wipe work data, were designed for apps that people operate and may not work as well for devices running AI agents. Because an agent works inside the employee's logged-in session, company records may show the employee doing what the agent did, and the agent's history and memory sit in the provider's cloud under the employee's account, beyond the reach of a remote wipe.

Loughlin wrote that none of this requires hacking, but the exposure is real and no new AI statute is needed to create it, with personal data given to an unapproved agent raising issues under the GDPR and US state privacy laws, protected health information entered into a personal agent possibly being a HIPAA breach, and routine flows of source code or pricing undercutting trade-secret protection. He wrote that EU law restricts the scope of employee monitoring and may require works-council consultation, and that US laws can limit employers' access to employees' personal accounts. He described three models likely to be applied role by role: access-only BYOD, in which personal devices reach corporate data only through a managed browser, app or virtual workspace; a sanctioned agent, in which an enterprise agent lets the organization control the agent even when it does not control the device; and company-owned devices for people in the most sensitive roles. He noted that the May 2026 guidance on agentic AI from CISA, the NSA and other governments recommends giving agents their own short-lived credentials and requiring human approval for high-impact actions.

Loughlin recommended that organizations assign ownership at the leadership level, naming an accountable executive, adding personal and unsanctioned agents to the enterprise risk register and reporting on them to the board committee that oversees cybersecurity risk. He also recommended revisiting the BYOD agreement to address which agents may touch company data, employee disclosure duties, a narrow commitment to preserve and produce work-related agent data, and offboarding certification that connectors are revoked and work-related memories deleted, covering phones and tablets and calibrated to local employment and privacy law. He advised updating legal-hold and e-discovery playbooks to add agent prompts, outputs, logs and memory to custodian questionnaires and hold notices, mapping roles and controlling the connection points where the law allows, updating incident response with scenarios for a hijacked or misused personal agent, and aligning related policies so they cross-reference each other.

Loughlin wrote that organizations that plan ahead will be better positioned to demonstrate reasonable governance to regulators, courts and customers, and that agent risks are developing quickly enough that organizations are changing their BYOD programs in the short term before settling on a longer-term model. He wrote that it is a good idea to make the sanctioned path easier than the personal one and to focus controls on the connection points the organization owns. He wrote that BYOD rests on the premise that a company can manage the risk of devices it does not own, that agents using employees' credentials on those devices test that premise, and that BYOD is unlikely to disappear but programs are likely to change.

Articles.Title: Advanced AI Agents Should Prompt Companies to Act Fast on BYOD

stories.Headline: Lawyers see AI take over research and drafting while human judgment stays essential
stories.Summary:
The article, published by LLM GUIDE on November 14, 2026 and updated November 15, 2026, was written by Mubin S. Khan, a Canadian-Bangladeshi journalist and Columbia Journalism School graduate based in Montreal. It examines which areas of law will be most resilient to artificial intelligence for lawyers pursuing an LL.M. in 2026. Khan reports that AI is taking over tasks once central to lawyers' work, from research and document review to drafting contracts and legal memoranda. The article draws on interviews with Shikha Shukla of Osuji & Smith Lawyers in Calgary, Anna Gorodetsky of Major, Lindsey & Africa, and Andrew Perlman, dean of Suffolk University Law School. Khan has more than two decades of experience in journalism, policy research and higher education, and has written for The Guardian, The Sunday Times and The Daily Beast.

Shukla holds an LL.M. from Canada's University of Calgary and leads the employment law practice at Osuji & Smith Lawyers in Calgary. Gorodetsky is a UC Berkeley-trained lawyer and partner specializing in in-house counsel recruiting and board services at Major, Lindsey & Africa. Perlman is dean of Suffolk University Law School, and Shukla is a founding member and board member of the Foot In The Door Initiative, which helps internationally trained lawyers gain Canadian legal experience. The article names the University of California, Berkeley Law, the University of Calgary Faculty of Law and Suffolk University Law School in Boston, Massachusetts. It also lists Suffolk's LL.M. in Global Law and Technology and its Master of Laws in Legal Innovation & Technology.

Shukla says AI is already useful for summarizing documents, constructing timelines from emails, comparing contract clauses and drafting routine correspondence, but she warns against relying on it where mistakes are costly. She says there are many horror stories of AI hallucinating case citations that look real, which lawyers have carelessly used in court without verifying, and that this can be fatal to a case. Gorodetsky says employers increasingly expect lawyers to use AI to work faster, and that producing a polished document is less of a differentiator when the first draft is easier to generate. Perlman points to new positions emerging within law firms and legal departments, AI-native firms and legal technology companies serving people who previously could not afford legal services. Perlman says we have to ask not just what legal jobs will be preserved but which jobs will be created as a result of AI.

Shukla says trial advocacy, negotiation and conciliation all depend on reading the room, judging credibility, understanding emotions and knowing when someone is psychologically ready to settle. She says clients facing dismissal are often dealing with lost income and professional identity, not merely a legal dispute, and she identifies personal accountability and applying existing employment and human rights laws to AI-driven decisions as areas requiring lawyers. Perlman says lawyers are called counselors for a reason and that people will still want human counsel on important issues, even if that counsel is enhanced and informed by AI. He says society may choose to reserve certain responsibilities for humans even if AI becomes technically capable, including judicial decisions affecting civil liberties, prosecution, public defense and aspects of lawmaking. Gorodetsky identifies situations involving incomplete facts, high stakes and competing interests as particularly dependent on human expertise, saying AI can contribute to the analysis but someone still has to ask the right questions, weigh the trade-offs, earn trust and take responsibility for the recommendation.

Perlman says traditional legal skills, including sound judgment, problem-solving, advocacy, negotiation and client counseling, remain essential, and that lawyers need to know the law well enough to realize when AI is wrong. Shukla says someone asking about severance is often really asking whether they were treated fairly and what happens next, and that AI doesn't pick up on how they feel, only what they say. Gorodetsky says she would be cautious about calling any practice area AI-proof, because resilience depends heavily on the responsibilities within a role, and she contrasts a commercial lawyer negotiating a strategically important partnership with one primarily processing standardized agreements. She expects complex negotiations, investigations, disputes, board counseling and regulatory strategy to remain particularly dependent on lawyers, and says product counseling, privacy, cybersecurity and AI governance also present opportunities. Perlman says future lawyers must combine traditional expertise with the ability to deliver legal services more efficiently using AI, and that we need future lawyers to understand how to use AI to deliver services better, faster and cheaper.

Gorodetsky advises LL.M. graduates to develop substantive expertise, understand the industries they serve and seek practical experience under experienced lawyers, and says cross-border experience and language skills can be valuable for internationally trained lawyers when aligned with employers' needs. Shukla emphasizes learning the fundamentals before relying heavily on technology, saying that if you outsource your learning, you lose the ability to catch its mistakes. She recommends gaining courtroom, negotiation and client-facing experience early, becoming proficient at supervising AI tools and exploring fields where law and technology intersect. Shukla says your personality, communication skills and a reputation for good judgment are ultimately what get clients to hire you again. The article also links to related LLM GUIDE pieces, including one from June 23, 2026 on how law schools are teaching LL.M. students to work alongside AI and one from October 19, 2026, a student blog by Addys Rojas Villegas on a University of Houston LL.M. student's journey from Venezuela to the U.S.

Articles.Title: What Areas of Law Will Be Most AI-Resilient After Your LL.M.?

stories.Headline: Samsung breaks ground on a $34 billion HBM packaging expansion in Asan
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics broke ground on a high-bandwidth memory packaging expansion at its Onyang manufacturing complex in Asan, South Korea, with a planned investment of ₩46 trillion, or approximately $34 billion, according to a November 12, 2026 investment announcement. The program includes five advanced packaging production lines and is scheduled to begin operations in 2028. Of the total investment, ₩6 trillion is allocated to facility construction and ₩40 trillion to equipment. The new production line is scheduled to begin operations in June 2028, a year earlier than originally planned. The announcement came during a period of tight memory supply.

The new facility will contain approximately 31,000 square meters of cleanroom space across three floors. The project will expand the Onyang campus's total floor area from 270,000 to 420,000 square meters, an increase of approximately 55.6%. Approximately 87% of the ₩46 trillion program is allocated to equipment, with the remaining 13% directed toward construction. The equipment expenditure will occur in phases across the broader five-line program rather than representing an immediate commitment for the newly announced building alone. Samsung's new Onyang facility is primarily a back-end packaging operation rather than a new DRAM wafer fabrication plant.

Samsung said the investment is intended to strengthen its ability to compete with SK hynix and Micron in the next generations of HBM. The company's June 2028 target represents the beginning of operations, not necessarily full-volume production. Meaningful additional supply could arrive later, depending on equipment installation and customer qualification schedules. Samsung is committing substantial capital to expand HBM production during a period of tight memory supply, yet the new facility will not begin operations for approximately 18 months. The new facility will not begin operations until 2028, leaving current memory shortages largely unaffected.

SK hynix announced in August 2026 that it would invest approximately ₩54.3 trillion in two additional semiconductor fabrication projects, including ₩35.2 trillion for its Yongin Y2 facility and ₩19.1 trillion for its Cheongju M17 facility. The company expects the M17 cleanroom to open in December 2028, followed by the Y2 cleanroom in June 2029. Micron is also developing substantial additional DRAM manufacturing capacity in the United States, including projects in Idaho and New York. Equipment suppliers like KLA and Lam Research get paid while fabs are built, so they profit even if memory prices later collapse. The convergence of these projects raises the possibility that additional DRAM fabrication and HBM packaging capacity will enter production during the same period, potentially increasing supply faster than demand if AI infrastructure investment moderates.

The Information Network estimates that global HBM revenue increased from $21.1 billion in 2024 to $38.7 billion in 2025, representing growth of approximately 83.4%. Revenue is projected to reach $50.5 billion in 2026 and $63 billion in 2027. Annual revenue growth is expected to moderate from 83.4% in 2025 to 24.8% in 2027. The market is projected to expand by approximately $12.5 billion in 2027, compared with $11.8 billion in 2026.

Memory manufacturers face the risk that today's aggressive capital spending will produce excess capacity if HBM demand growth moderates. HBM memory dies are manufactured in front-end DRAM wafer fabrication plants, while advanced packaging facilities assemble those dies into vertically stacked memory products. Increasing packaging capacity does not independently increase the supply of DRAM wares. Finished HBM production requires sufficient quantities of qualified memory dies, advanced packaging equipment, and acceptable manufacturing yields.

Advanced HBM packaging requires specialized processes involving wafer thinning, die stacking, bonding, inspection, and testing. Increasing the number of stacked memory dies also raises the difficulty of maintaining acceptable manufacturing yields. The convergence of these investments is significant because memory supply has historically been influenced by the collective capital spending decisions of a relatively small number of manufacturers. When several producers expand simultaneously, the resulting capacity additions can eventually exceed demand, particularly if customers reduce inventories or end-market growth slows.

HBM introduces additional complexity because manufacturing capacity must be allocated between conventional DRAM and HBM products. New manufacturing capacity must ultimately generate sufficient revenue and operating profit to justify the investment. Facility opening dates do not represent full production capacity. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Samsung’s $34 Billion HBM Bet Raises Memory Glut Risks - 24/7 Wall St.

stories.Headline: Detectify launches Agentic Tooling to help AI agents verify software vulnerabilities in live applications
stories.Summary:
The Swedish application security firm Detectify AB launched its Agentic Tooling on November 16, 2026, to help organizations verify suspected software flaws. This new suite of tools allows artificial intelligence agents to test whether vulnerabilities in running applications can actually be exploited. The launch also includes a Security Ledger designed to record evidence for every test to ensure the results are authentic. These tools are specifically aimed at DevSecOps teams who struggle to trust the reports generated by their AI agents.

The system requires the use of loop engineering to run AI agents in automated workflows triggered by events like continuous integration runs. It integrates with the Model Context Protocol or a command-line interface to work with a customer's existing agents in their own environment. The tooling utilizes Alfred, an AI system launched in March 2025, along with attack surface data and payload assessments from ethical hackers. This setup creates a verification factory where agents read code and test live applications from an external perspective.

Chief Executive Rickard Carlsson explained that agents often fabricate proof to please users, making it impossible to know if code is truly secure. He stated that the company intends to build proof that an agent cannot fabricate by using an append-only ledger. This ledger is written by Detectify rather than the agent to separate actual test results from unsupported AI conclusions. Carlsson noted that the tools are available on request and build upon a server announced in May.

The release addresses a critical need because Detectify's H2 2026 Cyber Hygiene Index found that 90 percent of high-severity vulnerabilities remained exposed for over 90 days. Additionally, research from Tencent Holdings Ltd. and Fudan University showed that 76 percent of static-analysis alerts were false positives. The company is backed by investors including Balderton Capital (UK) LLP, Inventure, First Fellow Partners Oy, SquareOne App Ltd, and Insight Partners. Insight Partners took a majority stake in the company in October 2024.

Articles.Title: Detectify’s Agentic Tooling lets AI agents test suspected flaws in running applications

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang leaves Nvidia as CEO amid espionage investigations and a scandal
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang left his role as chief executive officer of Nvidia during a stormy week in November 2026. He departed in disgrace following a scandal involving an internal affair and allegations of ties to Chinese espionage. The former leader is now the subject of investigations by the U.S. Congress and intelligence authorities. These probes focus on suspicions that AI chips were possibly diverted to China. Huang reportedly called himself a piece of shit before he quit the company.

The exit follows a landslide victory for the Democratic Party in the U.S. midterm elections. This political shift may increase regulatory burdens, power costs, and permitting hurdles for data centers. Nvidia has executed over 120 investments this year, with equity totals reaching 124 billion dollars by July. The firm poured 60 billion dollars into 200 startups, including xAI, Anthropic, and OpenAI. Nvidia also committed 36 billion dollars for computing capacity and 20 billion dollars for data center leases.

Jensen Huang personally decided many deals and managed a chain of circular financing. He previously argued that no new laws were needed and that companies should run as fast as possible. Huang claimed the probability of humanity going extinct within ten years was zero percent. He believed that doomsday narratives were irresponsible and that speed did not compromise product safety. He served as the most forceful voice for AI optimism and acceleration.

Matt Witheiler of Wellington Management stated that Nvidia is a four trillion dollar company regardless of its CEO. He noted the firm posted 100 billion dollars in revenue last quarter, growing 100 percent from a year earlier. The International Monetary Fund is monitoring the sector but says it is too early to conclude a broad reassessment. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva previously said AI investment helped the global economy during a Middle East energy shock. Competitors like Intel, Broadcom, and AMD are affected as they try to break Nvidia's dominance.

The articles state that Nvidia became a money pipeline for the AI ecosystem rather than just selling GPUs. The company provided financing to help its invested startups secure power and data centers. These startups then used that funding to buy Nvidia GPUs. This structure created a cycle of investment and purchasing that relied heavily on the network of the CEO. The industry has operated on a conviction that it needs more data centers, power, and computing.

Existing contracts and partnerships are not expected to evaporate in the short term. Computing demand may shift to other suppliers rather than disappearing entirely. The supply chain across the AI industry could diversify as a result of this leadership change. It remains open whether a second figure like Huang can emerge to lead the case for acceleration. The long term impact on AI investment, profitability, and productivity is not yet determined.

Articles.Title: AI's Loudest Accelerationist Exits as Regulatory Risk Builds - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Lai Mohammed urges media literacy and ethical AI regulation at Caleb University lecture
stories.Summary:
Alhaji Lai Mohammed spoke at a public lecture on November 14, 2026, in Imota, Lagos. The former Minister of Information and Culture urged citizens to embrace media literacy and verify information. He also called for the ethical regulation of Artificial Intelligence to protect the public interest. This event marked the maiden edition of the Caleb University Public Lecture series. The lecture focused on defending truth against disinformation and fake news in the digital age.

The lecture took place at Caleb University in Imota, Lagos, on November 14, 2026. It addressed the theme of fake news, disinformation, and Artificial Intelligence in the digital age. Mohammed warned that uncontrolled deepfakes could lead to information nihilism where truth is no longer believed. He stated that AI creates convincing falsehoods and causes people to dismiss authentic evidence as fake. These changes require citizens to verify all information before they choose to share it.

Alhaji Lai Mohammed is responsible for calling for the ethical regulation of Artificial Intelligence. He explained that the greatest danger of AI is the tendency to dismiss authentic evidence. Vice-Chancellor Professor Olalekan Asikhia said universities must be strongholds of ethical fact-checking and intellectual integrity. Registrar Mr. Mayokun Olumeru reaffirmed that the university will produce graduates who are custodians of truth. Principal Information and Media Expert Olawale Adekoya said the university was honoured to host Mohammed.

The event attracted various students, media executives, and leading scholars who attended the lecture. These groups are affected by the spread of deepfakes and the rise of information nihilism. The attendees witnessed the presentation of a commemorative plaque to Alhaji Lai Mohammed during the event. This plaque recognized his contributions to national communication and public policy in Nigeria. The university aims to ensure its graduates can identify and combat digital disinformation.

The articles provide background on the role of universities in maintaining intellectual integrity. They highlight the specific dangers posed by the uncontrolled spread of Artificial Intelligence and deepfakes. The text establishes Alhaji Lai Mohammed as a distinguished figure in media and public relations. It describes the university's goal to produce credible graduates who can defend the truth. The lecture series was inaugurated to address these modern challenges in the digital age.

The university will continue its commitment to producing graduates who serve as custodians of truth. Scholars and media executives will likely continue discussing the regulation of Artificial Intelligence. The articles leave open how the government will implement ethical AI regulations in Nigeria. They do not state if other universities will adopt similar ethical fact-checking strongholds. No further details are provided regarding the specific laws needed for AI regulation.

stories.Headline: Barclays cuts 5,000 jobs as banks expand AI use across operations
stories.Summary:
Banks have been expanding their use of artificial intelligence across operations, customer service and compliance during the third quarter of 2026, while shifting some employees toward higher-value work, according to CNBC. Barclays unveiled layoffs in functions where AI is being deployed, and UniCredit and Santander said technology was freeing employees for more valuable tasks and improving processes. U.S. giants such as JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs are making similar changes in staffing and workflows. The moves came as lenders reported quarterly results that brought their use of AI into sharper focus.

Barclays plans to cut 5,000 jobs, about 5% of its workforce, in 2026, with roughly 60% of the reductions affecting support functions including developer roles, though the bank said AI is not responsible for all the cuts. Santander said its AI initiatives generated 194 million euros in business value in the first nine months of 2026, and UniCredit reported its best-ever quarterly profit of 3.3 billion euros. The Financial Times reported on Oct. 7 that HSBC could cut around half of management and specialist roles, and as many as 70% of financial adviser roles, in its U.K. wealth business. JPMorgan managers have been told to avoid hiring as the bank deploys AI, CFO Jeremy Barnum said on the third-quarter earnings call, and Goldman Sachs said it intends to constrain headcount growth.

UniCredit CEO Andrea Orcel called AI an opportunity to accelerate and a lever the bank did not anticipate it would have, saying on CNBC's Squawk Box Europe on Nov. 9 that it was working extremely well. Santander CFO José García Cantera told the same program on Oct. 28 that AI helps decrease low value-added processes so employees can focus on more valuable ones, affecting both revenue and costs, and that it is difficult to say how much comes from AI. ABN AMRO CEO Marguerite Bérard said on Nov. 11 that AI supports anti-money-laundering checks and makes the bank easier to run and scale while preserving human judgement. KBW's Andrew Stimpson said the cuts are partly but not solely due to AI and have tended to come from back-office and support functions rather than the front office.

A KBW study published in September found customer service was the most frequently cited use case for AI among European banks, followed by operations, identity checks and preventing financial crime, with just under half of tracked use cases aimed at cutting costs or improving efficiency. Analysts said wealth management and advisory are emerging as key tests of whether AI can boost revenues rather than only lower costs, with Ninety One's Sophia Whitbread saying the evidence is still strongest for improving service, engagement and employee productivity. Recruiter Mark Astbury of Morgan McKinley said demand is growing for specialists in AI, software engineering and data, and that banks will need to rethink how they develop the next generation of talent as entry-level positions become increasingly technical.

Articles.Title: AI is reshaping banking jobs – but its ability to drive profits remains unclear

stories.Headline: Anne Boden builds Lockwood, a digital bank for AI agent payments
stories.Summary:
Anne Boden, who founded the British neobank Starling and stepped down as its chief executive three years ago, is building a new digital bank called Lockwood that is designed to let AI agents make payments on behalf of customers, according to Sifted. She is putting the proceeds from her Starling share sales into the venture, which marks her return to fintech. The report says she has been working on the project with a small team and that the bank is aimed at a world in which AI agents handle transactions for people. The articles give no date for a launch and do not say whether Lockwood has applied for a banking licence.

The articles say Boden has invested in Lockwood alongside other backers, and they describe the bank as being built for payments made by AI agents rather than only by humans. They give no figures for how much has been raised, no timetable for when the bank might open, and no detail on which regulators it would need to satisfy. The report does not say how many staff Lockwood has or where it is based. It also does not say whether Starling itself is involved in any way.

Boden is described as the founder behind the new bank, and the articles say she is funding it from the proceeds of her Starling share sales. The report does not quote her at length on Lockwood, and it gives no statement from Starling or from any regulator about the plan. No one from Lockwood is quoted on the record about the bank's plans or its timeline. The articles do not say what Boden's role at Lockwood will be.

The context is that Boden built Starling into one of Britain's better known digital banks before stepping down as chief executive three years ago, and she has since been involved in other ventures. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the fact that the bank is being built, and they give no date for any launch or regulatory decision. They do not say whether Lockwood will seek a UK banking licence or operate under another arrangement. No further details on funding, staffing or timing are given.

stories.Headline: NetChoice sues New York to block a law requiring mental health warning labels on social media platforms
stories.Summary:
The tech industry group NetChoice filed a lawsuit on November 13 in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York. This legal action targets Attorney General Letitia James to block a state law before it takes effect on January 1, 2027. The lawsuit challenges Senate Bill 4505, as amended by Senate Bill 8827, which was signed by Governor Kathy Hochul last December. This legislation requires social media platforms with addictive features to display a state-approved warning about mental health harms.

The law applies to platforms using infinite scroll, autoplay, or algorithmic feeds, including Meta, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, Pinterest, X, and Tumblr. Users under 17 must see an unskippable warning for 10 seconds covering 25 percent of the screen daily. After three hours of use, and every hour thereafter, the warning must last 30 seconds and cover 75 percent of the screen. The text is based on a 2023 advisory from former Surgeon General Vivek Murthy regarding excessive social media use. Violations could result in civil penalties of up to 5,000 dollars per instance, along with restitution.

NetChoice argues that the law violates the First Amendment by forcing companies to carry a preferred government message. The group claims these interruptions block access to protected speech and may push adults toward age verification. They are asking the court to declare New York General Business Law sections 1520 to 1526 unconstitutional and void for vagueness. Attorney General Letitia James is responsible for enforcing the law, but her office declined to provide an immediate comment.

This legal battle follows a November 2025 ruling where a federal judge blocked a similar warning law in Colorado. NetChoice is currently pursuing similar challenges against laws in California and Minnesota to prevent similar mandates. Additionally, Meta, Google, and TikTok recently sued California over its ban on personalized feeds for users under 16. The outcome of the New York case will determine if the state can enforce these labels starting in 2027.

stories.Headline: HFS survey finds only 33% of AI-active enterprises meet their AI business case
stories.Summary:
Only 33% of 502 senior AI decision makers at AI-active enterprises said their biggest AI program met or beat its business case in an HFS Research, Rackspace survey, published November 12, 2026. The survey was conducted in August and September 2026 and reported by MarketScale on November 15, 2026. Success fell to 28% when AI spans several functions and reached 56% where AI is embedded in standard operations. HFS said the pattern points to a fixable gap: unclear ownership of live AI performance, cost and governance as one system. Almost every respondent, 96%, said they have significant governance gaps.

Respondents worked at companies with at least $100 million in annual revenue, across eight industries and four regions. All were running AI pilots or more, and 83% were operating AI in production or beyond. The survey was blind, naming no vendor, and HFS said the results describe AI-active enterprises, not adoption across the whole market. Among single-function users, 37% met or exceeded their business case, falling to 28% across several functions and rising to 56% where AI is embedded in standard operations. HFS cautioned that these are different groups and the data does not show that operating maturity causes better returns.

HFS founder and CEO Phil Fersht said the industry has built a large ecosystem selling models, platforms, infrastructure and consulting, and that when results fall short each party blames another. He said technology and talent are plentiful, but people and partners willing to own how the whole system runs after go-live are scarce. He said the one-third result should make the industry face how hooked it has become on selling AI rather than accepting responsibility for getting it to work. Rackspace CEO Gajen Kandiah said moving from pilots to production requires cost, security, governance and infrastructure readiness handled as one. He said customers need a single accountable operator that integrates, runs and keeps improving the environment across infrastructure, applications, data and AI.

For 78% of respondents, governance failures pose a bigger threat than technology failures to scaling AI, and 44% lack a single, consistent way to run AI in production. The release groups barriers to AI returns into fragmented accountability, unpredictable costs and governance gaps. Of respondents, 58% cite workforce productivity gains, 42% cite measurable cost reductions, 28% report better customer experience and 21% report measurable revenue growth. Across more than 300 banking AI case studies HFS reviewed, productivity made up 44% of use cases, with nearly 20% built around risk and decision-making. HFS president Saurabh Gupta noted the US bank efficiency ratio was 56.9 in 2018 and 55.6 today, attributing swings over 15 years to interest rates and the macroeconomic environment rather than productivity.

Technology spending at global banks has grown close to 9% a year on average, and AI spending is growing nearly 25% a year, yet only 13% of banks and capital markets firms have scaled AI across the business, according to the webinar description. The panel estimated $1.5 trillion in enterprise debt across technology, data, process and talent, which HFS recommends tackling with a two-velocity approach that fixes foundations while capturing value. HFS proposes a fix it calls a Services-as-Software Operator, which could be an internal team, existing providers under one remit or a managed services partner, holding day-to-day responsibility for live AI performance, cost and governance. The enterprise keeps its business context, policy, decision rights and legal accountability. Rackspace describes its Outcomes-as-a-Service model as resting on secure infrastructure, data foundations and forward-deployed engineering for sectors where governance, sovereignty and uptime are non-negotiable, with a Build | Operate | Innovate delivery model, more than 25 years of operating enterprise technology and vendor-neutral, model-agnostic capabilities.

Rackspace reported third-quarter 2026 results after the market close on November 9, with revenue of $609.1 million, down 9.25% from the same period a year earlier, according to Quiver Quantitative. The next day it announced an initial multiyear agreement with Together AI to support enterprise AI inference. HFS states that it has no outside investors and that companies cannot pay to influence its research or ratings, and the report's definition does not require outsourcing since an internal team qualifies. HFS's banking panel recommended that banks own their enterprise AI harness layer instead of renting it. Of respondents, 61% prefer one accountable partner across AI models, platforms and infrastructure, 74% of production-stage firms whose AI has not delivered hold that preference, 73% would pay a premium over raw infrastructure for fully managed AI with governance accountability, and 63% see the operator role as meaningfully different from what they buy today.

The report attaches a condition to the premium: providers have to show clear operational responsibilities and measurable outcomes to earn it. The banking panel offered a tiered pricing model that moves beyond effort-based contracts and a balanced business case built on productivity, prediction, personalization and performance. HFS says enterprises should settle who answers for performance, cost and governance after go-live, and how each is measured, before adding another function to a working AI program. The articles do not say whether any enterprise has adopted the Services-as-Software Operator model. The articles do not give the full report title or the names of the banking practice leaders and senior advisors on the webinar panel.

stories.Headline: Mark Cuban warns that people who ignore artificial intelligence will become dinosaurs within three years
stories.Summary:
Mark Cuban spoke at the Upfront Summit in Los Angeles during 2017 to discuss the future of technology. He warned that people who failed to understand machine learning, deep learning, or artificial intelligence would become dinosaurs within three years. This prediction appeared accurate as the world approached 2027 because the technology reshaped the finance, tech, and industrial sectors. Business owners who still operate without these tools are now compared to creatures in Jurassic Park.

Investors can seek wealth by using an index fund like the Invesco QQQ Trust to access top companies. This specific fund tracks the Nasdaq-100 and held 64.4 percent of its portfolio in technology at the end of October. As of November 10, the fund included Apple at 8.43 percent and Nvidia at 6.80 percent. Other major holdings include Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Tesla, and Meta, along with Advanced Micro Devices and Micron Technology. The fund carries an expense ratio of 0.18 percent, which costs an investor 18 dollars for every 10,000 dollars invested.

The author of the report believes that investing in artificial intelligence stocks represents the biggest wealth opportunity for this generation. He suggests that owning an exchange traded fund is easier than trying to pick individual winners in a complex market. The Magnificent Seven tech stocks now represent 33 percent of the total market capitalization of the S&P 500. He argues that ignoring the long term potential of this technology could lead to future regret for many investors.

The current infrastructure build out is massive while companies continue to find ways to make these capabilities profitable. The Invesco QQQ Trust was trading at 679.89 dollars as of November 13, 2026, despite a recent correction. Many of the leading companies developing these platforms are already seeing enormous growth in their market value. Investors are encouraged to look at diversified funds to avoid betting their entire portfolio on a single stock.

stories.Headline: Geoff Woods urges CEOs to use AI themselves before grading employees on it
stories.Summary:
Geoff Woods, founder of AI Leadership and former chief growth officer at Jindal Steel & Power, wrote a Fortune commentary published November 15, 2026, at 7:30 AM ET. In it he described standing on stage at the annual Great Places to Work convention in Las Vegas, where all 500 CHROs in front of him raised their hands when asked if their executive teams had mandated AI use. He said he asks at every speaking engagement whether every executive is using AI to make themselves more valuable. He wrote that leaders are mandating AI and expecting productivity gains from their workforce without holding themselves to the same standard. He argued that delegating AI adoption to IT, a Chief AI Officer or an outside consultant is abdication rather than delegation.

Woods wrote that CEOs and executive teams need to learn to use AI and become AI-driven leaders before they can build AI-driven organizations. He said he is starting to see companies increasingly tying AI goals and skills directly to employee raises and promotions. He wrote that whether compensation should be tied to AI skill depends on the company, and that for organizations that typically tie performance to specific skills that will grow in value it makes sense. He said that for companies that do not, it is a break from precedent but does not mean it is the wrong move. He wrote that his concern is when a CEO who does not use AI is the one making the call, and that by using AI he does not mean writing better emails but truly leveraging it to think strategically.

Woods said he first saw AI in December 2022, when he was Chief Growth Officer at Jindal Steel and ChatGPT had been out for about two weeks. He said he told himself he was really busy and would revisit it later, then thought about delegating it to his huge IT department or hiring a consulting company. He recalled a quote from his college mentor about focusing on mastering skills so valuable they will serve you no matter where you go, and said he knew then that AI would be one of those skills. He committed to using AI once a day, every day, and quickly realized he was using it for things that did not really matter, like writing better emails. He said he never received a promotion for the quality of his emails and began asking what it would look like to major in the majors.

Woods said he started using AI to ask him questions as a thought partner rather than asking it questions like Google, which he called the game changer. A few months into his AI use he spoke with Naveen Jindal, Chairman of Jindal Steel, who asked to see an example, and Woods opened his AI tool using the CRIT framework he had developed, standing for Context, Role, Interview and Task. He attached the annual strategic plan into a secure instance of ChatGPT, set the role as an aggressive, growth-minded board member with deep expertise in the steel industry vertically integrated from distribution to mining, and had it interview him one question at a time up to five questions. He said the AI asked sharp questions only someone who knew the industry would ask, pulled out context that was in their heads and laid out a real analysis of where the plan could break. He said Naveen's mind was blown, that Naveen said "This is incredible," and that he suggested driving it through the whole company with Naveen leading it as Chairman.

Woods said he knew almost nothing about AI but knew the power of asking the right questions, which led to a partnership with Google where he learned a lot about the tech. He said the more he learned about the tech, the less he realized how much the tech mattered, and that you can have the greatest technology in the world but will never unlock the value without winning the hearts and minds of your people. He said it became clear that AI adoption was about leadership, and that over his time at Jindal the market cap grew from $750 million to $12 billion over a four year period. He said this was done with the right strategic thinking, which AI directly supported throughout the company, and that it is not about AI but about the right strategic thinking. He said he resigned from Jindal Steel, wrote a book about what he learned and turned it into a company.

Woods said a question he gets asked often is what first piece of their own work a CEO should test with AI if they wanted to start this week. He advised starting by asking what the biggest problem facing the company is, the one that would unlock huge growth if solved, which he said focuses you on the 20% of work that drives 80% of your results. He advised writing a prompt using CRIT, describing context in detail, naming the kind of expert you wish could advise you, having AI interview you one question at a time and giving it a task such as giving the top three high-impact, non-obvious strategies. He advised not taking the AI response at face value, telling AI what you like, do not like and would change, and iterating until you are confident enough to act. He wrote that most companies measure AI adoption through usage metrics such as 80% of the workforce using AI every week, which he said is a good place to start but does not tell you whether people are using AI for high-value work.

Articles.Title: I helped grow a steel company from $750 million to $12 billion. CEOs should use AI before they grade employees on it

stories.Headline: Researchers find single inertial sensors and AI can recognize functional stroke activities
stories.Summary:
A systematic review published in Artificial Intelligence Review has synthesized evidence on artificial intelligence-based human activity recognition for detecting functional activities in individuals recovering from stroke. Researchers searched four major scientific databases, PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus, and identified seventeen studies that met their inclusion criteria, which collectively involved 224 individuals with stroke. The systematic investigation evaluated current implementations across sensing technologies, target activities, physical settings, and model architectures. According to the authors, artificial intelligence-based human activity recognition represents a promising methodology for detecting functional activity after stroke, offering the potential to support objective and ecologically valid clinical assessment, continuous monitoring, and targeted treatment strategies.

Inertial measurement units served as the predominant sensing modality across the literature, appearing in 12 of the 17 analyzed studies, or 70.6 percent. Notably, multiple reviewed studies demonstrated the technical feasibility of successfully recognizing relevant functional movements and activities using only a single recording device. Controlled clinical settings hosted the majority of the reviewed research, accounting for 11 of the 17 studies, or 64.7 percent, leaving real-world clinical validation limited to date. Nevertheless, investigators also deployed single-sensor configurations in home-based and simulated-home environments, indicating viable potential for scalable, low-burden, and unobtrusive activity tracking outside formal medical facilities.

In terms of algorithmic modeling, convolutional neural networks were identified as the most frequently implemented deep learning architecture across the included investigations. When traditional machine learning methods were applied, Random Forest emerged as the most common classifier utilized for recognizing functional stroke activities. The review noted that while multimodal sensing can enrich functional activity characterization, greater hardware and sensor complexity may diminish feasibility for prolonged continuous monitoring at home. Given methodological and reporting limitations such as confounding and reproducibility concerns, the authors concluded that future research must prioritize longitudinal validation in everyday environments, transparent code and data availability, and the enrollment of acute and severely impaired stroke populations.

stories.Headline: Indian tech CEOs meet New Jersey governor to discuss investment and AI partnerships
stories.Summary:
Indian technology chief executives met with New Jersey Governor Phil Murphy at a United States forum to discuss investment and artificial intelligence partnerships, according to a report published by New India Abroad on November 13, 2026. The gathering brought Indian technology leaders and New Jersey officials together to explore business and job opportunities in the state. The report did not name the executives who attended or say exactly where the forum took place. It also did not give the size of any investment discussed or the value of any partnership raised at the meeting.

The discussion centered on two subjects, investment and artificial intelligence partnerships, and the report frames the meeting as a way to explore business and job opportunities for New Jersey. The article gives no figures for money, jobs or projects, and it names no companies beyond describing the participants as Indian tech CEOs. It also gives no date for the forum itself, only the publication date of November 13, 2026. No agreements were announced in the report, and no timeline was given for any follow-up.

The report attributes the meeting to the office of the New Jersey Governor and to the Indian technology leaders who took part, and it credits a post on X by India in New York as the source of its image. It does not quote Governor Murphy or any of the executives directly, so their own words are not available in the article. The piece carries a byline for Richa Sharma, a correspondent at New India Abroad, and it was posted at 2:29 PM on November 13, 2026. The report describes the event only as a US forum and does not say which organization hosted it.

The context given is limited to the stated aim of bringing Indian technology leaders and New Jersey officials together to explore business and job opportunities. The article does not say what happens next, whether any delegation will follow up, or when another meeting might occur. It also does not say whether the governor was present in person or joined remotely. Beyond the publication and posting details, the report offers no further dates, numbers or names for the reader.

stories.Headline: Shanghai police arrest 15 people for using AI to forge a luxury restaurant bill to boost liquor sales
stories.Summary:
Shanghai police arrested fifteen people on November 14, 2026, after discovering a forged restaurant bill. An online liquor seller used artificial intelligence software to alter a genuine receipt from the Peace Hotel. The fake document showed a dinner for six people that totaled 517,127.60 yuan. This forgery included two bottles of 1997 Romanée-Conti priced at 230,000 yuan each.

The scheme required the use of AI to change amounts and substitute the hotel's wine list with products from a private company. To make the image go viral after November 8, the group used batches of accounts and paid for bulk reposting. The investigation involved the Huangpu district police and officers from the suspects' home province. Four individuals, including a boss surnamed Zhao and colleagues surnamed Wang and Dong, now face criminal compulsory measures.

The Huangpu district police stated that Zhao organized his employees to create the fake bill and a staged video. They explained that the goal was to use manufactured virality to increase liquor sales for the company. Authorities noted that the group fabricated false information about a business to deceive the public. The police notice cleared the Peace Hotel of any involvement in the fake luxury dinner.

The forgery was first exposed by internet users who noticed mismatched English names and incorrect service charges. These readers also realized the specific wines listed were not sold by the hotel. This case highlights how generative tools are being used for commercial scams in China. The eleven other suspects involved in the operation received administrative punishments for their roles.

stories.Headline: StoredTech expands AI-powered managed IT services to speed issue resolution and detect risks
stories.Summary:
StoredTech, a managed IT services provider based in Queensbury, New York, has expanded its use of artificial intelligence and automation to enhance IT service delivery, accelerate issue resolution and strengthen proactive support for clients, the company announced on November 15, 2026. Building on its established use of technology in managed IT operations, the company is combining AI-enabled capabilities with the expertise of its technicians and engineers to improve service consistency, responsiveness and the overall client experience. The approach emphasizes human expertise alongside automation, allowing technicians to spend less time collecting information and reviewing historical support requests and more time diagnosing complex issues, collaborating with clients and identifying the root causes of IT problems. Rather than replacing human decision-making, AI supports technicians by providing relevant insights and recommendations, while employees remain responsible for evaluating suggested actions, determining appropriate solutions and providing feedback to improve the technology based on their operational experience.

StoredTech, powered by Titan, incorporates Titan's proprietary AI-enabled technology into its managed IT services to give technicians greater visibility into client support requirements. The technology consolidates relevant service histories, established procedures, client-specific instructions and diagnostic data, enabling support teams to assess potential causes of technical issues and determine appropriate remediation steps more efficiently. The expanded capabilities also support a more proactive approach to IT management and cybersecurity risk mitigation, and when a potential risk is discovered within one client's IT environment, the company's automated agents immediately evaluate other client environments for identical risks. According to internal service data, the company has achieved 54% faster response times and a 25% reduction in service tickets opened compared with its performance before adopting the technology.

David Andrade, President of StoredTech, said the company has long believed that investing in technology could help its teams deliver faster, more reliable and more secure service. He said its people bring the expertise, relationships and understanding of each business, and that equipping them with cutting-edge proprietary AI technology creates opportunities to build their skills, take on more complex work and do more for the clients and communities they serve. He also said a quick fix has limited value if the same problem comes back tomorrow, and that the company wants to understand what is causing an issue and address it properly. Giving teams better information helps them resolve problems more effectively and gives clients more time to focus on their own work, he said.

Looking ahead, StoredTech plans to further develop its AI-powered service capabilities by incorporating employee expertise and client feedback into ongoing improvements. The company aims to strengthen its ability to anticipate client requirements, address technical challenges more effectively and help organizations maximize the value of their IT investments as their operations expand. Founded in 2010, StoredTech is an AI-powered managed IT services provider with offices in Queensbury and Albany, New York, and Raleigh, North Carolina. The company helps businesses and organizations operate more securely, efficiently and effectively through comprehensive IT support and management, cybersecurity, cloud solutions and physical security.

stories.Headline: UAE lawyer says companies face liability for harm from AI-generated advice under civil law
stories.Summary:
Under UAE law, liability for AI-generated advice or decisions that cause financial loss, legal violations or harm may be considered under general principles of civil liability, contractual obligations and any applicable sector-specific legislation, according to Ashish Mehta, founder and managing partner of Ashish Mehta & Associates, writing in Khaleej Times on 15 November 2026. The UAE Civil Transactions Law does not establish a separate liability regime specifically for AI-generated outputs or advice or work rendered on the basis of AI-generated advice, he wrote. Article 245(1) of Federal Decree-Law No. 25 of 2025 promulgating the Civil Transactions Law provides that, subject to special legislations, the chapter applies to liability arising from a harmful act committed by a natural or legal person. Article 246 provides that every act causing harm to another obligates its perpetrator to compensate for the damage, even if the perpetrator lacks discernment. Article 247 distinguishes harm caused directly, where a guarantee is due without any condition, from harm caused by causation, where no guarantee is due unless the perpetrator was a transgressor or acted intentionally, or the act led to the harm.

Liability may depend on the role each person played in the development, deployment or use of the AI system, the nature of the act or omission involved, and whether a sufficient connection can be established between that conduct and the damage suffered. Using AI as a tool would not by itself necessarily exclude liability on the part of the person or entity responsible for its use. A company may be liable where an AI system is used in its business operations and the resulting harm can be attributed to the company's acts or omissions, including inadequate assessment of the system, insufficient safeguards or a failure to appropriately monitor its use. Article 645 of the Civil Transactions Law defines a professional company as a company established by one or more persons licensed to practice a liberal profession, or thereby with others, whose purpose is to practice that profession, unless the law or the agreement provides otherwise. Article 651 provides that each partner is personally liable for their professional faults towards the professional company and the rest of the partners, and the professional company is liable for the faults of the partners vis-à-vis third parties.

Article 651 also provides that the professional company is liable for any act or conduct carried out by the manager or managers in the ordinary course of management, and for any act carried out by one of its employees or agents whenever such person has the authority to act on its behalf and the third party has relied on such authorization in dealing with it. Any provision in the articles of association of a professional company permitting approval of the exemption of any person from any personal liability borne thereby in their capacity as a current or former manager shall be void. Professional companies remain liable under UAE law for professional services they provide, regardless of whether rendered by a manager acting in the ordinary course of business or an authorised employee, and regardless of whether the service deliverables relied on advice generated by artificial intelligence. Such liability may not be expelled by the professional company's constitutional documents or other agreements. Article 3.2.1 of the AI Ethics: Principles and Guidelines (December 2022), issued by the UAE Ministry of State for Artificial Intelligence, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications, provides that accountability for the outcomes of an AI system lies not with the system itself but is apportioned between those who design, develop and deploy it.

Article 3.2.2.1 of the AI Ethics Guidelines states that AI operators and AI developers should consider designating individuals to be responsible for investigating and rectifying the cause of loss or damage arising from the deployment of AI systems. Article 3.5.1 provides that AI developers should ensure AI systems will not cause any unintentional harm and adverse impacts. The AI Ethics Guidelines also provide procedures through which individuals affected by significant AI-assisted decisions may challenge those decisions and seek human review, but the Guidelines expressly describe themselves as non-binding and should be read as policy guidance rather than as a standalone basis for imposing legal liability. Where AI-generated advice or decisions by a company result in financial loss, legal violations or harm to an individual, the individual shall have a right of recourse against the company itself, and if the service was rendered by a partner, the partner remains personally liable to the company for any loss suffered as a result of such third-party claim or action.

As to a manager who was not acting in the ordinary course of business or an unauthorised employee acting in bad faith, the company may subsequently take action against such partner, manager or employee, including termination of employment. Article 614 clause 3 of the Civil Transactions Law provides that if the manager of the company exceeds the powers specified in the contract, he shall be liable for any damage that befalls the company as a result of such act. Clauses 2, 3, 4 and 9 of Article 44 of Decree Law No. 33 of 2021 on the Regulations of Employment Relations allow an employer to dismiss an employee without prior notice, after a written investigation and by a written and reasoned decision, in specified events. These include an employee committing an error resulting in gross material losses to the employer, or deliberately causing harm to the employer's property and admitting the same, provided the employer notifies the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation within 7 working days of being aware of the occurrence.

They also include violation of the establishment's bylaws on work and workers safety, where such instructions are in writing and posted in a visible place and the employee has been advised thereof, and failure to perform main duties under the employment contract despite a written investigation and two warnings of dismissal in case of recidivism. Clause 9 covers an employee abusing his position with the aim of obtaining personal gains and profits. Any claims by a company against an AI developer shall be subject to the contractual terms governing their relations. The applicable provisions cited are Federal Decree-Law No. 25 of 2025 promulgating the Civil Transactions Law and the AI Ethics: Principles and Guidelines (December 2022).

Ashish Mehta is qualified to practise law in Dubai, the United Kingdom and India, and full details of his firm are on www.amalawyers.com. Readers may e-mail their questions to news@khaleejtimes.com or send them to Legal View, Khaleej Times, PO Box 11243, Dubai. The article states that the information provided is intended for general guidance and does not constitute legal advice, and recommends seeking formal legal counsel. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Progress Software's Ed Keisling says AI token costs now come out of salaries and bonuses
stories.Summary:
Ed Keisling, chief AI officer at Progress Software, said in a November 15, 2026 CDOTrends article by Winston Thomas that the era of nearly free tokens ended as little as nine to 12 months earlier. He said that money must now come from somewhere, such as employee salaries, bonuses or travel. He described the gap between expectations and reality in AI deployment as far more complicated than executives expect. He compared it to his early career, when his team shipped finished Sun hardware and Oracle software stacks to banks instead of letting each bank install them. He said that work was much more difficult in practice than on paper.

Accenture surveyed 750 executives in 17 countries and found they expect per-token prices to fall 19% over two years while consumption grows 78%. GitHub moved every Copilot plan to token-based billing on June 1, 2026. Accenture found only about one dollar in five of token spend can be tied to a financial return. One in three organizations ran out of its annual token budget before year-end, and fewer than one in 12 use chargeback. By April 2026 Uber had used its full-year budget for AI coding tools and now limits each employee to USD1,500 a month in token spending per agentic coding tool.

Keisling said employees should see their own spend and managers their team's, with budget thresholds that force a conversation about whether work justifies the money. He said nothing should be deployed to a production or even test environment without cost controls in place. He said Progress wired cost telemetry into every agent before release and shut down internal agents after comparing spend with output, saying there was no ROI there. He called dumping everything into a growing context window probably the most expensive route and pointed to retrieval-augmented generation instead. He said getting data ready for a small language model takes months and that governance and observability tooling simply does not exist as a complete package.

The FinOps Foundation notes provider bills show spend by API key or project, not by business unit or cost center, and tooling around a production agent can make up 40% to 60% of feature spend. Gartner predicts companies will use small, task-specific models at least three times as much as general-purpose LLMs next year. IBM found high levels of shadow AI added USD670,000 to the average breach cost, and Ramp data reported by Axios showed 28% of corporate OpenAI chat spending in February flowed through personal consumer plans. Keisling said there is a good chance some data sent to frontier models ends up training them, while OpenAI states it does not train on API or enterprise data by default. Accenture's research suggests only about one-third of workloads must stay sovereign.

Progress describes itself as providing context and control for AI, including control over cost, and bought agentic RAG startup Nuclia in 2025. Progress sells agentic RAG as a service starting at USD700 a month. TypeSafe AI's Jev launched with USD5 in starter credit, which the company says buys about 120 million tokens. Keisling said newer small models are orders of magnitude cheaper than mid-tier ones, and he pins cheap models to routine tasks while saving frontier models for hard ones. He also points to a new class of decision models that classify and choose rather than write.

Keisling scores agents that act on four dials: the access the agent holds, the financial impact of its decisions, how fast a bad change can be reversed and the damage to reputation. He said companies should put a dollar on it and test the agent before it ships. He said what matters is how big a box you were able to put the agent in, in terms of tools, skills and budget. The article says most companies are still drawing theirs. The article ends by saying tokens got cheaper but ready did not.

stories.Headline: Foreign investors withdraw nearly US$50 billion from Asian equities over AI and cash burn concerns
stories.Summary:
Foreign investors withdrew nearly US$50 billion from Asian equities during October, marking the largest monthly outflow since June. This sell-off targeted tech-linked stocks in South Korea, Taiwan, India, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, and the Philippines. The retreat was driven by concerns over the cash burn of hyperscalers and fears that US midterm elections would bring tougher artificial intelligence regulations. These worries persisted after Democrats won elections in states where opposition to new data centers has increased.

The net withdrawal totaled US$49.8 billion, with Taiwanese stocks seeing a net loss of US$30.7 billion, the highest since January 2008. South Korean shares experienced a net outflow of US$14.6 billion, while Indian stocks lost US$3.6 billion for a second straight month. Indonesian and Thai markets saw outflows of US$938 million and US$199 million, though Vietnam and the Philippines gained US$122 million and US$109 million. In early November, foreigners offloaded another US$22.6 billion, including US$19.8 billion from Taiwan and US$8.3 billion from South Korea.

Wael Makarem of Exness stated that the outflows showed a retreat from AI positions due to doubts about profitability and infrastructure spending. He noted that tighter environmental reviews and regulations were expected to hinder chip demand and data center construction. Scarlett Liu from BNP Paribas suggested that investors were drawn to the resilience of the S&P 500 compared to the MSCI Asia ex-Japan index, which fell 6.9 per cent in October. She also mentioned that some investors moved money into US Treasuries as the 10-year yield reached 5.3 per cent in early October.

Herald van der Linde of HSBC upgraded India to overweight on Monday, citing reasonable valuations and resilient earnings. This positive outlook is reflected in the fact that cross-border investors have put a net US$5.7 billion into Indian equities so far this month. Other analysts believe investors are reallocating capital from Asia toward developed markets. This shift follows a period where the MSCI All Country World Index declined by only 1.7 per cent during October.

stories.Headline: Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon says Anthropic can retrain Mythos with a fraction of the original compute
stories.Summary:
Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic, said on X that Anthropic can already retrain its Mythos model with what he called a fraction of the compute originally needed. He said a slide from Anthropic's IPO roadshow was a major reason he quit the company after only about four months. The chart shows how much compute Anthropic needs over time to train its models, and its axis is compressed so that a 10x and a 100x increase barely look different. Coxon said the curve still climbs steeply, which he argues shows that algorithmic efficiency is improving not just quickly but at an accelerating rate.

Coxon wrote that the plot is insane and that he is surprised Anthropic made it public. He argued that Mythos, which he described as a major capability jump in the spring, was not a one-time deviation but a point on a superexponential trend. The roadshow slide shows a pre-training compute multiplier for code over time, with a logarithmic y-axis, and Coxon said the steep climb from July 2024 to October 2026 points to superexponential algorithmic progress. Anthropic notes that the data points are based on internal estimates and are for illustration only.

Coxon said algorithmic improvements are on the verge of being automated, which is why he wants frontier model development paused next year so competitors can catch up. He wrote that a pause would commoditize human-level intelligence and would only harm OpenAI and Anthropic. He previously trained AI models at OpenAI and, most recently, at Anthropic, and he drew wide attention in September with public warnings about the risks of advanced AI systems. Those warnings were echoed by other protagonists in the industry, and one of their fears is that advanced, self-improving AI could get out of control.

Articles.Title: Anthropic can already retrain Mythos with "a fraction of the compute originally needed," says former researcher Coxon

stories.headline_source: Anthropic can already retrain Mythos with "a fraction of the compute originally needed," says former researcher Coxon

stories.Headline: Criminals steal about €100 million from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa in a cyberattack
stories.Summary:
A highly organized criminal group targeted the French banking and insurance group Crédit Mutuel Arkéa in a major cyberattack during late 2026. The attackers first compromised a third-party service provider on October 27 to infiltrate the bank's infrastructure. Starting on Sunday, November 1, the hackers siphoned approximately €100 million, or about $112 million, from the organization's accounts. They used instant payment systems to move the funds into legitimate European bank accounts before transferring the money to cryptocurrency platforms.

The heist required the creation of fake Fortuneo IBANs to initiate payment orders from the bank's accounts to external destinations. On Tuesday, November 3, the bank discovered the fraud and immediately blocked external access to its information system. To stop the theft, the organization disconnected from the interbank payment system, deleted the fake accounts, and updated its credentials. Blockchain analyst ZachXBT recorded suspicious withdrawals over $106 million on November 2, later raising that estimate to over $133 million. Bitquery tracked $108.8 million in USDC moving through OKX, Crypto.com, and Kraken within 21 hours.

Julien Carmona and the bank's chairman described the incident as a new type of robbery carried out by a well-equipped group. The chairman stated that artificial intelligence was very likely involved in the attack, although he provided no specific technical details. Carmona suggested that advanced AI might have supported the criminals, but the bank has not yet provided concrete evidence of its usage. The bank noted that customer accounts and Fortuneo systems remained unaffected by the breach.

The security breach began outside the bank's network, and the name of the compromised provider remains undisclosed to protect similar companies. Most of the methods used, such as credential theft and money mules, existed long before the mass adoption of artificial intelligence. Experts believe AI could have assisted the group with reconnaissance, coding, or creating documents to open the fraudulent accounts. No criminal group has claimed responsibility for the theft at this time.

Articles.Title: French Bank Drained of €100M in Potential AI-Powered Heist - hi-Tech.ua

stories.Headline: Cyber law professor Sizwe Snail ka Mtuze urges an independent AI institute for South Africa
stories.Summary:
Sizwe Snail ka Mtuze, a professor of cyber law at Nelson Mandela University and managing director of Snail Attorneys, said the Information Regulator should not also serve as South Africa's artificial intelligence regulator. He was among the initial members who set up the office of the Information Regulator, the country's data privacy enforcer, in December 2016, and he spoke at the 2026 Governance Risk and Compliance Summit hosted by ITWeb last week. In his presentation he reflected on the regulator's gains and where he believes it can improve, and he argued against AI regulation sitting with the Information Regulator. Instead, he supports an independent AI institute or regulator that would coordinate with the Information Regulator on data issues, saying that where aspects have to do with data infringements, an independent AI institute can work together with the regulator.

Asked whether the absence of an AI governing body raises concerns given the fast pace of AI, he said the urgency of an AI institute is apparent because of the pace of AI development, and he noted that South Africa's draft National AI Policy was withdrawn earlier in the year. He said the president should create this institute by proclamation and give it certain powers to start setting up, so that when the AI policy comes there is already an organisation dealing with these matters. He added that creating an institute now would not hurt, and that government should move towards creating this AI institute and then create legislation around it. The Information Regulator, headed by advocate Pansy Tlakula, was set up to monitor and enforce compliance by public and private bodies with the Protection of Personal Information Act and the Promotion of Access to Information Act, and POPIA came into force on 1 July 2021 after a year-long grace period for organisations to comply.

Snail ka Mtuze described POPIA as a strong but improvable law, noting that the 2013 legislation is a little behind the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation of 2018, and he said Europe has five years of experience that South Africa does not have under POPIA, with gaps for improvement most certainly existing. He also highlighted questions around juristic persons' personal information and overlap between POPIA, direct-marketing guidance and the National Consumer Commission. He touched on the regulator's milestones, such as enforcement notices it has issued, with First National Bank and a TVET college among the most recent to be found in breach of POPIA, and he said private sector organisations have proactively engaged with the regulator, updated systems and trained staff. He emphasised that compliance must reach all employees, including cleaning staff, rather than only executives, and he said the regulator has done a good job ordering certain organisations to give information to people who wanted to access groundbreaking matters, with even the State Security Agency taken to task at some stage.

He cited the regulator's crackdown on the Department of Justice and Correctional Services, which finances its costs, and said that as early as 2020 the justice department was getting hacked while remedial meetings were held, with enforcement notices issued in the regulator's last term. He said the state getting sued by the state, with the state paying the money into the fiscus again, may not have achieved much in terms of what it looks like for the public, but the regulator made it clear that everyone needs to comply, whether an individual, the private sector or the state. On the matric results saga with the Department of Basic Education, he said his views are public and that he believes an examination number is personal information, which section one of POPIA makes clear. He said that with all due respect to the judges of the Pretoria High Court they may have just gotten it wrong, but that the Supreme Court of Appeal will be heard on the matter, and that this is a true test not just for the regulator but for the judiciary. Under POPIA, organisations must inform the Information Regulator if they expose the personal information of data subjects to unauthorised third parties without their approval, and perpetrators can face fines of up to R10 million or 10 years of imprisonment, depending on the seriousness of the breach.

stories.Headline: China's first fully AI-generated feature film flops at the box office
stories.Summary:
China recently released its first fully AI-generated feature film titled Sanxingdui: Future Past, but the project flopped at the box office. The production was created without any human actors or a traditional camera crew to film the scenes. According to data from the tracker Beacon Pro, the movie earned only about 1.8 million yuan, which is roughly 270,000 US dollars. This meager return occurred after the film had spent three weeks playing in theaters across the country. The 100-minute science fiction story requires viewers to imagine a world decades in the future where rogue algorithms cause catastrophe.

To prevent this disaster, the characters must decipher warnings hidden inside bronze artifacts from the ancient Shu kingdom. The film's reported budget was tens of millions of yuan, meaning the final earnings were well below the initial costs. Audiences rejected the movie because of its disjointed plot and visuals that appeared far too stiff. Viewers described the movie as being obviously AI, which contributed to the lack of ticket sales in cinemas.

This failure happened even as short AI dramas continue to boom on smartphones throughout China. The contrast suggests that while small AI clips are popular, full length AI features may struggle. The production attempted to merge ancient history with futuristic technology, but the execution failed to attract a wide audience. More to follow.

Articles.Title: No actors, no crew, no ticket sales: why China’s first AI feature film bombed
