stories.Headline: Chinese students attend AI and robotics study tours at industrial bases and museums
stories.Summary:
During mid-November 2026, primary and middle school students across China participated in popular study tours focused on artificial intelligence and robotics. These educational trips took place at industrial bases, museums, and science centers to bring emerging technologies closer to younger generations. In Jinan, Shandong Province, an embodied intelligence industrial base expected over 5,000 young visitors during the autumn break and the following weekend. Meanwhile, a science carnival in Qingdao, Shandong, attracted more than 2,000 students through twelve interactive challenges and six inquiry-based courses.

These programs require a shift from simply operating high-tech products toward a deeper understanding of the underlying logic of artificial intelligence. Effective learning should cover core AI aspects such as perception, reasoning, learning, decision-making, and interaction to help students recognize both capabilities and limitations. From November 6 to 10, the Jiangsu Science and Technology Museum offered science experiment shows and maker activities to encourage broader exploration. Other families visited the Shanghai Science and Technology Museum for AI-themed programs that combined hands-on crafts with guided tours of astronomy and ecosystems.

Li Qingdu, an AI and robotics researcher and educator, stated that these programs should develop problem-solving skills through practice rather than basic operation. Li cautioned that educational frameworks for these tours remain immature because the trend has only developed rapidly over the past three years. Parents like Qiu Shuhua from Jiangsu Province noted that while previous generations focused on history, today's children use these events to imagine the future. Su Zizhou, a mother from Shenzhen, emphasized the importance of combining hands-on learning with professional explanations to introduce technology in an age-appropriate way.

Articles.Title: China's AI study tours gain traction during autumn school breaks, but should prioritize sustained learning over operating high-tech products: expert - Global Times

stories.Headline: Hong Kong lawmakers urge government to tighten AI laws to combat scams and pornography
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers in Hong Kong called for the government to tighten artificial intelligence regulations after a new global index was released on November 14, 2026. The city ranked 50th out of 70 economies for AI governance according to a report from the Switzerland-based International Institute for Management Development. This first-ever World Digital and AI Ranking report placed the region 11th overall and fourth in Asia, trailing behind Singapore and the Chinese mainland. The United States took the top spot on the list for overall competitiveness in the digital and AI sectors.

The current situation requires the government to move beyond general guidelines to create more specific and enforceable laws. Lawmaker Johnny Ng argued that the city must do more to protect young people from scams and pornography. Fellow lawmaker Simon Lee suggested that the city should roll out new AI legislation in several distinct phases. He emphasized that the government should prioritize the monitoring of high-risk AI systems and the spread of deepfakes. These changes would address the gap between the city's strong infrastructure and its lagging governance.

Lawmaker Johnny Ng stated on a radio show that the city has guidelines but lacks sufficient laws for certain critical areas. Simon Lee added during the same broadcast that the existing regulations are simply not enough to handle modern threats. Chief Executive John Lee addressed these concerns during his Policy Address in September 2026. He mentioned that the government is currently looking at instituting legislation to combat AI-enabled crime and regulate deepfakes. These officials believe that stronger legal frameworks are necessary to maintain safety and security.

The context for these demands is the city's high performance in talent and infrastructure compared to its poor governance ranking. While the region remains competitive globally, the lack of specific laws creates vulnerabilities for the general public. The government is now tasked with balancing technological growth with the need for strict oversight of emerging tools. Future actions will likely focus on the phased implementation of laws to target the most dangerous applications of artificial intelligence. More to follow.

Articles.Title: HK 'needs to step up act on AI laws on porn and scams' - RTHK News

stories.Headline: Nearly 70% of aides and lobbyists expect AI safety rules to pass in the 120th Congress
stories.Summary:
A Canvass survey published by Punchbowl News on November 15, 2026 found that nearly 70% of respondents expect artificial intelligence safety rules to pass in the next Congress, which will be the 120th. The survey combined senior congressional aides with leaders of the wider lobbying world, drawing on top Capitol Hill staff and K Street professionals. Those respondents see the next Congress as the time for action on artificial intelligence safety. The article presenting the survey was dated November 15, 2026, and appeared in Punchbowl News. The survey result points to a shift in expectations for AI guardrails, with nearly 70% of those polled saying they view safety rules as likely to pass in the next Congress.

The 120th Congress is the body the respondents identified as the one that would take up the issue. The article did not give a specific date for when a vote might occur or what the rules would contain. It also did not say how many people took part in the survey beyond describing them as senior congressional aides and leaders of the wider lobbying world. Democrats have rallied behind the idea that artificial intelligence needs legal guardrails, according to the same article, but they are divided on how to tax the tech. That division is the only detail the article offered on the substance of the debate, and it did not say where Republicans stand.

The article also linked to separate coverage on Florida asking a court to stop OpenAI development and on what the Trump-Xi meeting means for tech. No lawmaker or staffer was named as responsible for the push, and the article carried no direct comment from any official. The article did not say what happens next beyond the survey finding, and it did not give a timeline for when AI safety legislation might be introduced or voted on. It presented the 120th Congress as the window respondents expect, without naming a committee, a sponsor or a draft bill. The piece was a preview of premium tech coverage, and the full story was available only to subscribers.

stories.Headline: US Supreme Court agrees to hear Robinhood appeal over IPO shareholder lawsuit
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court agreed on Nov. 13 to hear Robinhood's appeal of a ruling that revived a shareholder class action over its July 2021 initial public offering. The court granted Robinhood's petition, No. 25-944, but limited it to the Section 11(a) omissions question and left out Robinhood's separate Item 303 question. The case, Robinhood Markets v. Sodha, will decide how much interim financial information a company must put in an IPO prospectus before its quarterly results come out. Investors sued in late 2021, saying the registration statement left out material information about a shift in Robinhood's revenue mix and declines in key performance indicators.

The investors also cited falling cryptocurrency trading volume after a first quarter boosted by the GameStop meme-stock surge. Robinhood went public on July 30, 2021, a month after its second quarter closed, and the investors say the registration statement left out second-quarter 2021 data. The court limited its review to whether an issuer can be liable under the misleading-omissions prong of Section 11(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 for failing to disclose material interim financial information. The question asks whether such liability applies without an additional inquiry to determine whether the omission rendered any affirmative statement misleading. The defendants include Robinhood and its IPO underwriters, among them Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan Securities.

A federal judge in San Francisco dismissed the suit, and in an Aug. 29, 2025 decision the Ninth Circuit revived it. A Robinhood spokesperson told CNBC the company was pleased the Supreme Court had agreed to hear its case and looked forward to presenting its argument. The Ninth Circuit panel said the registration statement contained only limited information about second-quarter performance, and the stock fell after Robinhood reported those results. The Ninth Circuit held that an issuer can be liable for omitting material interim data without a separate finding that the omission made a specific statement misleading. Robinhood's petition argued the Ninth Circuit's rule is broader than the statute's text and conflicts with other circuits, including the First Circuit's extreme departure test for interim results.

The court asked the Solicitor General for the government's views in June. The government's brief, filed Oct. 7, recommended granting review limited to a reworded version of Robinhood's first question and said the second question, on Regulation S-K Item 303, did not warrant review. The investors argued that leaving out Item 303 means their Section 11(a) claim will go forward in the district court however the first question is resolved. Business groups including the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association filed briefs backing Robinhood's petition. Law firm Alston & Bird warned the Ninth Circuit's rule could invite forum shopping into the Ninth Circuit.

The investors do not claim any historical figure in the filing was wrong, and their case rests on omissions alone. Section 11 imposes near-strict liability on issuers and underwriters for flaws in a registration statement, so the standard for omissions sets how much intra-quarter data companies feel obliged to disclose before pricing a deal. The ruling will land as the largest IPOs in years come to market, including Anthropic's. The court has not yet scheduled argument.

The case is one of the most closely-watched intellectual property disputes of the generative AI era, and its outcome will shape how UK copyright law applies to AI models trained overseas. The High Court handed down its first instance judgment in November 2025, delivering a mixed outcome that largely favoured Stability AI. Getty succeeded on a small part of its trade mark claim, but its copyright claim ultimately failed, and because Stable Diffusion was trained outside the UK, Getty had dropped its primary copyright claims during the trial. Getty's remaining copyright case was one of secondary infringement, namely that Stable Diffusion was an infringing copy imported into and distributed in the UK.

The High Court accepted that an AI model can be an article even though it is intangible, but held that an infringing copy must be a copy. Because Stable Diffusion's model weights had never stored Getty's images, the model could not be an infringing copy. The key question in the appeal is whether an AI model can be an infringing copy for secondary copyright infringement if the model itself has never contained a copy of those works. The relevant provision of the Copyright, Designs, and Patents Act 1988 is section 27(3), and Getty's position is that making a model includes training it, in turn involving the copying of images.

Getty argues the law does not require the finished model to itself contain a copy of the works it was trained on. The British Recorded Music Industry Limited has been given permission to intervene in support of Getty and warns the High Court's approach could allow AI developers to train models offshore and bring them back into the UK. BPI cites two recent German cases where the Munich Court found that AI models did contain copyright works on which they had been trained, having memorised them. Stability AI argues that whether something is a copy depends on what is actually produced, not on how it was developed.

stories.Headline: UK adults spend over $1.3 billion a year on AI tools as paying users reach 5 percent
stories.Summary:
Brits are spending more and more on artificial intelligence, with one in twenty adults in the United Kingdom now paying for AI tools and spending more than $1.3 billion a year in total. That five percent share is still early days, but it is a fast ramp, since it was 1% two years ago and 2.5% a year ago. London is the hotspot, and the professional skew is predictable, with those involved in tech, finance, education and PR most likely to pay. Claude's share of that spending has quadrupled in a year, and the newsletter asks whether the trigger was the improved harness on Claude Cowork.

Agent-based shopping is still early, since Uber says four rides out of 320 million during Halloween week were booked by agents. The writer's Instinct agent secured an iPhone Duo on Tuesday, a job that involved checking Apple's website every few minutes from 7 am. William Gildea made his first purchase using his Instinct agent, sweaters for winter, and Hannah Petrovic's agent booked a squash court for a showdown with Marija Gavrilov. The writer says he would still reach for the app to book an Uber, but finding finicky, complicated products is a perfect job for agents.

On energy, adding wind to solar and batteries cuts the median cost from $105 to $86 per MWh, and north of Milan and Montreal it falls from $164 to $99. Based on hourly modeling over ten years, Kingsmill Bond and Daan Walter reckon that sun and wind mostly cover for each other, except for a difficult combined lull for about a week every four. Ember also finds that 83% of the 750GW of fossil plants being planned sit where reliable renewables, with a bit of gas backup, cost under $100/MWh. The writer's take is that technology costs will keep falling, but redesigning the grid into a largely renewable-based one also requires a better cost of capital and financial instruments that match energy prices to the volatility renewables bring.

stories.Headline: Professor Hoang Van Kiem proposes a three-tiered model to develop talent in gifted schools in the AI era
stories.Summary:
Professor Hoang Van Kiem, former Chairman of the State Council for Professor Titles in Information Technology, wrote in Thanh Nien Newspaper that talent development in specialized and gifted schools needs to change in the age of AI. The article was published on 15/11/2026, in commemoration of the 30th anniversary of the High School for the Gifted, Vietnam National University, Ho Chi Minh City. For decades, specialized schools and gifted schools have contributed to training many scientists, mathematicians, engineers, artists, and others who have made significant contributions to society. The article appeared amid ongoing debates surrounding admissions and training in specialized schools. The piece was presented by Thanh Nien Newspaper and carried by Vietnam.vn.

The article says talent is the result of the interaction of individual potential and biological characteristics, family and social environment, quality of education and teachers, opportunities to access knowledge and technology, training, experience, and creativity, and motivation, passion, and perseverance. It proposes a three-tiered talent development model: Tier 1 foundational competencies including mathematics, language, science, technology, arts, physical education, emotional intelligence, and humanities. Tier 2 is development of specialized talents in mathematics, computer science, natural sciences, languages, arts, social sciences, and emerging fields. Tier 3 is interdisciplinary creativity with scientific research, technological innovation, AI projects, digital art, entrepreneurship, and practical problem-solving. It proposes a model of Gifted High School, Youth Research Center, Creative Space, and Open Academic Community, with five components.

The article says teachers need to discover hidden potential that grades don't reflect, ignite passion and a desire for exploration, and guide students to think independently without relying on AI. It says they should impart research experience and scientific standards and educate students on character, ethics, responsibility, and compassion. It says the philosophy should shift from selecting the elite to unleashing talent, from selecting gifted students, intensive training, student competitions, and achievement to discovering potential, unleashing abilities, research and innovation, talent development, and contribution to society. It says competitions and Olympiads still play an important role in identifying and nurturing exceptionally talented students but should not be the sole objective of gifted education. It says achievement is a milestone, not the ultimate goal of gifted education.

The article says a student who doesn't win an Olympic medal can still become an outstanding scientist, a technological innovator, a talented artist, or an innovative entrepreneur. It says a student who wins numerous awards also needs to continue developing independent thinking, creativity, and adaptability to new problems. It says a student who excels in mathematics shouldn't just study math but needs exposure to computer science, physics, music, art, data science, and practical applications. It says a student who excels in literature shouldn't be judged solely on writing ability but needs philosophical thinking, social observation skills, artistic creativity, and communication skills. It says specialized schools will have to compile statistics on what jobs their graduates are doing after graduation.

The article says the Imperial Academy, established in 1076, is a symbol of Vietnam's tradition of training talent for the nation. It says the modern system of specialized high schools in Vietnam mainly emerged in the 1960s, and specialized mathematics education began in 1965 with a specialized mathematics class at Hanoi University, the predecessor of the specialized school model at the University of Science, Vietnam National University, Hanoi. It says Hanoi ,  Amsterdam High School for the Gifted commenced its first academic year on September 5, 1985, formed by consolidating the specialized classes of several high schools in Hanoi. It says that on July 14, 1993, Deputy Minister of Education and Training Tran Chi Dao signed a decision to establish the specialized high school system for mathematics and computer science at the University of Ho Chi Minh City. It says that on July 4, 1996, Minister of Education and Training Tran Hong Quan signed Decision No. 2693/GD-ĐT establishing the High School for the Gifted, Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City.

The article says future gifted high schools should develop according to the model of Gifted High School, Youth Research Center, Creative Space, and Open Academic Community. It says connecting with universities and research institutes is a key advantage that should be strongly promoted at the High School for the Gifted under Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City, where students can receive guidance from university lecturers, scientists, and business experts and participate in seminars, research projects, and academic activities appropriate to their age. It says student laboratories should provide opportunities for research projects on AI, robotics, biology, materials, environment, energy, music, and digital art. It says the article also covers proposals for admission to specialized schools based on subject groups and subject combinations and proposed changes to the entrance exam for specialized 10th-grade classes. It leaves open what students, parents, and teachers say about those proposed changes.

Articles.Title: Talent development in specialized schools and gifted schools needs to change in the age of AI. - Vietnam.vn

stories.Headline: Justice Edward Muriithi gives Kenya six months to create a national AI policy and legal framework
stories.Summary:
The High Court issued a formal notice to the government on November 15, 2026, regarding the use of artificial intelligence in public services. This legal action followed a challenge brought by activists John Wangai, Peter Agoro, and Antony Manyara who highlighted the lack of a comprehensive framework. These individuals argued that the absence of governing rules for AI systems across various public offices posed a risk to the citizenry. The court intervened to ensure that the state addresses these regulatory gaps to protect the public.

Justice Edward Muriithi granted the government a period of six months to finish creating a national policy and a legal framework for AI. While the court declined to force Parliament to pass specific legislation within 90 days, it emphasized the necessity of these guidelines. This new requirement aims to prevent violations of fundamental rights, including access to food, clean water, and social security. The framework must also cover essential services such as healthcare, education, sanitation, and adequate housing for all Kenyans.

Justice Edward Muriithi stated that the state carries a constitutional obligation to implement legislative and policy measures for the protection of its people. He explained that these actions are necessary to safeguard the basic rights of citizens from potential harms caused by unregulated technology. The judge emphasized that the government must take proactive steps to ensure that AI deployment does not undermine human dignity. By setting this deadline, the court holds the state accountable for the ethical integration of technology into public administration.

Articles.Title: Court puts State on notice over use of AI in public services - Daily Nation

stories.headline_source: Court puts State on notice over use of AI in public services

stories.Headline: AI Lawsuit Jersey 2026: Settlements, Eligibility and Filing
stories.Summary:
New Jersey faces three major AI class actions in 2026, according to lawfold.com, with the largest, Martinez v. TechHire Solutions, covering over 15,000 job applicants in the Newark metro area who claim an AI tool scored them lower based on zip code. The second, Doe v. SocialAI Corp, involves 8,000 New Jersey residents whose likenesses were used without consent to generate synthetic media. The third targets automated lending platforms and alleges AI loan denials disproportionately affected Black and Latino borrowers, with a class estimated at 12,000 applicants.

The Martinez case was certified by Essex County court in January 2026, the SocialAI Corp motion to dismiss was denied in February 2026, and the lending case began discovery in March 2026. The state attorney general filed two enforcement actions this year, both targeting AI vendors selling untested hiring tools to New Jersey employers. The cases invoke the 2025 AEDT Act, which gives workers a private right of action and requires a bias audit within 12 months of use, annual re-audits every 12 months, public disclosure, and candidate notification before AI use. Penalties run $500 per day for a missed initial audit, $1,000 per day for a missed re-audit, $500 per violation for non-disclosure, and $250 per applicant for missing notification. Deepfake victims can sue for statutory damages of $1,000 per incident under the 2025 privacy expansion, and the updated privacy framework took effect in January 2026, requiring explicit opt-in consent for AI data use.

Damages range from $500 to $2,500 for unauthorized data scraping under the NJ Consumer Fraud Act, $1,000 per violation for hidden AI data use, $1,000 to $5,000 for biometric misuse, and $5,000 per child for children's data harvesting. A 2025 state study found a 34% disparity in AI-driven loan approvals, against a 9% gap for human loan officers. The articles attribute the claims to New Jersey workers who say automated systems denied them jobs unfairly, and to plaintiffs who argue that non-compliance with the AEDT Act itself proves negligence. The articles state that employers must now prove their AI tools are bias-free and that companies that fail face penalties under the 2025 AEDT Act. The articles say the state attorney general filed the two enforcement actions, that penalties could exceed $10 million per case, and that the NJ Division on Civil Rights is actively investigating.

The articles state that the EEOC has referenced New Jersey cases in its own guidance. The articles say staffing agencies are the biggest targets and are named as co-defendants in multiple suits, and that at least four Fortune 500 firms paid undisclosed sums to New Jersey applicants. The articles state that over 20,000 workers have reported suspicious rejections since 2024, that over 40,000 New Jersey workers may be owed compensation, and that most claimants can expect between $200 and $5,000. The articles say the combined class size exceeds 35,000 people, that tech, finance, and staffing face the most exposure, and that the lead court is Essex County Superior Court. The articles state that retail chains face class actions over facial recognition data collected in New Jersey stores and offices.

The articles state that New Jersey passed the AEDT Act in 2025, that it was the first law of its kind in the state, and that the state leads the nation in AI regulation enforcement. The articles say New Jersey expanded its privacy laws in 2025 to cover synthetic media and that the updated privacy framework took effect in January 2026. The articles state that the claims fall under the NJ Law Against Discrimination, the NJ Consumer Fraud Act, the NJ Fair Housing Act, the NJ Biometric Privacy Act, and a NJ COPPA Extension. The articles say the law does not require proof of intentional discrimination and that disparate impact alone is enough under New Jersey law. The articles state that many employers missed the first audit deadline, creating a wave of new claims in early 2026.

The articles state that filing deadlines are approaching fast for several claims and advise workers rejected by AI systems to keep all emails, and deepfake victims to document screenshots, URLs, and timestamps. The articles do not name the defendants in the lending case, the employers or agencies named as co-defendants, the four Fortune 500 firms, or the retail chains facing biometric claims. The articles do not give the filing deadlines, the amounts paid in the undisclosed settlements, or the outcomes of the two enforcement actions. The articles do not state when the three class actions will next be heard or how the 34% disparity study was conducted.

stories.Headline: Google launches Universal Cart while Nvidia unveils agent safety platform for banks
stories.Summary:
Google and Nvidia introduced new technologies in late 2024 to influence how consumers choose payment methods and how banks manage automated software. Google launched its Universal Cart service across Search and the Gemini app in the United States on October 15 to help shoppers track prices and select payment options. Meanwhile, Nvidia announced the Open Agent Safety Platform on September 28 to provide security frameworks that keep artificial intelligence agents within specific operational limits. These separate developments suggest that financial institutions must now compete for transactions while simultaneously governing software that acts on behalf of their customers.

The Universal Cart tool utilizes Google Wallet to recommend payment methods based on available benefits, which may change how card issuers compete for spending. Nvidia's safety platform combines activity restrictions with a monitoring system that intervenes when an agent exceeds its permitted boundaries. Citi and J.P. Morgan Chase are collaborating with Nvidia on this shared safety technology to ensure software does not move beyond established limits. Additionally, BBVA announced on October 21 that it would explore this approach to maintain oversight as the bank expands its use of complex AI agents.

Google stated that its new shopping tool keeps consumers in control by allowing them to complete purchases through Google Pay or merchant websites. The company clarified that retailers remain the sellers of record and continue to provide all necessary customer support and confirmations. Nvidia explained that its technology distinguishes between instructions telling an agent what to do and independent controls that enforce what it can actually do. These companies believe that their tools will help banks manage the risks associated with automated decisions and the visibility of card benefits.

These shifts require card teams to understand how shopping assistants present benefits and risk teams to establish strict permissions for autonomous software. Banks must now determine exactly when a human must intervene to prevent AI agents from operating outside of their authority. While it remains unclear if consumers are ready to delegate every financial decision, these tools identify the next operational priorities for the industry. Financial institutions must ensure their products remain competitive when software helps customers choose while maintaining rigorous internal security.

Articles.Title: Google and Nvidia Bring Banks to AI’s Checkout Test

stories.Headline: GDC report finds 40% of game developers use generative AI while 55% see a negative industry impact
stories.Summary:
The Game Developer's Conference released its latest State of the Game Industry report, which found that 40% of game developers actively use generative AI in their work, according to PC Gamer. The report surveyed over 2,600 respondents from all corners of the industry, PC Gamer reported on 14 November 2026. The same report found that 55% of those surveyed said generative AI is having a negative effect on the games industry. PC Gamer's Rick Lane wrote the article about the findings. The report showed a slight uptick in AI use alongside dominant negative sentiment toward the technology.

The 40% figure marks a slight increase from 36% last year, the report found. Of workers over 45, 54% stated they use generative AI, and men were more likely to use AI tools than women, according to the report. Indie developers were less likely to use it than studios working on premium, free-to-play, and mobile-exclusive games. Among AI users, nearly three-quarters said they use it for research and brainstorming, while 56% said they use it for code generation and debugging. Use dropped to 22% for concept art and visual ideation and only 7% for player-facing features.

The negative view rose 1% from the start of 2026 and was up 25% from 2025, the report found. Meanwhile, 35% said the impact was mixed, and only 8% believed generative AI is having a positive effect. The report concluded, with the help of AI sentiment analysis tools, that industry professionals are forming a more nuanced view rather than taking an all-or-nothing stance. The report also highlighted new concerns that AI use leads to skill atrophy and loss in professional and personal development. Developers were also taking a dimmer view of using generative AI for player-facing features.

PC Gamer reported that developers who see a bright new future in the tech have increasingly clashed with those concerned by the ethical, artistic, and labour implications of tools like ChatGPT and Claude Opus. The article said the tech is becoming harder to avoid, since a casual Google search in 2026 technically counts as using AI. It said the effects of AI on the games industry, particularly agentic coding tools, have become more pronounced in 2026. Platforms like Steam and itch are wrestling with a dramatic increase in AI slop games, the article said.

Use of the tech among developers has triggered heated debates in spaces like the IGF awards, according to the article. The report was covered by Eurogamer before PC Gamer's article, which cited it. The survey drew respondents from all corners of the industry, PC Gamer reported. The report's conclusions were reached with the help of AI sentiment analysis tools, it should be noted, according to PC Gamer.

The article described generative AI use as one of the most contentious topics in the games industry. The report is the latest State of the Game Industry report from the Game Developer's Conference. The articles do not say when the full report will be published or what further findings it contains. They do not give the exact survey period or the full methodology beyond the 2,600-plus respondents.

They do not name the developers or studios surveyed. They do not say how the report defines generative AI use or which specific tools respondents reported using beyond the examples of ChatGPT and Claude Opus. They do not give any response from GDC beyond the report's conclusions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Experts warn banks may hold hung debt deals as AI infrastructure boom faces political uncertainty
stories.Summary:
Banks may be left holding debt deals tied to the AI infrastructure investment boom, experts warned, after a tech-led stock market rout wiped more than $3.2tn off US equities in a single day. The sell-off followed early November's Democratic wins in key states such as Texas, Georgia and Ohio, which account for around 38 per cent of planned US data centre capacity. OpenAI's Stargate data centre project, planned with a capacity of 1.2 gigawatts when fully built, faces growing political uncertainty. The Banker reported these developments on 16 November 2026, in an article by Anita Hawser.

The warning concerns so-called hung debt deals, which are loans banks have committed to provide but cannot sell on to investors. Banks may be insulated from direct losses, according to the article, but their links to private credit pose a less visible threat. The article gives no further figures on the size of the debt at risk or on which banks are exposed. It also does not say what happens next, beyond describing the political uncertainty facing the Stargate project.

The article attributes the warning to experts, who are not named, and it does not record any statement from a bank, a regulator or a government official. Responsibility for the debt deals is not assigned in the text, which describes the risk in general terms rather than naming the institutions involved. The only named project is OpenAI's Stargate data centre, which the article links to the political uncertainty rather than to the debt warning directly. No one quoted in the article responds to the experts' warning.

The context given is the recent tech-led stock market rout and the Democratic wins in Texas, Georgia and Ohio, states that account for around 38 per cent of planned US data centre capacity. The article presents these events as the backdrop to the warning about hung debt rather than as established causes of it. It does not say what happens next, and it gives no timetable for resolving the debt deals or for the Stargate project. The piece is an analysis of risk, not a report of losses already taken.

Articles.Title: Could banks be left holding the debt if the AI boom falters?

stories.Headline: IBM and MeitY Startup Hub sign MoU to support indigenous deeptech startups
stories.Summary:
IBM and the MeitY Startup Hub said on Tuesday that they had signed a Memorandum of Understanding to support the indigenous deeptech startup ecosystem, according to a report published on October 13, 2026. The agreement gives startups access to IBM's technology expertise, skilling programmes and development initiatives. The collaboration combines MeitY Startup Hub's nationwide innovation network with IBM's enterprise AI, hybrid cloud and quantum computing expertise. It is meant to help high-potential startups build, validate and scale technologies for India and global markets. It also complements IBM Ventures' ongoing engagements in India by expanding pathways for enterprise technology startups to connect with customers, investors and industry experts.

As part of the collaboration, startups will get access to IBM's portfolio of enterprise technologies and innovation platforms to solve business use cases. This includes technical guidance and enablement on technologies such as IBM watsonx, an enterprise-ready AI and data platform, IBM Bob, an AI coding agent for enterprises, and IBM Sovereign Core, an AI-ready software stack for digital sovereignty. Startups will also receive technical orientation on IBM's hybrid cloud and quantum computing, along with security and automation solutions. The collaboration will focus on enterprise proof of concepts, sovereign AI innovation, open-source ecosystem development, founder mentorship, technical skilling, and opportunities for startups to showcase their solutions to enterprises and investors. A key priority will be identifying and nurturing promising innovators from Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, broadening access to India's growing deep tech ecosystem.

Panneerselvam Madanagopal, the CEO of MSH, said the collaboration with IBM aims to strengthen indigenous deep tech capabilities, foster technology-led entrepreneurship and create greater opportunity for innovators to build solutions that contribute to a Viksit Bharat. Sandip Patel, the Managing Director of IBM India and South Asia, said the collaboration reflects a shared commitment to fostering innovation and strengthening the country's deep-tech startup ecosystem. Patel said these startups are playing a pivotal role in shaping the future of technology-led growth for India and the world. He said that together with MeitY Startup Hub, the aim is to help founders innovate faster, scale responsibly and build solutions that address both national and global challenges. Patel added that the goal is turning promising innovation into real-world impact.

stories.Headline: Anthropic plans an IPO within a week as seven AI giants invest 26 billion dollars
stories.Summary:
Anthropic plans to launch its initial public offering within the next week. This artificial intelligence leader is preparing for a blockbuster entry into the public markets. Seven major technology giants have committed to investing in the company. These investments will occur through a private placement alongside the IPO. The move comes as the company seeks a massive cash infusion.

The company is eyeing a market cap of around 1.4 trillion dollars, down from 2 trillion dollars. Seven giants, including Alphabet, Nvidia, and Microsoft, will invest 26 billion dollars at the IPO price. Other investors include Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Micron, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. Anthropic reported 33.2 billion dollars in revenue for the nine months ended September 30. This revenue represents a growth of 1,206 percent over the previous year.

Anthropic is responsible for the updated prospectus that reveals these upcoming investments. The company needs these funds because it remains unprofitable despite its rapid revenue growth. It reported a net loss of 104 billion dollars in the most recent period. This loss is worse than the 25 billion dollar loss recorded in the prior year. Most losses were tied to non-cash charges related to convertible notes and derivative liabilities.

Investors are cautioned that the stock is risky even at a 1 trillion dollar valuation. The success of Anthropic could benefit infrastructure providers like Nvidia and Alphabet. Alphabet may benefit specifically because Anthropic uses Google Cloud infrastructure for its operations. The recent SpaceX IPO serves as a reminder that high valuations can limit stock gains. Some analysts suggest that investors do not need to rush to buy the stock.

The company had an 81 billion dollar annualized revenue run rate as of October. Its operating loss shrank to 1.3 billion dollars from a previous 5.2 billion dollar loss. Anthropic is currently planning a massive build-out of its artificial intelligence capabilities. The company is moving from a research and development phase into a global rollout. This transition is described by analysts as the second act of the AI industry.

The company will go public next week to secure the committed 26 billion dollar investment. It remains uncertain if revenue growth will continue at its current fast pace. The final valuation will determine if the stock trades at 12.3x or 17.3x annualized revenue. The articles leave open whether the IPO will top the 75 billion dollar SpaceX record. It is unclear if the share price already reflects the company's business progress.

Articles.Title: Forget SpaceX: This Potential Blockbuster IPO Has Attracted $26 Billion From AI Giants

stories.Headline: AI drafts legal briefs but lawyers still hold responsibility for judgment
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence now drafts legal briefs and organizes case law in minutes. This technological shift occurred by November 15, 2026, according to Seoul Economic Daily. Junior lawyers previously spent entire nights reading records and revising drafts manually. Now, these colleagues receive completed drafts before their morning coffee even cools. The technology replaces the long hours once required for building basic legal skills.

The system can sort through tens of thousands of emails overnight without pay. It can also instantly pull together manuals for handling Fair Trade Commission inspections. In cartel cases, the first leniency applicant has its fine waived entirely. The second applicant to come forward receives a 50 percent reduction in fines. These specific rules mean a single order can change a company's fate.

Lee Chang-hoon is an attorney at the law firm Shin and Kim. He says that responsibility for brief contents cannot be handed to machines. Lee believes lawyers now sell professional judgment rather than just providing information. He notes that AI delivers wrong answers with composure and fabricates rulings. He argues that AI cannot take the blame for a lawyer's mistakes.

Some lawyers in the United States were sanctioned for citing invented case law. These fabricated rulings are described as plausible but are disasters for clients. Flustered employees may try to delete emails during on-site inspections by investigators. Commissioners at plenary hearings do not read AI prepared answers before asking questions. Clients are affected because they need advice on which options to choose.

Lawyers used to believe that working longer hours helped them build more skill. AI can now write opinion letters and prepare anticipated questions for hearings. However, it cannot stop an employee from deleting evidence during a raid. It cannot grasp the true intent of a commissioner's question during a hearing. AI cannot walk a chief executive through reputational damage or employee fallout.

Lawyers must still recommend decisions amid uncertainty and take responsibility for outcomes. They must guide executives on whether to rush into a leniency application now. The articles leave open whether the lawyer's job will disappear with late nights. They do not state if more lawyers will be sanctioned in America. The future of the profession depends on the value of human judgment.

Articles.Title: AI Can Draft Legal Briefs, But Lawyers Still Carry the Judgment - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Google threatens to block school search access if New York City bans AI, a reader says
stories.Summary:
The New York Daily News published a “Voice of the People” readers’ letters column on November 15, 2026, at 3:00 AM EST, with the email address voicers@nydailynews.com. A Forest Hills reader wrote that Google threatened to block schools’ search access if the NYC Department of Education bans AI. An Olivebridge, N.Y., reader wrote that Alaska’s Senate race was still too close to call as of Friday. That reader wrote that with 88% of votes recorded, Democrat Mary Peltola led by 3,975 votes. A Western Springs, Ill., reader wrote that Elon Musk spent at least $474 million supporting Republicans in the midterm elections.

The Forest Hills reader wrote that the DOE has over-relied on Google for the classroom, assignments, and grade-tracking and testing by computer. The Western Springs reader wrote that about $224 million was spent on races in Texas, where Musk’s SpaceX and Tesla are headquartered. That reader wrote that SpaceX is dependent on government decisions and contracts, and that Musk wants to build a data center in Texas to support Tesla’s testing for autonomous driving. The Olivebridge reader wrote that Peltola’s opponents are Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan and the Independent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who has received 4,199 votes. A Beacon, N.Y., reader wrote that Gov. Hochul’s recent reelection was a mandate, and that the SUNNY Act and the Healthy Homes Right to Know Act have passed the New York State Legislature and await her signature.

The Forest Hills reader wrote that Google’s goal is profit above all and to use our children as guinea pigs to teach its computer system. That reader wrote, “I’d be surprised if the DOE stood up to Google.” The Olivebridge reader wrote that a high-ranking Republican asserts that Dan S. Sullivan should be given the votes that Daniel J. Sullivan received, and identified this Republican as Trump. That reader called the assertion a clear perversion of the election and an insult to every Alaskan, and likened it to the “I just want to find, uh, 11,780 votes” suggestion in the 2020 presidential election. The Manhattan reader wrote that Chuck Schumer may want to ride into the sunset after his term is over, leaving a legacy of regaining his majority leader position.

The Forest Hills reader wrote that AI is quirky at best and wrong 50% of the time, and that students don’t read, want to double check or seek other sources. The Western Springs reader wrote that Musk bought more political speech than millions of ordinary people combined, but that with a strong wave against Republicans his candidates did not do well in this election. That reader wrote that many elections are a lot closer, and in those, huge contributions can be decisive. The Manhattan reader wrote that Schumer snubbed Abdul El-Sayed in favor of Haley Stevens and didn’t direct funding support to Angie Nixon, who came within a hair of defeating the miserable GOP candidate in Florida.

The Manhattan reader wrote that Elissa Slotkin and Bernie Sanders want an open selection process and for prospective candidates to provide a concrete plan for affordability and accountability. The Hamilton Square, N.J., reader wrote that in 1968 two Olympians from the U.S. raised their fists in a Black Power salute and were suspended, and that a few years ago Colin Kaepernick was chastised and punished for taking a knee on a football field. Al Sharpton and civil rights leader Ben Crump held a press conference at Sharpton’s National Action Network. stories.Headline: Malaysia partners with Singapore and US to stop AI chip smuggling
stories.Summary:
Malaysia is working with Singapore and the United States to stop chip smuggling, according to a statement released on November 13, 2026. The Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry is checking with local Customs to see if chips brought into Malaysia were re-exported legally. This action follows a 2025 probe by Singapore authorities into several companies, including the cloud computing firm Megaspeed and officer Alice Huang. Alice Huang is a suspected Chinese spy whose affair with Jensen Huang led to the resignation of the Nvidia chief executive. The Malaysian government is now bracing for expected US controls on high-performance artificial intelligence chips and remote compute deals with Chinese firms.

The government has tightened rules since July 2025, requiring permits for US AI chips to leave Malaysia, though importing them remains license-free. Regulations do not require data centres to name end users, but stakeholders estimate half of the 1.4-gigawatt capacity serves the Chinese market. Nvidia requires cloud partners, such as conglomerate YTL, to provide customer information and cap Chinese business at 49 percent of services. YTL Power lost RM5.5 billion, or an eighth of its market value, starting November 10 as investors gauged exposure to Megaspeed. MITI clarified that verification visits at data centres where Speedmatrix, the Malaysian arm of Megaspeed, is a tenant are part of regular monitoring.

Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Ghani said on November 10 that Speedmatrix was not under investigation due to a lack of credible evidence. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim stated on November 13 that Malaysia has not received formal requests from Singapore or the US but will collaborate. He noted that Malaysia is a trading nation that welcomes investments but wants to ensure that all rules are being followed. MITI denied that it has cleared Megaspeed or its local subsidiary of any wrongdoing amid the fallout in the data centre sector. These statements followed revelations over the weekend regarding Jensen Huang's affair, which increased security concerns in Washington over US technology.

Banking executives said that financing deals for about half of upcoming data centre projects in Malaysia have been halted, with delays up to six months. An unnamed investment analyst warned that significant implications for customer concentration and contract enforceability exist if Megaspeed accounts for much of YTL's capacity. David Black of BlackBox Research stated that there will be additional compliance costs, though he warned that a total chip export ban is counterproductive. A digital economy official said the news ruffled feathers, but for now, the situation remains business as usual while they wait. Taylor's University professor Ong Kian Ming suggested that tougher controls could be an opportunity for Malaysia to become a secure AI investment destination.

Data centre investments surged to RM95.8 billion, or 43.9 percent of total approved investments in the first half of 2026, from RM1.25 billion in 2021. This boom is now stalling as lenders avoid companies that might be subject to US probes, according to a local investment bank executive. The executive noted that without graphics processing units, data centre players cannot offer compute, even though demand still outstrips the current supply. Ong Kian Ming, a former deputy minister, suggested that Malaysia should increase MITI's powers to crowd in domestic demand and reduce Chinese dependence. He also mentioned that the upcoming Asean summit in Manila could be a forum for Asean to engage the US on these issues.

The industry is now waiting for clarity from Washington to determine when the stalled financing deals for data centre projects can resume. Malaysia may escalate oversight and implement more progressive policies to shift its AI data centre demand away from Chinese-related sources. Asean may use the unveiling of the Digital Economy Framework Agreement details at the Manila summit to discuss these technology controls. The articles leave open whether the US will launch formal probes into other Malaysian data centre players or implement a total export ban. It remains unclear if the current verification visits by MITI will lead to formal charges against Speedmatrix or other local firms.

stories.Headline: Catching the signals sooner: AI’s role in proactive pharmacovigilance
stories.Summary:
A key message at this year’s World Patient Safety Congress was that pharmacovigilance is evolving from a reactive, compliance-driven function to a more predictive and science-led discipline, pharmaphorum reported on 16 November 2026. As therapies for chronic diseases expand globally, safety organisations face an unprecedented volume of evidence from ICSRs, clinical studies, scientific literature, electronic health records and real-world data. The challenge is no longer data collection but timely identification and interpretation of clinically meaningful safety signals within increasingly complex and heterogeneous datasets. Highly trained safety physicians and scientists often spend significant time aggregating and reviewing information rather than on signal evaluation, causality assessment and benefit-risk analysis. Artificial intelligence offers the potential to strengthen pharmacovigilance by accelerating evidence synthesis, supporting earlier signal detection and enhancing risk surveillance.

AI is not a replacement for medical judgement but enables a human-guided, scientifically grounded approach in which technology augments expert evaluation. The expansion of chronic disease therapies makes ongoing safety monitoring more demanding as medicines are used over longer periods by people with varying underlying health conditions and alongside other treatment. Diabetes patients are increasingly treated with combinations of glucose-lowering agents, cardiovascular therapies, obesity medicines and renal-protective treatments. Healthcare is becoming more connected through continuous glucose monitoring, digital health applications, wearable devices and remote patient monitoring. A potential safety concern may involve not only the medicine and an adverse event but patient characteristics, treatment duration, concomitant medications, disease progression, lifestyle factors and real-world treatment patterns.

The traditional process flows sequentially from collection of Individual Case Safety Reports to signal detection, signal validation, scientific assessment and regulatory action. AI is unlikely to replace pharmacovigilance processes but can enhance them as an additional analytical layer identifying weak signals and emerging patterns across multiple sources of evidence. The system ingests millions of data points, allowing AI to autonomously identify unusual patterns, which are escalated for medical safety review, signal validation, scientific assessment and risk-mitigation action. More advanced agentic AI coordinates tasks across connected workflows with clear escalation points for human review, and biopharma companies reduce operational effort by 30-50%, accelerate regulatory reporting, identify safety signals earlier and reduce the risk of inspection findings, product recalls and patient safety events. For larger safety reports, AI can pull together relevant evidence and draft sections while human experts review and sign off the conclusions.

AI does not establish causality, validate safety signals or make regulatory decisions, which remain the responsibility of qualified pharmacovigilance professionals, medical safety physicians, epidemiologists and regulatory authorities. The next opportunity is looking beyond individual reports to evidence in electronic health records, claims data, registries, clinical studies and scientific literature. If an older diabetic patient takes multiple treatments simultaneously, individual reports may not make the connection apparent, but AI-supported analysis across appropriate sources could bring that pattern to specialists’ attention sooner. Initiatives such as the FDA’s Sentinel programme and EMA’s DARWIN EU network demonstrate the importance of broader real-world evidence in safety assessment and highlight why AI is becoming critical. No pharmaceutical company has a complete view of patient experience, so collaboration is required, and underlying illnesses, concomitant medicines and reporting biases still require scientific assessment.

Sanjeev Sachdeva leads advisory and business process services globally for the life sciences unit at Tata Consultancy Services and is a member of the unit’s core leadership team. He drives strategic direction, business and IT advisory, thought leadership, industry collaboration and technology innovation, with more than 30 years of experience in business and technology transformation. He partners with customers across R&D, manufacturing, supply chain and commercial to adopt new technologies, processes and operating models. Sachdeva is a regular contributor to industry and academic forums including the Wharton Mack Institute for Innovation Management, DIA, PHUSE, PHORUM and IIT Delhi. He also speaks at industry roundtables and has authored white papers on AI enabled transformation in drug safety, clinical development, personalised medicine, digital health, quantum computing in life sciences, the future of the lab, blockchain, the metaverse and AI in regulated industries.

Governance by design requires defined responsibilities, quality standards, escalation routes and a traceable record of source information, AI outputs and human decisions that stands up to scrutiny. Validation before deployment is only the beginning, and teams must monitor whether systems continue to perform as intended and intervene when output becomes unreliable. This creates new skills requirements in data quality and AI oversight, and human expertise becomes more valuable as reviewers need the evidence, time and authority to challenge rather than simply approve outputs. As highlighted at the World Patient Safety Congress, AI’s greatest value lies in enabling safety organisations to shift from reactive reporting to predictive risk management, identifying emerging risks earlier so safety teams can intervene sooner and strengthen patient protection. The future is an AI-native safety enterprise where AI handles data-intensive processes and experts focus on critical medical decisions, enabling faster insights, earlier risk mitigation and greater confidence in patient safety.

Articles.Title: Catching the signals sooner: AI’s role in proactive pharmacovigilance

stories.Headline: Cisco raises AI infrastructure sales forecast as Cerebras and CoreWeave beat estimates
stories.Summary:
Cisco reported quarterly results that beat estimates on both revenue and profit, and it raised its forecast for AI infrastructure sales to hyperscalers to $9 billion for the fiscal year, more than double the prior year, according to an article by Brian Sozzi published on Yahoo Finance on November 13, 2026. Cerebras, an AI infrastructure company, also beat on sales and earnings, and it guided to a core gross margin of 47% to 49% and sales of $310 million to $330 million for the current quarter, against analyst estimates of a 42.1% margin and $271 million in sales. CoreWeave beat on the top and bottom lines earlier in the week and pushed back on the view that it would need high-yield debt to fund growth, and its shares rose 22% over the week. The article tied the moves to an AI trade that may be back after an early fall slumber, in a week dominated by coverage of scandals involving Jensen Huang, whom the article described as having lost the CEO role at Nvidia. Cisco CEO Chuck Robbins said the company was executing against its strategy and seeing growing demand as customers invest in infrastructure for what he called the AI or SI era, and KeyBanc analyst Brandon Nispel said the stock looks attractively valued after earnings.

Barclays analyst Tom O'Malley said key customers remain intact and Cerebras is adding new hyperscalers, but the industry is seeing delays across many providers that are slowing the OAI ramp and could push the timing of revenue. O'Malley added that the stock had fallen 33% over the past month against a 14% drop in the SOX index, and he said clearing the bear case and adding customers should more than offset industry-wide concerns about those delays in the near term. Cerebras shares rose 13% in premarket trading on Friday, and the article said the new focus should be on execution of OAI and the new customer set. CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said the company already has a robust pipeline of customers competing for capacity, and at current pricing levels the 2027 renewals would generate approaching $4 billion of incremental annualized revenue with no additional capex required. Intrator said that figure grows to nearly $10 billion of annualized incremental revenue when 2028 renewals are included, and he said that if data center construction across the sector were to slow, installed compute would become scarcer and GPU pricing might stay higher for longer.

The article listed related headlines, including one saying Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang addressed a CoreWeave stock plunge and said he was optimistic, and another saying CoreWeave stock sank as the resignation of Jensen Huang rippled through the AI trade. The article gave no further detail on the Huang resignation beyond those references and the mention of scandals. stories.Summary:
Ninepoint Partners LP filed and obtained a receipt for a final prospectus qualifying units of the Ninepoint Anthropic HighShares ETF, the company announced on November 13, 2026. The ETF is expected to begin trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange under the ticker ANHI, subject to satisfying the TSX's original listing requirements. Trading is expected to start the business day following the completion of an initial public offering by Anthropic, PBC, currently anticipated on or about November 19, 2026. The ETF combines leveraged exposure to Anthropic, the company behind Claude, with a professionally managed covered call strategy designed to generate income. Ninepoint is based in Toronto and oversees approximately $8 billion in assets under management and institutional contracts.

ANHI will offer a management fee of 0.29% and intends to pay twice-monthly cash distributions, like other ETFs in the Ninepoint HighShares suite. The ETF seeks long-term capital appreciation through purchasing and holding, on a levered basis, Class A common stock of Anthropic, and regular cash distributions. ANHI will hold up to 100% of its total assets, including assets acquired with borrowings, in Anthropic Class A common stock and write covered call options on up to 50% of those holdings. The covered call strategy will be reviewed monthly for cash flow sustainability, and the risk rating is High. The ETF is considered an alternative mutual fund under applicable securities legislation, permitting strategies generally prohibited for conventional mutual funds, such as investing up to 20% of net asset value in a single issuer, borrowing cash, short selling beyond conventional limits and employing leverage.

Karl Cheong, CFA, Executive Vice President and Head of ETFs at Ninepoint Partners, said Anthropic's upcoming public listing is an opportunity to invest directly in the company, and he anticipates strong interest from Canadians seeking TSX-listed exposure. Cheong said Ninepoint designed ANHI to provide Canadian investors a way to participate in Anthropic's growth potential while seeking regular income through a covered call strategy. Ninepoint is the investment manager of the ETF. The ETF does not have a fixed distribution amount, and the amount of ordinary cash distributions may fluctuate, based on the Manager's assessment of prevailing market conditions.

The 2026 tournament will take place from November 15 to 22 at Inalpi Arena in Turin, Italy. NTT DATA is a global leader in AI, digital business and technology services. The partnership gives NTT DATA a global stage to showcase how AI, data and technology can support human potential. Elite tennis brings together skill, judgment and the ability to adapt under pressure.

NTT DATA will host a Tech Corner in Turin where visitors can see computer vision, Physical AI and advanced AI infrastructure applied to real-world scenarios. Those scenarios include monitoring, safety, construction and humanoid robotics. The space will also house the Mental Economy Gym, powered by Formula Medicine, an Italian company specializing in sports medicine and human performance. Guests there can take on digital challenges that measure indicators such as concentration, reaction and mental workload. At the Fan Village court, NTT DATA will showcase an on-court experience presented by FITP, combining cognitive and physical monitoring with AI-powered computer vision.

Kazuhiko Nakayama, President and CEO of NTT DATA Group, said what makes sport extraordinary is ultimately human, citing the ambition to push boundaries, the courage to take risks and the determination to achieve more. He said technology has the power to unlock even greater possibilities by helping people see what was previously invisible and discover new ways to improve. As an AI Consulting Partner of the Nitto ATP Finals, he said, NTT DATA wants to celebrate human potential while demonstrating how technology can expand what people can achieve. He said NTT DATA combines AI capabilities with deep industry expertise to help clients transform their businesses and create new value. The partnership is the latest in a series of sporting partnerships that bring NTT DATA's global brand positioning statement, "Intelligence to Impact," to life.

IT Brief UK reported that the partnership places the technology group alongside one of men's tennis's best-known season-ending events. The report said NTT DATA will use the tournament to show how AI, data and related systems can generate performance insights and support decision-making under pressure. IT Brief UK said the announcement reflects a wider trend in professional sport, where tournaments, teams and governing bodies use technology partnerships to enhance fan experiences and collect more detailed information on athlete preparation and match play. The report said tennis has become a testing ground for data-led analysis, with systems used across officiating, broadcast coverage and training. IT Brief UK said the demonstrations will place tools used in industrial and operational settings into a consumer-facing environment, linking them to measurable human activity rather than back-office processes.

It describes itself as one of the world's leading AI and digital infrastructure providers, with capabilities in enterprise-scale AI, cloud, security, connectivity, data centers and application services. As a Global Top Employer, NTT DATA has experts in more than 70 countries. NTT DATA is part of NTT Group, which invests over $3 billion each year in R&D. NTT DATA said the partnership reflects its belief that intelligence comes not only from AI and technology, but also from human expertise and deep industry understanding. stories.Headline: Majority of Indians prefer instant AI health answers over waiting for doctors in BCG survey
stories.Summary:
A Boston Consulting Group global survey found that 61 percent of Indians prefer instant AI health answers over waiting for doctors. This study was conducted during July and August 2026 and included 9,914 consumers across 10 different countries. The findings were published on November 15, 2026, by Sumit Jha in a report about the consumerisation of health care. This shift shows that more people in India are using digital technology to seek medical information instead of professionals. The report indicates that patients are increasingly seeking greater control over their treatment decisions, convenience, and their healthcare expenditure.

India scored 66 out of 100 on the Healthcare Consumerization Index, ranking second behind China, which scored 72. The United Arab Emirates ranked third at 63, while Brazil followed in fourth place with a score of 62. In India, 60 percent trust digital health information as much as professional advice, which is 19 percentage points above average. Additionally, 78 percent of Indian respondents want more control over treatment choices, and 73 percent want control over costs. Around 68 percent expect retail level convenience, and 58 percent view medicines as common consumer goods.

Chris Meier of BCG stated that consumer patients are reshaping rules to expect more intuitive, responsive, and personalized health care experiences. He is a managing director and senior partner who co authored the report on the consumerisation of the health industry. Sabrina Kristic, also a managing director and senior partner, noted that health care decisions are more complex than cosmetics. She warned that these decisions have potentially serious consequences, even if products blur the line between health and lifestyle categories. Both authors believe that providers must now balance patient choice and convenience with clinical quality and patient outcomes.

Millennials were most likely to prefer instant AI answers at 52 percent, followed by Generation Z at 47 percent. Baby boomers showed the lowest preference for these digital tools, with only 25 percent choosing AI over a doctor. Doctors from Harvard and Johns Hopkins warn that AI mass surveillance can cause chronic anticipatory stress and physical sickness. Vulnerable groups, including undocumented immigrants, may avoid clinics or pharmacies due to a fear of persecution from surveillance tools. These experts argue that AI surveillance is a structural determinant of health that can create avoidable health inequities.

The BCG report explains that digital platforms can improve information access but may also expose users to fragmented services and misinformation. People with limited digital literacy or confidence may be excluded from these new digital first models of health care. Meanwhile, the New England Journal of Medicine highlights how private companies now control the data ecosystems used for surveillance. Traditional surveillance required human oversight, but AI can continuously comb through social media, financial transactions, and geolocation records. This allows private actors to analyze vast amounts of personal data and share it with government agencies.

Next, healthcare providers must find ways to balance transparency and convenience with equity and the overall quality of patient outcomes. Clinicians can help by documenting patient fears about data usage to provide evidence for policymakers and various legal litigators. Some states, including Washington, Nevada, and Connecticut, have passed laws to extend privacy protections to certain consumer health data. More than 20 state attorneys general have sued the federal government for sharing Medicaid data with Palantir and ICE. The articles leave open whether AI will serve population health or become a driver of structural harm.

stories.Summary:
Marius Meiners predicts a retail revolution where artificial intelligence chooses what people buy and which businesses receive their money. This shift involves digital personal assistants learning consumer needs and completing routine purchases without being asked by the user. Some companies already report that chatbots drive up to 30 per cent of their total sales conversions. The process involves AI agents searching the internet, comparing various prices, and recommending products based on budgets. This transformation could become one of the biggest retail revolutions in history by automating everyday shopping and services.

The technology requires users to have personal AI assistants to handle groceries, clothes, restaurants, and other everyday services. Some brands generate between 20 and 30 per cent of sales through ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity platforms. To unlock on-device AI, users may need an iPhone 18 Pro or a Pixel 11 with 12GB RAM. These devices use compact 3-billion-parameter models for local text cleanups but rely on remote data centers for reasoning. This architectural reality means that 12GB of RAM is now the baseline for entering the AI world.

Marius Meiners, the co-founder and chief executive of Berlin-based Peec AI, is responsible for these retail predictions. He believes that personal AI assistants will become universal because they will be incredibly useful for every consumer. Meiners stated that these tools will know exactly what people want, where they eat, and where they stay. He argued that technology should make lives easier and free up time by handling annoying routine decisions. He suggested that AI can make these routine decisions better than humans could make them for themselves.

Retailers are affected because they risk losing customers if AI overlooks products or uses outdated prices and inaccurate information. Businesses must understand how shoppers find products and which sources AI platforms use to avoid losing sales to competitors. Gabriel Zamora, a senior writer at PCMag, notes that tech giants charge top dollar for these pocket supercomputers. He argues that cloud-reliant AI agents are quietly reducing modern smartphones to glorified dumb terminals for the users. People who enjoy shopping for luxury or expensive goods will still be free to shop for themselves.

The background shows that shoppers are increasingly turning to ChatGPT and rival platforms for advice before spending their money. Conventional website analytics may fail to reveal the actual influence that AI currently has on various buying decisions. Tech companies use marketing to imply that phones are autonomous supercomputers equipped with potent Large Language Models. However, neither Apple nor Google has promised 100 per cent cloud-free AI that operates exclusively on the device. Silicon Valley often obfuscates the truth regarding how devices hand off execution to remote data centers.

Brands are urged to ask customers where they find products and how they make decisions about those specific items. AI models already have a massive impact on consumer behaviour, but the full extent remains hidden from brands. The future involves AI assistants anticipating purchases and finding the best deals to complete routine transactions autonomously. The articles leave open whether smartphones will continue to rely on the cloud for sophisticated reasoning tasks. It remains unclear how many retailers will successfully adapt their data to be accurately read by AI.

stories.Headline: Google DeepMind and University of Chicago researchers test AI agents to scale public policy consultation
stories.Summary:
On November 11, 2026, researchers from Google DeepMind and the University of Chicago published a preprint on arXiv about pluralistic AI agents. This study evaluated how autonomous software representatives could represent citizens during deliberations regarding artificial intelligence governance to scale public consultation. The team tested these agents to see if they could capture diverse public input while identifying various operational risks. This research aimed to address low civic engagement and technical barriers that often hinder traditional public consultation on AI regulation. The final results were published by the CASRAI Editorial Board on November 15, 2026, as a four minute read.

The system requires three stages starting with an agent interviewing a person or persona to capture qualitative values and core priorities. Next, agents participate in structured multi-agent discussions using anonymized aliases, and finally, a policy-writing agent synthesizes the consensus into rules. The team, including Jacy Reese Anthis, Ken Burke, David Madras, Crystal Qian, Meredith Ringel Morris, Logan Cross, Caroline Pantofaru, and Utsav Prabhu, tested this. They used models like Claude-Opus-5, GPT-5.6-Sol, GLM-5.2, Kimi-K3, Mistral-Large, and Gemini-3.6-Flash across 5,947 deliberations using conjoint analysis. The study also involved 746 verified human participants recruited through Prolific across six different AI safety topics.

The investigators stated that pluralistic agents should function as amplifiers of public engagement rather than autonomous replacements for democratic institutions. They noted that prompt phrasing functions as de facto procedural rulemaking because verbosity and cooperativeness dictate the final policy outcomes. The authors emphasized that institutional researchers must implement safeguards against prompt manipulation and establish clear audit trails for agent interviews. They also argued that human stakeholders must retain ultimate ratification authority over any policies created through algorithmic consensus. The researchers highlighted that without transparent moderation algorithms, consultations risk skewing outcomes toward the most assertive delegates.

Human participants reported concerns regarding personal agency, noting that delegating deliberation prevented them from engaging in direct social learning. These participants felt that using proxies stopped them from updating their own viewpoints during the debate process. The study affected research administrators, ethics boards, and policy researchers by providing empirical benchmarks on how autonomous proxies deliberate. While participants preferred direct personal participation, pluralistic agents recovered 82 percent of the procedural justice gap against a baseline. When choosing between pluralistic agent proxies and direct deliberation with other humans, the participants split evenly at 50-50.

Traditional consultation mechanisms struggle to keep pace with rapid deployment cycles as universities and funding agencies navigate frontier AI safety. Public consultation often fails because institutions cannot disclose confidential technical details to broad audiences and citizens lack specialized engineering jargon. The researchers found that in 1,000 deliberations with 368 personas, agents matched desired priorities in 90 percent of cases. Direct human participation achieved an average attitude shift of 15.4 percentage points, while pluralistic agents produced a 13.9 point shift. This background shows that agents can solicit granular input on technical choices like computational safety thresholds and laboratory boundaries.

Next, university Research Ethics Boards must recognize the ethical nuances of algorithmic proxy representation when reviewing participatory research protocols. Institutions may adopt these multi-agent tools to improve democratic throughput while maintaining human oversight of the final policy decisions. The articles leave open how to standardize prompt calibration to prevent assertive agents from dominating the deliberative process. There is no mentioned solution for the loss of social learning that humans experience when using AI proxies. The text does not specify which specific AI safety topics were used for the 746 human participants.
