stories.Headline: OpenAI and Anthropic support congressional efforts to block China from accessing AI chips and tools
stories.Summary:
OpenAI recently backed a bipartisan congressional effort to block China from accessing artificial intelligence chips and chipmaking equipment this November of 2026. This support follows the recent ouster of Jensen Huang as the chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp on Thursday, November 13, 2026. Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, is expected to travel on Air Force One to China this week with President Donald Trump. Trump is scheduled to arrive in China on Wednesday to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's leader Xi Jinping. These events occur during the APEC summit as the United States considers new legislation to tighten export controls on high-end technology.

Congress is weighing three proposals, including the AI Overwatch Act, the Match Act, and the Chip Security Act, to be attached to defense legislation. The AI Overwatch Act, pushed by Jim Banks and Elizabeth Warren, seeks to freeze existing Nvidia chip sales rules for 18 months. The Match Act aims to restrict chip tools from ASML Holding NV, while the Chip Security Act requires mechanisms to prevent smuggling. These measures target the diversion of Nvidia processors and the activities of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company under investigation for improper chip smuggling. All three bills must pass before the end of the year to become law, provided President Donald Trump does not veto them.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has pushed for months to blacklist Megaspeed, while he criticized Howard Lutnick for slow-walking the Commerce Department's restrictions. Lutnick is accused of allowing Nvidia to use loopholes to sell advanced chips to China and giving the company unfettered rule-making access. The White House stated it maintains complete confidence in Lutnick, though some sources question how many lives the secretary has left. A senior US official said the Nvidia scandal should not bear on the China trip or figure in conversations with China. Representative John Moolenaar stated that Nvidia must change corporate practices and appoint leadership that makes national security its top priority.

Nvidia allies and trade groups argue that these provisions would harm the ecosystem of companies that are tied to the chipmaker's business. Democratic lawmakers claim the administration has failed to enforce existing export restrictions on AI chips since Donald Trump returned to office last year. The Justice Department is conducting an espionage probe into Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive suspected of being a spy for China. Alice Huang had an affair with Jensen Huang, which led to a board investigation and his eventual resignation from the company. Anthropic PBC has also expressed support for tougher controls on AI chip exports and tightened access to sophisticated chipmaking equipment.

Jensen Huang previously used his influence to kill the Gain AI Act, which required chipmakers to ensure no US customers sought chips. The current push for legislation gains momentum because Huang was a longtime foe of stricter export controls and diminished Nvidia's Capitol Hill clout. Bipartisan support includes House Speaker Mike Johnson, New York Democrat Hakeem Jeffries, and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, though John Thune remains undecided. China's Ministry of Commerce previously vowed to take necessary measures to safeguard interests after the House Foreign Affairs Committee advanced similar bills. China has previously deployed export controls on rare earth minerals to retaliate against the United States for ratcheting up chip controls.

The administration remains wary of new policies that could imperil the delicate trade truce with China, which expires on January 10, 2027. Lawmakers and administration officials continue to negotiate the exact terms of the three bills, meaning the proposals could still be scrapped entirely. It remains open whether the legislation will pass by the end of the year or if Trump will threaten a veto. The outcome of the Justice Department's espionage probe into Alice Huang and Megaspeed may further influence the final legislative language used. The articles leave unclear if Howard Lutnick will regain his footing after clashing with Scott Bessent and other Trump administration officials.

stories.Headline: Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution showcase AI data center battery systems at RE+ 2026
stories.Summary:
Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution will compete at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas starting November 17. These two companies will showcase energy storage systems and backup power solutions for artificial intelligence data centers. They disclosed their participation plans on November 15 for the three day renewable energy trade show. The event draws about 40,000 visitors and 1,300 companies to the largest renewable energy show in North America. Both firms are targeting North American orders by emphasizing their local production capacity for these battery systems.

LG Energy Solution will use a 279 square meter booth to show the JF3 AC LINK with US-made LFP batteries. This product increases energy density by 26 percent and uses AI and digital twin technologies for grid stabilization. Samsung SDI will exhibit the SBB 2.0 using locally produced LFP prismatic cells in a 20-foot container. Samsung will also show the U8A3 prismatic battery using lithium manganese oxide for uninterruptible power supply applications. LG will display the JP6 Rack for UPS and BBU products based on cylindrical 2170 batteries.

Kang Chang-beom of LG Energy Solution said stable power storage and efficient operations are essential for AI industry growth. He stated the company will become an energy platform by combining battery technology with intelligent operations and North American production. Samsung SDI claims the U8A3 is the first to pass all UL Solutions large-scale indoor fire test criteria. An industry official noted that companies now focus on profitability rather than the cutthroat competition seen in the past. This shift follows a trend where the three major battery firms moved toward making profits this year.

The competition affects Big Tech clients like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google who need cooling and power for AI chips. LG Energy Solution is sitting out a 1,180MW South Korean auction, leaving Samsung SDI and SK On to compete. This auction totals about 7.08GWh in storage capacity, which is larger than the first two rounds combined. Samsung SDI has about 15GWh of production capacity in South Korea with roughly 5GWh of remaining supply. SK On has about 3GWh of LFP capacity converted from an EV line in Seosan for deliveries.

Samsung Electronics previously spent 1.5 billion euros to acquire Germany's Flakt Group for data center climate control technologies. The company is now pursuing US cooling maker Modine to gain North American production facilities and customer networks. Modine recently began mass producing 2 to 3 megawatt chillers at a 63,400 square meter plant in Grand Prairie, Texas. Modine's data center revenue reached 439.7 million dollars in the third quarter, which is up 95 percent from last year. Samsung is also building a 240 billion won production line in Gwangju to start operating in early 2028.

Samsung may acquire Modine for 7.5 billion to 8 billion dollars through a merger agreement or a tender offer. The deal requires approval from two-thirds of voting rights, meaning about 35.41 million votes in favor are needed. LG Electronics is also competing by building a chiller plant in Virginia to begin operating in the first half of 2027. Other competitors like Daikin and Vertiv are expanding through acquisitions to win large projects from North American Big Tech firms. The articles leave open whether Samsung shareholders or Modine's board will ultimately agree to the proposed acquisition.

It says that understanding the financial impact of tax decisions, maintaining data consistency and identifying potential risks early are becoming increasingly important. The discussion also explores the link between financial and taxable results and how digital tools can help businesses detect discrepancies.

The interview further covers how AI can support tax professionals in managing requests, analysing information and identifying potential risks proactively. It highlights the view that technology should complement, rather than replace, professional judgement in tax decision-making. The articles give no further numbers, dates or names beyond the publication date and the interviewee's name and title. No specific changes, requirements or figures are attached to the discussion in the articles provided.

Responsibility for the views rests with Tural Jahangirov in his role as Manager at KPMG Azerbaijan, and the interview is attributed to kpmg.com. He frames the expanding role of tax as a shift toward understanding financial impact, keeping data consistent and spotting risks early. He presents digital tools as a way to help businesses detect discrepancies between financial and taxable results. He also presents AI as support for managing requests and analysing information, while professional judgement remains central.

The context is a tax function that is moving past calculations and compliance toward broader financial insight and risk awareness. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the themes raised in the interview. They offer no timeline, no follow-up steps and no commitments from any organisation. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Singapore probes Super Micro over potential false declarations regarding server purchases
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Home Affairs identified Super Micro Computer as part of a larger probe into potential false declarations regarding server purchases. This investigation began in February 2025 and involves the US-based server supplier, which has known links to the chipmaker Nvidia. Singapore authorities stated on November 12 that the firm has provided limited cooperation during the ongoing inquiry. The government also noted that the US Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation provided limited assistance despite repeated requests since September 2025.

The probe involves Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed and alleged Chinese spy, who was barred from re-entering Singapore in February. US authorities are investigating whether entities linked to Huang attempted to smuggle Super Micro products into China. Separately, co-founder Yih-Shyan Wally Liaw and two other men were charged in the US for conspiring to divert 2.5 billion US dollars of AI technology to China starting around October 2023. Additionally, two Super Micro employees were among nine people indicted in Taiwan for illegally exporting 130 B300 servers to Chinese customers.

Super Micro stated on November 13 that it has been responsive to inquiries and fully cooperated with officials in the US, Taiwan, and Singapore. The company denied that Megaspeed was ever a customer and claimed to maintain a robust compliance programme to protect American innovation. Regarding the US charges, Wally Liaw pleaded not guilty, while former contractor Ting-Wei Willy Sun pleaded guilty to four counts including smuggling and defrauding the country. The firm continues to operate a small office in Singapore located at Metropolis Tower 1 in Buona Vista.

stories.Headline: Democratic election wins and data center moratoriums push AI buildouts out of the US
stories.Summary:
Democrats won sweeping victories and local moratoriums on data centers during the midterm elections. These results embolden opponents of the artificial intelligence buildout across the United States. Successful Democratic candidates campaigned on stopping new construction to protect water and electricity. Other Democrats seek broader AI regulations to prevent job losses and dystopian outcomes. These changes will begin in January when Democrats control Congress and several state capitals.

Democratic control will extend to state capitals in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, and Iowa. Goldman Sachs analysis suggests moratoriums could delay as many as 45 percent of planned centers. Alphabet announced a 15 billion dollar data center push in Malaysia after the elections. Anthropic is seeking global locations to reduce concentration risks in its IPO filing. The GAIN AI Act was passed by the Senate in October 2025.

Stanislav Kazanov of Innowise said the election simply accelerated an existing trend of migration. He noted 26 percent of 633 gigawatts of new capacity is in states with halts. Kazanov explained that programs responding to American users must remain close to those users. Mike Intrator of CoreWeave stated that the results show how firms should build responsibly. Thomas Anglero of MerkabaPhi AS said frontier model owners must keep data centers locally.

President Donald Trump worries that these delays put the United States at a global disadvantage. Hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, and Alphabet are already investing in Asian data center buildouts. Aaron Henry of Foundeast Asia Co. Ltd. expects Thailand, India, and Malaysia to capture shares. Arnold Platz of General Future Holding views the shift as diversification rather than a total exodus. Kearney reports demand shifting toward Hungary, Greece, Portugal, and Scandinavia away from Germany and France.

The United States currently holds 45 percent of global data centers, while Europe has 28 percent. Asia held 15 percent of the world's data centers as of late last year. McKinsey projects Asia will account for 34 percent of global data center demand by 2030. Potential growth is also seen in Indonesia and Vietnam, as well as Poland and Hungary. Some developers are expanding existing campuses to avoid fights at new locations in the U.S.

The new Democratic Congress may renew the push for stricter AI export controls on chips. This focus follows a potential Chinese intelligence operation involving Alice Huang and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia president and CEO after reports of an affair with an executive. Future investment depends on who can deliver reliable power and water on a predictable timeline. The articles leave open whether the U.S. will maintain its lead in the global race.

stories.Headline: Developer Jakub Jankiewicz argues AI-generated code should be Open Source
stories.Summary:
A developer and writer named Jakub Jankiewicz published a blog post on November 15, 2026, arguing that all code generated by artificial intelligence should be released as Open Source. He based his argument on the fact that AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since Richard Stallman announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code, he wrote, was scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution, and the models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code, he argued, feels like license laundering.

The post makes two main demands, one legal and one practical, and it names the licenses it wants used. Jankiewicz argued that purely AI-generated code is not written by a human and therefore should not be copyrightable, citing the Monkey Selfie dispute as the foundation for that principle in the United States and noting that the U.S. Copyright Office later cited that precedent regarding AI. He added that Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI-generated images to be tagged as Public Domain, while acknowledging that copyright laws differ across the globe and that countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, he wrote, developers and companies should explicitly release AI-generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero license.

Jankiewicz is the person responsible for the argument, and the post reflects his own stated position rather than any company or organization. He conceded that code is not always fully manual or fully automated, but he said developers increasingly rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like that, where humans put little effort beyond writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source, he wrote. The article does not describe any enforcement mechanism, policy change or response from companies, and it offers no indication of what happens next beyond the author's call for developers and companies to adopt Open Source or CC0 licensing.

stories.Headline: Psychologist Eichenberg says AI chatbots bridge therapy waiting times but cannot replace professional care
stories.Summary:
People who struggle to find a therapist or need help faster than a counselling appointment can be set up are turning to general chatbots such as Gemini, Claude or ChatGPT, which seem like understanding listeners, according to an article published by The Star on Sunday, 15 Nov 2026. The article says many of us, especially the young, are using these chatbots as conversation partners for advice and to discuss problems, and it asks why not mental health conditions too. It adds that this comes with limitations and risks, and that psychologists it checked with were clear that AI is no substitute for psychological help from a person. In Germany, anyone looking for a place on a therapy programme has to wait an average of 20 weeks, says Christiane Eichenberg, head of the Institute for Psychosomatics at Sigmund Freud Private University in Vienna. Eichenberg, a psychologist and author of a book about Artificial Intelligence and Psychotherapy, says the gap in care is by no means the sole reason for the popularity of chatbots, which are available round the clock and are non-judgemental.

She says we can communicate with them without having to fear judgement or stigma, and that talking to a computer or phone makes it easier for many people to open up. She says you feel less pressure to put on a brave face and can express feelings such as sadness more intensely. The article says some people turn to general chatbots to discuss their everyday stress, feelings or anxieties, while other AI-based chatbots and applications have been developed specifically with a focus on mental health and are designed to help users reflect on their emotions, overcome fears or manage stress. Eichenberg says some AI-based mental health programmes have been scientifically evaluated and operate based on a clinically validated treatment protocol, and that the effects are comparable to those of psychotherapy when the systems have been used for four to eight weeks according to the research available so far. However, the article says it remains unclear how stable and long-lasting these effects are.

Kevin Hilbert, Professor of Clinical Psychology and Psychotherapy at the Health and Medical University of Erfurt, says an attentive, caring and always-available listener is appealing at first for most of us. The article says initial studies suggest that the use of artificial intelligence for mild psychological distress may be more effective than doing nothing at all, and that the systems may help in such cases by empowering users, helping them organise their thoughts and supporting them in their self-reflection. Hilbert says initial studies have also shown quite good results when it comes to anxiety, high stress or early symptoms of depression, but the article says there is overall not yet enough research to draw definitive conclusions. Eichenberg says specialist therapeutic chatbots may be particularly useful for bridging waiting times or to complement traditional therapy, and that they can support self-management, serve as a training ground for role-play for example, or provide valuable real-time support in acute stressful situations. She underlines that the bots are no substitute for psychotherapy.

stories.Headline: Meta expands AI age estimation on Instagram to apply teen account protections
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms announced in a statement dated November 9 that it is expanding its AI-powered age-estimation technology to find Instagram users it suspects are teenagers, even when they signed up with an adult birthdate. Accounts flagged this way are automatically moved into Teen Account protections, which Meta says will reach millions more teenagers across the world. The Epoch Times reported the move on November 10, 2026, and Biometric Update covered it the same day. Meta describes the protections as built-in safeguards that limit the content teens see, the time they spend on the app, and who can contact them. The company says some teens misrepresent their age online to reach experiences they are not old enough to use.

Starting this month, parents in the United States on Instagram will receive a notification explaining how Meta applies the age-appropriate protections and how they can help make sure their teen is logged in with the correct age. Teens aged 13 to 15 need parental permission to make some account protections less restrictive. Those aged 16 and 17 have more freedom to change certain settings, but still face restrictions, such as content limits, that cannot be altered without a parent's approval. Meta says it is continuing to roll out the technology on Facebook, and later this year it will begin launching similar measures globally on Threads. The company has also started using Apple's age-range signal in Australia as an additional way to help determine users' ages.

Meta is the company behind the expansion, and it says it uses AI and other signals to estimate a user's age. Larry Magid, CEO of the nonprofit ConnectSafely, explained the method in a November 6 post on Meta's website. He said the signals include profile information, comments, posts, captions and bios, such as references to school grades or birthdays, and that Meta can also analyze visual patterns in photos and videos. Magid stressed that this visual analysis is not facial recognition, because it looks for general characteristics suggesting an underage person in order to estimate an age range, not to identify anyone. He added that Meta deactivates suspected under-13 accounts and requires proof of age to prevent their deletion.

Meta also said it has long supported legislation requiring age verification and parental consent at the app store level. It argues that one verified signal from a person's device, shared consistently with all apps, is far more effective and privacy-preserving than asking every platform to verify age separately. Meta says it uses Apple's signal voluntarily, but that teens will get inconsistent protections across apps while sharing and using the signal stays optional for app stores and developers. It describes its own AI system as a backstop that can correct mistakes and feed them back to the app store for correction across all the apps a teen uses. Meta also says it has set a strong standard for age assurance and is investing in stronger technology to catch accounts that may belong to children under 13.

Biometric Update's Joel R. McConvey criticized the approach, writing that Meta responds to calls for platform accountability by hitting the problem sideways, in a game of misdirectional tennis. He argued that the age inference system is a form of profiling whose methods, accuracy and privacy implications are not subject to the public scrutiny applied to independently evaluated third-party tools. He also said it removes user choice, applying a model that recalls U2 pushing its album onto everyone's iPod. He noted that effective age assurance tools exist and that Meta already works with vendors, notably Yoti for facial age estimation on Instagram, and he said data from Australia shows how unserious the company has been about following laws it dislikes. Teens are the people directly affected, and the Electronic Privacy Information Center, through Megan Iorio, voiced support for California's AB 1709, saying design features that manipulate kids are the problem.

The expansion follows a roughly $18.1 billion settlement Meta reached in August with multiple U.S. jurisdictions over allegations of endangering children. Those lawsuits accused the company of deliberately designing its platforms to be addictive, knowingly exposing children to mental harms, and misleading people about the safety of its products. Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion to settle suits from 47 states, territories and the District of Columbia, and $1 billion to settle a Texas suit. As part of the deal, Meta agreed to institute age-verification protocols, content controls and time limits for children. Biometric Update reports that the agreement involves 52 bipartisan attorneys general and makes about 30 percent of the payments conditional on TikTok and YouTube adopting comparable measures and making matching payments.

Meta, Google and TikTok filed separate lawsuits on November 4 seeking to stop California from enforcing Assembly Bill 1709, a new state law meant to protect children under 16 from the effects of social media. The law bars platforms from offering underage children features judged psychologically exploitative that could cause compulsive use, including autoplay videos and personal recommendations. Platforms are obligated to delete the accounts of children with such features. The companies allege that the measure violates First Amendment free speech protections. The Epoch Times also notes that Meta recently settled with a teen during a trial over social media addiction claims, which the articles cite without giving details.

In the weeks ahead, U.S. parents on Instagram will begin receiving the notifications, while the technology keeps rolling out on Facebook and reaches Threads later this year. The articles do not say how accurate Meta's age estimation is, how many teens it has identified, or whether the system will face independent evaluation. They also leave open whether Apple's age-range signal will spread beyond Australia, and whether app stores or developers will be required to share and use it. The outcome of the lawsuits from Meta, Google and TikTok against California's AB 1709 is likewise undecided. Biometric Update adds that the company's statements about online safety rest on credibility it may not have.

stories.Headline: Telefónica blocks 500,000 fraudulent calls daily in Spain and launches Llamadas Molestas alerts
stories.Summary:
The articles report that AI-powered fraud could cost firms USD $11.5 billion by 2027, according to CFOtech, and that Telefónica publishes a running series of position papers and blog posts on digital security framing the problem as a question of trust. The analysis, dated November 16, 2026, pulls together what Telefónica, CFOtech, TELUS Digital, E*TRADE and a handful of named practitioners say about AI-enabled fraud, what defenses they recommend, and where the market is heading. The articles state that AI now writes the scam, clones the voice and builds the fake colleague, and that the bill is climbing. The articles state that when any voice, face or message can be faked, the old shortcuts for deciding who to believe stop working. The articles state that the Maileva hack exposed 22 million people's data recently, and that every leak of personal data hands scammers fresh raw material for convincing impersonation.

The articles state that CFOtech's report puts the potential cost of AI-powered fraud to firms at USD $11.5 billion by 2027, a figure the articles say cannot be verified from the headline alone and should be treated as a directional estimate rather than a measured loss. The articles state that Telefónica's Spanish operations block approximately 500,000 fraudulent calls every day, and that on 16 March 2026 Telefónica launched Llamadas Molestas, a service that alerts users to potentially unwanted calls using predictive models that analyze patterns associated with spam and nuisance calling. The articles state that Telefónica says its security capabilities include 12 Security Operations Centres built to detect and respond to potential incidents. The articles state that TELUS Digital lists the preferred multi-factor method as an authenticator app or hardware device, not SMS, and that high-value transactions should require two or more independent approvers. The articles state that E*TRADE's consumer-security guidance lists fraud warning signs as urgency, secrecy and demands to act now.

The articles state that Ben Colman, chief executive officer of Reality Defender, defined the problem in a KCBD report on voice-cloning scams, saying a deepfake is a piece of media, audio, video, images where a real person is either AI-generated or AI-manipulated using tools available to anybody with just a Google search. The articles state that Telefónica's guidance for organizations focuses on knowing which AI systems are in use, who uses them and what data they touch. The articles state that Telefónica recommends four moves for organizations deploying AI: discover which AI systems are in use, identify the users and the data they access, protect models against known attacks, and monitor model behavior continuously for malicious patterns. The articles state that Telefónica's AI-risk framework adds security-by-design measures such as access controls, security assessments, continuous monitoring and protection of physical and digital infrastructure, plus employee cybersecurity training. The articles state that Telefónica says industry-wide anti-fraud work increasingly combines AI-driven detection, advanced authentication, intelligence sharing and consumer education.

The articles state that Telefónica Tech applies AI and automation inside its Security Operations Centres to analyze large data volumes and prioritize threats for human analysts, and that the company says AI can improve cybersecurity by spotting anomalous patterns and emerging risks in real time. The articles state that automation takes over repetitive security tasks, freeing specialists to focus on complex decisions and incident response. The articles state that ET Edge Insights ran a piece under the headline that AI scams overtake phishing as cybercrime turns into an industrialised business. The articles state that a human fraudster might run a handful of convincing scams a day, while an automated pipeline can run thousands and tailor each one. The articles state that the confirmed picture has three parts: AI is being used to create convincing impersonations, deepfake audio and video, fake personas and other deceptive content at scale; that capability feeds AI-enabled fraud and phishing, which threaten both users' digital trust and their financial security; and the recommended response is a mix of personal habits, organizational process and technical monitoring, not a single product.

The articles state that Telefónica's published material treats deepfakes, advanced phishing campaigns and increasingly sophisticated digital fraud as the growing risks tied to malicious AI use. The articles state that Telefónica's security writing stresses that identity replication makes the authenticity of digital interactions more important for customer relations, identity verification and fraud protection. The articles state that Telefónica describes a prevention model that spans the whole incident lifecycle, from anticipation through prevention to detection. The articles state that readers once learned to spot phishing by its flaws, such as odd grammar, a mismatched logo or a clumsy greeting, and that AI removes most of those tells. The articles state that an earlier report on fake GTA VI downloads carrying the Vidar infostealer showed how quickly a hyped launch becomes bait.

The articles state that the cost has more than one layer: direct losses such as a fraudulent wire approved after a convincing fake call, then investigation and remediation costs, then the slower damage to customer confidence. The articles state that a customer who doubts a brand's messages stops acting on any of them, including the legitimate ones. The articles state that the articles stick to confirmed figures and clearly label their own judgment calls because the fraud space attracts more guesswork than almost any other corner of tech. The articles state that the articles' own read is that the training line deserves more attention than it gets, since most successful fraud still ends with a person pressing a button. The articles state that tooling shrinks the number of bad messages that reach that person but never reduces the stakes of the ones that do.

stories.Headline: Omani SMEs use AI to improve productivity and cut costs
stories.Summary:
The first article, published by CNN on November 16, 2026, discusses what it calls the originality gap and the search for competitive advantage in the AI era, though the text provided contains mostly page code rather than the article's reporting. The second article, published by Zawya on November 14, 2026 and written by a staff writer for the Oman Daily Observer, examines how small and medium-sized enterprises in Oman can turn artificial intelligence into a competitive advantage. It says AI is no longer reserved for large corporations or businesses with substantial financial resources, and that even relatively small businesses can now use AI tools for tasks that once required considerable time, specialised expertise and additional staff. Those tasks include responding to customer enquiries, analysing sales trends, managing inventory and preparing financial reports.

The article says AI can help Omani SMEs improve productivity, reduce costs and become more competitive, and that the real question is not whether businesses should adopt AI but how they can use it effectively to generate tangible economic benefits. It gives examples: a small retail business can use AI-powered tools to analyse purchasing patterns, identify popular products and forecast future demand, which helps owners make better inventory decisions, reduce unnecessary stock and minimise waste, while restaurants and hospitality businesses can use AI to understand customer preferences, manage bookings, improve marketing and respond to enquiries more efficiently. Marketing is another area of benefit, since AI tools can now assist with producing marketing content, translating communications, identifying potential customer groups and tailoring promotional campaigns, work that previously required dedicated employees or external agencies. Financial management also offers opportunities, as many small businesses struggle with cash-flow management, expense monitoring and financial planning.

The article argues that SMEs play an important role in Oman's economic diversification, employment generation and development of local supply chains, so businesses that become more productive through technology can potentially expand operations, improve service quality, reach new customers and compete in regional markets. It cautions that adopting AI should not become an objective in itself, because buying software or subscribing to an AI platform does not automatically translate into higher productivity or profitability, and businesses first need to identify where they face operational difficulties and whether AI can offer a practical solution. It says a small enterprise might begin by automating customer enquiries or improving inventory management rather than investing in expensive and complex systems, and that starting with manageable applications, evaluating results and gradually expanding their use is a more realistic approach. It also lists challenges that cannot be ignored, including data privacy, cybersecurity, the accuracy of AI-generated information and the risk of excessive dependence on automated systems.

The article says government institutions, universities and the private sector can contribute through practical training programmes, SME-focused digital advisory services, collaboration with technology providers and affordable access to AI solutions, and that universities can connect research and technical expertise with real business challenges. It notes that Oman's National Digital Economy Programme and its second phase for 2026 to 2030 provide a policy framework for accelerating digital transformation and encouraging businesses to embrace emerging technologies, and that the next step should be ensuring these ambitions translate into practical improvements at the level of individual enterprises. It concludes that the competitive advantage of AI will not belong only to businesses that adopt the most advanced technology but to those that understand how to use it intelligently, responsibly and productively, and that for Oman's SMEs the opportunity now is to turn that potential into measurable economic value.

stories.Headline: Malaysia investigates Megaspeed subsidiary over alleged diversion of Nvidia AI chips
stories.Summary:
Malaysian police opened an investigation in April 2025 regarding United States allegations that high-performance artificial intelligence chips were illicitly procured and diverted through the country. The probe focuses on whether Malaysia served as a transit hub for Nvidia chips or if local proxy companies were involved in the scheme. Authorities are specifically investigating Speedmatrix, a subsidiary of the Singapore-based company Megaspeed International, which operates as a tenant at Malaysian data centers. This investigation follows reports that Megaspeed may have steered advanced technology to China in violation of United States export rules.

The investigation is being conducted under the Strategic Trade Act 2010 and involves several regulatory agencies. These include Bank Negara Malaysia, the Inland Revenue Board, the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission, Customs, and the police. While Speedmatrix can bring chips into Malaysia without a permit, any entity exporting, re-exporting, transshipping, or transiting high-performance US AI chips has required a permit since July 2025. The Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, known as MITI, is the lead agency coordinating with a task force called STAC.

Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail stated that the government is taking these allegations seriously and that the investigation is very complex. He noted that progress is regularly conveyed to MITI so the information can be shared with relevant parties. MITI added that providing false information to customs authorities is a serious offense and confirmed that Speedmatrix has never been cleared of any wrongdoing. The ministry is working closely with authorities in Singapore and the United States to determine if chips were re-exported illegally.

This situation coincides with the immediate resignation of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang as president, chief executive officer, and board member on November 12, 2026. His departure followed a scandal involving Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive and suspected Chinese spy who was barred from entering Singapore in February. The controversy has reportedly wiped nearly half a trillion dollars off the market capitalization of Nvidia. Malaysia is now considering stronger controls to curb chip smuggling as the artificial intelligence sector faces significant uncertainty.

stories.Headline: Samsung breaks ground on HBM packaging plant in Asan and moves opening to June 2028
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics broke ground on a high-bandwidth memory packaging plant on November 12, 2026, to expand the artificial intelligence server supply chain. This new facility is located at the Onyang campus in Asan, South Korea, and focuses on advanced packaging for HBM memory. The company is accelerating the project to meet the rising demand for server memory used in various modern artificial intelligence systems. Construction of the plant is the first project under a regional industrial mega-project program led by the South Korean government. The facility is now scheduled to begin its operations in June 2028, which is one year earlier than previously planned.

The project requires 6 trillion won, or 4.48 billion dollars, for construction and 40 trillion won for advanced equipment installed in stages. Total medium and long term investment for the Onyang expansion is roughly 46 trillion won, including three clean-room floors of 31,000 square meters. Samsung Electro-Mechanics is investing 8 trillion won in package-substrate production for central processing units and graphics processors in the Chungcheong region. Samsung Display is investing 67 trillion won in an 8.6-generation production line for information technology displays within the same South Korean region. Samsung Electro-Mechanics will also spend 4.27 trillion won in South Korea and 2.51 trillion won in Vietnam for flip-chip ball grid array substrates.

The South Korean Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources announced the groundbreaking and said it would coordinate permits for the new projects. The ministry also stated it would help the company secure necessary transport infrastructure along with essential water and electricity for the site. Samsung said during its third-quarter earnings announcement that it had already completed negotiations over HBM supply volumes for the year 2027. The company noted that customers continued to seek additional supply, which prompted the decision to move the plant opening date forward. Samsung Electro-Mechanics disclosed in September that its substrate expansion for high-performance computing applications will start mass production in September 2028.

Customers seeking more high-bandwidth memory are affected by packaging capacity, which is a separate manufacturing step from producing the memory wafers. Advanced packaging connects stacked memory dies with processors and other components, making it a critical constraint on the finished HBM supply. The expansion at the Onyang campus was prompted because the existing Samsung campus in Cheonan has run short of available space. This makes Onyang a major production base for advanced AI memory to support the needs of various global technology customers. The project is part of a broader investment program across the Chungcheong region to bolster the regional industrial economy.

The South Korean government identified 112 materials, components and equipment suppliers with additional investment plans totaling about 23.6 trillion won around the projects. HBM combines stacked memory dies with high-speed connections for AI accelerators, which are essential for the operation of AI servers. The government is supporting these industrial projects by managing the infrastructure and permits required for the massive scale of the investments. Samsung Electro-Mechanics is focusing its substrate investments on AI servers and other high-performance computing applications to meet the growing market demand. These efforts are part of a strategic move to secure the supply chain for artificial intelligence hardware in Asia.

The investment for the Onyang plant will be deployed over several years, with equipment spending following the initial construction in phases. Samsung has not disclosed the planned output capacity of the new plant or the specific customer commitments for the facility. The company has also kept the expected financial returns from the 46 trillion won investment private at this current stage. It remains open whether the increased capacity will fully satisfy the rising demand for AI server memory by June 2028. stories.Headline: Connecticut passes a law requiring AI chatbots to remind minors they are AI every hour
stories.Summary:
A letter to the editor in The Globe and Mail on Nov. 15, 2026, said a large proportion of projected massive investment in computing power for artificial intelligence will be used for utterly trivial purposes. The writer said his fantasy football team, picked by artificial intelligence, earned a C grade from the AI and stood last in his division. He said one rare win came against a manager whose starting lineup had only three active players. He said AI should be treated like mainframe computing of 60 years ago, only accessible to those with a serious need for it. He urged readers to consider how much power and carbon footprint of an energy- and water-hogging data centre would go to gaming, AI-generated cat videos, pornography, trivia, fake job applications and academic fraud.

The letter said a hockey playoff pool started in 1979, and this past April one team picked JJ Peterka on Buffalo. The writer said he noted Peterka was on Utah, not Buffalo, and the team admitted using AI for the pick. He said Peterka, who played on Buffalo the prior season, got zero points in the playoffs and that team lost the pool by 10 points. He said the next best player, whom they would have picked on Buffalo without AI, got 10 points, and they would have tied for first place. He said a nine-time champion asked whether AI made the pick.

A letter by Joanne Nesti in HK Now, received Nov. 12, 2026, and published Nov. 13, 2026, said artificial intelligence is the biggest technological advance in our lives, for better and worse. She said as many as two-thirds of all teens in the United States use AI chatbots, and we can't let this technology keep growing without a chance to rein it in. She said bad advice, questionable motives and a drive to keep users engaged have caused tragedies already, and we need to protect our children from the worst outcomes. She said she voted for the legislation earlier in 2026 and is proud to have done so. She said as a grandfather she is concerned about her own grandkids' safety, and as the owner of a manufacturing company she has seen how quickly technology can evolve.

Nesti said that as of Jan. 1, 2027, Connecticut will have a new control in place to better monitor the use of AI, days after youth likely receive new phones, tablets and laptops for the holidays. She said a new law passed earlier this year will cover several AI issues, and one piece will directly impact families. She said under the new law chatbots will have additional controls to prevent them from developing close relationships with humans, and a bot must remind a user it is AI every three hours for adults and every hour for children. She said before a minor starts using an AI chatbot, as of Jan. 1, 2027, operators must prevent it from engaging in harmful conduct. She said some news stories described AI companions and chatbots encouraging the public to consume unsafe substances, encourage unsafe behavior like disordered eating, or even commit violence.

Nesti said AI systems will need to be updated as of Jan. 1, 2027, to prevent this harmful conduct. She said another change requires AI chatbots to pick up on thoughts of suicide or self-harm and direct a user to help, such as suicide and crisis lifeline numbers. She said this will help address the needs of struggling youth, leaving them less susceptible to falling victim to chatbots. She said any violations of the law will be enforced by the Attorney General's office. She said the law isn't meant to prevent AI or technology companies from operating their products, but meets the disturbing and tragic stories heard in recent years and tries to prevent them from happening again.

Nesti said these changes aren't going to put OpenAI or Anthropic out of business and aren't going to impact the free market. She said Connecticut is the seventh state to regulate AI companions, so the state is not going out on a limb by itself. She said the state needs to stay safe and protect its youth from threats. She said putting guardrails on AI will help. The letter said the views stated are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of the editors, who welcome supporting or opposing views on any published item.

The Globe letter said letters to the editor should be exclusive to The Globe and Mail, include name, address and daytime phone number, and be kept to 150 words or fewer. It said letters may be edited for length and clarity, and submissions can be sent by e-mail to letters@globeandmail.com. The HK Now letter said it was received Nov. 12, 2026, and was published Nov. 13, 2026, by Joanne Nesti. The HK Now letter ended mid-sentence with the words putting guardrails on AI will help u. The Globe letter was published Nov. 15, 2026, at 06:00:00Z.

stories.Headline: FuelCell Energy joins federal StabilityMax program to test fuel cells for AI data centers
stories.Summary:
FuelCell Energy, a fuel cell company headquartered on Great Pasture Road in Danbury near the Bethel border, will take part in a three-year federally funded program to test whether fuel cells can provide electricity to data centers where there are rapid fluctuations in power consumption. The company announced the project in a release dated Nov 13, 2026, reported by staff writer Rob Ryser. The program is known as StabilityMax. Under the project, FuelCell Energy will develop a fuel cell test facility in Danbury, creating a national laboratory-supported testbed for evaluating integrated power solutions for AI data centers. The federal government wants to know whether fuel cells, which already power commercial and industrial facilities, can handle the heavy demands of artificial intelligence data centers.

The project runs three years and is led by the U.S. Department of Energy's National Laboratories of the Rockies. FuelCell Energy reported 425 employees worldwide last year, most of them at the company's Danbury headquarters and its Torrington manufacturing plant. FuelCell planned to keep its staffing levels the same. Details about the StabilityMax grant program, such as how much federal money is involved, were not disclosed. The pairing of fuel cells with data centers made news in October when a developer proposed to reinvigorate a 1.3-million-square-foot office structure in Danbury by bringing in a data center and using fuel cells to power it.

Mayor Roberto Alves said Thursday that FuelCell Energy's participation in the national research effort is a strong example of the innovation and expertise rooted in Danbury. Alves said he was pleased to see a Danbury company working with leading national labs on the challenge and looked forward to learning what the project demonstrates about performance, cost and the effects on the electric grid. Kathleen Blomquist, the company's director of communications, said the project isn't about testing whether fuel cells can power data centers because they can. Blomquist said the question is how to optimize a fuel cell-based power system for the rapidly changing demands of AI infrastructure, including how fuel cells, batteries, power electronics and advanced controls work together as computing loads fluctuate. Zhiwen Ma, a principal investigator at the National Laboratories of the Rockies, said fuel cells combined with data centers provide unique solutions to meet the power demands of AI infrastructure.

Ma said that through the project, NLR will help demonstrate how integrated fuel cell systems can rapidly respond to data center power needs while limiting impacts to the utility grid and ratepayers. Shankar Achanta, chief product and technology officer at FuelCell, said the insights gained through the work will help optimize system designs, validate performance under real-world conditions, and support future deployment of fuel cell-based solutions for digital infrastructure. The company's release said that as AI adoption accelerates, data centers are driving unprecedented demand for electricity and creating rapid fluctuations in power consumption. A data center is an umbrella term for computer processing plants that support all the ways artificial intelligence is used today. Public concern about energy usage by data centers has made headlines across Connecticut and the region.

A fuel cell makes electricity from fuel and air, eliminating the need to burn fuel. The company's headquarters sits on the city's east end. A FuelCell Energy power plant stands on Triangle Street in Danbury. The three-year project isn't as much about testing whether fuel cells work but about applying the technology to the next level. The federal government also wants the work to limit impacts to the utility grid and ratepayers.

The articles do not say when the three-year project begins or ends. The articles do not disclose how much federal money is involved in the StabilityMax grant program. The articles do not say what results the test facility is expected to produce or when. The articles do not say whether the October proposal for the 1.3-million-square-foot Danbury office structure is connected to the StabilityMax project. The articles do not say what the national laboratory-supported testbed will cost or who beyond FuelCell Energy will run it.

AMD expects revenue to increase by more than 80% in 2027, fueled by healthy growth in the data center business. AMD sees the server CPU total addressable market jumping to $220 billion by 2030. stories.Headline: Kukoon Rugs and Seating Matters adopt AI to scale operations and boost staff productivity
stories.Summary:
Traditional industries in Northern Ireland began adopting artificial intelligence to become more competitive, as reported by Darran Mashall on November 15, 2026. Two specific companies, Kukoon Rugs and Seating Matters, have integrated this modern technology into their daily business operations. These firms use the software to scale their operations and improve the overall productivity of their various staff members. The adoption of these tools allows these traditional businesses to modernize their processes while maintaining their historical roots. This shift is happening across different sectors, including carpet making and the manufacturing of specialist clinical seating.

Kukoon Rugs, a family firm in Newry, County Down, uses AI daily in finance, commercial, marketing, supply chain, and product departments. Seating Matters, located in the Sperrin Mountains outside Limavady, exports clinical seating to healthcare facilities in the US and Australia. The products from Seating Matters have also appeared in television dramas such as Coronation Street and Emmerdale. These companies sell their goods online and through some of the biggest retail chains found across the UK and Ireland. The technology is used to sift through data, such as finding a relevant email from six years ago.

Chief Executive Paul Vallely says AI allows his team to perform more accurate, efficient, faster, and more thoughtful work. He believes the technology removes the most boring tasks from office roles and increases the excitement and engagement of his team. Managing director Martin Tierney states that AI has revolutionised back office functions like accounting, finance, and pulling data from 20 sources. Tierney claims that while AI will not replace jobs, a person who knows how to use AI could replace a worker. He compares the power of artificial intelligence to a calculator on steroids that makes accountants more productive.

Staff members at Seating Matters are affected by the technology, which Tierney says has actually led to new jobs being created. He notes that the technology is poor at customer service but excellent for managing laborious tasks and avoiding filing cabinets. Vallely argues against claims that AI negatively impacts creative industries, stating it releases time for more research and analysis. The employees are encouraged to use the software to solve problems and speed up mundane tasks within specific guardrails. These guardrails ensure that no patient information or financial information is ever put into the AI software.

Northern Ireland has a long manufacturing tradition, becoming world famous for shipbuilding and linen after the Industrial Revolution in the 19th century. Rug making is also an ancient skill that has existed in the Newry area for a very long time. The articles explain that the basic products may not change, but the design, creation, and marketing processes are changing. Tierney mentions that in the 1800s, people feared calculators would replace accountants, but the technology only increased their productivity. This historical context shows a pattern of traditional roles evolving through the introduction of new tools like Excel.

The companies will continue to use AI to handle mundane tasks while ensuring a human always checks the final work. Seating Matters will keep using the software to flesh out ideas through a chat interface without needing an IT degree. The articles leave open whether other traditional industries in Northern Ireland will follow this path to remain competitive. stories.Headline: Wealth advisers pitch charitable giving help to new AI millionaires
stories.Summary:
Wealth advisers courting newly minted AI millionaires are pitching a service beyond the usual portfolio management, namely help in giving money away, according to advisers and clients described in a Wall Street Journal report published by Mint on 15 November 2026. Anthropic is planning to go ahead with its stock-market debut the following week, a listing expected to create another wave of fortunes only months after SpaceX produced a similarly large bonanza. Many of these new clients are in their 20s and 30s and have had little time to think about managing wealth that appeared effectively overnight. Some prospective clients want to give away 25% of their wealth or more, so advisers must show they can structure charitable giving, align investments with values and measure the impact of the money.

Advisers often suggest donor-advised funds, known as DAFs, because they give the donor an immediate tax deduction while allowing grants to charity at a time of the donor's choosing. A common strategy is to fund a DAF with shares of highly appreciated stock, which lets the donor avoid the capital-gains taxes that selling the shares would trigger. DAFgiving360, formerly Schwab Charitable, said it received more nontraded pre-IPO shares and private-business interests in the fiscal year ended 30 June than in any previous year, and it has seen unprecedented numbers of new DAFs opened and funded this year. The seven co-founders of Anthropic have pledged to donate 80% of their equity to charity, and the company's IPO prospectus outlines a donation-matching program letting employees give equity awards to charity. OpenAI offers to match employee contributions to DAFs through a partnership with the provider Daffy.

Akash Magoon, chief executive of the AI startup Adonis, said that at 30 and unmarried the idea of parking money in a trust for a child he does not have is hard to fathom. A prominent bank invited him and other prospective clients to a New York Knicks game at Madison Square Garden during the NBA semifinals last spring, and although he enjoyed it, a follow-up meeting left him feeling the advisers had not tailored the pitch to his circumstances, including his philanthropic goals. Julia Reed, national director of charitable consulting at DAFgiving360, said the ability to advise on charitable giving is front and center and nonnegotiable, adding that these wealth creators tend to focus on giving back to their communities and seeing results in their lifetime. Shirl Penney, chief executive of Dynasty Financial Partners, said these clients buy into the idea that AI is powerful and can do a lot of good but can also eliminate jobs, and feel an obligation to give back. Dynasty is on an internal list of wealth-management firms provided to Anthropic employees, according to people familiar with the matter.

Magoon, raised in Baltimore by Indian immigrants, aims to give away at least 10% of his wealth in line with the Sikh religion, and after selling his interest in the AI-enabled insurance benefits tool Nayya in 2022 he worked with advisers at Merrill Lynch who helped him set up a DAF. He contributed nearly $200,000 to the fund and used it to pay for a scholarship for five students a year to attend his alma mater, the University of Maryland, and study computer science or economics, with recipients required to be born and raised in Baltimore. He recently renewed the scholarship for another five years and said he wants his adviser to educate him on the different mechanisms for being charitable. Amir Memon, managing partner of OneWell, said advisers there helped three clients pool tens of millions of dollars to create a joint foundation earlier this year, and Haley Schaffer, who founded Waypoint West about a year ago, said old-school private banks pursuing newly wealthy young clients face a disconnect. Charitable consultants say only a handful of major philanthropic gifts have come from AI founders so far, so a flood of donations is not necessarily imminent.

stories.Headline: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh opens a San Francisco Fed conference on AI and productivity
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh will open a conference at the San Francisco Fed on Monday at 9 a.m. Pacific with 15 minutes of remarks. He will then spend most of the morning leading panels with Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison, Stanford economist Nick Bloom, and venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, per the published agenda. The topic is how artificial intelligence, and what the Fed calls superintelligence, will change productivity and jobs. The Fed lifted the upper bound of its target range to 4.00% in September, from 3.75%.

Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter, above the 2% to 3% range considered healthy trend growth. In the week ending November 13, the 10-year Treasury yield rose from 4.86% to 5.15%, and the 30-year reached 5.47%. Data centers could use up to 12% of U.S. electricity demand by 2028, according to Energy Department projections. The independent market monitor for PJM Interconnection, which runs the largest U.S. power grid, concluded that data center load growth is the primary reason for its tight supply and high prices. Inflation-adjusted average hourly earnings were $11.26 in October, a preliminary figure, down from $11.38 a year earlier.

The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index fell to 48.1 in September, a level associated with recessions. Warsh said at Jackson Hole in August that we have come to a hinge point in history and called AI potentially a new factor of production. He asked whether AI would cause a significant, sustained rise in productivity across the economy. He also asked who ends up with the gains: chipmakers, cloud providers, AI developers, other businesses, or consumers. At his October 28 press conference, he said productivity growth is strong and capital investment robust, while noting inflation has run above target for close to six years.

He said capital spending sits at a historically high share of GDP, led by high-tech investment. Warsh has said the task force's findings will inform future policy judgments, not dictate immediate decisions, so Monday is unlikely to bring a rate signal. Unemployment sits at 4.1%, so AI has not caused mass layoffs, and it also has yet to show up in paychecks. Core Personal Consumption Expenditures prices, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, rose 0.3% in September.

If AI raises the economy's speed limit, the Fed can let growth run faster without tightening, and if it doesn't, today's AI building boom starts to look like old-fashioned overheating. If productivity rises fast enough to lower the cost of producing each unit, the Fed could hold or cut rates while growth stays strong. If spending keeps outpacing the efficiency gains, the Fed is dealing with a classic overheating economy, and long-term yields above 5% could then stick. The bond market is pricing in that second scenario, and it is up to AI to prove otherwise.

Warsh was sworn in as Federal Reserve Chair on May 22 under intense pressure from President Donald Trump to lower interest rates. The $31 trillion Treasury market is sending Warsh a signal. The efficiency gains come later, but the construction bills are due now. Two things are worth tracking: whether Warsh presents strong productivity as a reason for patience on rates, and the next reading of core Personal Consumption Expenditures prices.

Cooler readings alongside 3% growth would be the first real evidence of an AI productivity boom. The articles leave open whether AI will bring a rapid productivity miracle or gradual gains, and whether it will make price stability easier or harder to achieve. They also leave open who ends up with the gains from AI. The articles do not say what the conference panels will conclude.

Around 1,000 servers suspected of serving as bases for advanced artificial intelligence-driven cyberattacks have been online since October, a Japanese-led international investigation showed on Nov 14, according to Kyodo News. The probe was carried out by the Japan Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre, known as JPCERT/CC, in cooperation with overseas cybersecurity firms. The investigation found that the servers may have used AI to search for vulnerabilities and to target websites worldwide. Hacking, which previously required time even for those with specialised knowledge, has become easier with the emergence of high-level AI, the reports said.

JPCERT/CC began its investigation in early October and identified AI tools in the discovered servers, and it is tracking 600 to 700 of them. According to the centre, most of the servers hosted AI-powered platforms such as the penetration-testing tool Artex, and they appeared to be searching for system vulnerabilities and attempting to steal configuration files. One server contained traces of a programming support tool created by AI from the US company Anthropic, which suggested that attackers weaponised AI to enhance their hacking capabilities. Some publicly accessible servers contained tools for analysing the internal structure of smartphone applications and programmes for testing system vulnerabilities, and attackers are believed to have analysed apps and attempted unauthorised access through interfaces that exchange information with external systems. Servers hosting the tools can be set up in physical facilities or operated through virtual frameworks, the articles said.

Ken Sajo, an analyst at JPCERT/CC, warned that AI is still in the early stages of being used for cyberattacks and that more sophisticated attacks will increase in the future. The articles did not name any other officials or give further statements from the organisations involved. The reports, published by The Straits Times and The Mainichi on Nov 15, 2026, both credited Kyodo News and carried the same account of the investigation. The articles did not say what happens next beyond the centre's continuing tracking of the servers.

stories.Headline: Rajasthan chief secretary V Srinivas meets UNESCO in Jaipur to discuss a proposed AI ethics course for public officials
stories.Summary:
Rajasthan Chief Secretary V. Srinivas held a meeting with a delegation from UNESCO in Jaipur on November 13 to discuss the implementation of a globally recognised course on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, according to reports dated November 13 and 14. The proposed course, which was designed by UNESCO, is aimed at strengthening the knowledge, skills and competencies of public officials in the effective, ethical and responsible use of AI in governance and public administration. The course seeks to equip government officials with the necessary understanding of emerging AI technologies and their practical applications in governance. It will focus on building institutional capabilities to harness the potential of AI while ensuring that its adoption remains ethical, transparent, accountable, inclusive and aligned with public interest.

The course will also familiarise officials with the opportunities and challenges associated with the use of AI in government functioning, including its role in improving administrative processes, enhancing decision-making and strengthening public service delivery. Emphasis will be placed on developing an understanding of responsible AI practices and ensuring that technological advancements are adopted with due consideration for ethical principles and governance standards. The initiative is aligned with the objectives of the Rajasthan AI/ML Policy 2026, which envisages promoting the adoption of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning across various sectors, including government administration. The collaboration with UNESCO is expected to provide public officials with access to globally recognised expertise and learning resources, enabling them to better understand and apply AI-based solutions in their respective areas of work.

The initiative is expected to strengthen the institutional capacity of the State Government, promote informed and responsible use of emerging technologies and facilitate the integration of AI into governance processes. It will also contribute towards making public administration more efficient, responsive and citizen-centric, while ensuring that technology-driven interventions remain guided by ethical considerations and public welfare. The reports do not say what the Chief Secretary said at the meeting, and they give no further details on who else took part or what was agreed. The articles also do not state what happens next, beyond describing the course as proposed and the collaboration as expected to deliver these benefits.

stories.Headline: Grok forecasts XRP may fall to $0.80 by year-end at 35% odds
stories.Summary:
Grok AI forecast on November 14, 2026, that XRP may fall to $0.80 before the end of 2026, a 17% drop from its current price of $0.96. The forecast was reported by Sam Daodu in articles published by 24/7 Wall St. and finance.yahoo.com. Grok's projected downside target of $0.80 is based on insights from crypto analyst Ali Martinez. The AI assigns a 35% chance that XRP will reach this price before December 31. In the past week, XRP has already decreased by 17.4%, down from roughly $1.16.

XRP is currently trading below its 20-day average of $1.20 and its 50-day average of $1.33. XRP is also 73.7% lower than its all-time high of $3.65. Grok identifies three support levels below the current price, each derived from different analytical tools. The $0.90 level is about 6% beneath the current price and marks the lower edge of a weekly descending channel, intersecting with a rising trendline from the 2020 to 2021 lows. The $0.87 level is approximately 9% below and is tied to the 0.786 Fibonacci retracement level derived from the previous surge from around $0.10 to $3.69.

The $0.84 level is about 12% lower and is the 100-month simple moving average, which Grok considers the lower boundary of a supportive range between $0.84 and $0.90. For Grok's prediction to materialize by year-end, XRP will need to breach all three support levels within approximately six weeks. Grok lays out three possible scenarios for XRP's year-end price, with two suggesting it will finish above $1. The bear scenario gives a December 31 price of $0.82, a 14.5% change from $0.96, with a 30% probability. The base scenario gives $1.05, a 9.5% change, with a 50% probability.

The bull scenario gives $1.40, a 46% change, with a 20% probability. The combined probabilities of the base and bull scenarios indicate a 70% chance that XRP will end 2026 above $1. The bear scenario would require a significant Federal Reserve shock, such as a half-point rate hike on December 9, or a hawkish outlook that would push Bitcoin below $60,000. When Grok made its forecast, Bitcoin was trading around $65,300, meaning an 8% drop to $60,000 is plausible. XRP typically follows Bitcoin's movements.

The model identifies two events that could help avoid the bear scenario: Bitcoin reclaiming and maintaining a price above $75,000 heading into year's end, and a return to net inflows into U.S. spot XRP funds. If XRP reaches $0.80, Grok anticipates it would take about eight weeks to rebound above $1. Grok's most probable year-end price for XRP is $1.05, about 9.5% higher than the current price but still below the 50-day average of $1.33. The model accounts for the oversold RSI near 19, which could signal a bounce, while also considering extreme market fear and ongoing fund outflows that might limit further upward movement. Grok also notes that Bitcoin is trading just under its 200-week average and that interest-rate expectations are shifting.

This prediction is driven by extreme market fear, and the Crypto Fear and Greed Index currently reads 13, indicating panic. Additionally, $1.23 billion in crypto liquidations occurred within a 24-hour period, showing that many leveraged positions were forcibly closed as prices declined. Investor confidence is waning, as shown by $19.1 million in outflows from U.S. spot XRP funds between November 9 and 13. These funds had $1.15 billion in net assets on November 13, down 24.8% from $1.53 billion on October 15. XRP's relative strength index, which measures momentum, is nearing 19, well below the oversold threshold of 30.

Grok's most likely price for XRP on December 31 is $1.05, with a bear case of $0.82 and a bull case of $1.40. The model estimates a 70% likelihood that XRP will close 2026 above $1. If it drops to $0.80, Grok expects about eight weeks to recover above $1 again. The articles leave open how XRP will trade between now and December 31 beyond the three named support levels. The articles also leave open whether the Federal Reserve will deliver the half-point rate hike on December 9 that the bear scenario requires.

stories.Headline: TARSBOT and Aptiv partner to develop and scale industrial embodied AI robots for smart manufacturing
stories.Summary:
TARSBOT and Aptiv signed an agreement to deepen their strategic collaboration on embodied AI. This event took place on November 16, 2026, in the city of Shanghai. The signing occurred during the 9th China International Import Expo, which is known as the CIIE. Both companies intend to advance the development of industrial robots for real production environments. This partnership focuses on integrating advanced computing with robotic systems for smart manufacturing.

Aptiv expects to deploy 100 TARSBOT A-Series industrial robots by the end of 2026. These robots cover 8 manufacturing process categories and 33 application scenarios, including flexible assembly and production management. The companies plan to achieve mass production in 2026 using Aptiv high-performance computing platforms. A larger project targets a fleet of 1,000 units with support from the Jiading District Government. The first batch of robots is already operating at an Aptiv smart factory site.

The two companies are responsible for validating applications in real industrial environments to improve their technology. They stated that production insights will support the iterative development of the AI World Engine. This AWE system serves as the general-purpose foundation model for TARSBOT embodied AI robots. The partners aim to combine end-to-end AI capabilities with established engineering expertise and rigorous standards. Their goal is to support efficient and reliable deployment of these robots at scale.

Manufacturers worldwide are affected because they face growing demand for intelligent automation and greater supply-chain efficiency. The collaboration aims to demonstrate that scalable deployment can be validated in practical industrial settings. Embodied AI is emerging as an important force for advancing next-generation productivity for these manufacturers. The high-performance computing platforms provide reliable compute for perception, decision-making, and motion control functions. Intelligent power distribution solutions from Aptiv will also be integrated into the TARSBOT robots.

TARSBOT and Aptiv have already been working closely to develop China's first industrial embodied AI robot fleet. The first phase of this project is currently being implemented at an Aptiv production site. This initial work focused on adapting robots to real production processes and specific manufacturing requirements. The signing at the CIIE marks a transition to a more systematic and scaled phase. The companies are utilizing China's rich real-world manufacturing environments to connect robotic systems with applications.

Looking ahead, the partners will build a validated industrial reference for replicating embodied AI across additional scenarios. This effort is intended to create broader opportunities for smart manufacturing on a worldwide scale. They will continue to integrate computing platforms to support stable operation on real production lines. The articles leave open the specific timeline for the full 1,000 unit fleet deployment. They also do not specify which other manufacturing scenarios will be targeted for future expansion.
