stories.Headline: Anthropic develops AI systems about twice as fast as a year ago, METR finds
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is reportedly developing its artificial intelligence systems around twice as quickly as it was a year ago, according to an analysis released Thursday by an independent monitoring group. The Berkeley, California-based nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research reviewed Anthropic's internal data and interviewed staff. Anthropic invited the researchers as it prepares for its Wall Street debut. The findings were released amid debate over the potential for AI models to elude human control with catastrophic consequences. The analysis was reported by Scripps News on November 15, 2026.

METR's assessment was based on about 11 weeks of Anthropic's internal data, from mid-August through late October, as well as employee interviews. METR said it was given "unprecedented access to internal data" on Anthropic's AI research and development process. The group said Anthropic's redactions limited how it could communicate more detailed estimates of acceleration. METR also reviewed a public risk report Anthropic published in August and a private version, and said the public report "overall understates the level of acceleration that was occurring." METR said Anthropic appears to have made as much progress on benchmarks in the past year as between October 2023 and October 2025.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for the AI industry to slow its work so safety measures can catch up during the research group's assessment period. In a Sept. 12 essay, he urged the AI world to "slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models." Co-founder Sam McCandlish said in a lengthy post on X Thursday that many of METR's conclusions match his own, writing that "AI is speeding up our research, but it's hard to say exactly how much." McCandlish, also Anthropic's chief architect, said the company plans to release a report with its own analysis of the speed of AI progress within Anthropic in the coming weeks. He said sharing "exactly what is driving the speedup isn't the right thing to do" because it is "commercially sensitive" and "risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster."

METR said it believed much of the reason for the faster development is the help of AI itself, and Anthropic has said its Claude chatbot increasingly helps the company develop newer versions of itself. METR said it could confidently rule out the growth of computing power used in training AI models as the reason for the acceleration. The researchers said there were no "bottlenecks" such as restrictions on computing power or data holding back Anthropic's AI progress. METR said Anthropic researchers described significant "signs of life" implying AI could soon make highly significant and fully autonomous contributions to model training.

The San Francisco-based company is planning to go public later this month in what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever. METR has conducted evaluations on model capabilities for Anthropic, OpenAI and other labs for years. The nonprofit is funded through donations and does not accept compensation for its work, but AI companies it has partnered with have provided access and tokens. The findings are significant because details about the technology and its risks have been provided primarily by AI companies, which have been encouraged by President Donald Trump's administration to police themselves on matters of safety.

Amodei's September essay said AI advances have been driven primarily by recursive self-improvement, which he defined as "AI's growing ability to build the next generation of AI." In that essay, Amodei championed external evaluators embedded within leading AI labs and highlighted METR as an appropriate third-party evaluator. McCandlish said the work with METR began "well before and is separate from the embedded third-party evaluators that are part of our commitment to pacing the frontier." He added that "it's a good illustration of why we think evaluators are a good idea."

McCandlish acknowledged the redactions make it harder for others to "check METR's work," and said the company continues to weigh the pros and cons. METR said it could be overstating its findings because the acceleration might be limited to "well-specified tasks" that can be graded automatically or with a language model. METR said there were some internal disagreements and uncertainty among its team, but the group said it believed the company's rate of improvement had doubled. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said at the time that he also supported the idea of independent evaluators with employee-like access.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA, SK Telecom and Rebellions sign sovereign AI infrastructure agreement in Seoul
stories.Summary:
On November 9, 2026, at NVIDIA AI Day Seoul at the COEX convention centre in Gangnam District, Seoul, NVIDIA, SK Telecom and Rebellions signed a strategic memorandum of understanding to build sovereign AI infrastructure. Rebellions Chief Executive Officer Sunghyun Park, SK Telecom Chief Technology Officer Chung Suk-geun, Ashish Karandikar, Vice President of NVIDIA’s NVLink Fusion division, and SK Telecom President and CEO Jung Jai-hun attended. The initiative is backed by South Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT under Deputy Prime Minister and Minister Bae Kyung-hoon. Rebellions will connect its next-generation Rebel R200 neural processing units to NVIDIA’s computing platform via the NVIDIA NVLink Fusion interconnect. Rebellions will develop rack-scale inference systems based on the NVIDIA MGX modular server architecture, while SK Telecom will deploy and validate the hardware across its domestic AI data centres.

SK Telecom plans to pair the heterogeneous systems with its proprietary foundation models, including A.X K2, and public-facing services under the government’s ‘AI for All’ project. The partners target commercial deployment of the integrated Rebel R200 systems in 2028. NVIDIA GPUs execute the compute-heavy prefill stage, while Rebellions’ Rebel R200 NPUs run the decode stage. NVLink Fusion is a scale-up interconnect allowing custom third-party ASICs and XPUs to communicate directly with NVIDIA GPUs and CPUs at NVLink bandwidth within a server rack. MGX provides standardized rack footprints, liquid cooling paths, and power distribution compatible with Open Compute Project standards, giving Rebellions access to established original design manufacturer supply chains.

Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA, said sovereign AI gives nations the power to turn their language, culture and expertise into intelligence. Sunghyun Park, cofounder and CEO of Rebellions, said the announcement marks a turning point, opening a new chapter for sovereign AI by connecting Korea’s AI silicon and models with global systems technology. Jung Jai-hun, President and CEO of SK Telecom, said linking SKT’s AI data centers, proprietary AI models including A.X K2, and public-facing AI services developed under the ‘AI for All’ project will strengthen full-stack sovereign AI competitiveness. Bae Kyung-hoon, South Korea Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Science and ICT, said the collaboration enables Korean-developed NPUs to enter the computing infrastructure market alongside NVIDIA through NVLink Fusion. Bae said the government will actively support this collaboration to deliver tangible results.

The disaggregated GPU-NPU model directly impacts academic high-performance computing centres, national laboratories, and university research computing divisions. Academic facilities face strict power and cooling ceilings, and running monolithic GPU clusters for conversational models wastes energy on memory-bound decoding loops. Offloading token generation to energy-optimized NPUs advances institutional goals for sustainable HPC by reducing power consumption per token while maintaining low inference latency. For AI systems researchers, NVLink Fusion offers an accessible environment for investigating heterogeneous memory hierarchies, KV-cache transfers, and mixed-precision execution without proprietary interconnect barriers. As research funding agencies increasingly demand environmental audits, calculating a rigorous compute FLOPs estimate alongside token-per-watt throughput will be vital for grant compliance.

Sovereign AI infrastructure allows universities to safeguard sensitive research assets, including clinical health records, genomic datasets, and proprietary patent disclosures. Serving models on domestic sovereign clouds complies with strict data protection mandates and aligns with broader national data infrastructure standards. Researchers deploying split architectures must record firmware and runtime configurations carefully to guarantee a reproducible AI experiment across heterogeneous clusters. The tripartite alliance follows SK Telecom’s June 2026 agreement with NVIDIA to construct gigawatt-scale AI factories in South Korea using NVIDIA’s DSX modular architecture, with an initial facility planned for 2027. Founded in 2020, Rebellions previously developed the Atom NPU and its flagship Rebel R100, which featured a chiplet architecture using fifth-generation high-bandwidth memory.

The consortium has outlined a four-stage roadmap toward production readiness. In 2026, 2027, Rebellions and NVIDIA will finalize the Rebel R200 physical design and validate NVLink Fusion signaling inside prototype NVIDIA MGX chassis. In 2027, SK Telecom will deploy prototype MGX systems within its domestic AI data centres to evaluate power efficiency, thermal stability, and performance on A.X K2 models. In 2028, commercial deployment of Rebel R200 rack systems will begin in SK Telecom data centres, supporting public services under ‘AI for All’ and offering compute to universities and enterprises. Following domestic validation, the consortium plans to market the MGX sovereign AI infrastructure package to global telecom operators and sovereign cloud providers.

stories.Headline: Microsoft opens a digital innovation center in Kuwait with the government to scale trusted AI adoption
stories.Summary:
Microsoft announced on 15 November 2026 the opening of the Microsoft Digital Innovation Center (MDIC) in Kuwait, established through a partnership between Microsoft and the State of Kuwait government. The center is designed to connect trusted technology, government priorities, customer challenges and the local innovation ecosystem in one collaborative environment. Government entities, customers, startups, developers and students will be able to experience Microsoft's AI, cloud, cybersecurity and digital capabilities firsthand there. They can also explore relevant use cases, build skills and identify pathways from ideas to implementation, according to the announcement.

The MDIC is meant to support Kuwait as it moves from AI experimentation toward trusted adoption at scale, with a growing focus on practical outcomes, national capability and long-term competitiveness. Developing national talent will be central to its mission, with pathways for citizens, government employees, students, developers and startups to build practical AI skills. Hands-on experiences will include workshops, demonstrations, open-house sessions, developer engagement and student-focused programming. The opening is described as the latest example of Microsoft's long-term commitment to Kuwait and its support for the country's digital transformation under New Kuwait Vision 2035.

Omar Saud Abdulaziz Al-Omar, Kuwait's Minister of State for Communications and Information Technology, said the center represents an important step toward a knowledge-based, AI-powered economy. He said stronger collaboration between government, technology leaders and national talent creates the environment needed to turn AI's potential into tangible outcomes for institutions, the economy and people. Naim Yazbeck, President of Microsoft Middle East and Africa, said Kuwait has a clear ambition to use AI as a driver of economic growth, better public services and new opportunities. He said the center is about helping turn that ambition into action and helping organizations move beyond experimenting with AI to delivering meaningful impact at scale.

Alaeddine Karim, General Manager at Microsoft, said the center reflects the company's long-term commitment to Kuwait and that its focus is not technology for technology's sake. He said the aim is to work alongside government, businesses and the ecosystem to solve real challenges, build local capabilities and translate AI into meaningful outcomes. He said Microsoft wants the MDIC to be where ideas move into action and where organizations can confidently take the next step in their AI journey. The announcement did not give a specific opening date beyond 15 November 2026, nor did it name further next steps.

stories.Headline: Peter Ward says profitability traps stop managed service providers adopting AI
stories.Summary:
Peter Ward, managing director of Dijital Team, told ARN that many managed service providers are caught in profitability traps such as underpriced agreements, hidden delivery costs and expanding service obligations, which limit their ability to experiment and adopt AI. He said industry data shows the average net profit for providers is 6 per cent, and that 25 per cent of MSPs are financially underwater and not making any money at all. Ward said service gross margin is the biggest driver in the MSP space, and that getting it right means everything flows through to the bottom line. He added that operating expenses in any IT business are fairly constant, so providers need to get the costs of tooling, labour and delivery right.

Ward said profitability is a key lever because the more profitable a business is, the more it can invest and grow, and that profit is needed to experiment. He said many organisations have moved from break fix to managed services and felt the impact of cloud, and now need to re-engineer and reskill to succeed in AI, which is very hard without a profitable business. He also said that for every extra $1 an MSP puts on its bottom line, it means $5 extra when the business is sold, which matters amid significant merger and acquisition volumes in the market. Ward's insights came from Dijital Team's conversations with thousands of MSPs at events and conferences, and he launched his book The IT Sales Playbook over 12 months ago.

Ward said many MSPs followed the processes in that book and built their ability to acquire new customers, which led him to write The MSP Profitability Playbook to help organisations turn back into profitability. The book includes diagnostic tools, practical worksheets, an owner scorecard and a structured approach to implementing changes over a 90-day period. He said that if all the boats in the harbour can be lifted, the tide rises together and that helps create a great outcome for everybody. In May, Dijital Team launched its Better Business Pathway enablement program, developed by customer enablement manager Diana Drury, which focuses on five operational challenges: service, finance, people, sales and go-to-market operations. Drury said at the time that the MSP and technology service provider market needed guidance along those five pathways, and that one of the biggest pain points she has heard is the unspoken struggle to figure out all of the shiny stuff and how to get it into a business and make it better.

Articles.Title: Profitability traps holding MSPs back from experimentation and AI

stories.Headline: Mohammed Bin Rashid School of Government launches fourth AI ethics cohort with IEEE
stories.Summary:
The Mohammed Bin Rashid School of Government launched its fourth executive education cohort recently. This programme focuses on artificial intelligence ethics in the age of agentic AI. The school collaborated with the IEEE Standards Association and its own research centre. Registration is now open for professionals to join this pioneering training initiative. The course will take place from 23 to 26 November 2026.

The training occurs at the MBRSG premises located in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. It prepares students for the IEEE CertifAIEd certification as an AI Ethics Professional. The curriculum covers accountability, transparency, privacy, and algorithmic bias through four days of training. A specialized workshop is scheduled for 20 November 2026 during Dubai Future Week. The programme supports a UAE goal to deploy agentic AI across 50% of government sectors.

Executive President Dr. Ali bin Sebaa Al Marri is responsible for the school. He stated that expanding agentic AI adoption requires governance frameworks that keep pace with technology. He noted that enhancing public sector talent ensures these technologies are deployed responsibly. Al Marri said building capacity to navigate transformations is a central pillar of the mission. He believes these efforts align with the Annual Government Challenge launched by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid.

The programme targets government leaders, policymakers, and strategic planners from public and private sectors. It also affects governance, risk, and compliance officers and specialists in data and digital transformation. These professionals will learn to evaluate autonomous systems against international standards to identify risks. Participants will use ethical frameworks to support the safe deployment of these intelligent systems. The training helps them integrate ethical considerations when designing agentic AI within their organizations.

The school aims to strengthen national capabilities in AI governance within the public sector. This mission drives public policy development and aligns executive education with current technological shifts. The programme uses the globally recognized IEEE CertifAIEd standard for evaluating autonomous system ethics. It includes practical case studies on implementing generative and agentic AI within the UAE. These efforts reinforce governance practices rooted in accountability, transparency, and privacy protection.

Participants will receive a completion certificate from the school after finishing the four days. They may then pursue the IEEE CertifAIEd certification by fulfilling professional experience criteria. Candidates must also pass an IEEE accredited examination to become certified AI Ethics Professionals. The articles do not state the total cost of the registration for the cohort. They also leave open the specific number of professionals who will enroll in the programme.

stories.Headline: Han Won-seok admits using AI to cheat on state exams and turns himself in to Seoul police
stories.Summary:
Han Won-seok, aged 34, admitted to using artificial intelligence to cheat on a state exam. He confessed via a video on his attorney Lee Don-ho's YouTube channel on Sunday. The man cheated on the Certified Tax Accountant examination after publicizing his performance online. He turned himself in to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency following public suspicion. This is the first known case of a successful state exam candidate admitting AI cheating.

Han used a micro-camera to send photos of questions to AI and viewed answers on a smartphone. He scored 159 out of 160 on the first-stage test, including a perfect tax law score. The average tax law score for other examinees was 30.18 out of 100. He also admitted to using the same equipment during the Certified Public Accountant examination. The Suneung exam for 550,000 students is scheduled for this coming Thursday.

Ha Joon-kyung, a policy chief at Cheong Wa Dae, said agencies must prevent AI cheating. He stated that authorities should use all possible methods available at the current technology level. He also requested that test management not create unnecessary anxiety for students using medical equipment. The presidential office said it is paying special attention to the case of Han. HRD Korea said it would file a complaint against Han for obstruction of official duties.

The Democratic Party of Korea said those responsible must be held accountable according to the law. People Power Party spokesperson Choi Bo-yoon criticized the government for failing to develop technology-based solutions. He noted that radio-frequency detectors failed to find AI glasses during a mock HRD Korea test. Online commentators are calling for scrutiny of other tests due to unusually high scores this year. One candidate achieved the first perfect score in the 19-year history of the Legal Education Eligibility Test.

The tax accountant exam is difficult and often requires years of full-time study to pass. Critics noticed Han's study materials showed little wear and contained a misspelling of a key term. Han previously claimed his high scores were due to good fortune and his study methods. HRD Korea had previously reviewed his first-stage grading on Friday and found no irregularities. Camera footage from the examination room did not show Han wearing any suspected AI glasses.

Cheong Wa Dae will deploy personnel to detect AI cheating and strengthen training for proctors. The government will look into suspicious cases in state qualification exams to see if AI was used. HRD Korea will consult with the Finance Ministry and the National Tax Service on follow-up measures. Police have assigned the case to a metropolitan investigation unit following the confession of Han. The articles leave open whether previous examination results will be scrutinized or overturned.

Articles.Title: AI cheating case raises scrutiny over test administration ahead of Suneung

stories.headline_source: AI cheating case raises scrutiny over test administration ahead of Suneung

stories.Headline: AI cameras detect nearly 19,000 potential driving offences in a two week West Midlands trial
stories.Summary:
An artificial intelligence trial uncovered nearly 19,000 potential driving offences during a two week period. The trial took place in March and used AI powered cameras to detect dangerous road behaviours. One image showed a driver drinking from a bottle of wine while another driver inhaled from balloons. Cameras also captured drivers holding mobile phones and people failing to wear their seatbelts. One shocking image showed a front seat passenger holding an unrestrained small child on their lap.

Cameras were installed outside Ladywood fire station in Birmingham and Fallings Park in Wolverhampton. Ladywood saw 11,045 potential seatbelt offences and 1,163 potential mobile phone offences. Fallings Park recorded 6,030 potential seatbelt offences and 757 potential mobile phone offences. The West Midlands Combined Authority funded the trial with the police and fire service. No enforcement was planned as a result of this specific two week AI camera trial.

Road Safety Commissioner Mat MacDonald said the findings highlighted a huge problem with regional driving behaviours. He stated that the results pointed to a widespread culture of potentially lethal behaviours behind the wheel. MacDonald, an NHS doctor, said he was not surprised by the high number of mobile phone users. He noted that it is almost impossible to walk a street without seeing someone dialling and driving. He expressed hope that this technology could eventually be rolled out more widely in the region.

Police and crime commissioner Simon Foster said the trial findings were deeply concerning for the authorities. Dr Christophe Bastien of Coventry University said the technology offers an objective way to understand motorist behaviour. He noted that risky behaviour remains more common than many people think based on these results. Bastien said AI systems are not perfect and should support rather than replace existing police enforcement. The trial affected drivers in Birmingham and Wolverhampton who were captured by the AI sensors.

Road safety data from 2025 linked unfastened seatbelts to 133 deaths on roads in the UK. The same 2025 data showed that mobile phone use was linked to 32 deaths across the country. Mat MacDonald was appointed as the new road safety commissioner in January 2025. He previously served as the chairman of the campaign group known as Better Streets for Birmingham. The AI cameras were trained to recognise specific patterns like drivers using their mobile phones.

The trial was stopped earlier than planned because of the high number of detected road offences. Officials are now talking about the resourcing needed to make this technology viable on the roads. MacDonald said the ultimate goal is for the number of camera activations to reach zero. Foster is evaluating the results to see how AI can be used for future police enforcement. The articles leave open whether the technology will be officially adopted for permanent road enforcement.

Articles.Title: Driver drinking from wine bottle among shocking images captured by AI cameras

stories.Headline: Startup Fortune advises teams to version AI agent prompts in Git and tag every release
stories.Summary:
On 15 November 2026, Startup Fortune published a guide on versioning prompts for AI agents before a bad edit reaches production. The guide says prompts, tool descriptions, few-shot examples and the model name all change agent behavior, so all of them belong in Git. It says a release file names the live prompt version, and a rollback means editing a single line. It says the first version takes about two hours. It says nothing crashes when a prompt edit breaks an agent, which just gets quietly worse at something nobody was watching.

The guide says to keep the system prompt, tool descriptions and exact model ID in a Git repo and tag every release. It says to have the app read a small release pointer so a rollback is a one-line change, not a redeploy. It says to build an eval set of 20 to 30 real cases from your own logs and run each case at least three times. It says to block any prompt change that fails a must-pass case or drops the overall pass rate against production. It says to stamp the prompt version on every trace, and after any revert add the failing conversation to the eval set.

The guide says xAI said an unauthorized change had been made to the system prompt of its response bot, and that it would start publishing its system prompts on GitHub so people could see every edit. It says the fix xAI chose is one you can copy today. It says the prompt often sits in a dashboard text box, a Notion page or a string buried in a Python file, and someone tweaks it on a Tuesday because one customer complained. It says tool descriptions are the sneakiest, and rewording "look up an order" to "look up an order or refund" makes the agent call that tool for refund questions it used to hand to a human. It says to pin a dated model snapshot where your provider offers one, not a moving alias.

The guide says Microsoft 365 Copilot was hit by EchoLeak, tracked as CVE-2025-32711, through a crafted email its victim never opened. It says teams can limit the damage with narrow credentials, per-task tool lists, domain allowlists and human approval for irreversible actions. It says Langfuse's prompt management lets you attach labels to prompt versions, and your code fetches whichever version carries the "production" label. It says LangSmith keeps commit hashes for prompts and lets you pull by tag. It says a solo founder with one or two agents doesn't need either, because a Git repo and a release file will do.

The guide says in May 2025 xAI's Grok began answering unrelated questions on X with remarks about South Africa. It says Air Canada was ordered to pay about C$812 in February 2024 after its chatbot invented a refund policy. It says OpenAI began rolling back a GPT-4o update on April 29, 2025, after the model turned noticeably flattering, and later published a post on what its testing had missed. It says Promptfoo, an open-source tool, is built for this, describing prompts, test cases and assertions in a YAML file and running it from the command line. It says thirty cases at three runs each is about a hundred calls, a modest bill on most models.

The guide says to send the new version to a slice of traffic first, say 10 percent of conversations, or run it in shadow mode where it answers but the customer still sees the old reply. It says to run a rollback drill once, on a quiet afternoon, pushing a deliberately bad version to staging, flipping it back and timing it. It says to look at the eval set monthly, adding cases from new failures and dropping ones about features you've removed. It says not to change the prompt and the model in the same release, and to treat a model upgrade as its own versioned change. It says not to share one prompt across several agents, and to give each agent its own folder and its own tags.

Articles.Title: How to Version Prompts for AI Agents Before a Bad Edit Hits Production

stories.headline_source: How to Version Prompts for AI Agents Before a Bad Edit Hits Production

stories.Headline: European leaders discuss AI risks to elections at Dublin summit
stories.Summary:
European governments are concerned that states or organised actors could use artificial intelligence to spread misleading content and manipulate public opinion, even to influence election results, according to a report by Filip Polo in Politis. Cyprus' 2028 presidential election is not outside the scope of these concerns over foreign interference and electoral manipulation through artificial intelligence, the report said. Fabricated videos, images and audio recordings that appear authentic can be mass-distributed to mislead voters and shape public opinion. Officials argue the risks go beyond false news, since an organised campaign can damage candidates' credibility, confuse voters and set the election agenda. The issue was discussed with particular emphasis at the informal European Council summit in Dublin on 13 November, where European leaders held a dedicated discussion on artificial intelligence for the first time.

President Nikos Christodoulides told the summit that the malicious use of technology to influence elections threatens all EU countries and that prevention must be in place before interference occurs. Speaking on the sidelines in Dublin, he referred to recent incidents involving schools and to election developments in Romania and other countries, saying the threat concerns the whole European Union. Asked whether Cyprus is also at risk, he said that once such phenomena are recorded in other member states, all countries are vulnerable. He noted that 2027 will be a year of elections across Europe, making it more important for citizens to be informed and for governments to adopt preventive measures. He said authorities should not simply analyse malicious actions after they occur but should have a framework in place so such actions cannot take place.

At EU level, efforts are under way to introduce specific measures to prevent and counter disinformation and electoral manipulation, and these initiatives are expected to apply to Cyprus as well. Leaders also discussed Europe's position in the global race for artificial intelligence, noting a strong research base and dynamic start-ups but heavy dependence on non-European providers for advanced models, computing power, microchips and cloud infrastructure. Arthur Mensch, co-founder and chief executive of France's Mistral AI, presented the prospects for a stronger European ecosystem, and Geoffrey Hinton, awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2024, highlighted the broader challenges of the technology's development. On 10 November, the Council of Ministers approved Cyprus' first National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, with a horizon extending to 2032, aiming to make the country a trusted artificial intelligence hub in the Eastern Mediterranean. Christodoulides said the technology sector contributes around 15% of Cyprus' GDP and announced a visit to the United States at the end of November to attract companies and encourage the return of Cypriot professionals working abroad.

stories.Headline: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander corrects reporter who cites false AI stat and warns against trusting AI
stories.Summary:
On Friday, the Oklahoma City Thunder lost 113-112 to the Los Angeles Clippers at Intuit Dome in an NBA Cup game, their third straight defeat, despite Shai Gilgeous-Alexander scoring 40 points. During the postgame press conference, a Los Angeles reporter asked Gilgeous-Alexander a question built on a statistic about his first-half assists that the reporter had taken from an AI-based search engine. Gilgeous-Alexander, the reigning back-to-back NBA MVP, corrected the reporter by saying the figure was a false stat. After Gilgeous-Alexander gave a routine answer about his efficient 40 points, the reporter admitted in a joking way that the incorrect stat had come from AI. The reporter then quipped, "Gotcha, don't trust AI," and Gilgeous-Alexander replied as he walked off the podium that people should definitely not do it.

The exchange changed nothing about the result, which saw the Clippers score the final seven points to escape with the one-point win, and Gilgeous-Alexander missed a shot at the buzzer. The loss was Oklahoma City's third in a row and dropped the Thunder in the NBA Cup, while Gilgeous-Alexander's 40 points came in a losing effort. The articles give no further numbers, dates or names beyond the 113-112 score, the 40 points, the two MVP awards and the Intuit Dome setting. Coverage of the moment spread through HoopsHype, ClutchPoints, Awful Announcing, Thunder Wire and other outlets, with headlines calling Gilgeous-Alexander the NBA's preeminent Anti-AI King. The articles do not say whether the reporter or his outlet faced any discipline, correction or policy change after the exchange.

The reporter is responsible for the incorrect statistic, having relied on AI search results without cross-checking the information, as Awful Announcing noted most people hardly do. Gilgeous-Alexander said the stat was false and, when the reporter joked about not trusting AI, told him not to do it and definitely not to do it. The articles do not name the reporter or identify his outlet beyond describing him as an LA reporter. The Thunder star's response drew praise online, with fans saying they love when players put media in their place and calling him the man. The articles do not quote the reporter beyond the few words of the quip.

The context is a difficult stretch for Oklahoma City, which the articles describe as a growing injury crisis and a depleted roster, with fans noting half the team is out. Gilgeous-Alexander has admitted the Thunder are maybe having their toughest stretch ever, and coverage says coach Mark Daigneault cannot ask him to become everyone as supporting players must step up. The articles do not say what happens next for the reporter or his outlet, and they give no follow-up beyond the exchange itself. Oklahoma City's next game and any response from the team or the reporter are not covered in the articles provided.

stories.Headline: Avanade finds New Zealand firms face pressure to accelerate AI adoption but struggle to prove financial returns
stories.Summary:
New Zealand organisations are under growing pressure to accelerate their adoption of artificial intelligence, but most are struggling to show a financial return on those investments, according to new research from Avanade, a Microsoft specialist. The Build Beyond Limits: AI Reality report was based on a survey of 3,600 business decision-makers across 11 markets, including Australia and New Zealand, and it found a widening gap between how organisations see their AI maturity and how far they have actually changed their operations around the technology. Globally, 77 per cent of organisations described themselves as established, advanced or AI-first in their AI journey, and 72 per cent said they were confident their teams were using AI effectively. However, only 18 per cent said they had fundamentally reshaped the way teams operate around AI, and in Australia and New Zealand 84 per cent said they had not fundamentally reshaped how they work with what AI makes possible, including new ways of working, products, services or business models.

The research found that 88 per cent of respondents in Australia and New Zealand said their organisation needs to accelerate AI transformation urgently, even though 68 per cent reported that AI investments have yet to generate financial returns that justify the expenditure. Only 43 per cent said they use business value and return-on-investment metrics to assess AI progress, while 66 per cent had not formally calculated AI's financial return and had it reviewed by finance leaders or senior management. Budget pressures are also emerging, with 26 per cent of organisations in the two countries citing limited funding or pressure to demonstrate ROI quickly as a major barrier to becoming an AI leader. Just 23 per cent reported transformational improvement in what employees could achieve, and the same proportion reported such improvement in operational efficiency and business cost reduction, while 39 per cent said they believe colleagues are using AI in ways compliance teams would not approve of, above the global average of 32 per cent.

Doug Robinson, chief executive of Avanade Australia and New Zealand, said the high adoption rate was a positive sign, telling Reseller News that most clients said they were going great until asked about return on investment, when two-thirds said no. He described a move from hobby AI to enterprise AI, saying people have used the technology first and then brought it to corporates, and that a lot of shadow AI is developing in organisations before they realise it can interrogate corporate data as well as their large language models, which is where the return starts coming. Robinson said the 16 per cent who have already materially changed their business is the number to watch, and he expects it to grow from 16 to 32 to 60 per cent as AI becomes enterprise ready, with ROI following. He said New Zealand organisations are not short on AI ambition but are short on evidence, and that you cannot accelerate adoption responsibly if you cannot say what your AI investment is returning, which most currently cannot.

stories.Headline: President Ramaphosa leads South African delegation to Silicon Valley to study AI ecosystem
stories.Summary:
President Cyril Ramaphosa arrived in California on Saturday, 14 November 2026, for a working visit to Silicon Valley, leading a high-level, multi-stakeholder South African delegation to gain insights into the global artificial intelligence ecosystem and inform South Africa's approach to the development, adoption and application of AI. The delegation comprises representatives from government, academia, business, research institutions, technical experts and university students, reflecting the country's commitment to an inclusive, collaborative and multi-stakeholder approach to harnessing the opportunities presented by AI. The programme includes engagements with leading technology companies, investors, researchers, academics and AI experts, as well as technology demonstrations and knowledge exchanges, exploring frontier AI, robotics, data infrastructure, cloud computing, digital innovation and the practical application of AI across various sectors. A key component is engagements with leading academic institutions on the implications of AI for technology, security, the economy, business and the labour market, as well as emerging developments in robotics and technological research.

The programme also features the South Africa AI Opportunity gathering under the theme Building the African AI Economy: Infrastructure, Investment and Innovation, bringing together South African and international stakeholders to explore how South Africa can position itself as a competitive AI hub on the African continent. Discussions focus on AI infrastructure, data centres, computing capacity, energy requirements, investment opportunities and the growth of a competitive start-up ecosystem, while other areas include the application of AI in government and industry, law enforcement and public safety, AI safety and security, governance, skills development and the future of work. The delegation also engages with technology and infrastructure companies to gain insights into emerging technologies, investment trends and developments shaping the global AI ecosystem, seeking to identify opportunities for investment, knowledge exchange, skills development and the strengthening of South Africa's technological capabilities. The visit provides an opportunity to learn from countries and institutions at the forefront of AI development, understand the associated risks and challenges, and consider how South Africa can develop an enabling policy, regulatory and skills environment to support responsible AI adoption.

The President is accompanied by the Ministers of Finance; International Relations and Cooperation; Science, Technology and Innovation; Trade, Industry and Competition; Communications and Digital Technologies; Electricity and Energy; Small Business Development; and the Presidency, as well as South Africa's Ambassador to the United States of America. Media enquiries were directed to Vincent Magwenya, Spokesperson to the President, and the statement was issued by The Presidency in Pretoria. The visit also promotes South Africa as an investment destination, showcases progress in economic reforms, including through Operation Vulindlela, and highlights opportunities for investment in the country's digital economy, research capacity and innovation ecosystem. South Africa seeks to harness the transformative potential of AI while safeguarding digital sovereignty, policy autonomy, data protection and responsible AI governance, ensuring that technological advancement contributes meaningfully to inclusive economic growth and development.

stories.Headline: Jeff and Sandy Teper give NYU Stern $5 million to launch an annual student AI startup challenge
stories.Summary:
Jeff Teper, Microsoft's Executive Vice President for Apps and Agents, and his wife Alexandra "Sandy" Teper have donated $5 million to New York University's Stern School of Business to establish the Teper Innovation Challenge, an annual competition for students. The gift, reported on November 15, 2026, creates a contest designed to help students develop AI-powered startups and solve real-world business problems. The initiative will provide hands-on experiential learning opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students, with more than $100,000 in annual prize funding for winning teams. The competition will formally launch during the spring 2027 semester, featuring separate tracks and awards for undergraduate and graduate students.

Student teams in the Teper Innovation Challenge will develop AI-native solutions to business challenges, giving them opportunities to experiment with emerging technologies and explore entrepreneurial ideas. The annual competition will encourage students to build and test their concepts, evaluate results, and develop practical applications for artificial intelligence. Beyond the competition, the Tepers' contribution will expand access to frontier technology for Stern students and support the thoughtful integration of advanced AI tools into the school's educational experience. Jeff and Sandy Teper both graduated from NYU Stern, with Jeff earning his bachelor's degree in 1986 and Sandy graduating in 1985, and they met while attending the school.

Jeff Teper currently serves as Microsoft's Executive Vice President for Apps and Agents, and he previously launched and grew SharePoint into a billion-dollar business. He has led teams through major technology transitions involving cloud computing and artificial intelligence, and he was among the inaugural industry leaders to join NYU Stern's Tech Board. Over the years, Teper has hosted Stern students at Microsoft in Seattle, sponsored experiential learning projects in New York City, and advised faculty developing one of the first agentic AI courses at a business school. The new challenge expands his involvement with the university by providing students with opportunities to develop practical AI-building skills.

NYU Stern Dean Bharat Anand said the gift will give students opportunities to experiment with emerging technologies and develop entrepreneurial ideas. The university believes advances in AI are making it easier for individuals to transform ideas into tangible products and businesses. The Teper Innovation Challenge is intended to encourage students to explore those opportunities while learning how artificial intelligence is changing business and the economy. Jeff and Sandy Teper said they had an incredible experience at NYU spanning software engineering and business during the personal computer revolution, and that with the even larger artificial intelligence transformation they are thrilled to support Stern students as they explore, collaborate, and create opportunities in this next wave of technology and the economy.

stories.Headline: Jamaica's government signs MOU with investors to explore AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness announced on Sunday that the Government has approved the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding with a group of investors to explore the establishment of artificial intelligence infrastructure in Jamaica. He made the announcement while speaking at the Jamaica Labour Party's Special Delegates Conference at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James on November 15, 2026. Holness did not provide details on the MOU during his address to the party conference. The Prime Minister said Jamaica is to explore the establishment of AI facilities as part of efforts by the Government to maximise economic opportunities and position Jamaicans to participate in the industry.

Holness said the Government recognises the revolution being brought about by AI and wants to position Jamaica to benefit from it. He said the goal is for Jamaica to have a footprint and not only be a consumer of the technology, but to be part of the creation of the technology. The Prime Minister said his administration intends to pursue this so that children can have jobs in the new economy that will be created using artificial intelligence. He said the AI task force established by the Government is providing advice on what needs to be done in this regard.

Holness argued that Jamaica cannot be left behind in the global AI thrust, describing the moment as the cusp of another transition and revolution in technology. He said this revolution is going to increase the productivity of mankind far beyond what can even be imagined now. He repeated that Jamaica cannot be left behind again. The Prime Minister did not give a timeline for the exploration or name the investors involved in the MOU.

stories.Headline: Majority of Australians believe AI risks outweigh benefits according to Lowy Institute poll
stories.Summary:
The Lowy Institute commissioned a mini-poll in October 2026 to gauge how Australians feel about artificial intelligence. Research fellow Charles Lyons-Jones reported that public wariness of the technology has become entrenched. Sixty-five percent of respondents believe the risks of AI outweigh the benefits. This figure is unchanged from a previous poll in March 2026. It represents a thirteen point increase from the results recorded in 2024.

The National AI Plan released in December 2025 aims to make Australia a leading destination for data centre investment. The government set expectations in March for developers regarding innovation, jobs, water, energy, and the national interest. Data centre companies raised at least AU$35 billion in 2026, which is 46 percent higher than in 2025. The Productivity Commission estimated that AI could add over AU$116 billion to economic activity over ten years. These figures contrast with a 1.2 percent margin of error for the 3,028 residents surveyed.

The Reserve Bank flagged that AI investment could increase input costs and add to capacity pressures. This bank also cut its productivity forecast for 2026 while data centre construction added to price pressures. The Reserve Bank raised interest rates three times since March 2026 as inflation remained above target. The Lowy Institute noted that government policy may be outpacing public sentiment regarding these technologies. They suggested the government might need to reckon with trade-offs between public sentiment and geostrategic imperatives.

Seventy-six percent of Australians worry that AI will lead to fewer jobs over the next twenty years. This concern is the joint-highest of any country surveyed and exceeds the median of 46 percent. Fifty-two percent of respondents expect AI to widen the gap between rich and poor, second only to South Korea. Only 23 percent are comfortable with businesses using AI from China, while 36 percent trust AI from the United States. These views reflect a general distrust of the two superpowers acting responsibly in the world.

A Pew Research Center survey of 37 countries found Australians are among the most concerned about AI. Six in ten Australians were pessimistic about economic performance over five years in the March poll. This pessimism was higher than during the Covid pandemic or the Global Financial Crisis. China's National Intelligence Law requires developers like Zhipu and DeepSeek to cooperate with state intelligence agencies. Sixty-two percent of people in March viewed cyberattacks from other countries as a critical threat.

The government relies on the alliance with the United States to keep the region's AI future tied to America. Seventy-three percent of Australians in March said this alliance was important to their national security. In the United States, voters in dozens of local ballot measures recently backed limits on data centres. The articles leave open whether public sentiment will swing to support American AI in the future. They do not state if the government will change the National AI Plan.

stories.Headline: South African author Coral Hart publishes nearly 400 AI-assisted romance novels since February 2025
stories.Summary:
Coral Hart, a South African author with around 14 years of experience in publishing, has released nearly 400 books since February 2025, or roughly one book every other day, according to reporting from the Straits Times cited by Futurism. She initially wrote a few dozen romance novels the traditional way before switching to a blend of ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok to generate her prose. Hart uses more than ten pen names to conceal her identity when she actually sells the books. She told Agence France-Presse that ChatGPT is really good at dialogue but terrible at prose, while Claude is terrible at sex drives. Grok, she said, builds the spicy scenes even though it is completely unhinged at other moments.

Dividing her output of 370 total novels by the days since February 1, 2025, gives a rate of one book for every 1.75 days, or about four books per week. Hart said recent advances in large language models mean she can now draft the whole book in one sequence. She has received tens of thousands of hate messages about her process, yet she thinks of herself as something of an ambassador for it despite the infamy. She told AFP that for the last 16 years nobody had asked her what her creative process was.

Hart also said the technology is here and will not be switched off or unplugged because a bunch of authors said so. Hart is the person responsible for the books, and she has defended them as selling well and as the product of a workflow she is happy with. She described herself to AFP as an ambassador for AI-assisted writing, and she brushed aside the criticism from authors who want the tools shut down. The articles do not say what happens next beyond her stated intention to keep going.

Articles.Title: Author Says the Hundreds of Full-Length Romance Novels She Publishes Every Year Are Very High Quality in Spite of AI Usage

stories.headline_source: Author Says the Hundreds of Full-Length Romance Novels She Publishes Every Year Are Very High Quality in Spite of AI Usage

stories.Headline: Career experts advise job seekers to build networking relationships before asking for help
stories.Summary:
Online job applications have become easier to send but harder to get noticed through, because employers increasingly use automated screening tools to evaluate large numbers of applicants, according to the Associated Press. Employment experts say that having inside connections from professional networking can help job seekers stand out when the robots threaten to reject a resume outright. LinkedIn career expert Catherine Fisher said networking is important whether or not someone is searching for a job, and that it is not just a nice-to-have because it sets a person apart and gives an edge. The advice was reported by Newser on November 15, 2026, in an article that also carried an unrelated item about Kalshi dropping Donald Trump Jr.

The experts offered several tips, starting with developing relationships before asking for help. Indeed career strategist Matt Berndt said networking is about relationship-building and that a common mistake is approaching it transactionally, meaning people reach out only when they need something. Instead of asking about job leads straight off, he suggests approaching contacts for specific career information or advice, such as asking about the job market and compensation where a contact works if you are thinking about relocating. Another way to start a conversation is to follow people on social media and comment on their posts.

Nisha Chittal, chief of staff at Vox, said first messages to a hoped-for professional contact should be brief and to the point. If you are inquiring about openings, she advises against asking vaguely about upcoming opportunities that would match your qualifications, and suggests instead asking whether the contact has or knows of openings for a specific position. Chittal also said a quick no to an online application does not necessarily close the door, because a personal recommendation is worth a shot since many recruiters are bombarded with applications and appreciate hearing about promising candidates. She said that generally if you have that kind of referral, someone will give the application a serious look, and that it is a tough environment to be job searching right now, so anything that makes a personal connection helps when there are many hundreds of applicants for a job.

Articles.Title: How to Bust AI Guardrails in Job Hunt: Networking

stories.Headline: Huawei unveils architecture to network one million AI processors into a single supercomputer
stories.Summary:
Huawei detailed its Peerium architecture and UnifiedBus 2.0 interconnect on November 11, 2026. This system allows the company to network one million AI processors into one supercomputer. Technical reporting and analyses by Live Science confirmed these operational mechanisms. The architecture was first unveiled conceptually at the Huawei Connect 2026 summit. Engineering briefings reported by SDxCentral on November 4, 2026, expanded on these details.

The system uses Nested Bulk Synchronous Parallel, Unified Memory Addressing, and Decentralized Peer-to-Peer Interconnects. UnifiedBus 2.0 consolidates ten protocol specifications, achieving 800 GB/s bandwidth and 2 microsecond latency. Hardware includes LinkBlade optical backplanes, LinkDevice ports at 1.6 Tb/s, and UBG Switches with 1,024 radix fan-out. The Atlas 950 SuperPoD integrates 8,192 Ascend 950DT accelerators, while Atlas 960 and 960E use Near-Packaged Optics. These components replace 196 km of copper cabling across a 4,096-NPU pod.

Liao Heng, chief scientist for HiSilicon, said the infrastructure is tailored for frontier AI models. He noted that six to seven Chinese laboratories target models with 10 trillion to 40 trillion parameters. Rotating Chairman Eric Xu stated that unifying one million processors is a baseline requirement for efficiency. ICT Business Group CEO Yang Chaobin emphasized opening the UnifiedBus standard to open-source communities. Yang mentioned collaborations with the OpenJiuwen project and the DeepSeek Harness optimization framework.

Independent semiconductor analysts said that real-world scaling efficiency faces severe fault-tolerance and thermal overhead challenges. They noted that mean time between failures drops dramatically in million-chip installations. University high-performance computing centers and national laboratories are affected by these architectural shifts. Compliance managers must track evolving restrictions governing hardware exports and cross-border computational collaborations. Research institutions face a bifurcation between the Nvidia CUDA ecosystem and Huawei's Ascend/CANN stack.

Huawei adopted an interconnect-centric philosophy to counteract United States Department of Commerce export controls. These restrictions limit advanced foundry nodes under 7nm and cutting-edge high-bandwidth memory modules. Domestic foundries face yield and density limits compared to global leaders like TSMC. Huawei used CloudMatrix 384 to pack five times the accelerator density per rack than Western equivalents. This approach diverges from Ultra Ethernet Consortium, PCIe Gen 6, and Compute Express Link specifications.

An Atlas 950 SuperCluster with 256,000 computing cards is currently operational in Chinese test environments. Commercial shipments of modular Atlas 950 SuperPoD systems will begin by early 2027. Engineering teams are now testing the next-generation Atlas 960 and Atlas 960E architectures. The articles leave open how the system will handle 100-trillion-parameter models projected for 2030. They do not specify the exact date for the full million-chip deployment.

stories.Headline: AI Dosing Tool Standardizes IVF Drug Starts Without Changing Birth Rates
stories.Summary:
A pilot real-world study at Peking University Third Hospital tested an algorithmic dosing tool called POvaStim in assisted reproduction. Researchers led the single-centre observational study, published in Frontiers in Endocrinology, on women undergoing in vitro fertilization or intracytoplasmic sperm injection. The team matched 119 women whose clinicians used POvaStim against 119 propensity-score-matched controls managed by conventional experience-based judgement. The controls were managed under gonadotropin-releasing hormone antagonist protocols. The study enrolled consecutive women between August 3 and December 31, 2022, at the Center for Reproductive Medicine at Peking University Third Hospital.

The tool standardizes initial gonadotropin dosing during ovarian stimulation, and the study included standard antagonist cycles using follitropin alfa, follitropin beta, or urofollitropin. Mild stimulation regimens were excluded, and matching drew on a candidate pool of 4,877 conventionally dosed cycles. Matching used one-to-one nearest-neighbour propensity score matching without replacement within a caliper of 0.2 standard deviations of the logit score. Matching was based on body weight, gonadotropin preparation, and an ovarian reserve score derived from age and anti-Müllerian hormone. Twenty-six algorithmic cycles could not be matched within tolerance and were excluded, and post-matching standardized mean differences stayed below 0.08.

The authors emphasized that the investigation compared two composite care strategies, clinicians supported by POvaStim versus clinicians relying on unassisted clinical judgement. They cautioned that the absence of hospital admissions does not prove equivalent safety, because elevated ovarian response in the algorithmic arm was actively mitigated through increased elective embryo cryopreservation. They noted that conditioning on fresh transfer introduces post-treatment selection bias, as transfer decisions depend directly on ovarian response. They stated that separating artificial intelligence effects from physician attributes will require future factorial or cluster-randomized trials comparing clinicians across explicit experience strata with and without decision support. They also noted study limitations including the single-centre design, unmeasured outpatient hyperstimulation, and restriction of algorithmic assistance strictly to starting doses while omitting POvaStim's dynamic inhibin B adjustment module.

Under conventional practice, physician-selected doses yielded a standard deviation of 69.8 international units per day and an interquartile range of 87.5 international units per day. Clinicians using POvaStim recorded a standard deviation of 44.7 international units per day and an interquartile range of 50.0 international units per day, a 43 percent narrower interquartile range and a 2.43-fold lower variance confirmed by an F test yielding a p-value of 2×10⁻⁶. After adjustment, residual standard deviation was 16.2 international units per day with algorithmic guidance versus 49.4 international units per day in controls. Median cumulative gonadotropin consumption reached 2,175 international units in the algorithmic group compared to 1,950 international units in controls, alongside a higher median daily dose of 225.0 versus 195.0 international units per day. When researchers retrospectively applied POvaStim to control patients, the model recommended near-identical mean starting doses of 216.36 versus 216.42 international units per day.

Protocol instructions required algorithmic clinicians to round calculated doses upward to commercial pen increments, placing administered doses above recommendations in 94.1 percent of cycles and driving 38 percent of the gap. Control clinicians unknowingly prescribed below model recommendations in 69.7 percent of cycles, accounting for 62 percent of the 27.4 international units per day difference. Cumulative live birth occurred in 49.6 percent (59 of 119) of the algorithmic group versus 50.4 percent (60 of 119) of controls, an absolute risk difference of -0.8 percent with a 95 percent confidence interval of -13.5 to +11.9 percent (p = 0.897). Cumulative clinical pregnancy occurred in 56.3 percent (67 of 119) of algorithmic patients versus 63.9 percent (76 of 119) of controls, a risk difference of -7.6 percent with a 95 percent confidence interval of -20.0 to +4.8 percent (p = 0.234).

Median retrieved oocyte counts were 14 in the algorithmic group compared to 13 in controls, while median normally fertilised two-pronuclear embryos were 7 versus 6 and good-quality embryos were 5 versus 5. Fertilisation rate per inseminated oocyte was significantly lower in the algorithmic cohort, with a median of 0.58 compared to 0.69 among controls (p = 0.010). Conventional insemination was used in 68.1 percent of algorithmic cycles compared to 52.9 percent of controls, and among conventionally inseminated cycles rescue intracytoplasmic sperm injection was required in 8.6 percent (7 of 81) of algorithmic cases versus none (0 of 63) in controls. No patient in either arm developed severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome requiring hospital admission.

Elective whole-embryo cryopreservation for non-genetic indications occurred in 46.2 percent (55 of 119) of the algorithmic arm versus 34.5 percent (41 of 119) of controls (p = 0.064), with hyperstimulation prevention the primary motivation in 83.6 percent and 78.0 percent of freezes respectively. Retrieval of at least 15 oocytes occurred in 47.9 percent versus 38.7 percent of cycles, while freeze-all procedures for preimplantation genetic testing were more frequent in controls at 13.4 percent versus 1.7 percent. Among women receiving a fresh transfer, clinical pregnancy was significantly lower in the algorithmic group at 51.9 percent versus 72.4 percent in controls (interaction p = 0.048), though this lost significance after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.100). No interaction appeared for live birth.

Primary clinical outcomes were assessed after two years of longitudinal tracking extending to a fixed data-lock date of December 31, 2024. In the primary analysis, treating 16 patients without an embryo transfer as non-events, sensitivity analyses evaluating complete cases, adjusted models, and matched-pair structures yielded consistent results. Because the study was not designed as an equivalence or non-inferiority trial, the wide confidence intervals cannot rule out clinically important outcome differences. Total fertilisation failure occurred in one algorithmic cycle and zero control cycles, while cycles without blastocysts did not differ significantly between arms.

Articles.Title: AI Dosing Tool Standardizes IVF Drug Starts Without Changing Birth Rates

stories.Headline: Collin Hansen warns pastors that AI cannot replace scripture and prayer
stories.Summary:
Collin Hansen, editor-in-chief of The Gospel Coalition website, raised the question of whether pastors can trust artificial intelligence in an essay titled "Why AI Will Write Your Next Sermon," and he discussed the issue further in a telephone interview with columnist Terry Mattingly, whose piece was published on November 15, 2026. Hansen said AI had become a nearly daily part of his life over the past couple of years, as it has for many others, and that he has found help with home repairs, diet and exercise plans, meal preparation, trip planning, personal health assessments, and even baseball swing and pitching advice for his son. The deeper question, he said, is how AI will handle the problems pastors face as the faithful wrestle with parenting and careers, marriage and morality, sin and forgiveness, questions that affect work in the pulpit as well as private hospital conversations and prayers. Hansen said the software professionals who build these platforms struggle to separate factual questions from those focusing on ethics and morality, and he warned that pastors who seek AI help with sermons need to understand that. He asked whether AI means people do not have to study and remember the Bible as much, and said that doing so turns what used to be Bible study into some kind of science that can be chopped into pieces and processed, perhaps with another AI program.

He said the computer system does not recognize what happens in counseling, evangelism, apologetics and deathbed ministry, where there is a difference between asking AI to supply the answers you need and your own personal, intimate familiarity with the scriptures, and he said those distinctions will be lost on people who think these tools will make things more efficient. Religious leaders and pastors need to pause and ask what they are being efficient for, what they are trying to accomplish, what they will say to these people and how they will pray for them if they are not formed in the scriptures and in prayer themselves, he said. The article cited the third annual "State of AI in the Church" survey, conducted by AIforChurchLeaders.com, ChurchTechToday.com and others, which found that AI has moved from novelty to normal, with 93.5% of church leaders actively engaging with or exploring AI in their ministries. Two years ago 13% totally opposed the use of artificial intelligence in church work, and now only 2.4% say that, while 43% of church leaders reported using AI every day, double the 2024 rate, and 78% used AI weekly or more, up from 43% in 2024. The survey also found that 64% of participants used AI when doing sermon research or writing, and that a mere 9% of churches have a formal policy on using AI agents.

A Lifeway Research survey of Protestant pastors yielded more modest numbers, with less than 50% saying they are using AI, only 10% describing themselves as regular users and 32% experimenting with it, while 18% were intentionally avoiding AI and 20% claimed they were simply ignoring AI trends; 62% of pastors in that survey worry that users are not being honest about how they were using AI in ministry, and 55% affirmed that God has always shared His Word through people and AI isn't a person. Hansen said everyone knows AI programs can help users who are not gifted writers or speakers appear more literate, but it is also clear that these platforms struggle to separate questions about facts and those about doctrine. He said AI knows better how to answer Bible questions than a seminarian or an average pastor, but that a person will not get good, ethical, trusted advice from AI unless they ask for it. If pastors ask about the Ten Commandments, he said, they will hear the mean ethical take of an AI engineer in Silicon Valley in the year 2026, a human pretending to be an objective computer, and they will not hear the God who thundered on Mount Sinai.

Articles.Title: MATTINGLY: Can pastors trust AI?
