stories.Headline: Non-sonographers use AI guidance to capture quality heart scans in rural mobile unit
stories.Summary:
Healthcare personnel without prior clinical ultrasound training acquired high-quality echocardiographic scans in a mobile examination unit serving rural United States communities, aided by real-time artificial intelligence guidance and centralized expert evaluation. The independent preliminary research was scheduled for presentation at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 through November 9 in Chicago under Abstract Poster MDP2290. The work was conducted as part of the broader Risk Underlying Rural Areas Longitudinal cohort study, known as the RURAL study. The investigation evaluated whether non-specialists could reliably capture research-standard cardiovascular images directly within geographically isolated localities. The approach seeks to bring advanced diagnostic tools closer to rural residents while expanding rural participation in cardiovascular clinical research.

The observational study cohort comprised 4,597 volunteer adult participants spanning ages 25 to 65, with a cohort average age of 48 years. Women represented 67 percent of the enrolled population, and at enrollment 63 percent self-identified as white adults, 35 percent as Black adults, and 2 percent as Hispanic adults. Mobile operations ran within a dedicated mobile health unit that visited ten rural counties across Alabama, Kentucky, Louisiana, and Mississippi between November 2021 and June 2026. Each participant completed examinations within a single 3.5-hour scheduled appointment inside the vehicle. The echocardiograms were performed by fourteen non-sonographer healthcare workers, including nurses, nursing assistants, and computed tomography technologists with no prior background in cardiac ultrasound, who completed a standardized two-hour training curriculum divided into four structured modules, with three operators requiring retraining following preliminary reviews.

Principal investigator Dr. Gerald S. Bloomfield and the Duke Clinical Research Institute established a centralized quality assurance framework to address the gaps. Study author Dr. Sanjana Ravi, an internal medicine and pediatrics resident at Duke University School of Medicine in Durham, North Carolina, said echocardiography is among the most valuable research tools in cardiovascular science yet delivering it in rural communities has proven difficult. Dr. Ravi noted the conventional framework requires an expert sonographer in a hospital or specialized imaging center, resources severely limited across rural areas. She also cited a pronounced scarcity of cardiovascular imaging specialists available to review recorded images and a shortage of local clinicians who can communicate diagnostic results to patients. Dr. Ravi expressed surprise at how quickly nurses and computed tomography technologists adapted to the technology.

Dr. Lee H. Schwamm, a member of the American Heart Association volunteer committee on AI and Technology Innovation who was not involved in the study, observed that one in five Americans lives in a rural area, severely restricting access to critical diagnostic testing and specialty medical care. Dr. Schwamm, senior vice president and chief digital health officer of Yale New Haven Health System and associate dean of digital strategy and transformation at Yale School of Medicine, noted that if confirmed through subsequent trials, this paradigm could serve as a valuable operational blueprint for other diagnostic specialties. The study set a performance target requiring scans within a fifteen-minute operational window. Of the 4,597 completed heart examinations, 98 percent captured all six standard echocardiographic views mandated by the protocol, and Duke core laboratory experts rated scans adequate more than 99 percent of the time. Diagnostic-quality rates for individual anatomic views ranged between 77 percent and 94 percent, and operators met the 15-minute target in 81 percent of sessions with a median scan duration of 9.5 minutes.

Echocardiography uses high-frequency ultrasound waves to generate dynamic, moving visual representations of cardiac structure and function. According to American Heart Association guidance, physicians order this non-invasive test for heart murmurs, damaged heart valves, or unexplained chest pain, and it is standard practice for congenital heart defects, documented myocardial infarction or stroke, or prior rheumatic fever. The conventional clinical pathway depends on specialized sonographers in hospital departments or dedicated outpatient imaging facilities, which remain scarce throughout rural regions. Experts identified critical results in 133 scans among the 4,597 asymptomatic volunteers, most commonly a left ventricular ejection fraction of less than 50 percent. The study team communicated 99 percent of these critical findings to participants within three days of image acquisition.

The investigators noted the trial design included no direct head-to-head comparison between images from AI-guided non-sonographers and experienced professional sonographers scanning the same patients. Reproducibility of structural measurements was evaluated internally within the Duke core laboratory and not independently validated against external imaging core laboratories, and inter-operator variability was not systematically evaluated. The protocol relied on a single commercial brand of artificial intelligence software and a single academic core laboratory, so alternative platforms or facilities will require separate verification and validation studies. Findings from this rural cohort may not extrapolate to non-rural populations or settings lacking support from an experienced academic core laboratory, and the investigation did not examine whether returning critical results influenced subsequent clinical care or long-term cardiovascular health outcomes. Because the study was presented as a scientific meeting abstract, the findings have not undergone formal peer review and are preliminary until publication in a peer-reviewed journal, and the American Heart Association notes that abstract conclusions represent solely the views of the study authors and not official association policy.

Articles.Title: AI-Guided Non-Experts Perform Quality Mobile Heart Scans in Preliminary Rural Study

stories.headline_source: AI-Guided Non-Experts Perform Quality Mobile Heart Scans in Preliminary Rural Study

stories.Headline: Psychologist Sebastian Ocklenburg proposes psychological evaluations for AI developers
stories.Summary:
On November 15, 2026, Psychology Today published a personal perspective by Sebastian Ocklenburg, Ph.D., asking whether psychological evaluations are needed for AI developers. Ocklenburg is a professor for research methods in psychology at the Department of Psychology at MSH Medical School in Hamburg, Germany. The article was reviewed by Jessica Schrader. Ocklenburg wrote that AI companies have warned about the risk of AI going rogue and causing harm to humans. He argued that another potential risk may be mentally unstable AI developers purposefully building harmful AI tools.

Ocklenburg cited the American Psychological Association's 2017 guidelines for occupationally mandated psychological evaluations, published on February 24, 2017. He wrote that psychological evaluations are occupationally mandated in some jobs in many states of the U.S., including police officers, people working in prisons, firefighters, people working with the FBI, pilots, air traffic controllers and people working in nuclear power plants. He wrote that in some jobs evaluations may be conducted with people already employed if they show signs of impaired mental health or thinking abilities, including physicians and other healthcare workers. He described the March 24, 2015 crash of a Germanwings passenger plane in the French Alps, in which a pilot with severe mental issues purposefully crashed the plane with 150 people on board, killing all passengers. He wrote that AI developers do not routinely undergo mental health screenings.

Ocklenburg wrote that he believes occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers should be considered. He wrote that professional organizations for psychologists, companies that make hiring and employment decisions in relation to the development of AI tools, and government agencies involved in the regulation of tech companies should consider such evaluations. He wrote that more psychological research is needed into whether severe, untreated mental health conditions in AI developers could lead to the risk of real harm for other human beings. He wrote that occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers could help ensure that only mentally stable people are involved in the development of frontier models with the potential to cause real harm to humans. He wrote that no one knows how likely catastrophic events akin to the Germanwings airplane catastrophe would be in the field of AI development and what impact they would have.

Ocklenburg wrote that over the last few weeks there has been a lot of discussion in the media about the extent to which rogue AI agents may potentially cause harm to humans in the future or even kill all of humanity. He wrote that experts debate whether AI agents turning on humanity is a real risk or not. He wrote that one potentially more likely risk of AI often gets ignored. He wrote that just like a pilot could cause a plane to crash on purpose, an AI developer could purposefully build AI models that lack the necessary checks and balances to prevent them from hurting humans, or even an AI that exists with the purpose to harm humans, for example by performing hacking attacks on critical infrastructure. He wrote that AI does not need to turn rogue by itself to harm humans, because one developer doing so on purpose could lead to massive economic and personal harm.

Ocklenburg wrote that a scenario like this seems more likely to occur in the near future than AI turning rogue by itself, so measures to prevent such an incident are needed. He wrote that mental health conditions like antisocial personality disorder, which has been linked to violating the rights of other people without feelings of guilt, and dark personality traits such as psychopathy mean such a scenario is not entirely unlikely. He wrote that the big AI companies themselves warn about the potential risks of AI. He wrote that the Germanwings incident highlighted how important it is that people who work in high-risk fields and have a responsibility for the survival of others are mentally stable. He wrote that his research focuses on left-handedness and brain asymmetries.

Ocklenburg wrote that he believes occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers should be considered, and the article gives no further steps beyond that recommendation. The article leaves open how likely catastrophic events akin to the Germanwings airplane catastrophe would be in the field of AI development and what impact they would have. The article leaves open whether severe, untreated mental health conditions in AI developers could lead to the risk of real harm for other human beings. The article gives no date for when such evaluations might be introduced or by which body. The article gives no response from AI companies, psychologists' organizations or government agencies to the proposal.

Articles.Title: Are Psychological Evaluations Needed for AI Developers?

stories.Headline: A systematic review finds AI achieves high accuracy in cancer imaging but needs prospective multicenter validation
stories.Summary:
A systematic review of 180 peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 found that artificial intelligence systems, particularly those using deep learning, show consistently high performance in cancer detection and prognostic modeling across imaging modalities and tumor types. The review was published in Discover Artificial Intelligence, volume 6, issue 1, Article 1531, by N. A. R. Mohamed in 2026. The article reporting it appeared on bioengineer.org on November 15, 2026, written by Nathaniel Bowman and sourced to Scienmag. The study selection followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines to identify original research applying artificial intelligence to major oncological imaging tasks. Each investigation was evaluated for methodological quality using the QUADAS-AI framework.

The review covered computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography, mammography, histopathology, dermoscopy and endoscopy. Several high-quality cohorts achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values exceeding 0.90 for cancer detection. In whole-slide histopathology, certain curated datasets enabled models to reach an AUC of 0.99 for identifying metastases. Mammography-based deep learning models for breast cancer screening reported AUC values between 0.89 and 0.96. Lung cancer screening studies using 3D convolutional neural networks trained on over 42,000 CT scans achieved an AUC of 0.94.

The authors emphasize that prospective, multicenter trials are the necessary next step to verify robustness in routine clinical workflows. The review cautions that retrospective validation studies may be susceptible to selection bias and limited demographic diversity. The reviewers identified persistent limitations in reporting standards concerning patient selection, data flow and timing. Approximately 20 percent of studies lacked clear documentation of recruitment methods or exclusion criteria. The authors state that sustained clinical adoption depends on rigorous prospective, multicenter validation, standardized reporting and navigation of regulatory and workflow integration requirements.

The review notes that deployment must occur without increasing the reporting burden on clinicians or introducing workflow complexities. It states that ongoing monitoring of system performance is essential, as models may require periodic updates against evolving scanner technologies and changing clinical protocols. The review identified radiomic signatures as essential tools in modern precision oncology. It notes that federated learning approaches can mitigate privacy and data-sharing constraints by allowing collaborative model training without centralized patient data. The review states that regulatory science frameworks increasingly emphasize structured reporting standards such as CLAIM.

Only 21 percent of the included studies performed external validation using independent datasets. Only 14 percent incorporated multicenter datasets. The review identified a transition from simple classification tasks to complex multimodal and foundation model architectures. Vision transformers and self-supervised pretraining methods have emerged as particularly influential in enhancing representation learning for volumetric and cross-domain data. Benchmark datasets such as BRATS facilitated advancement of U-Net and V-Net architectures, with transformer-based models like UNETR further improving 3D tumor segmentation accuracy.

Future research priorities identified by the review include robust, outcome-based clinical endpoints, federated multicenter validation strategies and continued development of explainability frameworks. The review states that the highest clinical evidence currently supports AI as an adjunctive tool in breast and lung cancer screening, metastatic detection in digital pathology, and classification of dermatologic and endoscopic lesions. It notes that integrating tools into picture archiving and communication systems and electronic health record workflows requires overcoming medico-legal, technical and process-oriented hurdles. The review cites predicting responses to neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy in rectal cancer without excessive manual intervention as highlighting practical utility. The article leaves open how these validation, reporting and integration requirements will be met.

stories.Headline: Researchers develop deep learning model to predict nasopharyngeal carcinoma recurrence risk from biopsy slides
stories.Summary:
Researchers conducted a multicenter retrospective study to forecast nasopharyngeal carcinoma recurrence risk. They used a weakly supervised deep-learning computational pathology framework for this purpose. The study was completed by November 15, 2026, across three Chinese tertiary medical centers. The system analyzes routine hematoxylin and eosin stained biopsy whole-slide images. It stratifies progression-free survival in patients with locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

The study involved 253 patients with stage III to IVA undifferentiated non-keratinizing nasopharyngeal carcinoma from 2012 to 2025. Nanfang Hospital, Jiangsu Cancer Hospital, and Shandong Cancer Hospital and Institute served as the three centers. A training cohort had 149 patients, while internal validation had 52 and external testing had 52. The model used a ResNet-50 convolutional neural network and a binary risk score cutoff of 0.450. Images were digitized at forty times optical magnification with a resolution of 0.25 micrometers per pixel.

The research team developed an attention-based multiple-instance learning model to evaluate biopsy images. They stated that traditional clinicopathological factors and standard tumor-node-metastasis staging provide limited resolution for predictions. The team noted that visual evaluation of biopsies remains inherently qualitative and subjective. They claimed their model extracts robust prognostic signals without requiring laborious manual annotation of tumor margins. This approach allows for individualized risk assessments to determine if patients need treatment intensification.

Clinicians struggle to identify which patients can safely avoid excessive therapy-related toxicities. Patients with locally advanced disease are affected, representing seventy percent of new diagnoses. These individuals often receive induction chemotherapy followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy. Some higher-risk subgroups may also receive adjuvant systemic therapy and immune checkpoint inhibitors. The model helps distinguish between high-risk and low-risk patients to improve these clinical decisions.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is an epithelial malignancy with aggressive local invasion and systemic dissemination. It has the highest global incidence in southern China, East Asia, Southeast Asia, and North Africa. Standard treatment relies on definitive radiotherapy paired with platinum-based chemotherapy. However, treatment responses and recurrence patterns vary widely among patients in identical clinical stages. Conventional pathological examinations cannot systematically parse high-dimensional spatial microenvironmental characteristics across entire slides.

The model achieved a 3-year progression-free survival area under the curve of 0.721 in external testing. It correctly identified sixteen out of seventeen patients who experienced disease progression within three years. The gated attention model outperformed four alternative pipelines, including Vision Transformer and ResNet-50 mean pooling. The articles do not state how this tool will be integrated into daily clinical practice. They leave open whether the model will be tested in other global populations.

stories.Headline: Stanford review finds AI boosts task completion but not durable learning across 52 causal studies
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, Stanford University's SCALE Initiative released an expanded evidence review examining 52 causal studies on artificial intelligence in education. The review found that AI tools frequently enhance real-time task completion and student confidence. It found that durable learning gains remain highly inconsistent. The review cautions university researchers, institutional review boards, and evaluation teams that passive cognitive offloading often undermines conceptual retention compared to structured pedagogical scaffolding. The report is titled The Evidence Base on AI in K-12: A November 2026 Review.

The report was published by the AI Hub for Education within the Stanford Center for Opportunity Policy in Education, the SCALE Initiative. It was authored by Seth Walker, Lily Fesler, JP Martinez Claeys, Chris Agnew, and Susanna Loeb. The synthesis expands a March 2026 baseline of 20 papers by adding 32 newly published causal studies released between October 2025 and June 2026, bringing the total evidence base to 52 rigorous investigations. The Stanford repository enforces strict methodological criteria, including only randomized controlled trials and well-identified quasi-experimental designs. The March 2026 review included zero student-facing causal studies in operational U.S. elementary and secondary schools, while the November update captured the first five domestic K-12 trials, though most research remains concentrated in adult and higher education contexts.

The authors highlighted a notable shift in setting toward the first five domestic K-12 trials. The core finding across the 52 evaluated studies is that educational outcomes diverge sharply based on whether AI provides cognitive scaffolding or enables cognitive offloading. When tools deliver Socratic guidance, clarify misunderstandings, and structure problem-solving steps, students achieve modest gains in conceptual mastery comparable to human tutoring. When students use models to offload intellectual tasks such as generating complete essays, code, or mathematics solutions, durable learning declines. In-session task completion accelerates, but unassisted post-tests reveal marked performance deficits compared with peers using traditional learning materials.

In multiple randomized experiments, students using AI reported elevated confidence, decreased anxiety, and perceived mastery, yet their objective exam scores failed to demonstrate measurable academic advantage. Generative fluency often conceals genuine comprehension deficits. Generative platforms reduced teacher preparation time for lesson plans, reading level adaptations, and grading rubrics without compromising curricular quality as assessed by subject-matter experts. Automated diagnostic systems providing feedback to novice tutors improved pedagogical technique and pupil outcomes. In classrooms where teachers relied heavily on automated instructional prompts, spontaneous teacher-student interaction declined, occasionally dampening student motivation.

Across evaluated platforms, students rarely logged the dosage required for measurable academic impact unless usage was mandatorily integrated into structured class periods. Following the rollout of foundational models in 2023, vendors widely promoted AI as an automated one-on-one tutor capable of rapid learning acceleration. Commercial claims overwhelmingly rested on correlational customer surveys lacking control groups. The Stanford SCALE Initiative established the AI Hub for Education Research Repository in early 2025. Independent coverage by Education Week underscored the tension between school district technology procurement and the finding that homework offloading undermines student retention.

Analysts emphasized that districts have deployed significant funding without established pedagogical guardrails governing home use. Reporting in Chalkbeat highlighted equity concerns, noting that under-resourced schools often lack the staffing needed to guide student AI interactions effectively. Researchers quoted across both outlets echoed Susanna Loeb's conclusion that AI is not a uniform intervention, but a medium whose efficacy is defined by how educators structure student engagement. Educational AI studies must incorporate delayed, unassisted post-tests to distinguish real skill retention from transient tool assistance. Investigators should formalize outcome measures and analytical models in advance by completing a study protocol preregistration, preventing selective reporting in a field facing commercial pressure.

Institutional review boards must adjust evaluation standards, and protocol assessments in classroom environments must evaluate cognitive risks and control-group fairness alongside privacy protections when students are exposed to task-offloading software. Experimental reproducibility requires detailed sharing of prompt templates, model versions, and interaction logs. Researchers should support their findings with an open data availability statement and maintain compliance via institutional responsible conduct of research training programs. The Stanford AI Hub for Education will continue updating its repository monthly.

stories.Headline: SIU School of Medicine and Springfield Memorial Hospital fund a $2 million AI device to teach patient communication
stories.Summary:
Springfield Memorial Hospital and its Foundation joined the Southern Illinois University School of Medicine in putting $1 million each toward a new artificial intelligence and Extended Reality device for the Ed Curtis Laboratory for Innovation in Medical Education, and the technology was shown to the public and to Memorial Health Foundation donors last week. The device is meant to help students and doctors learn how to talk with patients and their families about the care those patients are receiving. The story was reported by Capitol City Now on November 15, 2026, with Elston Lacy and Will Stevenson credited on the piece. The laboratory’s team has been working on this kind of research since early 2025. According to an October news release from the SIU School of Medicine, the ECLIME team has launched more than 20 research projects focused on improving educational outcomes since early 2025.

That work explores how AI can deliver timely feedback, strengthen communication skills and support learning while preserving the essential role of faculty mentorship. The new device combines artificial intelligence with what the school calls extended reality, and its features are expected to be valuable both to students and to working professionals. The investment by the foundation and the school totals $2 million. Pam Hulten, Director of the Springfield Memorial Foundation, said on the WTAX Morning Newswatch that the hospital has to do its part to train its workforce, including nurses and everyone within the hospital, and then the extension over with SIU. She said the institution has incredible and brilliant physicians, medical residents and students who are eager to have learning at their fingertips.

Dr. Traves Crabtree, Professor and Chair of the Division of Cardiothoracic Surgery at the SIU School of Medicine, also speaking on WTAX, described a concept in medicine called de-skilling. He said that if medical professionals look to AI for the answers on what a diagnosis is and how to work it up, there is a threat that the learner loses the ability to think about and develop clinical reasoning. He added that the school is not really in that space right now, and that what it is doing is finding opportunities in education where there are important things to teach or train but the resources or time are lacking. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the public and donor showing of the device last week.

stories.Headline: US agencies suspect Alice Huang of spying for China using Nvidia founder Jensen Huang
stories.Summary:
U.S. intelligence agencies suspect Alice Huang of spying for China's Ministry of State Security. She allegedly used a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang to obtain strategic information. This suspected operation came to light in November 2026. The scandal involves the founder of the artificial intelligence processor company Nvidia. Reports from The New York Times and Reuters first detailed the affair.

The suspected spy is Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese businesswoman. She is linked to Megaspeed, a Singapore company that bought advanced processors from Nvidia. Jensen Huang stepped down from his executive leadership role on November 12, 2026. The case involves state-of-the-art semiconductors, which are key strategic assets for the United States. These technologies are currently subject to strict export restrictions.

U.S. agencies believe Alice Huang was recruited to facilitate access for Chinese interests. Nvidia launched an independent investigation to see if its CEO was targeted. The company wants to determine if foreign intelligence operations penetrated its leadership. China has rejected all the accusations regarding this espionage operation. No public evidence proves that trade secrets were stolen or that Jensen Huang knew.

The investigation is significant because of the technological competition between the United States and Beijing. The reports affect the leadership of Nvidia and the diplomatic relations between nations. The New York Times and Reuters are the primary sources of these allegations. The case highlights how intimacy can be used for institutional penetration. It shows how intelligence services approach people with personal access to key figures.

History shows secret services often exploit romantic and sexual relationships to obtain classified documents. Examples include Rahab in Jericho, the dancer Mata Hari, and the Nazi Salon Kitty. The SS and Walter Schellenberg used a Berlin brothel to record foreign diplomats. Markus Wolf used Romeo agents, while Russian and Chinese networks employ similar honey traps. These methods identify personal vulnerabilities to influence political decisions.

Nvidia continues its internal probe to find the extent of the security breach. It remains unclear if Alice Huang successfully transmitted any sensitive technical data. The articles do not state if U.S. officials will file formal charges. They leave open whether other Nvidia executives were targeted by Chinese intelligence. The final results of the independent investigation have not been released.

stories.Headline: Federal Reserve economists find AI data center commitments top $1 trillion while productivity gains stay muted
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, the Federal Reserve Board published working paper FEDS 2026-074, titled Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence, with DOI 10.17016/FEDS.2026.074. Federal Reserve Board economists Nick Carollo, Leland D. Crane, Daniel Garcia Molina, and Joseph Nichols authored the paper. The paper documents that U.S. capital commitments for artificial intelligence data centers have surged past $1 trillion. It also finds that aggregate macroeconomic productivity gains and labor market disruptions remain muted. The paper evaluates how generative AI infrastructure is rippling through national accounts.

Planned domestic data-center construction climbed from roughly $300 billion in 2024 to more than $1 trillion in announced pipelines by 2025. Using the project forecasting methodology from Brandsaas et al. (2025), the authors estimate baseline annual data-center investment will step up from $100 billion in 2024 to over $880 billion by the end of 2027. That exceeds 2.0% of U.S. GDP, with approximately one-third of the outlay funding physical structures. Two-thirds is absorbed by high-tech equipment including GPUs, TPUs, high-density memory, and server cooling systems. The authors calculate an import share of roughly 50% for high-tech compute hardware, with components primarily sourced from East Asian fabrication and packaging corridors.

Carollo and colleagues report that high-bandwidth memory and specialized printed circuit boards saw annualized price increases of nearly 8% through early 2026. This reversed a multi-decade trend of technological price deflation. Surging electricity requirements prompted a sharp rise in power-generation interconnection requests in late 2025. The paper finds generative AI has yielded negligible measurable impact on aggregate U.S. labor productivity and Total Factor Productivity. Econometric decomposition indicates recent post-2023 productivity pickups primarily reflect cyclical supply-chain normalization rather than AI diffusion.

On November 13, 2026, at the UC San Diego Economics Roundtable, Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson delivered a keynote titled New Technology, Old Questions: Productivity Puzzles and the Macroeconomy. Jefferson invoked Robert Solow's famous 1987 paradox that you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics. Jefferson noted that early personal computer investment in the late 1980s required more than a decade of organizational adaptation before aggregate productivity accelerated. Daron Acemoglu (2025) estimates cumulative TFP gains of only 0.7% over the next decade, while Filippucci et al. (2025) reach 0.3 to 0.9 percentage points annually. Jones and Tonetti (2026) and Demirer, Musolff, and Yang (2026) confirm coding agents accelerate syntax generation, but software deployment remains tightly bounded by human review and integration testing.

On November 12 at Yale University, Governor Michael S. Barr presented remarks on American Inequality and the Future of AI, analyzing findings from the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances. Barr warned that because AI infrastructure requires massive capital reserves, financial gains are heavily concentrated among top software firms and high-wealth equity holders. Governor Christopher J. Waller, in his November 10 speech at the Bank of England Watchers Conference on The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism, emphasized labor resilience. Waller noted that aggregate claims, vacancies, and payrolls show no sign of widespread displacement. New York Fed research (Abel et al., 2025) and independent market analysis from TradingView report that only ~10% of workers use AI daily, with firms primarily augmenting existing roles rather than reducing headcounts.

The Federal Reserve's November 13, 2026 Financial Stability Report says equity valuations are partly driven by enthusiasm for super intelligence and details rapid growth in data center debt. The working paper keeps its analysis distinct from the central bank's semi-annual Federal Reserve Financial Stability Report, which focused on debt liquidity and bank credit exposures. Foundation model providers capture ~19% of U.S. software gross output, and broad experimentation contrasts with limited intensive daily integration. NBER research by Alvarez et al. (2026) shows that data centers generate brief construction bursts but minimal long-term local employment. The findings carry operational lessons for university research offices, campus HPC directors, and sponsored programs teams navigating hardware scarcity and escalating compute costs.

stories.Headline: npj Digital Surgery opens AI surgical care collection with 2027 deadline
stories.Summary:
The journal npj Digital Surgery has opened a collection titled Innovation in Digital Surgery: Artificial Intelligence Across the Surgical Care Pathway, with a submission deadline of 12 July 2027, according to the collection page. The collection is edited by Marc D. Succi of Harvard Medical School and Arya S. Rao, also of Harvard Medical School, and it supports research related to SDG3, SDG4 and SDG9. The page says the collection highlights work that identifies unmet clinical needs and implements solutions leading to quantifiable improvements in patient care. It also says the collection confronts the traditional obstacles of translational innovation, including funding, intellectual property, commercialization and venture support.

The collection invites papers on preoperative risk assessment and perioperative decision-making, including studies of how digital and AI systems influence decision support in realistic surgical settings from triage through discharge. It also seeks work on computer vision, including vision-language models applied to laparoscopic, endoscopic and robotic video that can identify anatomy and assess surgical milestones. Natural language processing and generative AI are another focus, covering operative note generation, extracting information from the clinical record and preparing discharge paperwork, with particular interest in data governance, privacy, bias and regulatory considerations. Surgical training is also in scope, including AI-powered simulation, virtual and augmented reality curricula and digital competency assessment, while studies primarily about device or pharmacologic treatments fall outside the collection's scope.

The page says the collection welcomes submissions from all authors and not by invitation only, provided manuscripts fall within the scope of the collection and of the journal. All submissions are subject to the same peer review process and editorial standards as regular npj Digital Surgery articles, including the journal's policy on competing interests. The page says the Guest Editors have no competing interests with the submissions, which they handle through the peer-review process, and that peer review of any submission for which the Guest Editors have competing interests is handled by another Editorial Board Member without competing interests. The collection is not supported by sponsorship, and papers will be published as soon as they are accepted and then collected together and promoted on the collection homepage.

stories.Headline: Minghao Liu and colleagues review explainable AI that unifies formability and performance in additive alloys
stories.Summary:
A review published in Advanced Materials Joining on November 15, 2026 evaluates how explainable artificial intelligence can bridge the divide between defect suppression and mechanical optimization in additive manufacturing. The review was led by Minghao Liu, Wei Xu and colleagues. Laser powder bed fusion melts consecutive powder layers with focused laser beams. Localized energy deposition and rapid cooling rates of 10⁴ to 10⁶ K/s create severe thermal gradients. Traditional data-driven machine learning models correlate raw process inputs directly with bulk properties.

The review categorizes physical interpretability across four knowledge domains: physical metallurgy principles, cross-scale numerical information, microstructural image data and causal physical mechanisms. Physical metallurgy-guided support vector machines use thermodynamic driving forces and equilibrium phase fractions to constrain process schemes. First-principles calculations supply formation enthalpies and cohesive energies for high-entropy alloy designs. Calculation of Phase Diagrams methods supply non-equilibrium phase fractions, solidification intervals and transformation temperatures. Finite element modeling and molecular dynamics provide thermal stress distributions and solidification cooling rates.

The authors state that contemporary studies remain predominantly task-specific and single-objective, focusing either on defect mitigation or on mechanical strength. They emphasize that both formability and mechanical properties arise from the identical composition-process-thermal history pathway. They propose a unified multi-objective optimization framework structured around shared thermal history descriptors including local thermal gradient G, solidification front velocity R, cooling rate and remelting depth. They say coupling physics-constrained models with standardized multimodal databases and causal discovery algorithms will allow researchers to determine whether formability and performance objectives are driven by cooperative or competing metallurgical mechanisms. They add that establishing standardized repositories pairing raw process signals, three-dimensional defect geometries and mechanical performance measurements will be vital for training reliable multi-objective surrogate architectures.

Steels and titanium alloys represent the performance-first paradigm, where components achieve near-full density across broad processing windows but suffer anisotropic microstructures, cyclic thermal reheating and non-equilibrium phase evolution. In LPBF steels, statistical models paired with physical metallurgy descriptors mapped linear energy inputs to density and nanohardness with classification accuracies reaching 92.4%. Combining extreme gradient boosting with SHAP interpretability and NSGA-III multi-objective optimization enabled rapid design of ultra-high-strength stainless compositions. For Ti-6Al-4V, incorporating threshold stress intensity factors and Kitagawa-Takahashi envelope constraints into neural network loss functions improved fatigue strength prediction coefficients of determination from 0.70 to 0.82 and reduced mean absolute errors from 40.5 MPa to 29.9 MPa across 143 experimental samples. Combining three-dimensional micro-computed tomography defect volumes with deep neural networks identified maximum defect circumscribed sphere diameter and sphericity as primary determinants of fatigue life, attaining a test coefficient of determination of 0.946.

Aluminum alloys and nickel-based superalloys represent the formability-first paradigm, where hot tearing, liquation cracking, high laser reflectivity and wide freezing intervals dominate processing challenges. High-strength aluminum alloys including 2xxx and 7xxx series feature freezing ranges exceeding 100 K. Graph attention networks integrated with physical metallurgy knowledge graphs designed an additive aluminum alloy achieving 99.98% relative density without substrate preheating, with ultimate tensile strength of 454 MPa and elongation of 9.5%. In nickel-based superalloys, dual-parameter criteria evaluating heat resistance and deformation resistance mapped cracking susceptibility by quantifying elemental microsegregation. Trace additions of boron, zirconium and hafnium severely aggravate cracking by depressing the solidus temperature.

Incorporating causal transfer learning allowed researchers to predict fatigue strength in low-alloy steels from tensile data with as few as thirty training sets, achieving a verified 50 MPa fatigue strength increase. Physics-informed neural networks incorporate conservation of mass, momentum and energy to simulate molten-pool geometry and Marangoni convection. Phase-field dynamics modeled via the Allen-Cahn and Cahn-Hilliard equations describe dendritic growth and solute segregation during solidification. Mechanics-based fatigue formulations incorporate Basquin's law and stress-dependent variance rules. Currently available datasets are fragmented, typically reporting either defect characteristics or mechanical test metrics but rarely paired measurements from identical specimen batches.

Explainable methodologies have resolved biomechanical compromises in biomedical titanium alloys, with physical metallurgy descriptors including molybdenum equivalent, valence electron concentration ratio and d-electron parameters introduced into gradient-boosted decision trees trained on seventy-five compositions. Embedding these parameters as constraints within genetic algorithms enabled design of quaternary and quinary titanium-molybdenum-niobium-zirconium-tin alloys, both achieving stable single-phase beta structures with measured elastic moduli of 40 GPa and 37 GPa against predicted targets of 43 GPa and 39 GPa. Physics-informed neural network models incorporating Weibull distributions, finite element frequency mapping and Monte Carlo estimation established ultra-high-cycle fatigue predictions for Ti-6Al-4V, boosting crack propagation resistance by 20 to 30 percent while cutting development cycles by more than half. Quantum machine learning alongside high-throughput computing designed the lightweight Al85Cu5Li4Mg3Zn3 entropy alloy, exploiting rapid cooling to convert brittle intermetallics into hierarchical cellular eutectic structures and dense planar faults. Combining light gradient boosting with genetic algorithms introduced nanoscale titanium diboride particles into the aluminum matrix, promoting ultrafine equiaxed grains that suppress hot tearing and decoupling grain-boundary, Orowan, dislocation and solid-solution strengthening contributions.

stories.Headline: Nvidia probes CEO Jensen Huang over relationship with suspected Chinese intelligence asset
stories.Summary:
Nvidia launched an independent internal probe into CEO Jensen Huang on November 8, 2026, after he admitted to marital infidelity. The investigation follows allegations that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset for China's Ministry of State Security. Intelligence officials believe Alice Huang may have attempted to use the relationship to obtain sensitive information about advanced semiconductors and U.S. administration developments. While Huang apologized to shareholders and colleagues in a memo, it remains unproven if any classified secrets were leaked or if espionage occurred.

The board of directors formed a special committee of independent directors and external legal counsel to review potential risks to national security. This process occurs as House Committee Chairmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford requested a closed-door briefing with Huang on November 18. Additionally, Senator Chris Coons announced a congressional investigation on November 8 to examine the company's security protocols. The situation caused Madison Huang, a senior director at Nvidia, to cancel her November 8 visit to Seoul for Nvidia AI Day 2026.

The board stated they have no reason to believe company secrets were compromised and expressed continued confidence in the leadership of Jensen Huang. In his internal memo, Huang admitted he was not faithful to his wife and stated there is no excuse for his actions. Regarding broader security, Nvidia claims that meetings with Asian cloud customers involve only ordinary business information rather than trade secrets. The company is now requiring some Southeast Asian customers to use the Fleet Intelligence system to track the location of AI accelerators.

This controversy coincides with reports that Chinese firms Neumatrix and MagInfra may have bypassed export restrictions to obtain H200 chips. Allegations suggest Neumatrix is linked to the sanctioned private equity firm Wise Road, while MagInfra shares ties with the sanctioned server company Inspur. These findings have intensified government scrutiny of Nvidia's customer screening and the U.S. approval process for chip exports. The company continues to operate while facing increased political pressure and potential constraints on its global business strategy.

stories.Headline: Nvidia board removes CEO Jensen Huang following reports of extramarital affairs
stories.Summary:
The board of Nvidia prepared to remove CEO Jensen Huang around November 11, 2026, following several serious personal allegations. Huang eventually resigned as president, CEO, and board member after reports of affairs with two different women emerged. One woman is suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence, while the other is a senior executive at Nvidia. These events created the most serious leadership crisis in the history of the world's largest AI semiconductor company. The board considered meeting as early as November 11 to determine the future of the company's founder.

The board's decision followed allegations involving Alice Huang of Megaspeed in Singapore and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare. Powell joined the company in 2008 and reported directly to Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 with two engineers. Huang owns about 3.6 percent of the company, which lacks a dual-class share structure for enhanced founder voting rights. The board will now adopt a full chairmanship structure, and Colette Kress will serve as the interim CEO. Kress will also keep her current roles as the company's chief financial officer and executive vice president.

Independent directors hired attorney Joon Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to lead an independent investigation. Huang wrote a letter to employees on November 8 admitting he was unfaithful to his wife and apologizing. He initially expressed his intention to remain in his position before the allegations regarding Kimberly Powell became public knowledge. When the New York Times contacted him about the reports, Huang told the reporter not to reach out directly. Neither Kimberly Powell nor the company issued an official response to the reports regarding the alleged extramarital relationship.

Investors fear a leadership vacuum because Huang personally managed over 60 direct reports and led all major company decisions. The FBI and U.S. intelligence officials are investigating whether Huang shared national security secrets with Alice Huang of Megaspeed. China's Foreign Ministry denied the spy allegations and told the United States to stop fabricating narratives for technology blockades. Market reactions were sharp, with shares dropping 8.1 percent to 159.59 dollars, erasing 340 billion dollars in market value. Analysts like Stacy Rasgon noted that the transition would be difficult because Huang and Nvidia were essentially one.

Huang transformed Nvidia from a gaming chip maker into an AI leader, introducing the GeForce 256 GPU in 1999. In 2006, he developed CUDA, and he later secured early support from Sega and cooperation with TSMC founder Morris Chang. He built strong ties with Samsung Chairman Lee Jae-yong, SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, and firms like Microsoft and Google. Huang also persuaded President Donald Trump to ease export restrictions and committed 90 billion dollars to various partnership deals. Despite these successes, the New York Times reported that Huang had rejected internal succession planning for several years.

The board is now searching for a permanent successor to replace the founder who led the company for 33 years. Potential candidates mentioned by media include Apple's Johny Srouji, Arm CEO Rene Haas, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, and Lori Huang. Other unlikely candidates include AMD CEO Lisa Su and Intel's Lip-Bu Tan, while the U.S. Congress tightens export controls. The investigation will now examine internal controls and compliance with the company's code of conduct regarding the reported affairs. It remains open whether the leadership change will ripple across the broader AI ecosystem and affect global capital flows.

stories.Headline: Nvidia board investigates CEO Jensen Huang over conduct and potential foreign intelligence ties
stories.Summary:
Nvidia shares dropped as much as 8.79 percent to 170.24 dollars on November 9 after reports emerged regarding Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang. The company founder admitted to being unfaithful to his wife in a recent internal memo, while the board of directors launched an independent investigation into his conduct. This probe examines whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation involving Alice Huang, a former senior executive at a semiconductor firm. U.S. intelligence authorities suspect that Alice Huang may have been recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security to approach the executive.

The current scrutiny follows a 40 page report published on May 13 by Culper Research which alleged that Nvidia evaded U.S. export restrictions. Culper Research estimated that over 20 percent of computing revenue for fiscal 2026 was linked to China through a Singaporean firm called Megaspeed. The report claimed Megaspeed received funding from Alibaba and saw its debt and equity grow from 33 million dollars in 2023 to 3 billion dollars by late 2024. It also noted that 2.9 billion dollars in refundable deposits of unclear origin were transferred to subsidiaries like the Malaysian company Speedmatrix.

The board of directors hired outside legal experts to lead the investigation but stated they have no reason to believe company secrets were compromised. They expressed continued confidence in Jensen Huang, although the executive previously described his interactions with Alice Huang as routine business contacts. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives warned that Huang might have to step down depending on the investigation results, which could create a leadership vacuum. Such a vacancy might disrupt product launches and investment decisions for the broader artificial intelligence ecosystem, including partners like OpenAI.

The controversy may lead to tighter regulatory scrutiny of Nvidia's business in China despite previous requests from Huang for the U.S. government to ease export restrictions. Since the Culper Research report was released, Nvidia shares have fallen about 20 percent while the S&P 500 has gained approximately 2 percent. The Chinese government has denied all allegations of espionage, and no specific spying activity has been confirmed by officials. Analysts believe that prolonged uncertainty regarding the future of the chief executive could threaten the overall stability of the company's management.

stories.Headline: Serval offers $30,000 signing bonuses to hire 100 AI-savvy engineers
stories.Summary:
A United States artificial intelligence startup named Serval offered large signing bonuses to attract skilled engineers during the fall of 2026. The company sought to hire 100 engineers who could apply artificial intelligence to various business lines and actual services. This recruitment drive occurred while large scale restructuring and layoffs were sweeping through the broader United States technology industry. The Wall Street Journal reported these details on November 14, 2026, regarding the firm's aggressive new compensation strategy.

New hires at Serval receive a signing bonus of 30,000 dollars and about 10,000 dollars in vacation travel benefits. Existing employees who refer new talent to the company also receive a bonus of 30,000 dollars for their help. Carlos Lesama, the head of talent acquisition at Serval, stated that the firm needs software engineers and AI adoption specialists. He noted that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are currently absorbing a large share of the available talent pool.

Mohit Bende, the chief executive of Karat, said the value of engineers with solid fundamentals who use AI efficiently is rising. Jill Hunstart, chief executive of Hunstart and Company in San Francisco, said firms prefer candidates with hands on experience over training. Ruth Thomas of Payscale stated that market value is rising before companies can establish adequate pay benchmarks for these AI skills. These professionals are affected by a bidding war that runs counter to general hiring patterns in the technology sector.

Payscale data shows median wage growth in the United States technology sector reached 6.4 percent in the third quarter of 2026. Other sectors grew slower, with government at 4.6 percent, architecture and design at 4.3 percent, and business services at 4.1 percent. Manufacturing saw growth of 4.0 percent, while DevOps engineers experienced the steepest wage growth at a rate of 16.5 percent. Customer support managers saw 9.5 percent increases, while security architects, software developers, and application engineers all saw growth around 5 percent.

Valentino Stoll, a 42 year old engineer from New Jersey, left a 260,000 dollar job in July for a smaller startup. Stoll received a raise and a promotion within months because of his experience applying artificial intelligence to various company products. Levels.fyi found that median base pay for new software engineers hired recently exceeded the pay of incumbents at the same level. This pay gap was about 4 percent at entry levels and widened to 17 percent for the most senior levels.

Competition for talent is expected to intensify as AI adoption continues to outpace the efforts of companies to overhaul pay structures. Recruiters now prioritize how effectively candidates have used AI tools in actual work rather than whether they completed training courses. The articles leave open how long these high signing bonuses will remain necessary to attract the desired caliber of talent. They do not specify if other startups will match the specific 30,000 dollar bonus offered by Serval.

TechGig is holding an exclusive live online masterclass called AI Upskilling: Build with AI on 1 December 2026, from 12:00 PM to 1:30 PM, led by Barnam Bora, who is Head of Developer Advocacy for Microsoft 365 & Copilot. The 90-minute session is aimed at software developers, engineers, AI enthusiasts, product managers, technology professionals, engineering managers, students and early-career professionals who want to move beyond AI fundamentals. According to the announcement, participants will explore practical AI skills including AI tool selection, environment setup, automation and building AI-powered solutions through hands-on experimentation. The article says the question is no longer whether AI will change the future of work but whether professionals have the skills to be part of that transformation. Participants will also receive a TechGig Certificate of Participation upon successful completion of the session.

The masterclass is built around six key learning areas, which are an AI-first mindset, AI tool selection, environment setup, AI-powered applications, automation and practical experimentation. Organisers say the session will help participants develop an AI-first mindset, explore modern AI tools and understand how to turn ideas into practical AI-powered solutions. It also aims to show how individuals can establish an effective environment for AI experimentation without getting caught up in unnecessary technical complexity. The stated objective is to help participants transition from being passive users of AI to confident professionals who can experiment, innovate and build with it. The article says curiosity, willingness to experiment and an interest in learning are all that is needed, and no AI expertise is required to get started.

Barnam Bora leads the session, and the article says his experience at Microsoft and Amazon spanning over 15 years provides a strong foundation for understanding technology adoption, developer ecosystems and platform innovation. It describes him as bringing valuable industry insights into how professionals can embrace emerging technologies and translate them into practical applications. The article says his extensive experience across technology, cloud platforms and AI innovation will help participants approach AI experimentation, select appropriate tools and develop confidence to explore new possibilities. Organisers argue that as organisations increasingly integrate AI into their operations, professionals who can identify opportunities, experiment with tools and build AI-powered solutions will be better positioned to adapt to changing industry demands. Registration is open at the link given in the announcement.

stories.Headline: South Korea orders audit of IT assets to counter AI-driven cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
The Presidential Office of South Korea ordered a comprehensive audit of information technology assets on November 15, 2026, to combat cyberattacks powered by artificial intelligence. This initiative targets the private sector, the government, and the military to ensure that security vulnerabilities are addressed before they become public. The National Security Office held a joint response meeting on November 13, which was chaired by third deputy director Song Ki-ho. During this session, participants reviewed a full survey of network and system configurations that has been ongoing since August.

The new strategy requires the establishment of a management system to accurately identify hardware and software assets across all sectors. This effort involves close cooperation between the National Intelligence Service, the Ministry of National Defense, and the Ministry of Science and ICT. Officials plan to accelerate the adoption of a software bill of materials to quickly identify systems affected by specific vulnerabilities. Additionally, the government will seek early warnings about security flaws from software vendors, overseas government agencies, and related professional communities.

The National Security Office explained that AI-enabled attacks are increasing while existing network diagrams often differ from the assets actually being operated. This discrepancy makes it difficult for individual institutions to respond quickly when new security vulnerabilities emerge in their systems. By securing information before it is publicly disclosed, the office intends to implement preventive measures more effectively. The goal is to create a more agile defense mechanism that can keep pace with the evolving nature of AI-driven threats.

stories.Headline: IIIT-B to showcase AI, DPI innovations at Bengaluru Tech Summit
stories.Summary:
The International Institute of Information Technology-Bangalore will showcase its research in artificial intelligence, digital public infrastructure, healthcare, telecommunications and smart manufacturing at the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026, which runs from Tuesday to Thursday. The institute will present projects ranging from digital identity systems used around the world to AI-based tools for healthcare monitoring, smart manufacturing and autonomous vehicles. It will also highlight its work on AI skilling and technology startups during the three-day event. The summit display brings together several strands of the institute's research under one roof.

The institute will showcase five digital public infrastructure initiatives, namely MOSIP, OpenG2P, CDPI, COSS and INJI, which together support more than 45 countries. MOSIP helps countries build national digital identity systems and is being rolled out in more than 30 nations, while OpenG2P assists governments in providing welfare benefits. CDPI and COSS support countries in developing digital public infrastructure, and INJI provides an open-source platform to issue, store and verify digital credentials. Healthcare research from the institute's Electronics and Health Research Centre will cover public health, surgery, assistive devices, self-care tools and Tele-MANAS. AI-based tools for remote health monitoring will be on display, including projects to predict sepsis risk, FatigueShield for fatigue and heat-stress forecasting, and ArogyaSense for identifying clinically relevant health information.

The IIIT-B COMET Foundation will showcase a prototype of Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces, a technology that uses electronically controlled surfaces to direct wireless signals, reduce interference and improve network coverage. The technology is particularly useful indoors and in private 5G networks, and the project was developed with support from the institute's Technology Innovation Hub under the Department of Science and Technology's NM-ICPS programme. The Karnataka AI Hub, supported by the State government and anchored at IIIT-B, will showcase initiatives to build AI capabilities for students, professionals, researchers and entrepreneurs. The institute's Web Science Lab will present AnumatiDPI, a consent management platform that allows individuals and organisations to control access to and sharing of their data.

stories.Headline: LTM adds its AI-QEM error mitigation tool to IBM Quantum Functions Catalog
stories.Summary:
LTM announced on 12 November 2026 that its AI-powered Quantum Error Mitigation capability, known as AI-QEM, had been added to IBM's Quantum Functions Catalog, and the company said it was the first global systems integrator to publish a function in that catalog. The catalog offers partner-built quantum software services that are meant to simplify quantum workflows and make experiments more efficient for researchers and enterprises. AI-QEM is offered as a circuit function, so users with eligible IBM Quantum access plans can apply it directly inside their Qiskit workflows. LTM said it had tested the capability on IBM Quantum computers across circuits of different sizes and complexities, including experiments involving more than 100 qubits.

The capability uses AI models to learn device-specific error patterns and estimate corrections through classical post-processing, according to the company. LTM said this improves result accuracy without additional quantum processing unit time, repeated circuit executions or extra qubits, which some conventional error mitigation techniques require, and that it reduces the cost and complexity of running useful quantum experiments. IBM's listing says AI-QEM uses circuit, backend and observable characteristics to learn correction factors and applies classical inference to mitigate noisy quantum expectation values. LTM did not disclose the accuracy improvements achieved or provide comparisons with other error mitigation methods. Other providers in IBM's catalog offer related tools, including Q-CTRL's AI-driven error suppression, Qedma's QESEM error mitigation function and Algorithmiq's tensor-network-based approach.

Scott Crowder, Vice President of IBM Quantum Adoption and Business Development, said in a statement that the AI-QEM function would allow IBM's users to mitigate errors faster and with fewer resources in their efforts to develop algorithms and applications. LTM said it continues to advance practical quantum applications across industries, including quantum optimisation solutions for a global insurer, hybrid quantum machine learning for critical infrastructure, and quantum-safe security programs for financial services and insurance organisations. The articles also note that LTIMindtree had earlier joined the IBM Quantum Network as its first Indian global systems integrator. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the availability of the function in the catalog.

stories.Headline: Tanisha Bansal leads a free AI agents masterclass on 28 November 2026
stories.Summary:
ET TechGig is holding a free live online masterclass titled AI Agents: From Demo to Real-World Deployment on 28 November 2026 at 4:00 PM, lasting 75 minutes, according to an announcement published on 15 November 2026. The session will be led by Tanisha Bansal, an AI and Technology Professional at Accenture Strategy & Consulting, whose expertise covers Generative AI, agentic systems, RAG, MCP, enterprise integrations, workflow automation, cloud technologies and AI evaluation. The class is aimed at AI and Machine Learning Engineers, Software Developers, Application Engineers, Cloud and Solution Architects, Generative AI Practitioners, Engineering Managers, Technical Leads and Enterprise Technology Professionals. It will include a 15-minute live Q&A in which participants can put questions to the speaker.

The masterclass follows a practical, architecture-first approach across six areas, starting with why AI demonstrations often struggle in real enterprise environments and moving through enterprise AI architecture built from models, RAG, MCP, tool calling and orchestration. It will show how an agent can interpret user intent, retrieve information, validate business rules, execute approved actions and verify outcomes through a worked example, and it will cover guardrails, security, evaluation, observability and human-in-the-loop approvals. The session also addresses measuring AI implementation through completed workflows and tangible business outcomes rather than the quality of generated responses, and it offers a structured framework for moving prototypes toward production. Registration is free.

The article frames the class around a gap it describes between agents that perform well in demonstrations and those that work reliably in real enterprise settings, saying successful implementation requires more than connecting a large language model to a tool. It says developers must handle security, permissions, validation, failure recovery and human approvals, and that the difference between an impressive demo and a dependable solution lies in how these components are engineered. The article states that professionals who understand how to build secure, reliable and production-ready AI agents will have an important advantage as organisations adopt autonomous workflows. It gives no further details on what follows the session beyond registration being open.

stories.Headline: SK Hynix accelerates HBM4 equipment installation for mid-2027
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix is accelerating its HBM4 production plans and will install new equipment by mid-2027, according to on-chain reports cited by KuCoin and Korean media outlet Etnews on November 15, 2026. The company is negotiating with partners to procure equipment for HBM4 production and is coordinating with suppliers of back-end processes such as bonding, cutting and testing to align on procurement timelines and quantities. A SK Hynix partner familiar with the situation said the company is advancing additional investments in HBM4 production equipment and accelerating related arrangements. The partner said the aim is to complete equipment delivery, installation and commissioning in the first half of next year, and some equipment must be delivered before the first quarter.

The expansion may be located at the P&T6 packaging and testing plant in Cheongju, North Chungcheong Province, South Korea, a semiconductor factory formerly known as M8 that SK Hynix selected in 2025 as its HBM production site. Since the beginning of this year, SK Hynix has been constructing HBM production lines at the facility, and one industry insider said the company plans to maximize the use of idle capacity there to expand HBM4 production. If the entire factory operates at full capacity, it could produce more than 20,000 additional HBM wafers per month, according to that insider. SK Hynix said last month during its third-quarter earnings call that its DRAM and HBM capacity for the next three years has essentially been sold out by 2029.

The reports describe the move as a significant development for semiconductor demand, and they note that SK Hynix still believes demand for HBM remains strong despite increased uncertainty in the AI industry due to factors such as the change in NVIDIA's CEO. The company plans to focus its investments on equipment for HBM packaging and testing, with operations scheduled to begin in the first half of next year. Several industry insiders in the semiconductor equipment sector provided the details on the negotiations and the Cheongju site. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the equipment timeline and the planned start of operations.

stories.Summary:
South Korea's SK Hynix is coordinating back-end process equipment orders with suppliers to expand its production capacity for HBM4, the next generation of high-bandwidth memory, according to the semiconductor equipment industry on the 15th. The company is using its Cheongju P&T6 fab as an additional production base and is moving up its schedule with a target of bringing in and setting up equipment in the first half of next year. It is in the stage of matching volumes and delivery schedules, centering on back-end equipment such as bonding, dicing and inspection, and is requesting first-quarter delivery for some items. The fab, formerly called M8, was designated by SK Hynix in 2025 as an HBM production site, and HBM lines have been built there since early this year.

One industry official said the plan is to make maximum use of idle space at P&T6, explaining that running the fab at full capacity could add more than 20,000 HBM wafers per month on a wafer basis. SK Hynix said at its third-quarter earnings briefing that its DRAM and HBM volumes were effectively sold out for the three years through 2029. Nvidia's decision to lower the bandwidth target for the HBM4 to be used in its next-generation AI chip Vera Rubin is also analyzed to have worked in favor of the expansion decision, because adopting a relatively easier-to-implement speed reduced the process burden on manufacturers. The move reflects a judgment that HBM demand remains solid even as uncertainty in the AI industry has grown following the change of leadership at Nvidia.

A senior executive at a back-end equipment company said SK Hynix is preparing large-scale orders and the industry is paying close attention, adding that the ripple effects of HBM market growth will begin in earnest. An SK Hynix official said the company has continued to place equipment orders in line with its plans and will respond to market expansion without disruption. Nvidia appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive officer and began the process of selecting a successor, and the company has said it will maintain existing customer contracts and product development schedules. The industry is watching the AI investment and semiconductor procurement plans the new management will present at Nvidia's quarterly earnings announcement scheduled for the 17th local time, since whether the new management changes its investment and supply chain strategy remains a variable in future HBM supply negotiations.

stories.Headline: Digantara raises $50m led by Reliance Industries to expand space situational awareness
stories.Summary:
Bengaluru-based spacetech startup Digantara has secured USD 50 million in a funding round led by Reliance Industries, according to a report published on February 2, 2026, which values the company at approximately USD 200 million. The round also included participation from 360 One Asset, Tokyo-based SBI Holdings, and entrepreneur Ronnie Screwvala, while existing investors Peak XV Partners and Kalaari Capital took part as well. The funding follows Digantara's announcement in December 2025 that it had completed a USD 50 million Series B round. The company was founded in December 2020 by Anirudh Sharma and specializes in space situational awareness and intelligence.

The fresh capital will fuel Digantara's global expansion, with a significant focus on the United States market, and will scale its production and satellite manufacturing capabilities. The company currently provides services to defense markets in India, the United States, the United Kingdom, Singapore, Australia, and Japan, and it plans to extend into Europe by mid-2026. Digantara's selection to participate in the Golden Dome missile system program, described as a multi-layered defense effort integrating ground, sea, air, and space-based systems, further supports its US push. Its proprietary space camera can monitor objects at a resolution of up to five centimeters, surpassing the industry standard of around ten centimeters. Digantara has three satellites operational in orbit, with the first two focused on space weather and the most recent dedicated to space object tracking.

The company operates an integrated platform named AIRA that combines sensing hardware, data processing, and analytics across space and terrestrial systems. Its infrastructure includes the SCOT constellation for space surveillance, the ALBATROSS series for missile warning and tracking, and SKYGATE, a network of ground-based sensors, with phased deployment scheduled throughout 2026 and 2027. The spacetech sector has seen a notable increase in venture capital interest over the past year, highlighted by Agnikul Cosmos raising USD 17 million in November 2025 at a valuation of USD 500 million and reusable rocket maker EtherealX securing USD 20.5 million earlier this month in a round co-led by TDK Ventures and BIG Capital. stories.Headline: Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke launches Entire with $60 million to store AI prompts alongside code
stories.Summary:
Entire Inc., a new startup founded by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, launched with $60 million in seed funding to build an AI-native code management platform, according to TechGig. The company says traditional tools like Git were designed for human-written code and do not effectively track AI-generated code. Entire's core idea is to store prompts alongside code so that AI-driven development can be managed better. The $60 million seed round was led by Felicis, M12, which is Microsoft's venture arm, and Madrona.

Notable angel investors include Olivier Pomel, the CEO of Datadog, along with Garry Tan and Jerry Yang. Entire argues that current systems such as GitHub and GitLab track file changes, commits, diffs and approvals but do not record the prompts given to AI agents. The company says saving only the output of AI-generated code without the prompts leads to inefficiencies and repeated mistakes. Its approach makes prompts first-class citizens in code management through a Git-compatible platform that logs prompts, records follow-up troubleshooting prompts, tracks third-party tools used by agents and stores token usage and generation metadata.

Entire says this workflow prevents repeated AI mistakes by saving remediation prompts so future agents can reuse that knowledge, and it improves transparency by letting developers inspect prompt logs. The company also says it reduces inference costs by letting teams check whether similar issues were already solved before querying an AI model again. Entire's first product is Checkpoints, an open-source tool on GitHub that at launch supports Claude Code and Gemini CLI and logs prompts, AI responses, token usage and context metadata. The company plans more integrations in the coming months and is developing a semantic layer to organize project history and make stored prompts searchable and reusable.

Entire currently has 15 employees and intends to double its team, and Dohmke compared the shift to a new software development model akin to industrial manufacturing. The company says AI-generated code brings challenges including lost reasoning context, repeated troubleshooting loops, a lack of institutional memory in AI sessions and rising inference costs. Entire is not trying to replace Git but to extend it for the AI era by turning prompts into reusable assets. The company's stated goal is to build the infrastructure for machines writing code, just as Git was built for humans writing code.
