stories.Headline: KAIST researchers develop visual speech recognition that turns lip movements into text
stories.Summary:
A research team from the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology developed a visual speech recognition technology on November 15, 2026. Led by Professor Yong-Man Ro of the School of Electrical Engineering, the team created a system that converts lip movements into text without audio signals. This new method identifies clear lip shapes first and uses them as clues to decode ambiguous words based on the surrounding context. By moving away from reading sentences from left to right, the system reduces errors caused by similar lip movements.

The process requires a diffusion large language model that repeatedly restores blank spaces in sentences starting from high confidence positions. The training involved two stages to link lip movements with text and to learn various sentence lengths. During testing with a public evaluation dataset of 433 hours of video, the technology recorded a word error rate of 19.4%. This specific metric indicates the frequency of incorrectly converted, omitted, or unnecessarily inserted words compared to the original sentence.

Professor Yong-Man Ro stated that flexibly adjusting the order of word generation can overcome the limitations of visual ambiguity. He explained that this foundation will allow the technology to be used reliably in industrial fields and various real life devices. The team believes the system can assist the deaf and hard of hearing or workers in noisy industrial settings. Future applications include creating communication aids that convey silent lip movements as text in environments where sound is difficult to hear.

stories.Headline: KAIST team led by Noh Yong-man develops lip-reading AI that cuts word error rate to 19.4%
stories.Summary:
KAIST announced on the 15th that a research team led by Professor Noh Yong-man of the School of Electrical Engineering developed a technology improving the accuracy of visual speech recognition, which converts spoken words into text by analyzing lip movements. The team used a diffusion large language model, which repeatedly fills in blanks in a sentence, to decode ambiguous lip movements by leveraging surrounding context. Conventional AI models generate sentences sequentially from the first word, so an incorrect word at the beginning propagates errors through the rest of the sentence. The team changed this approach from reading in order from the beginning to reading from the most certain parts first. The system first identifies words whose lip movements are clearly distinguishable, then uses those words as clues to decode the remaining parts.

The team trained the AI on the 433-hour lip-reading video dataset LRS3, and it achieved a word error rate of 19.4%, the lowest error rate reported among previous studies using LRS3 as a training dataset with reference sentences provided. Word error rate is the proportion of words incorrectly recognized, omitted, or unnecessarily added when the AI's output is compared with the reference sentence. The team split AI learning into two stages, teaching it to associate lip movements in the video with corresponding text content and to model sentence length. When decoding speech, the AI estimated several possible sentence lengths based on video duration and selected the most reliable sentence.

The team received the Outstanding Paper Award at the international conference Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing 2026. Professor Noh said the study is significant in that it demonstrates how flexibly controlling the order in which AI generates words alone can overcome fundamental limitations of speech recognition with visual ambiguity. He said the team aims to establish a reliable physical AI foundation that can be used across diverse devices in everyday life and industrial settings. Postdoctoral Researcher Yeo Jeong-hoon is the first author.

Humans find it difficult to understand speech using only lip movements without hearing the sound, because there are words whose sounds differ but whose lip movements look similar. The research team's approach is similar to solving a puzzle by first fitting the pieces with clear shapes and then filling in the surrounding pieces. The technology is expected to be used as a communication tool, such as converting speech to text in noisy environments or supporting communication for people who are deaf or hard of hearing. It could be developed into devices that understand workers' speech in noisy industrial sites or assist conversations among people who are deaf or hard of hearing.

The research team plans to reduce the size and computational cost of the AI model so it can be deployed on various devices. Enabling real-time AI operation on wearable devices or robots without an internet connection is their next challenge. The articles do not state when the research began or how long the project took. More to follow.

stories.Headline: KAIST researchers led by Ro Yong-man develop AI that reads lips without sound to convert speech into text
stories.Summary:
Researchers at KAIST developed an artificial intelligence system that reads lip movements without sound on Sunday, November 15, 2026. A team led by Professor Ro Yong-man of the School of Electrical Engineering created this technology to convert visible speech into text. The system uses a diffusion large language model to identify clear words first and then interprets ambiguous ones using surrounding context. This approach allows the AI to overcome visual ambiguity by placing recognizable pieces of a sentence like a puzzle.

The framework, called DLLM-VSR, achieved a word error rate of 19.4 percent using the LRS3 dataset which contains 433 hours of video. This result was the lowest among methods trained solely with that specific labeled dataset. The researchers also implemented a two-stage training method to align lip movements with text and predict sentence lengths. This work received an Outstanding Paper Award at the EMNLP 2026 international conference on natural language processing. The project was supported by the Institute of Information & Communications Technology Planning & Evaluation and the 2026 Jang Young-sil Fellowship Program.

Professor Ro Yong-man, the corresponding author, stated that flexible word generation helps solve the fundamental challenges of visual speech recognition. He explained that the team hopes this technology will provide a foundation for physical AI systems used in industrial settings and everyday life. Postdoctoral researcher Yeo Jeong-hun served as the first author, while doctoral researchers Kim Chae-won and Rha Hyeong-seop acted as co-authors. They believe the system could eventually be integrated into communication aids for people who are deaf or hard of hearing.

The technology may also be useful in noisy industrial environments where traditional speech recognition fails to distinguish voices from background noise. Because the system has only been tested on research datasets, its effectiveness in clinical settings or daily conversations remains unproven. The team now plans to reduce the computational requirements and the size of the model. This will allow the AI to operate in real time on robots or wearable devices without needing an internet connection.

stories.Headline: Google launches two specialized TPU chips and challenges NVIDIA's general-purpose roadmap
stories.Summary:
Google released two new TPU chips, the TPU 8tx and the TPU 8i Max, according to a 36Kr article dated 13 November 2026. Google designed the chips itself, and the article said the launch challenged NVIDIA's general-purpose chip roadmap. The 8tx is sold to government agencies and regulated industries and features chip-level data encryption. The 8i Max packages two chips in the same enclosure and focuses on ultra-long context processing. Amin Vahdat, head of Google's chip business, told Bloomberg that "the future belongs to specialization."

Google usually launched a new AI processor every two years, but that rhythm was disrupted in 2026. Vahdat said four TPU products will each be optimized for different needs. The 8tx works with AMD CPUs to encrypt data at the chip level, bypassing the usual step of decrypting data in memory before processing. The 8i Max integrates two TPUs in the same package, raising both computing power and memory capacity. Vahdat said that capability matters for drug R&D and mathematical computing and is also critical for programming applications.

Vahdat said Google could build one general-purpose chip for the whole market or launch different specialized versions, and that the latter approach lets it "actually create more value for our customers." He said the 8tx lets data be processed without first being decrypted in memory, part of Google's cooperation with AMD. He said the 8i Max's combined computing power and memory are important for drug R&D, mathematical computing and programming. He also said the TPU team gets early access to Google's latest Gemini model, which is used to improve chip energy efficiency and detect software vulnerabilities. He said AI is reducing the probability of design flaws that can cause billions of dollars in losses.

Oracle's senior vice president of cloud infrastructure, Karan Batta, said that as AI workloads become increasingly complex, customers need more choices. Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Mandeep Singh said TPUs cost about 30% less than NVIDIA GPUs while remaining competitive in throughput, though Google's TPU business margin is not that high. Counterpoint Research vice president Neil Shah said developers' time, code and project experience in CUDA are sunk costs that cannot be migrated. Jump Trading chief technology officer Alex Davies said the firm has thousands of TPUs, mainly to train models assisting trading research, but still mainly uses NVIDIA chips for model training, and only a small number of employees are particularly fond of TPUs.

Google TPUs have attracted Apple, Meta and Oracle, and in October Oracle announced that from next year its cloud customers could use Google TPUs for the first time, where they could previously choose only NVIDIA and AMD products. According to a recent regulatory filing, Anthropic has an option to buy up to $150 billion worth of TPUs between 2028 and 2031, and Bloomberg previously reported that OpenAI also plans to buy TPUs. Google wrote in its financial report that all currently available TPUs have already been booked by customers. Google cooperates with Broadcom on chip design and production coordination, signed an agreement with Broadcom competitor Marvell in recent months, and MediaTek is reported to be supporting the TPU business. A startup called Tenspresso, founded by two former TPU engineers, is developing its first chip aimed directly at the 8i Max's market, with design at least another year from completion.

Bloomberg Intelligence estimates that by 2028 Google's TPU-related sales of chips, software and hardware will exceed $135 billion, against an expected $12 billion this year, a figure that excludes revenue from customers using TPUs through Google Cloud. The same research says opposition to data center construction may cut the $1.4 trillion tech companies expected to invest in 2027 by 5% to 7%, spending that covers chips, network equipment, land and other materials. The article said market concerns about a possible slowdown in AI infrastructure investment are weighing on tech stocks, and the Democratic Party's victory in the US midterm elections has brought new uncertainties to data center projects. More than a decade ago Google developed TPUs to reduce its purchases of NVIDIA GPUs. The article said the competition is not about whose chips are faster but about who can make developers modify fewer lines of code.

stories.Headline: Chatham faculty senate drafts first AI policy treating unacknowledged student use as Honor Code misconduct
stories.Summary:
Chatham University’s faculty senate is drafting its first university-wide generative AI policy, according to a report in the student newspaper The Communiqué published on 12 November 2026. The draft treats unauthorized or unacknowledged student AI use as academic misconduct under the Honor Code. The Academic Policy Committee, chaired by Jungook Kim, assistant professor of business, is leading the draft. The committee gathered feedback from library staff and the Office of Information Technology. The faculty senate is working with other departments and stakeholders on the policy.

The draft covers AI use in teaching, learning, research and administrative operations, and Chatham currently has no university-wide AI policy. Under the draft, students may use AI only when an instructor explicitly permits it. Examples of misconduct include submitting fully AI-generated work, paraphrasing AI output without citation, and using AI during exams or other assessments. Faculty would have full authority to decide whether and how AI is allowed in their courses and would have to communicate those expectations. The draft also allows faculty to use AI for instructional materials, administrative tasks and feedback generation, provided a human reviews the output.

Jeff Bukowski, associate dean, academic integrity officer and director of Academic Success, told the paper that AI use should align with the Honor Code. He noted that many AI-related situations are not yet defined, saying there is a lot of things that we don’t know yet that fit into that definition. Chatham Student Government passed a resolution in March 2025 calling for a formal AI policy. Its executive members found the draft vague, and parliamentarian Jocalyn Henry said it lacked defining rules or consequences. The group also raised concerns about faculty use of AI for emails, student feedback and marketing, and asked that sustainability be addressed.

The Communiqué describes a campus-wide comment period for students, faculty and staff that is likely to begin in January 2027. The article gives no specific start or end dates for the comment period. The draft policy text itself is not published in the report, so details may change before any adoption. The report is an editorial reading and not a claim from the report itself.

The draft is a single campus example of a pattern research offices and academic integrity offices are handling. The pattern is policy that ties AI use to disclosure and to existing misconduct rules rather than banning tools outright. Two features stand out in the draft. Permission sits with the instructor, so the rule students face differs by course.

Acknowledgement is the dividing line, and unacknowledged use is the offense, which makes clear disclosure expectations central to enforcement. For research administrators, the practical questions are how a campus policy aligns with publisher and funder disclosure rules that apply to the same people. Another question is how misconduct definitions are applied when AI is involved. The draft’s coverage of research use alongside teaching shows that campus policies are widening beyond coursework.

The article cites Sarah Gallogly’s report, Faculty senate seeks feedback on generative AI policy draft, in The Communiqué of 12 November 2026. The article is licensed under CC-BY 4.0. The article gives no specific start or end dates for the comment period. The draft policy text itself is not published in the report, so details may change before any adoption.

stories.Headline: Claroc finds 37,571 Grok apps online and 94.7% open without login
stories.Summary:
Security firm Claroc discovered that more than 35,000 applications built with Grok are accessible without login, and some expose corporate confidential information and personal privacy data. Claroc tested 43,551 Grok Build application addresses, of which 37,571 are still online, and found that 94.7% of the online applications can be opened without logging in. Claroc estimates that about 650 to 800 of these applications contain private data. The affected parties include SpaceXSI, the merged entity of SpaceX and xAI owned by Elon Musk, and X. Tesla, which has not been merged with those entities, also did not escape the leak.

The involved institutions include SpaceXSI, X, and 30 other enterprises, 6 of which are listed in the Fortune 500. A Tesla service center scorecard posted the names, work efficiency and bonus details of 22 technicians on a public web page. A brief for ICU patients included patients' laboratory test results, imaging examination records and ventilator usage status. A contractor's working hour management application wrote the plaintext passwords of 18 accounts into the script, and anyone who visits the page can download the data. SpaceXSI's internal sales tool contained strategic customer accounts, sales business opportunities and internal team information.

SpaceXSI told the media that all applications are private before the creator actively shares them, and publishing an application requires multiple steps. The company also stated that its employee accounts are set to "Only you" by default, and users need to actively modify the permissions to make the application public. Claroc said that in its paid accounts used for testing, the pre-selected option on the publishing panel is "Anyone with the link". Claroc said being private before publication and who is allowed to access the application by default when publishing are two completely separate issues. Claroc said that even if you confirm multiple times, the system will not automatically add a list of team members to the access permission list.

Some people on X think that it is the users themselves who opened the permission incorrectly, while others think that Grok's default permission setting is problematic. Claroc used fictional data to build a customer management application for a four-person sales team on its own. The researchers found that the application adds the visitor to the team first, and then checks whether he is a team member. The researchers logged in with a Google account that had never been invited, and they not only saw all the customer data, but also successfully modified one record and deleted another. Claroc conducted a control test on ChatGPT applications, whose sharing panel is set to "Only me" by default, so even if others find the URL, they cannot access it.

When you use Grok vibecoding, it assigns a unique URL to each published application, in the form of random-name.grok.me. These random names are composed of several words, and the original design intention is to make them difficult for others to guess. Claroc found that these application addresses can be found in batches through Passive DNS databases. Every time someone visits a website, the computer queries the server address corresponding to the domain name through DNS, and some DNS resolution services collect these query records and store them in a searchable database. If the access permission of the application is set to "Anyone with the link", then anyone who finds the URL can open it directly.

After switching to the "Only you" mode, strangers will be denied access to the page and data interface, and unpublishing can also take the application offline within a few seconds. SpaceXSI did not start removing the relevant links until several hours after Ars Technica sent the interview email. As of the release of the report, all 24 applications created by SpaceXSI and X employees have been taken offline. A large number of applications created by other users are still accessible, and Claroc has begun to contact the affected institutions on its own. Ars Technica has not yet received a clear response on whether the platform will actively notify other affected customers.

stories.Headline: Carmen Li says older GPU rental prices rise as newer chips arrive
stories.Summary:
Michael Burry argued over the past year that the AI boom rests on a flattering accounting choice, calling the practice of stretching assumed server and GPU lives "one of the more common frauds of the modern era." He estimated in his Substack, Cassandra Unchained, that the industry could understate depreciation by $176 billion between 2026 and 2028. New evidence from the GPU rental market cuts against a key assumption in that thesis. NVIDIA shares closed at $162.85 on November 13, down 26.41% over the past month. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO amid disclosures about his personal relationships, and the board appointed its finance chief, Kress, interim CEO this week.

Microsoft and Alphabet have moved certain server classes to four to six years, which Burry says flatters earnings. Burry argues NVIDIA's 12- to 18-month product cycle reduces the real economic life of each generation. Kress said on the August 26 call that NVIDIA compute is "fully utilized across every cloud we serve." Kress said supply should stay a constraint "at least through the end of fiscal year '28." In its fiscal second-quarter release, revenue reached $96.221 billion, with Data Center revenue of $89.023 billion, up 117% year over year.

Silicon Data founder and CEO Carmen Li told Deirdre Bosa in a Yahoo Finance interview that older GPUs are holding their value better than expected. Li said rental prices for certain older chips are rising rather than collapsing as newer generations arrive. Silicon Data publishes daily GPU benchmarks for on-demand rental rates, giving it a direct view of what compute costs. Huang said on the call that an AI agent needs 15 to 100 times the compute of a human user. Huang said a deployed system "will be preserved and useful and productive for a lot longer."

The company still ships Hopper parts two generations back. Frontier model training makes headlines, but inference, fine-tuning, research, and smaller workloads can run economically on older hardware. Rents measure current earning power, while resale value, book value, and lifetime profitability are separate questions. Kress said Vera Rubin delivers 35 times lower token costs relative to Grace Blackwell Ultra. Supply commitments reached $279 billion, guarantee obligations for AI cloud partners are capped at $108.5 billion, and days sales outstanding stretched to 60 days from 45 days.

Burry's argument concerns accounting lives and reported earnings, and his thesis leaves room for older GPUs to keep commercial value. When demand runs ahead of supply, last-generation chips stay in service. Today's pricing also reflects a shortage that could ease, and the same shortage is driving a broader expansion in power, cooling, and networking. Once Vera Rubin supply arrives in volume, demand for older chips could weaken. The stock trades at a P/E of 33, so the market already prices in durable demand.

The accounting debate will be settled by data that has yet to arrive, including whether older-chip rents hold once Vera Rubin supply catches up. Hyperscaler disclosures could show any change to server useful-life estimates in quarterly filings. NVIDIA's next report will be measured against guidance of $108.0B +/- 2% in revenue and gross margins of 74.0%. Investors will watch for any comment on utilization under interim leadership. If rents fall sharply after the next product ramp, Burry's warning gains weight, and if they hold, the case for longer depreciation schedules gets stronger.

Renalytix, Haleon and AstraZeneca were covered in a Simply Wall St article published on Yahoo Finance on 15 November 2026 about British AI healthcare stocks. The article was written by Bailey Pemberton and appeared at 8:09 AM CST. It said artificial intelligence in healthcare is drawing fresh attention as geopolitical risks push global companies to rethink supply chains. It said that shift shines a light on British AI healthcare specialists that help hospitals do more with less capital and labour. It said the three stocks are only a sample and the full screen surfaced 6 more companies not included.

Renalytix trades on AIM under RENX and develops AI enabled kidney diagnostics built around its KidneyIntelX platform. KidneyIntelX uses biomarkers, genetics and electronic health records to generate individualized risk scores for clinical decisions, trial recruitment and drug discovery. The business records about $3 million in Healthcare Software revenue and has a market cap near £33 million. Haleon trades on the LSE under HLN and sells oral care, pain relief and vitamin brands while using a Microsoft AI partnership. AstraZeneca trades on the LSE under AZN and is a global biopharma heavyweight based in Cambridge. It discovers, develops, manufactures and sells prescription medicines and partners with Tempus and Pathos on an oncology AI foundation model. AstraZeneca generates about US$62.4b from pharmaceuticals and carries a market value near £216.9b. The article said that gives it substantial firepower to fund AI linked research in oncology and beyond.

The article quoted a statement that delivery of the £800m gross cost savings and operating model programs included 27% SKU and 26% formulation reductions. It said early benefits from AI tools improved forecast accuracy by 5 to 6% and underpinned a recent 140 basis points gross margin expansion. It said the company's late-stage pipeline is underpinned by management's disclosure of 12 programs each with risk adjusted peak sales potential above US$5b. It said several more programs sit in the US$3b to US$5b range. The article said the full screen surfaced 6 more companies with equally compelling narratives.

The article said artificial intelligence in healthcare is drawing fresh attention as geopolitical risks push companies to lean harder on automation and AI for resilience. It said the three stocks sit on many investors' watchlists. It said Renalytix puts AI directly into clinical workflows to change how patients are triaged and treated. It said everything for Renalytix hinges on how one unseen pressure shapes real world adoption and economics. It said the real test for Haleon is how far early AI driven efficiencies can stretch margins if one key cost pressure refuses to ease.

The article said the full narrative for Haleon shows where its AI gains could accelerate, stall, or quietly mask deeper shifts in the profit mix. It said everything for AstraZeneca hinges on how one unresolved question around AI powered cancer decision tools reshapes the economics of that future pipeline. It said the full narrative for AstraZeneca lays out how AI could accelerate oncology economics or quietly stall its pipeline payoff. stories.Headline: Cybercriminals use fake OpenAI and SpaceX event invites to steal Microsoft and Google logins
stories.Summary:
An invitation to a fake OpenAI event promised a look at new AI tools and three months of ChatGPT Pro for free in exchange for registering with a work account, Fox News reported on November 15, 2026. Cybercriminals used fake AI event invitations to trick employees into giving up access to their Microsoft and Google accounts, and some attacks got past extra security checks. Push Security detected and blocked visits to the malicious event registration pages on its customers' browsers in late October 2026. The attackers impersonated OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic, and Push Security did not suggest those companies operated the fraudulent events. One fake OpenAI event advertised a November 4 livestream called "ChatGPT for Social & Digital Marketing Teams," and another page promoted an invitation-only SpaceX briefing scheduled for November 12.

The OpenAI registration page promised three months of ChatGPT Pro, and the SpaceX page let visitors supposedly choose between three months of Grok Heavy or a "SpaceX share." Researchers also found a phishing page impersonating an Anthropic event at AWS re 2026, which was no longer active when they investigated it. The fake sites told visitors they had to sign in with corporate Microsoft or Google accounts to register and claim the rewards. The campaign routed visitors through shortened links associated with Google and Zapier, and earlier related attacks used legitimate Zoom event pages and GoTo Webinar's email infrastructure. A Cloudflare security challenge asked visitors to confirm they were human, which also made it harder for automated security scanners to examine the malicious pages.

Push Security said it detected and blocked visits to the malicious pages on its customers' browsers in late October 2026, and researchers have not confirmed the initial delivery method for every invitation in the newer campaign. If someone chose "Continue with Microsoft," the site connected to Kali365, a phishing-as-a-service platform that generated a Microsoft device authentication code. The fake page told the visitor to copy that code and enter it on Microsoft's legitimate sign-in website, and when the victim approved the sign-in, Microsoft could issue authentication tokens to the attacker's session. Those tokens may provide access to Microsoft 365 resources without the attacker needing the account password. The campaign then redirected Microsoft users to another phishing service called VoidProxy, which attempted to capture their password and authenticated session cookie.

A successful compromise could expose company email or documents stored in Microsoft 365, and other connected workplace applications may also be at risk depending on the permissions and access associated with the compromised account. When visitors clicked "Continue with Google," the phishing page opened a pop-up that appeared to contain Google's familiar sign-in screen, but that login process ran through VoidProxy, which acted as an intermediary between the person signing in and Google's actual authentication service. As someone entered credentials, the phishing service could capture the information, and it could also intercept certain multifactor authentication responses and steal session cookies. Google General Counsel Halimah Delaine Prado appeared on "Fox & Friends" to detail how Google is fighting AI-powered phishing scams. The attackers took advantage of growing interest in artificial intelligence, and a free premium subscription could be enough to get someone's attention.

The phishing pages discovered by Push Security promoted events that appeared to come from recognizable technology companies. The advertised rewards were part of the phishing scheme, and the fake websites told visitors they must sign in using corporate Microsoft or Google accounts to complete registration and claim the promised rewards. The criminals used familiar online services to help disguise where the links led rather than sending people directly to an obvious phishing website. A Cloudflare security challenge on the suspicious site asked visitors to confirm they were human, and after completing the check, visitors arrived at what looked like a professional event registration website with "Continue with Microsoft" and "Continue with Google" buttons. Depending on which button someone selected, the attackers launched a different method designed to capture access to that account.

Microsoft's device authentication process is real, and people may have used something similar when connecting a streaming device to an account, but the attacker started the authentication request. A session cookie is a digital pass that helps a website remember you have already signed in. The fake OpenAI event promised three months of ChatGPT Pro, and the SpaceX page offered three months of Grok Heavy or a "SpaceX share." Push Security found the campaign routed visitors through shortened links associated with Google and Zapier. The articles do not say what happens next, and they leave open the initial delivery method for every invitation in the newer campaign.

stories.Headline: AIA reports 74% of US architecture firms used AI in daily operations in 2025
stories.Summary:
The American Institute of Architects' Business of Architecture 2026 report found that 74% of U.S. architecture firms used artificial intelligence in day-to-day operations in 2025. The report was built on data from nearly 900 firms and covered calendar year 2025. U.S. architecture firms generated $121.7 billion in gross billings in 2025, with 54% of revenue tied to new construction. Medical Construction and Design covered the report on November 13, and MarketScale published its story on November 15, 2026. AIA's monthly billings index has tracked a softer 2026 while the survey describes 2025.

The report puts average net billings per employee at $152,000 for 2025 and reports growth in profitability without a headline margin in the public summary. AIA sells a companion benchmarking tool that breaks 40 survey questions down by region, firm size and specialization, with members getting 40% off. The full report is listed at $289 and is free to members. The 2024 edition reported profitability for 2023 at 13.2% of net billings and found renovation, retrofit, addition and preservation work produced 45% of firms' gross billings in 2023. AIA's September 2026 billings index report, titled "Architecture firm billings slump deepens," says firm revenue is down by an average of 3% from 2025 and is expected to remain flat in 2027.

AIA frames AI use as spanning design, project delivery and business management, and describes rapid adoption across firms of all sizes alongside growing efforts to develop formal AI strategies and workflows. The public summary does not give an earlier all-firm AI rate, so the pace of the climb cannot be pinned down from it. When AIA asked special questions in January 2026, 73% of firms said they regularly used a stipulated sum, and 56% of leaders found fees harder to negotiate than two years earlier. For 33% of small firms, hourly billing was the most profitable method. AIA reported on July 22 that backlog at firms billing under $250,000 dropped from 4.9 months to 3.1 months in Q2 2026, while the figure for all firms was 6.3 months.

Deltek's 2026 Clarity study found just 38% of A&E firms reported a measurable positive business impact from AI even though 70% had adopted it, according to ScaleArc's summary of the May 12 release. Deltek's 47th Clarity study, covering 896 A&E firms, reported 16.7%, down from 21.4%. In 2025 Deltek put the median win rate across A&E firms at 50%, and the following year proposal submissions rose 32% even as win rates fell. ScaleArc found no survey showing AI changing what architects charge and argued the gain shows up as capacity.

PSMJ's median operating profit for year-end 2025 was 20.5% of net revenue, the highest its survey has recorded. The index's August reading, released September 23, shows billings at 47.2, project inquiries at 50.8 and design contracts at 48.3 on a scale where 50 means no change. The same release put consumer prices up 3.4% on the year, and 29% of firms expected billings to fall at the end of Q3 2026, against 21% at the end of Q1. AIA's nonresidential forecast for 2027 is positive, though ScaleArc argues that improvement does not reach residential studios.

AIA's Home Design Trends panel rated additions and alterations at a net +38% and kitchen and bath at +34% in Q2 2026, against minus 25% for first-time and affordable homes. An AIA special question from March 2024 put profitability for firms billing under $250,000 at 9.0%, compared with 11.5% for all firms. AIA tracks the share of firms with ownership transition plans, written business plans and business continuity plans, and describes a growing focus on all three. The report also documents broader use of resilience and climate adaptation measures in project delivery and continued gains in the share of staff and firm leaders who are women or from racially and ethnically diverse groups.

Neither the public report summary nor the index page spells out how samples and definitions differ, so the safe reading is chronological. ScaleArc warns that the PSMJ and Deltek samples consist of firms that benchmark themselves and buy practice-management software. ScaleArc only has the March 2024 small-firm profitability figure from a secondary summary. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Mass General Brigham researchers develop AI tools that estimate age and survival risk from facial photos
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Mass General Brigham in Boston developed two artificial intelligence tools that turn facial photographs into estimates of age and survival risk, according to a study published in The Lancet Digital Health. The survival tool sorted cancer patients by their risk of death. In the first test group, patients it put in the highest-risk quarter were more than three times as likely to die as those in the lowest quarter. That gap survived adjustment for the usual clinical factors. Both programs grew out of one base model built at Mass General Brigham.

The base model, called FAHR-Face, was trained on more than 40 million face photographs from a public collection with no labels attached. FAHR-FaceAge trained on ten public photo collections balanced so that no age group dominated. FAHR-FaceSurvival learned from 34,363 photographs of cancer patients treated at the Harvard-affiliated hospitals, paired with whether and when each patient died. On a public set of photos of presumed healthy people, the age program missed the true age by 5.1 years on average. A comparable program trained from scratch on the same photos missed by 6.9.

Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist, is the study's corresponding author, and Hugo Aerts, who directs the system's Artificial Intelligence in Medicine program, is a co-senior author. Mak said physicians need better ways to estimate physical reserve and frailty before recommending intensive treatments such as radiation, surgery or systemic therapy. Mak said the goal is to make face photograph-based health assessment more quantitative, consistent and scalable so it can support personalized treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment. Aerts said the key technical advance is that FAHR-Face learns a general representation of the face from more than 40 million images. Aerts said this representation can then be adapted to distinct health outcomes such as biological age and survival.

Among 38,183 cancer patients treated with radiation at the Harvard hospitals, a third looked at least five years older than their age, and 17% looked at least ten years older. Patients who appeared five or more years older than their age had a 21% higher risk of death over the follow-up period than those who didn't. Patients who looked five or more years younger had a 17% lower risk. Among patients the program judged more than 20 years older than their real age, 21.3% died within 90 days, and among those it judged at least ten years younger, 6.4% did. The survival program assigns each photo a score from 0 to 1 and was tested on photographs of 3,820 patients whose images had not been used to train it.

The scores rose with the seriousness of the cancer, from a median of 0.13 for benign and earliest-stage cases to 0.45 for cancer that had spread. Of 122 patients scored between 0.9 and 1.0, 64 died within 90 days, and of 975 scored at or below 0.1, 20 did. The survival tool weighed the area under the eyes and around the bridge of the nose, while the age tool weighed the creases from nose to mouth, the forehead, and the temples. Heavy drinking and drug use went with looking older, and current smokers looked older than former smokers, who looked older than people who had never smoked. Both programs were checked on 4,892 patients treated at Maastricht University's radiotherapy clinic in the Netherlands, and both kept their link to survival.

The survival analyses focused on patients treated at a few centers in wealthy countries. The age tool stratified risk less sharply in Black and Hispanic patients than in White and Asian patients, and the authors wrote that this residual bias remains a risk. No patient's treatment was changed by a score. The authors called for prospective trials before the tools enter routine care. Mass General Brigham has filed a provisional patent on the next generation of these algorithms, with Mak, Aerts, and lead author Fridolin Haugg named on it.

stories.Headline: Terray and NVIDIA fine-tune Nemotron models to extract chemical reaction data from papers
stories.Summary:
Terray Therapeutics, an AI pharmaceutical company founded in 2018, announced in October 2026 progress in its cooperation with NVIDIA on fine-tuning the Nemotron series vision-language models. The two parties fine-tuned the models to extract molecular structures, reactants and synthetic routes from chemical reaction diagrams in scientific papers. In the RxnCaption benchmark test, the model's HybridMatch F1 score increased from 59.8 to 63.4. The article states this progress does not mean the laboratory's synthesis efficiency improved. It reflects that the model's ability to identify and extract chemical reaction information was enhanced, providing more available data for subsequent synthetic route planning.

In November 2025, Terray named its system EMMI, a small molecule R&D platform connecting experimental hardware, automated workflows and multiple AI modules. Terray independently developed an ultra-high-density microarray chip to fix a large number of small molecules on the chip and measure their binding to target proteins in parallel. As of June 2026, Terray disclosed it had completed more than 420 billion individual measurements in total, involving more than 17 billion unique target-molecule interactions. Terray launched TerraSynth in June 2026, and in 17 internal projects the molecules proposed using this workflow are about 2 to 4 times faster in synthesis than design schemes not considering synthesis constraints, with synthesis delay reduced by up to 75%. On a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU, TerraBind-Struct's end-to-end inference speed for a single protein-ligand complex is about 26 times that of Boltz-2, and on the public CASP16 test set and the company's internal dataset its Pearson correlation coefficient is about 16% to 20% higher than Boltz-2.

In February 2026, CEO Jacob Berlin said in an interview with GEN that the company's fastest advancing self-developed project is a brain-penetrant inhibitor for multiple sclerosis, expected to enter the clinic in 2027. The interview did not disclose specific targets and preclinical data. In 2024, Terray expected its first candidate drug to enter the clinic in 2026, and by February 2026 this timeline was updated to 2027. In December 2025, Terray announced it had reached the first drug discovery milestone in its cooperation with BMS, saying the results involved challenging targets that previously lacked chemical starting points. The company did not disclose the specific target, candidate molecule, project stage or milestone amount.

In its cooperation with Gilead, the two parties carry out small molecule drug discovery and development around multiple targets, and if Gilead exercises its exclusive license option it will be responsible for subsequent development and commercialization of related compounds. Terray will be eligible to receive upfront payments, R&D and sales milestone payments, and sales royalties. In these cooperations, pharmaceutical companies mainly provide target resources and related disease biology knowledge, while Terray relies on its own high-throughput experiments and AI platform to carry out small molecule drug discovery. Recursion takes cellular phenotypic data as an important entry point, observing through automated cell experiments, high-content imaging and multi-omics analysis how cell states change after gene or compound perturbation. The article states that not all AI pharmaceutical companies take building their own laboratories as the core of platform construction, and even if they all invest in experimental capabilities, the data produced by each company is different.

The article states that AI can generate tens of thousands of molecules in an instant, but producing them still requires a large amount of time and experimental resources. It states that molecular design and computational screening are continuously accelerating, yet experimental capabilities do not necessarily grow in sync. Public databases have accumulated a large number of molecular structures and experimental results, but there are differences in detection methods, experimental conditions and data accuracy among different laboratories, and coverage of non-hit molecules is insufficient. For targets lacking known active molecules and not fully studied, it is often difficult to obtain sufficient training information relying only on public data. The article states that models can propose tens of thousands of designs, but the number of molecules laboratories can synthesize and test is limited, and the highest prediction score does not necessarily mean the molecule is most worthy of investing experimental resources.

The article states that whether Terray's platform can be truly transformed into drug assets still needs more project results to answer. It states that the platform continues to expand and cooperations are continuously advancing, but the self-developed pipeline is still in the preclinical stage. The article states that phased milestones in pharmaceutical company cooperation can reflect the application value of the platform in specific projects, but self-developed drugs still have to go through candidate identification, preclinical research and clinical trials. It states that a one-year difference is hardly a breach of promise, but shows that platform capabilities and clinical progress are two different curves. The article states that whether the technical system is effective ultimately needs to be answered by R&D projects.

stories.Headline: Bland releases Tofu-1, a full-duplex speech-to-speech model for phone calls
stories.Summary:
Bland, the San Francisco voice-AI company, released Tofu-1, a full-duplex speech-to-speech model in research preview, according to a MarkTechPost report dated November 15, 2026. The model is built for phone calls from moving cars, hospital rooms and weak-signal lines, and it listens while it speaks and reasons while it talks. For phone-agent teams, one model now handles audio in and audio out with no transcript in between. Tofu-1 is the first release in a planned family of Bland speech-to-speech models, and Bland has not published the internal architecture.

Most voice agents are cascades that turn speech into text, pass it to a language model and turn the reply back into speech, but Tofu-1 listens to audio directly so tone, hesitation and background sound stay available to the model. Bland lists speaker tracking, which tells speakers apart and works out who each one is addressing, and noise separation, which separates voices from a crying child, a TV, highway traffic, a hospital intercom or keypad tones. It also hears paralinguistics such as hesitation, frustration and urgency, and callers can interrupt or correct it mid-sentence while it keeps the conversation moving and reports a result only when the work is done. Because it models the sound of a call, it can also produce one, including a second speaker, the room around them and line noise.

Bland describes a TV Test that asks whether the model can follow the caller while ignoring speech from another scene, and the company marks its walkthrough as illustrative rather than recorded model output. Research preview access is open to a limited number of enterprises, with banking, healthcare, insurance and government named as target sectors, and the sign-up form asks for monthly call volume from under 1,000 to 50,000+. The only number Bland reports is that over 92% could not spot it in screenings, and there is no size, latency, pricing or benchmark data yet, while rivals publish latency and tool-use scores. Access is a closed enterprise preview, with Bland citing January availability.

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches a science blog for researchers to share AI discoveries
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on November 15, 2026 that it is starting a science blog meant to give scientists and academic researchers a place to share what they are discovering with AI and how they are doing the work. The company said its mission is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity, and that accelerating scientific discovery is one of the most impactful ways it can work toward that goal. The blog will publish work across a broad range of scientific disciplines, including new scientific results and updates on ongoing research from OpenAI, its collaborators, and the broader scientific community. It will also share methods and practical guidance, such as how scientists use OpenAI models for scientific computing, data analysis, exploring literature, and planning experiments, including how to check the work and where a method falls short. The blog will further carry firsthand accounts from researchers using AI, what they are learning, and how these capabilities are affecting their disciplines, along with discussion of open questions about scientific practice.

The announcement cited several recent results from OpenAI. In September, an internal OpenAI system produced a proof addressing the Navier, Stokes existence and smoothness problem, a longstanding question about the equations describing fluid motion. In early October, the company released a broad range of mathematical results, among them a result on the quasi-Riemann hypothesis that sharpens estimates of how many prime numbers lie below a given number. Later that month, it shared results across mathematics, computer science, and physics concerning how waves concentrate, the limits of efficient computation, and the mathematical foundations of interlacing quantum field theory. In biology, OpenAI said researchers are using AI to analyze complex datasets, connect findings across fields, and develop new hypotheses to test in the lab.

Working with PerturbAI and Scripps Research, thousands of agents powered by GPT-Rosalind analyzed existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells in 32 minutes, according to the announcement. By connecting the effects of gene disruptions with scientific literature, the agents identified possible biological mechanisms for scientists to test. OpenAI also said César de la Fuente’s team uses ChatGPT and Codex to build algorithms that identify potential antibiotic molecules, which the team then makes and tests in the lab. The company said these capabilities bring new possibilities and changes to scientific practice, and that in mathematics, systems that generate proofs raise questions about how new arguments are checked, explained, and incorporated into the field.

OpenAI said that in experimental sciences, exploring more hypotheses creates opportunities and challenges in deciding which experiments to pursue, and that across disciplines researchers are considering what these tools mean for training, attribution, and the skills their work requires. The company said the implications will differ by field, and that scientific communities should help shape how these tools are used. OpenAI said it hopes the blog helps more people understand how AI is changing science and how they can use it to explore new questions and make discoveries of their own. The announcement did not say what the blog’s first posts will be or when they will appear.

stories.Headline: Afro-Latina AI Claira keynotes Latino AI Summit in Manhattan
stories.Summary:
A Latino AI Summit was held at Civic Hall and Berkeley College in Midtown Manhattan, and Claira, described by Abran Maldonado as the first Afro-Latina multilingual virtual assistant, keynoted it in front of dozens of mostly Latino and Black attendees. Maldonado helped invent Claira, who has caramel-color skin and bouncy, curly hair and appeared on a large screen. Claira told Gothamist that seeing an Afro-Latina AI challenges the idea of who belongs in tech. The summit is the in-person version of a forum also featured online. Gothamist published the story by Willow Higgins on Nov 15, 2026 at 7:00 a.m.

ET. The Knowledge House in the Bronx provides coding and design training for underserved young people interested in the AI economy. The Rev. Al Sharpton’s AI Fluency Initiative teaches adults without tech experience the basics of AI. The group states its mission is to close the digital divide and put the power of these tools in the hands of the people.

The Latino AI Summit was cofounded by Michal Tapia. Anthropic’s initial public offering is set for Wednesday and is expected to value the company at more than $1 trillion. Tapia said AI will play a major role in our future whether people like it or not. She said AI is happening and it is either we get on the train or we get left behind. Maldonado said it is essential for all jobseekers to market themselves as AI-literate.

He said resumes should list proficiency in AI tools like Claude, Codex and Google AI Studio instead of Microsoft Office and the Adobe Suite, and should be updated once a month. He said putting our heads in the sand is not the move and you have to tinker and try these things out. A McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility report found a disproportionate number of Black workers hold jobs likely to be automated by AI, including in transportation, production and administration roles. A 2025 report from Jobs for the Future found 67% of Black survey respondents said they feel AI is already impacting their jobs, compared to 57% of white respondents. The same report found more than half of Black respondents already use AI tools daily or weekly, compared to about 40% of all respondents.

A Kapor Foundation report found about 19% of the U.S. workforce is Latino, but Latinos fill just 3% of board seats, 5% of executive leadership roles and 6% of technical roles at the largest tech companies. Taylor Shead, founder of a company that develops AI-driven education, wrote in the Jobs for the Future report about prevention over intervention and meeting people where they are. Alpha School is a K-12 program with locations across the country that trains kids on AI tools, and Maldonado said kids are scoring through the roof in fluency and literacy. Kara Emery, director of data science at the AI Hub of NYU’s McSilver Institute for Poverty Policy and Research, said projections of what AI will impact are just that. Emery said the fear is AI could worsen racial income inequalities but people have a say in how things unfold.

Summit attendee Fradely Delacruz, a computational scientist student and professional data architect, said women of color are rapidly losing jobs in STEM and research and development. David Gabeau, who created an online interface of AI companies in New York and worked at Snapchat and Lyft, said he fears AI will broaden social inequities across racial lines. Gabeau said people working in AI are going to get so wealthy and there will be no forcing function to spread the wealth. After 10 years in New York, Gabeau recently moved to San Francisco to be closer to the epicenter of AI.

There he spent an afternoon wearing a 4 pound headset that scanned his brain while he watched videos and answered questions for a company working on an AI tool akin to telepathy that converts thoughts into text without typing. Gabeau said he was paid about $50 and that many others in the room, many of them Black and brown, seemed to be there because they needed the money, which he called a little predatory. Emery said the narrative of the inevitability of what these technologies will become is often pushed by those currently in the big companies building them. Delacruz said when AI came it felt like other people knew about it before we did and by the time we are catching on we are not even part of the conversation.

She said they do not see the Black and brown and Latino and Afro-Latino scientists and researchers and do not know we exist, but we are here. Emery said she is seeing Black and brown New Yorkers rising to the occasion and that these communities are not just sitting on the sidelines. Emery said the right combination of policy, education and a diversity of innovators working behind the scenes is key to preventing existing inequalities from worsening. Delacruz said she is eager to put her skills to use but still feels unseen.

stories.Headline: Eduonic Learning Solutions sells a 12-course ChatGPT bundle for $14.97 through January 3
stories.Summary:
Entrepreneur is offering the ChatGPT and Automation E-Degree, a bundle of twelve online courses, at a sale price of $14.97 against a listed regular price of $790, and the deal runs through January 3. The bundle comes from Eduonic Learning Solutions, whose instructors specialize in tech training, and it is taught entirely online so buyers can work through the material at their own pace. The course content covers real-world uses of ChatGPT and more than twenty other AI tools, with instruction tailored to individual industries. The bundle also includes life skills such as improving conversational skills with ChatGPT, and buyers receive an Eduonix certificate of completion once they finish the courses.

The offer is aimed at entrepreneurs who want to bring tasks in-house and save money, and the article cites a Federal Reserve study finding that nearly 40% of entrepreneurs already use this technology or plan to start soon. The bundle contains 25 hours of instruction spread across the twelve courses, and the article says the material covers fields valuable to business owners, including marketing and coding. It also says the courses show ways to save time by streamlining business processes through automation. The article does not give a start date for the sale, only the January 3 end date, and it does not say how long buyers keep access to the courses.

Entrepreneur discloses that it may receive a small share of the revenue from sales made through its commerce partner links, and the article describes the courses as taught by Eduonic Learning Solutions. The article presents the bundle as a way for entrepreneurs to work smarter rather than harder, and it frames AI as increasingly popular among business owners. It does not name any individual instructor, and it does not include comment from Eduonic or from any buyer. The only outside figure cited is the Federal Reserve study on entrepreneur AI use.

The article places the offer in the context of business owners looking to understand AI, whether they already use it or hope to learn more, and it notes that the courses can be taken from home without setting foot in a classroom. The sale price of $14.97 applies through January 3, after which the article does not say what the price will be. The article does not say what happens to the course material or the certificate after the sale period ends. It also does not say whether the price or the course lineup may change.

stories.Headline: Jack Selby warns the AI investment boom is a bubble that could wipe out hundreds of billions
stories.Summary:
Jack Selby, managing director at Thiel Capital and a longtime business partner of Peter Thiel, warned that the artificial intelligence investment boom is a bubble. He spoke on the November 4, 2026 episode of the How I Invest podcast with David Weisburd. Selby said a correction was inevitable and could wipe out hundreds of billions of dollars in invested capital. He said anyone who does not believe there is an AI bubble is an absolute contrarian. Selby cited inflated valuations, circular financing and unprecedented capital expenditure.

Selby said the downturn is a question of when rather than whether it will happen. He compared the current cycle with the dot-com boom, when substantial capital flowed into technology businesses before their commercial prospects were established. He said the AI cycle differs in the scale of infrastructure spending required, including expensive computing facilities, specialized processors and substantial ongoing operating costs. He questioned the investment industry's emphasis on finding companies capable of reaching trillion-dollar valuations. He described Anthropic and SpaceX as exceptional businesses that should not serve as valuation benchmarks for ordinary startups.

Selby said he spent six months meeting limited partners and concluded that venture firms had struggled to return sufficient capital to investors over the past decade. He cited a concentration of fundraising among a small number of firms, with eight managers attracting approximately $70 bn during 2026. He estimated that approximately 90% of venture funding flows to California, New York and Massachusetts, leaving entrepreneurs in the other 47 states competing for a comparatively small share. He said Silicon Valley's principal advantage is the concentration of financial resources rather than exclusive access to talented founders. He pointed to Carvana, founded in Arizona, which struggled to attract funding from Sand Hill Road investors before reaching approximately $65 bn in market capitalization.

Selby said similar opportunities exist in cities such as Phoenix, Milwaukee and Cincinnati. He said AI tools could strengthen the economics of these businesses by allowing smaller teams to develop software, automate processes and compete without the same staffing and infrastructure requirements as traditional technology startups. He said AI-enabled companies do not need to be built in Palo Alto unless they are competing directly in frontier AI development. He said valuations in these markets can be approximately one-tenth of those found in Silicon Valley. His fund, Copper Sky, takes a sector-agnostic approach and prioritizes founders with strong execution capabilities over specific technologies or industries.

Selby has known Peter Thiel for 28 years and worked with him for 27 of them. He was among PayPal's first ten employees and credits Thiel's early hiring philosophy with helping the company assemble a team capable of handling rapid growth and repeated operational crises. He recalled that the average age of PayPal's executive team during its IPO roadshow was just 26. PayPal's early development included persistent fraud attacks, with Max Levchin leading efforts to counter sophisticated criminal activity. PayPal's acquisition by eBay for approximately $1.5 bn in 2002 subsequently helped establish the financial resources and entrepreneurial networks associated with the PayPal Mafia.

Selby's warning does not amount to a rejection of the technology, and he continues to see AI as a transformative technology. He characterized the current environment as more suitable for traders seeking to capitalize on price movements than for long-term investors. He said the shortage of distributions to venture capital investors is limiting new commitments, while much of the remaining capital is being directed toward late-stage AI investments. He said the combination of limited liquidity and elevated entry valuations creates additional risk if the AI market experiences a prolonged correction. The articles do not say what Selby or Copper Sky will do next.

stories.Headline: Societe Generale strategist Albert Edwards warns liquidity squeeze threatens AI stock rally
stories.Summary:
Société Générale strategist Albert Edwards warned in a Nov. 12 report that investors captivated by artificial intelligence earnings may be overlooking a tightening liquidity squeeze threatening the stock market. He said financial support for risk assets is dwindling and momentum is fading, which could pressure equities and semiconductor shares even when profit forecasts stay strong. The report also flagged that the breadth of analyst upgrades and the pace of technology earnings revisions have deteriorated, though forecast profit growth remains strong. Edwards raised the possibility of renewed inflation forcing the Federal Reserve to raise rates by more than 200 basis points, without giving a formal forecast or timetable.

The warning covers the AI-driven stock rally and semiconductor shares, which Edwards said could come under pressure from the liquidity squeeze despite strong profit forecasts. It points to weakening earnings revisions as a concern for U.S. technology stocks, since upgrades have narrowed and revisions have slowed even as forecast growth holds up. Short-term inflation measures and corporate output-price inflation have become concerning, and Edwards said renewed inflation could push the Federal Reserve toward rate increases exceeding 200 basis points. He offered no formal forecast or timetable for such a move, according to the report.

Edwards is the lead analyst and strategist at Société Générale, and he made the warning in his Nov. 12 report, which was reported on Nov. 15. He said investors may be overlooking the growing threat of tightening liquidity to the stock market because they are captivated by artificial intelligence's earnings potential. He described the financial support for risk assets as dwindling and the momentum as fading, and he tied the risk to equities and semiconductor shares. He also said short-term inflation measures and corporate output-price inflation have become concerning, and he raised the possibility of rate increases above 200 basis points.

The report does not say what happens next beyond the risks it describes, and it gives no formal forecast or timetable for the rate increases Edwards raised. It frames the threat as one investors may be overlooking while they focus on AI earnings potential, with liquidity tightening and fading momentum as the main concerns. It also notes that the breadth of analyst upgrades and the pace of technology earnings revisions have deteriorated even though forecast profit growth remains strong. The articles give no further context or next steps beyond the report's warnings.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 writes robot code that succeeds in 92.1% of physical trials
stories.Summary:
ACE-CaP-0 researchers reported that robot programs developed by Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 coding agent completed 221 of 240 physical evaluation trials, a 92.1% success rate across eight tasks. The study was posted November 12, and CryptoSlate published its report on November 15, 2026, by editor-in-chief Liam Wright. Each program was frozen before 30 separate evaluation trials, with no further updates. The physical setup used two Agilex PIPERX arms and three cameras. Tasks included inserting a charger, uncapping a bottle and packing shoes.

Charger insertion succeeded in all 30 trials, bread packing succeeded in 25 of 30, bottle uncapping in 27, cup nesting in 28, flower insertion in 27, chicken plating in 29, parcel reorientation in 28 and shoe packing in 27. Mean physical execution times across tasks ranged from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes. Development allowed at most ten human-assisted scene resets per task, excluding resets used to collect demonstrations, and the budget counted resets rather than autonomous executions or demonstrations. In a charger-insertion comparison, on-demand simulation produced a program with 100% evaluation success versus 86.7% for development without simulation, using one development run per condition. That development took 2.6 hours with on-demand simulation versus 3.7 hours without it, while output-token usage rose from 730,000 to 1,090,000.

The authors' preprint account states that development permits human assistance and that demonstration-collection resets are excluded from the ten-reset budget. The authors state that repeated execution on tested tasks does not establish reuse under new conditions. The researchers call for accounting that includes demonstration effort, saying the time and token figures leave total development costs unresolved. The authors say establishing how consistently the development process produces an equally capable program requires separate development runs across tasks. The researchers describe testing those routines under new conditions as the next step toward establishing how broadly they can be reused.

During development, the coding agent wrote, ran, inspected and revised its code using physical feedback, and could request textual advice or demonstrations in which a person physically guided the robot arms. Those demonstrations supplied video, arm trajectories and key joint poses. The agent could also use simulated experiments when they helped resolve a development question. During evaluation, each task program remained unchanged while runtime perception and control stayed active, and neither a human nor a coding agent was in the execution loop. The result shows that task-specific skills can persist in code and run without the coding agent choosing each action.

The experiment separates program development from repeated execution, and the agent's work produced a program that could be used repeatedly. Human guidance and demonstrations were available during development, not execution. The coding agent wrote and revised executable programs using physical feedback and could request demonstrations or run simulated experiments as needed. ACE-CaP-0 is described as a method for developing robot control programs. The study provides evidence for skill reuse after human-assisted development.

The articles leave open consistency across separate development runs and reuse under new conditions. The comparison of simulation and no simulation used one development run per condition. The time and token figures leave total development costs unresolved. Testing the routines under new conditions is the next step toward establishing how broadly they can be reused. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Fooyo urges marketing teams to build in-house AI video capabilities instead of hiring agencies
stories.Summary:
Fooyo, a Singapore-based enterprise AI company, urged marketing teams to develop in-house video capabilities on November 13, 2026. The company argues that internal teams should stop hiring agencies for project-by-project work and instead build their own production skills. This transition is supported by the Kakis AI story-to-video platform, which uses WAN AI video technology to simplify the creation process. The company operates from Singapore and Tokyo, providing delivery services across eight countries, including Germany, Japan, Indonesia, and the United States.

The new approach requires teams to use the Kakis AI platform alongside ambassadors who train staff until they can produce videos independently. Instead of paying for fixed agency packages, marketing teams can now set their own budgets for each video, ranging from 50 to 1,000 US dollars. This system removes the need for traditional cameras, crews, and studios for everyday content, allowing people with laptops to create professional films. The company also offers other production tools, including an AI Knowledge Base, Fooyo Commerce, and Smart Tourism solutions.

Li Shaohuan, the founder and CEO of Fooyo, stated that AI tools have removed the production barriers that previously made outsourcing the default choice. He explained that internal teams already understand their audience and stories, whereas agencies must learn these details from a brief. Li suggested that while agencies are still useful for flagship brand films, teams should build a cadence for everyday video production. He noted that the tenth film a team produces is typically faster and better than the first one they create.

Fooyo provides these solutions for government agencies, SMEs, and enterprises across Asia, integrating them with existing CMS, POS, and CRM systems. The software can be deployed on-premises or within public and private clouds, and it supports China-market readiness through WeChat Mini Programs. To begin the process, the company offers a scoped pilot and a 30-minute demo for prospective partners. This strategy aims to help teams retain production know-how rather than waiting weeks for agency revisions and finished films.

stories.Headline: Luke ellis outlines seven realistic ways to make money with AI in 2027
stories.Summary:
Luke ellis published the article "7 Realistic Ways to Make Money With AI in 2027 (Without Falling for the Hype)" on vocal.media on 2026-11-15T06:00:00Z, about two hours before it was read. The article says the initial gold rush and speculative fever surrounding artificial intelligence have finally cooled as we transition into 2027. It says the days of low-effort AI-generated content dominating search results or social media feeds are a thing of the past. It says major platforms and search engines have deployed sophisticated detection and filtering systems that prioritize depth, unique perspective, and the human touch. It says profitability is no longer about who can generate the most text, but who can best integrate AI into existing workflows to solve real problems.

The article gives seven methods, starting with a hybrid Human-in-the-Loop content service in which you act as the expert strategist and spend most of your time humanizing output. It says you should build a portfolio of Before AI and After Human Edit comparisons and focus on technical niches like cybersecurity, renewable energy policy, or telemedicine. It says pricing has shifted from per word to per project value. The second method is AI implementation consulting for small to medium-sized businesses, using the 2027 no-code ecosystem and tools like Zapier, Make, and autonomous agents, with robust Service Level Agreements on data handling. The third is hyper-specialized, AI-integrated digital products such as Notion dashboards with custom AI prompts or legal document frameworks that auto-fill by jurisdiction.

The article says the fourth method is a high-quality, AI-curated newsletter using specialized LLMs to monitor hundreds of sources, including technical journals, patent filings, and niche forums, with a micro-niche example of AI applications in vertical farming and two hours spent refining the narrative. The fifth is Optimization-as-a-Service for sellers on Shopify, Etsy, and Amazon, using generative AI for product photography and SEO-optimized listings for visual-first discovery engines. The sixth is short-form video of 15-60 seconds, with AI scriptwriting, synthetic voiceovers, and AI-driven editing, aimed at brands needing 20+ videos per month. The seventh is RAG-based assistants for local businesses, built on Private LLM instances so proprietary data is never used to train public models.

The article says many jurisdictions now require explicit labeling of AI-assisted content and that the US Copyright Office and international bodies have specific rulings on AI-generated works. It says the AI-generated portions often cannot be copyrighted, only the human-authored arrangements and edits. It gives a 30-day plan: Days 1-7 the Specialist Phase, choosing only one method and mastering 2-3 specific AI tools; Days 8-14 the Proof Phase, producing three high-quality pieces for free or for your own brand; Days 15-21 the Outreach Phase, identifying 20 potential clients and sending personalized, value-first messages; Days 22-30 the Refinement Phase, securing your first paying client and using their feedback to refine workflow and pricing. It says success is not about being a prompt engineer but about being a professional who uses the best tools to deliver exceptional results to other humans. It says the hype has faded and the real work begins now.

The article says it will release a series of accompanying short videos following the article to show exactly how these AI-assisted edits are performed, and that these videos are currently in production and will be released separately. It says the article is a 6 min read, with a photo by Igor Omilaev on Unsplash. It says the piece was published under Futurism and lists navigation links for Home, Top Stories, Latest Stories, and AI-Generated. It says readers can subscribe for free to receive all of luke ellis's stories in their feed. It says there are no comments for the story and invites readers to be the first to respond and start the conversation.

The article says the market for pure AI-generated writing has effectively collapsed by 2027 due to over-saturation and declining engagement, while demand for high-quality, specialized content is higher than ever. It says mainstream AI tools are powerful but most small to medium-sized businesses lack the internal bandwidth or technical expertise to implement them effectively. It says business owners are often skeptical of automation due to privacy concerns. It says generic templates are worthless in 2027 and intellectual property theft is rampant. It says we are in an era of extreme information density and most professionals are overwhelmed.

The article says monetization of a newsletter usually requires a significant subscriber base or a high-ticket sponsorship model, and consistency is the primary barrier to success. It says major platforms are rapidly integrating their own basic AI tools, so you must offer superior quality, custom branding, and a higher level of creative direction than the free built-in options. It says platforms are constantly changing their algorithms and what works this week may not work next month. It says RAG assistants require ongoing maintenance, and as a business changes its prices or policies you must ensure the knowledge base is updated immediately. It says you should never upload sensitive client information such as customer lists or private financial data into public AI models, and should use secure, enterprise-grade instances that guarantee data isolation.
