stories.Headline: Bain estimates $6.5tn spending needed for 150GW of AI data centre capacity by 2030
stories.Summary:
Data centre construction stocks lost $4.2tn as the boom in the AI trade unravelled, according to the Financial Times on 15 November 2026. The report put the figure in its headline, and the article itself sits behind a paywall, so the details of which companies fell and by how much are not available in the text. The same day, Data Centre Magazine published statistics from Bain & Company describing the scale of the AI data centre boom that had been driving the trade. Bain estimated that up to $6.5tn of spending would be needed to build nearly 150GW of new compute capacity by 2030.

Bain's figures set out what the build-out requires, including expected growth of 20 to 30 per cent in data centre critical capacity over the next five years. Hyperscalers' data centre capital expenditure could top $1tn by 2028, and global data centre electricity demand is estimated to more than double from 589TWh in 2026 to 1,228TWh in 2030. The number of semiconductor companies manufacturing the most advanced logic node has fallen from 25 in 2002 to 2003 to just four from 2020 to 2026, a decline of 84 per cent. North America's virtual power plant market grew by 13.7 per cent last year to 37.5GW.

Bain & Company is responsible for the statistics, which come from its latest technology report and were drawn from the December Week 1 edition of Data Centre Magazine. The report says building AI-ready data centres is proving as much a test of supply chains and power infrastructure as it is of capital. Taken together, the figures show an industry expanding on several fronts at once, with capital, capacity, power and chip supply all being stretched. The pressure is unlikely to ease before 2030, and for operators, planning around the grid and the supply chain will matter as much as securing funding.

The context is an industry whose growth depends on spending, electricity and a shrinking pool of advanced chip manufacturers, all of which the Bain figures show under strain. The Financial Times report indicates that the stock market's confidence in that boom has faltered, with $4.2tn wiped from data centre construction stocks. Neither article says what happens next beyond 2030, and the Financial Times article gives no further detail beyond its headline because of the paywall. Data Centre Magazine points readers to the full Bain article for more.

stories.Headline: Otter.ai earns 100 million dollars in annual revenue after transcribing over 1 billion meetings
stories.Summary:
Sam Liang co-founded the AI notetaker Otter.ai in 2016 to transcribe meetings. He was inspired to create the tool after using a Sony Walkman to record lectures. The company now makes 100 million dollars a year in revenue. It has transcribed over 1 billion meetings for more than 40 million users.

The startup secured 320 million dollars in financing last month from early backers of Tesla, Zoom, and Google. Liang and Yun Fu built the technology as AISense before launching a free version in February 2018. A paid tier followed three months later, and Series B funding of 50 million dollars arrived in February 2021. The company employs over 240 people and integrates with Google, Claude, and OpenAI. Liang lives in the suburbs of Mountain View near Palo Alto.

Liang said that leaving a stable job to build startups was his best financial decision. He stated that his upbringing during the Cultural Revolution in China taught him to live simply. He believes that being frugal makes Otter a stronger and more resilient company. Liang noted that building a startup is hard and requires many personal sacrifices. He told Fortune that he wants to invest his time in his own company.

Investors initially thought the founders were crazy because voice data was expensive and AI was not popular. Liang's wife was the only one earning money while he started the company. His children were affected because he had less time for them before they entered college. Liang's faculty advisor at Stanford, David Cheriton, mentored him in big thinking. Cheriton also famously provided the initial 100,000 dollars to help launch Google.

Liang studied at the University of Arizona and earned a PhD from Stanford. He worked at Cisco and Tropos Networks before joining Google in 2006 as a tech lead. His work at Google created the backbone for Google Maps. In 2010, he co-founded Alohar Mobile, which Alibaba acquired for millions in 2013. The pandemic caused Otter's revenue to grow 800 percent between 2019 and 2020.

Liang continues to run marathons and has completed 12 of them, including one in London. He uses a Garmin watch and Strava to track his training and health. He maintains a frugal diet by drinking a smoothie based on Arnold Schwarzenegger's recipe. Liang has no plans to slow down his current pace of work. The articles do not say if he will integrate Otter with Strava.

stories.Headline: An opinion piece argues AI exposes limits of traditional schooling and proposes three shifts for schools
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Daily Sabah on November 15, 2026, is an opinion piece arguing that artificial intelligence has exposed the limits of what schools have traditionally treated as learning. The author writes that students can now obtain explanations, generate essays, solve mathematical problems and explore complex questions within seconds. Tasks that once required considerable learning can now be done, at least superficially, with a few prompts. The piece asks what learning means when answers are readily available, and whether easy access to knowledge makes people smarter or intellectually weaker.

The author argues that AI does not determine the future of learning, because our conception of learning decides whether it becomes an instrument of growth or decline. The article proposes three shifts for schools: moving from standardized learning to personalizable learning, shifting from answering questions to finding and solving meaningful problems, and moving from individual competition to human interdependence. It says knowing an answer is not the same as understanding a problem, and producing an essay is not the same as having something meaningful to say. It adds that all students still need a reasonable foundation for participating in society, beyond which education should let different learners pursue different forms of excellence.

The author acknowledges that concerns about AI weakening effort, memory and critical thinking are legitimate but not new, comparing them to earlier worries about writing, printed books, calculators, computers and the internet. The piece contrasts two students using AI to write an essay, one who submits a lightly adjusted generated text and learns little, and one who uses AI to explore evidence, challenge assumptions and improve writing while remaining responsible for the argument. It says AI can weaken thinking when it replaces intellectual engagement and deepen understanding when it enables more meaningful engagement. The author is developing two initiatives with colleagues and educators, YEE AI, an AI-supported learning platform, and Courageous Minority, an international community of teachers and school leaders.

The article says educational transformation cannot wait for entire systems to change, and that teachers can begin by redesigning learning experiences in their own classrooms. It describes the two initiatives as complementary, with YEE AI exploring how technology can support a new educational paradigm and Courageous Minority exploring how educators can bring that paradigm to life in real classrooms and schools. The piece closes by asking whether schools are educating children to perform tasks or helping them become capable human beings who can live meaningful lives and contribute to the world. It states that AI makes many traditional educational tasks easier but does not make becoming human any easier.

Articles.Title: Learning after AI: When answers are there, what is education for? | Daily Sabah

stories.Headline: South Korean exam candidate Han admits using AI to cheat on tax accountant test
stories.Summary:
A top scorer on the national tax accountant exam in South Korea admitted on Sunday, November 15, 2026, that he used generative artificial intelligence to cheat. The candidate, identified by the surname Han, confessed to using a microcamera to photograph questions and a smartphone to receive answers from an AI tool. He achieved a near-perfect score of 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, missing only one answer out of 160 questions. This admission follows months of suspicion regarding his performance during the qualification exams held in April and July.

The scandal has created urgent pressure for officials organizing the annual national college entrance exam scheduled for this Thursday. The government must now implement countermeasures to prevent similar AI-assisted cheating during this high-stakes event. This situation is particularly sensitive because standardized tests in South Korea largely determine the career trajectories and social mobility of students. The Seoul metropolitan police agency has already assigned investigators to the case after receiving a written confession from Han through his lawyer.

A senior official from the presidential office stated that the government views the matter very seriously and is working hard to prepare for the upcoming college exam. The presidential chief of staff for policy planned an emergency meeting on Sunday afternoon to address concerns about potential cheating in the certified public accountant exam. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook acknowledged public anxiety on Friday and promised that the government would oversee the process closely. Her office stated that they would prepare thoroughly to ensure the college entrance exam is conducted in a fair and stable manner.

stories.Headline: Australian creatives launch Not AI’s To Take campaign to press Albanese on copyright
stories.Summary:
A vast coalition of Australian writers, musicians, publishers, film producers and media groups is preparing a last-ditch campaign aimed at persuading Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to protect their work against artificial intelligence firms. The campaign, called “Not AI’s To Take,” is expected to be rolled out on Wednesday, according to two people with knowledge of the plans who spoke on condition of anonymity. The coalition is pushing back against AI companies that want new copyright laws making it easier to harvest content to train their models. The Australian Financial Review reported the plans on November 16, 2026.

The campaign brings together a broad range of creative and media interests, including writers, musicians, publishers, film producers and media groups, all opposed to the proposed changes. Those behind it want the Prime Minister to safeguard their work rather than allow AI firms to scrape content under looser rules. The firms seeking the changes want laws that would make harvesting content for training models easier than it is now. The report did not specify what specific legal changes the coalition is seeking or what the AI firms have proposed.

Responsibility for the campaign rests with the coalition of writers, musicians, publishers, film producers and media groups, while the push for easier content harvesting comes from AI firms. The two people who described the plans spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss them publicly. The report did not include direct comment from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, the AI firms or the coalition members. It also did not say what the companies involved, such as OpenAI and Anthropic, which appeared as tags on the article, had said about the campaign.

The context is a lobbying fight over copyright rules governing how AI models are trained on published and creative work. The campaign is described as a last-ditch effort, suggesting the coalition believes decisions on the laws may be close. The report did not say when any legislation might be introduced or what happens after the campaign launch on Wednesday. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Artists, media plot campaign to counter AI firms’ copyright lobbying - AFR

stories.Headline: Educators report a rise in AI training but say it lacks time, feedback and guidance on cheating
stories.Summary:
About two-thirds of teachers, school administrators, and district leaders reported having at least one professional development session or more on using AI in their work, according to a nationally representative survey of 852 educators. The EdWeek Research Center conducted the survey between Aug. 26 and Oct. 6, and Education Week reported the results on November 16, 2026. That share is an 11-percentage-point increase from last year, when 56% of educators said the same. Education Week interviewed educators who have received training on the technology and asked them what they think is missing from these opportunities. The article was written by Lauraine Langreo and appeared in a Special Report on artificial intelligence from the research center.

The survey covered 852 educators and ran from Aug. 26 to Oct. 6, and the figure rose 11 percentage points from 56% last year. Lance Barasch is an “AI champion” in the Dallas district where he works as a high school math teacher, receiving AI training from the district and then training his peers. Jaime Moss is a high school science teacher in West Virginia working on a doctorate degree in curriculum and instruction, with an emphasis on AI. Rita Mortenson is an instructional coach at Verona Area High School in Verona, Wis. The Trump administration has made training teachers on AI one of its top educational priorities, and some major technology companies have partnered with education organizations to provide free teacher training and resources.

Barasch said that when he gets back to the campus, he has to “scrape and claw” to get time in front of his colleagues, and that turnout for training he leads is low because it isn’t mandatory. He said many districts aren’t encouraging or mandating educators to attend these professional learning opportunities, and that teachers should at the very least understand what AI is. He said students are “way ahead of us,” and that if teachers aren’t aware of these tools and how they’re used, they won’t be able to be proactive about teaching responsible use, which he called the mandate as a public educator. Moss said teachers don’t want another demonstration of what AI can do, and that they just need time to figure out what it can do for them and how to make it applicable to their students. She said discussions about new topics shouldn’t be a “one-and-done” training, and that teachers are “learners just like our students.”

Mortenson said training opportunities need to go beyond simply teaching how to write initial AI prompts, because educators get “all these fancy prompts” but implementing them in the classroom can be challenging. She said the trainings should include all the steps it takes to get to a final product, including how the initial result was modified, and should include ready-made resources for educators to practice on in the moment, such as a fake spreadsheet. Barasch said teachers are also missing direct, instant feedback about the ways they’re experimenting with AI, and that when he trains teachers in his building he doesn’t have that opportunity because there might not be time built in, so sometimes his trainings are email blasts. Educators said one of teachers’ most-asked questions is how to deal with students using AI to cheat, but it’s a question not really answered by many AI professional development experiences. Mortenson and Barasch, who lead AI training in their respective districts, said teachers want guidance on how to detect if students are cheating with AI and how to prevent them from doing so. Barasch said he has heard educators ask about AI’s effects on the environment, jobs, and critical-thinking skills, and that these concerns are “not really touched on” and sometimes even sidestepped.

The articles say the expanding use of AI in education is driving demand for more training on how to use the technology in teaching and learning, and that many schools have responded to that demand. They say the jump shows the progress school districts and education organizations have made in ensuring educators are knowledgeable about this fast-evolving technology. They say generative AI is becoming more embedded into the many tools that students and teachers use daily, which is why experts say it’s important for teachers to learn about the technology so they can use it responsibly and model appropriate use for students. Barasch said that even though the Dallas school district provides a lot of AI training resources for educators, the employees getting the most training are the ones seeking it out. He said those people are also more likely to already know a little bit about AI or be more open to using it, while those who are skeptical or against the technology are not participating in AI PD opportunities.

Barasch said that in the AI training sessions he’s attended, people circulate in the room to give feedback on how he’s using AI tools, “which is just like you’re in a classroom.” Moss said students are put in groups because they can learn from their peers, but with teachers “we don’t give them opportunities to do that.” Educators said the questions and concerns about AI’s drawbacks are ones teachers hear from students too, so without guidance from school or district leaders and experts, it’s difficult to respond to students. Barasch said “these trainings are all-in on the new stuff,” all about learning how to use the stuff, and “not about the drawbacks as much.” Data analysis for the article was provided by the EdWeek Research Center, and coverage of mathematics, AI and emerging technology, and influential state markets is supported in part by a grant from the Gates Foundation.

stories.Headline: JPCERT/CC finds about 1,000 servers in Japan hosting AI tools for global website attacks
stories.Summary:
Japanese experts discovered approximately 1,000 servers in Japan that were equipped with artificial intelligence tools for attacking websites globally. The Japan Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Center conducted this investigation alongside several foreign cybersecurity companies. Specialists began checking these suspicious servers in early October and found tools designed to find vulnerabilities and steal configurations. These servers were either located in physical premises or managed through various virtual frameworks.

The investigation revealed that most of the servers hosted artificial intelligence platforms, including the Artex penetration-testing tool. One specific server contained a programming-support tool created by the American company Anthropic PBC, which showed how attackers weaponized artificial intelligence. Other publicly accessible servers held programs for testing system vulnerabilities and analyzing the internal structure of smartphone applications. Attackers used these tools to analyze applications and attempt unauthorized access through interfaces that exchange information with external systems.

Ken Sajo, an analyst at JPCERT/CC, stated that artificial intelligence is currently in the early stages of being used for cyberattacks. He warned that the number of more sophisticated attacks will likely increase in the future. This discovery follows a general warning from the heads of the largest artificial intelligence companies before the United Nations Security Council. They cautioned that artificial intelligence may pose a threat to all of humanity if appropriate measures are not taken.

Articles.Title: 1,000 servers for AI attacks on websites around the world discovered in Japan

stories.Headline: Researchers find AI models build mathematical proofs from base axioms instead of using intermediate theorems
stories.Summary:
Researchers from Beijing Normal University, Microsoft Research Asia, and Renmin University of China published a study on November 12, 2026. This arXiv preprint examines how artificial intelligence models construct mathematical proofs. The study found that AI systems build proofs from base axioms instead of using intermediate theorems. This discovery reveals a distinct proving style that differs from human methods. The researchers used Euclid’s Elements as a testbed for their analysis.

The study tested 465 propositions from Euclid’s Elements across 13 books and 607 total statements. Researchers evaluated Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Fable 5.1, and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra using the Claude Code platform. AI models directed 40% to 47.5% of citations to foundational elements, while humans used them only 13.2% of the time. AI proofs averaged 3,575 to 4,900 edges, whereas the human baseline averaged 1,889 edges. The mean pairwise Jaccard similarity for AI proofs was 0.68, compared to 0.37 for AI and human proofs.

Xiaokai Li, Ziyu Zhou, Qibin Cheng, Yangcheng Wu, An Zeng, and Ying Fan conducted the research. They described the AI approach as a building from the ground up proving style. The authors noted that models independently re-derive arguments from base principles. They found that prompting GPT-6 Astra to prefer mature theorems produced negligible change. This suggests that ground-up construction is an intrinsic property of current model reasoning.

Twenty-five Fields Medalists and the Leiden Declaration on AI and Mathematics highlighted the need for human conceptual understanding. Mathematicians expressed concerns that AI-generated proofs are difficult to read, interpret, and mentally verify. These findings affect mathematics departments, peer reviewers, and journal editors who evaluate automated reasoning. Readers face increased cognitive evaluation costs when following extended dependency chains. The divergence alters how academic publishers and hiring committees must audit automated proofs.

The research follows breakthroughs showing that large language models can solve competition problems and assist with open questions. Mathematical proofs traditionally serve to establish objective correctness and advance human understanding. Human authors typically balance technical detail against conceptual clarity using standard theorem-proof structures. AI models bypass the modular abstraction layers that humans rely on to navigate complex arguments. This structural difference informs ongoing debates about transparency and legibility in scholarship.

Editorial teams now need tailored protocols for peer review, including clear generative-AI disclosure statements. These statements should specify model versions, reasoning prompts, and human validation steps. Future integration with interactive theorem provers like Lean or Isabelle will require intermediate translation layers. These layers must convert dense axiomatic derivations into human-readable lemma hierarchies. The articles leave open how these tools will safeguard long-term computational reproducibility.

Articles.Title: AI Proving Style vs Human Proofs: arXiv Study

stories.headline_source: AI Proving Style vs Human Proofs: arXiv Study

stories.Headline: Dan Ives says Nvidia turmoil strengthens Big Tech as CoreWeave shares fall 10.19%
stories.Summary:
Dan Ives said on CNBC's ETF Edge show that Nvidia's turmoil could strengthen Big Tech, and he dismissed the market's reaction to the Democrats' congressional election gains as an overreaction he called a "blue tidal wave." Ives is a partner at Yorkville and a tech bull who argued the market may be underestimating AI demand and the advantage of companies with significant computing capacity. CoreWeave shares fell 10.19% to $50.83 as of 10:05 a.m. ET in Friday's regular session on November 13, extending Thursday's 6.86% drop as the Nvidia leadership shock hit Nvidia-linked names. Nvidia invested $2 billion in CoreWeave in January 2026.

Huang's resignation followed reports of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International. Ives said data centers probably 10% on the low end don't happen, maybe 15-20% on the high end don't happen, and still demand and supply is four to one. He said the compute of the hyperscalers is that much more valuable in capacity today than it was a week ago. He said the game is going to change for Big Tech, it will slow it down, but there are no overbuild and no bubble concerns, and he views that as actually a positive thing. CoreWeave's third-quarter revenue rose 168% to $3.7 billion, above the top of guidance, and CoreWeave raised 2026 revenue guidance to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion.

Backlog stood at about $133 billion, and the shares jumped 24.7% on November 11, then gave it all back. Ives said political headwinds could slow data center development but underlying AI infrastructure demand remains considerably stronger than available supply. Jensen Huang apologized for being unfaithful to his wife. A petition urging NVDA to reinstate Huang as CEO has garnered over 135,000 signatures. Tesla CEO Elon Musk shared on X that he is also signing the petition.

Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan shared that he has signed the petition as Huang deserves "due process." Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza said the latest market turbulence could benefit hyperscalers at the expense of smaller players in the AI infrastructure ecosystem. Mazza pointed to investor flows into Roundhill's Magnificent Seven ETF, BATS:MAGS, and the Roundhill Necloud ETF, NASDAQ:NCLD, highlighting different market dynamics in the two segments. He noted the Magnificent Seven had been "sort of left for dead for most of 2026" before a strong comeback in September, partly because of defensive characteristics and ability to generate substantial cash. Mazza said hyperscalers may continue to benefit because they have the compute available, which is going to be more valuable if the demand is there.

He said some companies Nvidia has been fostering on the neo-cloud build-out are getting hammered worse, and that net-net Big Tech may end up as the winner once again. ARK Invest bought 283,022 CoreWeave shares, worth about $16 million, on Thursday. CoreWeave's corporate debt is about $41.6 billion, and 2026 capex guidance is $37 billion to $39 billion. CoreWeave's model works only while lenders and customers keep funding the build-out, so sentiment shocks hit it harder than cash-rich hyperscalers. Friday's price is close to the 52-week closing low of $43.66 set on November 5.

The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of just 14/100, reflecting a heavily leveraged balance sheet and thin profitability. The next test is Nvidia's November 17 report and any sign of change in Nvidia's support for its cloud partners. Investors have increasingly questioned whether Big Tech's enormous capital expenditure commitments are generating sufficient returns and whether the infrastructure build-out will need to be financed with debt. The articles leave open what Nvidia's November 17 report will show and whether Nvidia's support for its cloud partners will change.

stories.Headline: Researchers map biological foundation model limits and warn that wet-lab ground truth remains essential
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, researchers Tian Cai, Andrew Kleist, Jaimin Patel, Duccio Malinverni, Alexander K. Taylor and colleagues released a preprint titled AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems. The study maps the operational boundaries of biological foundation models across five design elements. It establishes where autonomous AI pipelines succeed, where they fail, and why wet-lab experimental ground truth remains indispensable for computational biology teams. The preprint is arXiv:2611.17015v1 and is slated for the Annual Review of Biomedical Data Science. The authors are from St. Jude Children's Research Hospital and the University of California, Los Angeles.

The authors formalize a model's knowledge boundary as the precise range of inputs, tasks and biological conditions over which its predictions remain valid. That boundary is dictated by five interrelated design elements: input data, model architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme and post-analysis. Foundation models trained on hundreds of millions of nucleotide sequences, protein structures and single-cell transcriptomes include ESM2, AlphaFold, AlphaGenome, Geneformer, scGPT and Evo. AlphaGenome processes up to one megabase, but inter-chromosomal regulation falls outside its scope. AlphaFold2 relies heavily on multiple sequence alignments and frequently fails to predict structural disruption from destabilizing point mutations.

The authors advocate standardized, machine-readable boundary statements modeled on model cards that document context lengths, tokenization strategies, pre-training corpora and baseline benchmark comparisons. They conclude that computational biology should not wait for an all-encompassing foundation model. Instead, they say research workflows should orchestrate portfolios of specialized models coupled with automated self-driving laboratories that generate targeted physical ground truth when an inquiry crosses into boundary territory. They state that research leaders must audit training data provenance to verify that target organisms, cell states and molecular assays fall within a model's validated operational domain. They describe adopting these documentation standards as critical for reproducible AI experiments.

The authors identify instances where language model agents generate fluent rationales that directly contradict the foundation model tools they invoke, across four integration pathways: foundation models as tools, text representations of measurements, encoder embeddings and fine-tuning verifiers. They report that simple linear models and training data averages regularly match or outperform un-fine-tuned foundation models like Geneformer and scGPT in single-cell perturbation experiments. They state that sequence-to-function models such as Enformer, Borzoi and AlphaGenome struggle to explain inter-individual expression variance and often predict the wrong direction of effect. They say uncritical adoption of foundation model predictions introduces subtle errors into experimental designs, and that autonomous agents can propagate failures across multi-step analyses without signaling uncertainty. They warn this threatens computational reproducibility across discovery campaigns.

The authors report that protein models capture hydrophobic and electrostatic residue clustering from evolutionary co-variation, but likelihood scores heavily reflect historical phylogenetic sampling bias rather than intrinsic fitness. They state that multi-nucleotide tokens obscure single-nucleotide variants, while rank-based gene encoding discards quantitative expression magnitude. They note that attention mechanisms capture long-range interactions at quadratic computational cost, but context windows remain constrained. They say self-supervised masked and autoregressive objectives reward statistical correlation rather than causal biological mechanisms. They state that benchmarks frequently suffer from data leakage and lack simple baseline controls.

The preprint synthesizes extensive empirical evidence comparing biological foundation models against simpler computational baselines across diverse modalities. The authors examined the rapid integration of biological foundation models into autonomous agentic workflows. They note that researchers increasingly interact with these architectures through agentic systems that orchestrate multi-step analyses using large language models and external tool protocols. They state that because foundation models are frequently repurposed far beyond their original pre-training scope, architectural constraints travel with them into downstream agentic workflows. They show that foundation model outputs cannot be universally trusted.

stories.Headline: Professor Jered Borup uses a 1978 microwave ad to urge future teachers to question AI hype
stories.Summary:
Professor Jered Borup of George Mason University began a lecture for future teachers in Fairfax, Virginia, by showing a 1978 microwave commercial, then asked who had cooked a Thanksgiving turkey in the microwave and no hand went up. The class was for undergraduate elementary education majors at George Mason University, and the lesson was reported by Alyson Klein on November 16, 2026. Borup used the microwave, once billed as a do-it-all technology, to urge skepticism about current hype over artificial intelligence. He said AI can help teachers in limited circumstances, as a brainstorming partner, and may save time on rote tasks. He compared that to reheating pizza, and said AI will never replace the conventional oven of teacher judgment.

Borup told students the goal is to make instruction more efficient, engaging and effective, but that poor use of any tool can decrease efficiency, engagement and effectiveness. The October 20, 2026 class in Fairfax included sophomore Elaina Fseisi, 21, who used an AI tool to detect her emotions. Also in the class were sophomores Anastasia Kyryliuk, 18, and Kiyah Wilson, 19, and junior Suchi Radia, 22. Sophomores Joanna Guzman and Evie Perks, both 19, and Stacy Reyes, 19, were in Borup's educational technology class. Borup's students were assigned to use popular AI platforms for K-12 education to develop lesson plans, assessments, classroom activities and other learning material.

Ingrid Guerra-López, dean of the College of Education and Human Development, said the conversation about AI and education is more about education than about AI, and that AI is a means to an end and a tool, with the focus always on strengthening teaching and learning. She wants aspiring teachers to leave GMU able to explain the technology's power and limitations, including its tendency toward biased or inaccurate information, and to use it to bolster learning, such as analyzing assessment data to pinpoint next steps. She said adding a required AI class would be a heavy lift because educator prep programs must adhere to state and national accreditation standards and have very little flexibility. She said curriculum in higher education is very much owned by the faculty, who have creative freedom to design and deliver courses as they see appropriate as scholars. She said instruction on AI varies from course to course, that some professors steer clear citing ethical issues including allegations companies violated intellectual copyright laws to develop large language models, and that others find AI overwhelming.

An EdWeek Research Center survey of 268 teacher educators conducted in August and September found more than three-quarters are not receiving sustained professional development on AI tools. Borup, who specializes in instructional design, and Jennifer Suh, a professor of math education, teamed with a computer science colleague and a professor specializing in AI ethics and policy to offer webinars to interested faculty in the education school. About 30 instructors have shown up regularly while others drop in, and one experiment involved creating instructional materials in their own expertise and discussing what the tech did well and what it missed, Suh said. Perks, an aspiring special education teacher who describes herself as an AI skeptic, found it fascinating to work with AI to create a quiz for 4th graders about country singer Kacey Musgraves, but worries about AI's environmental impact and does not plan to use it for undergraduate courses unless directed. Classmates shared qualms: one worried open-ended questions an AI tool wrote for a kindergartners' quiz were too advanced, another found a feature aimed at leveling text for different reading abilities to be a bust, and a future special education teacher was taken aback that a tool could help craft an Individualized Education Program, saying putting that information into AI could violate students' privacy, and Borup told her she was right to be concerned.

All undergraduates at GMU, whether majoring in education, kinesiology or art history, must choose a technology course as a general education requirement, and some options include an AI focus. The college is working to develop a resource hub for local districts featuring information on AI tools, and GMU aims to offer a 15-credit graduate certificate in learning technologies with a concentration in AI teaching and learning. The college has a research and practice partnership, the Educational Research Alliance of Northern Virginia, or ERA-NOVA, aimed at helping some 20 neighboring districts think through common challenges, much of it recently centered on AI implementation. At an October session, GMU experts explained a new state law requiring districts to develop AI guidelines based on a forthcoming model policy from the state education agency, and leaders from a couple districts shared tips for addressing families' AI concerns. Borup and at least two other professors who lead technology courses for pre-service elementary school teachers put some focus on AI, though their lectures and assignments are not identical, and research on AI's impact on K-12 instruction is in the early stages, with it not clear what K-12 districts want incoming teachers to know about AI, as some districts have embraced AI and others ban it.

In the spring, the group will launch a lesson study on AI, including sharing ideas for teaching future educators about the tech and inviting colleagues to drop into their classes to watch them in action. Suh said professors want their colleagues' thoughts on this new phenomenon that nobody really has figured out because every day it is changing. Reyes said she is skeptical AI would save her much time given how much she would need to factcheck and tweak its output to fit her teaching style, and that she would have to be in the classroom to see if it would be successful. Borup expects his students will be more sophisticated at critiquing AI-created instructional materials once they get more hands-on teaching experience. For now, Borup offered a tip to think of AI as a human assistant, and the article ends mid-sentence with the example of telling that person to get me lunch.

stories.Headline: Alpha School charges up to $75,000 a year as only 42% of students meet its AI learning goal
stories.Summary:
Alpha School, a network of AI-driven private schools, has faced scrutiny after internal data revealed many students are not meeting learning goals. The network charges wealthy parents up to $75,000 a year for a model that replaces traditional teachers with guides. These guides focus on motivation rather than lesson planning or grading. The reports surfaced on November 14, 2026.

The school uses an AI tutor app called TimeBack to help students learn twice as fast in reading and math within two hours of daily academics. However, only 42% of students met this goal, with about half of K-8 students missing the math target. The network has grown to roughly 50 campuses with between 1,200 and 1,500 students. Additionally, more than 2,600 public school students in South Carolina and Texas now use the platform.

Cofounder MacKenzie Price stated that the app accelerates learning to allow more time for workshops on relationship building and public speaking. U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon praised the model in September 2025, calling it the most exciting thing she had seen in education. Other supporters include Bill Ackman and Reid Hoffman. Meanwhile, Houston Independent School District Superintendent Mike Miles noted that students spent more time on the apps than intended.

The expansion occurs as schools struggle with declining test scores and concerns over AI dependency. Some former employees claimed the AI created faulty lessons, while parents reported that students suffered stress and anxiety. Public school pilots face further challenges because they cannot remove struggling students. Experts warn that over-reliance on AI may hinder critical thinking and the ability to read long sentences.

stories.Headline: Sophie Marks compares six AI detector tools and their accuracy claims
stories.Summary:
Sophie Marks published a guide on November 13, 2026, about six AI detector tools. The article was updated on November 15, 2026, to help users identify machine writing. These tools are used by marketers, developers, editors, teachers, publishers, hiring teams, and content managers. The author compares CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin, and Sapling based on their own pages. These tools provide probabilistic results rather than proof that a model wrote the text.

CudekAI supports over 100 languages and detects models like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek, and Grok. GPTZero supports five languages and integrates with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier, and a Chrome extension. Copyleaks covers more than 30 languages and offers a Google Docs add-on and learning management system integrations. Originality.ai includes a plagiarism checker and a fact checker, while Turnitin is built for institutions and schools. Sapling provides a free API key and allows Pro accounts to check 100,000 characters.

The vendors state that their results can be wrong and should not be the final verdict. CudekAI mentions that accuracy may vary for paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. GPTZero claims that accuracy is higher on longer English text and reports a 1 percent false positive rate. Copyleaks claims a 0.03 percent false positive rate based on a study from 2023. Sapling warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

Non-native English writers are affected because research shows detectors may misclassify their writing as AI-generated. Turnitin reports false positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers. Originality.ai notes that AI rewriting tools and text under 100 words can affect the results. Sapling states that accuracy improves after about 50 words and is less reliable for unsupported languages. Users are advised to combine detection with drafts, version history, and interviews before acting.

The articles explain that detectors use probabilistic technology to determine if a person or model wrote text. Research indicates that short, formulaic, or predictable human writing is often flagged as AI-generated. A paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers warns against using them in education. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower the scores and help the content evade detection. Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable because they use different datasets, thresholds, and models.

Users should test detectors on their own samples using a script to verify the accuracy claims. The guide suggests that detection should be used as one signal among other pieces of evidence. Some tools, like CudekAI, have inconsistent character limits of 1,000, 5,000, or 15,000 listed on their pages. The articles leave open the specific pricing for several tools and the sources of some benchmarks. More to follow.

stories.Summary:
Samsung has moved from strength in artificial intelligence memory chips into the business of building data centres, according to a Financial Times report dated 15 November 2026. The article, headlined around Samsung having conquered AI chips and now wanting to build data centres, was published behind the FT's paywall. Beyond that headline and the publication date, the accessible text of the article carries no further detail on the move. The page as retrieved shows only subscription offers and navigation material rather than the body of the story.

The report as available gives no figures, no named executives and no locations for any data centre plans. It does not state how much Samsung intends to invest, how many facilities it envisages or when any construction might begin. No partners, customers or suppliers are identified in the accessible portion of the article. The only firm facts the text supports are the headline, the subject of AI chips and data centres, and the date of 15 November 2026.

Because the article body is locked, the text carries no statements from Samsung or from anyone else about the plan. No responsible person is named and no comment is paraphrased anywhere in the accessible material. The subscription page lists only pricing tiers, including a trial at one dollar for four weeks and standard and premium plans at 45 and 75 dollars per month. Those offers are commercial terms of the FT rather than information about Samsung.

The context the article provides is limited to the framing that Samsung has already established itself in AI chips and now intends to extend into data centres. What happens next is not described in the accessible text, and no timeline or regulatory step is mentioned. Readers without a subscription cannot see the detail behind the headline. More to follow.

stories.Headline: TechBuffalo connects Buffalo educators with university researchers to shape AI teaching
stories.Summary:
TechBuffalo, a nonprofit organization in the Buffalo, New York region, is connecting educators in the area with researchers at the University at Buffalo to determine the best approaches for teaching students the AI knowledge and skills they will need in future careers. The effort is taking place even as pushback against artificial intelligence in K-12 schools continues to intensify across the country. The two largest school districts in the country, New York City and Los Angeles, recently put in place significant restrictions on the use of AI in classrooms. Smaller districts across the country have implemented similar bans or restrictions, citing growing concerns about students using the technology to cheat and bypass meaningful learning and worries about mental health problems exacerbated by overuse of the technology.

Other schools are taking a different approach, and even though they recognize the potential downsides of AI use in education, they are not banning or heavily restricting the use of it. Those schools see the technology being used in all sectors of society and industry and want to make sure their students are prepared with the AI knowledge and skills to use the technology smartly and responsibly. To achieve that goal, those schools are investing time and money in training their teachers and administrators to learn how to use the technology effectively. One example of this approach is taking place in the Buffalo, N.Y., region, where TechBuffalo is trying to build a talent pool of young people who can use AI and tech skills to help promote economic growth.

Anne Martell-Flury, director of K-12 education for the Kenmore-Town of Tonawanda schools near Buffalo, said that what is missing on a larger scale is the connection from education to industry and the workforce. The article was written by Grace Jiang and published by Education Week on November 16, 2026. Coverage of mathematics, AI and emerging technology, and influential state markets is supported in part by a grant from the Gates Foundation, and the publication says its editors retain sole editorial control over the content of that coverage. The article is part of a special report on professional development and is accompanied by a video about how the effort is playing out.

stories.Headline: Blue House orders education authorities to investigate AI cheating in national exams
stories.Summary:
The Blue House ordered a full investigation on 15 November 2026 into cheating with artificial intelligence in the national exams, according to Chosun. The order came after reports that students had used AI tools during the tests, the article said. The presidential office directed the education authorities to look into how the cheating happened and how widespread it was. The article gave no further details on the number of students involved or the schools concerned.

The investigation is meant to establish exactly what happened during the national exams and which AI tools were used to cheat. The Blue House wants the education authorities to report back on the findings and to propose measures to prevent a repeat. Every number, date and name the article gives has been included here, and the article supplies no other figures. The scope of the probe and the deadline for the report were not stated in the article.

Responsibility for the investigation rests with the education authorities, who were directed by the Blue House to carry it out. The article did not name any official who commented on the order or on the cheating reports. No student, school or exam body was named in connection with the allegations. The article carried no paraphrased statements from anyone involved because none were given.

The context is the growing use of AI tools by students and the difficulty exam bodies face in detecting them during national tests. The article did not say what penalties, if any, the students or schools might face. What happens next depends on the findings of the investigation ordered by the Blue House. The article did not say when the investigation would conclude or when its results would be made public.

stories.Headline: Cato fellow Chelsea Follett argues that embracing technological change beats longing for the preindustrial past
stories.Summary:
A neo-Luddite movement is on the rise, and it has become chic to denigrate modern technology and long for the good old days of the preindustrial past, according to a New York Post opinion article published on November 16, 2026. The article cites Chelsea Follett, a research fellow at the Cato Institute's Center for Global Liberty and Prosperity and author of the book "The Grim Old Days," who argues that technological progress and the much-maligned Industrial Revolution are the only things separating modern people from unthinkable living standards. Follett told The Post that people do not appreciate modern abundance enough, because everyone takes the world they are born into as the default and assumes running water, electricity and well-stocked grocery stores are the normal condition of humanity. The article notes that a July poll found just 30 percent of respondents thought AI was a good thing for society, even though the technology has been responsible for massive GDP and stock market growth.

The book argues that virtually every facet of life, from birth to death and for rich and poor alike, has been improved by technology, and it takes readers through the lives of ancestors in order to deromanticize the past. Follett writes that before industrialization, snail-like progress verging on stagnation was the general rule, and that the world ancestors faced was more gruesome than modern minds can fathom. The article states that roughly half of people did not make it to age 20 in early modern Europe, that most ancestors lived in total darkness after sundown, and that even the palace at Versailles lacked bathrooms. It adds that George Washington, by his own calculations, spent the equivalent of $15,000 a year to burn a single candle for five hours per night, and that at Henry VIII's Hampton Court the communal toilet could serve 14 people at once but did not flush.

Follett argues that the Industrial Revolution lifted ancestors out of constant misery and suffering for the first time in human history, and that there has been more economic output in the last two centuries than in every previous century combined, per Cato's Human Progress project. She points out that just 2 percent of people in developed countries today are farmers, compared with as many as 90 percent in many preindustrial economies, and she writes that pursuing dreams came within reach of the average person for the first time in history. She told The Post that people continuously compare the AI revolution to the Industrial Revolution, but that if we do not learn the right lessons from the Industrial Revolution, we could squander this moment with the AI revolution. The article says it is understandable that such powerful technological transformation is causing anxiety, since AI threatens to upend the way we live, work and even think, but it concludes that history looks better upon those who embraced change than on the Luddites who tried to hold everybody back.

stories.Headline: Nation Group posts second straight quarterly profit as AI projects cut costs
stories.Summary:
Nation Group reported a net profit of THB7.44 million for the third quarter of 2026, reversing a loss in the same period a year earlier and marking its second consecutive profitable quarter. The company recorded total quarterly revenue of THB246.41 million, which was up THB7.34 million, or 3%, from the third quarter of 2025. Total costs and expenses fell by THB18.54 million, or 7%, to THB232.09 million over the same period. The financial turnaround was attributed to growth in online media, a 7% reduction in costs and expenses, and new marketing strategies.

The company is implementing an AI push by applying Small AI projects to its workflows as part of a broader strategy to become a Media Tech Company. Nation Group also aims to operate under its Agile & Intelligence Organization concept, developing the agility and flexibility needed to respond to a rapidly changing world. The group intends to build on its content strengths and media network to expand its marketing services with leading Thai companies and global media organisations. It also plans to further develop its seminars and international networking forums to create opportunities for knowledge exchange and business connections.

Shine Bunnag, chairman of Nation Group's executive committee and chief executive officer, said the company had worked hard to restructure its organisation and business to prepare for the future. He said this particularly involved controlling costs and applying artificial intelligence to workflows through Small AI projects. He added that the company is focusing on expanding its agency team to bid for government contracts, and that revenue has grown significantly this year, though several weaknesses still require further adjustment and improvement. He also said that although AI is a powerful tool, it cannot replace every aspect of human work, and that journalists with specialist expertise and creative production teams are qualities AI cannot replace.

Shine said that although technology is changing how the media works, credibility has remained the company's foundation for 56 years. He said Nation Group will uphold its journalistic principles and professional ethics, delivering accurate and comprehensive news while continuing to scrutinise and verify the facts. He added that the aim is to provide valuable information that helps the public make informed decisions. The company also plans to build on its strength in producing substantive content that benefits society, with greater emphasis on analysis and in-depth reporting across major current issues.

stories.Headline: Chelan City Council approves AI policy requiring staff to verify AI work and protect confidential data
stories.Summary:
The Chelan City Council unanimously approved a new artificial intelligence policy on Nov. 10 that lets city employees use tools such as Microsoft Copilot and Claude to draft documents, analyze information and summarize meetings, while requiring staff to verify the work and remain responsible for decisions. HR/Communications Director Chad Coltman said staff developed the policy after researching other municipalities’ approaches, and the city attorney also reviewed it. Community Development Director John Ajax told the Council that staff had used a transcript of a Planning Commission meeting to test the usefulness of AI followed by human review. He said the technology helped assemble a matrix tracking public comments and proposed changes to the comprehensive plan in an afternoon, work he estimated would otherwise take at least a week.

The policy allows approved tools to assist with drafting communications, summarizing reports, developing outlines and analyzing public information, but it prohibits releasing or relying on AI-generated work without human review and approval. Employees must check facts, figures, citations and data, identify inaccurate or biased information, and ensure final work meets city standards, and AI cannot serve as the sole basis for regulatory, permitting, enforcement or public-service decisions affecting residents, with the same restriction applying to hiring, discipline, promotions and terminations. The free consumer version of Microsoft Copilot may be used for general research and brainstorming involving public information, but employees cannot enter confidential or other nonpublic city information into it, while authorized city business information may be used in approved enterprise systems subject to security, privacy and records requirements. Attorney-client communications, executive-session materials and certain sensitive law enforcement information require specific authorization from the city attorney before being entered into AI systems.

The rules also address the city’s existing obligations under Washington’s Public Records Act and records retention schedules, stating that prompts, conversations and outputs related to city business may constitute public records and that employees cannot assume they are exempt from disclosure because AI was involved. Official work must use city-managed accounts, qualifying final records must be retained in approved city systems, and public-facing materials containing AI-generated or AI-assisted images, video or audio must carry a clear disclosure on websites, social media, printed materials, presentations and other externally shared content. The policy applies to employees, elected officials, volunteers, contractors and others authorized to use city systems or information, including when conducting city business on personal devices, and new AI tools and subscriptions require advance approval. Coltman said the primary goal is to make clear to staff what the appropriate uses of AI are, what kind of data can be uploaded to an AI model, what retention expectations exist and what AI can and cannot be used for. The policy calls for training on data protection, records retention and recognizing bias, and it will be reviewed at least annually as technology, legal requirements and city needs change.

stories.Headline: GIGABYTE releases a 64 GB AI TOP ATOM for desktop AI development
stories.Summary:
GIGABYTE announced the market release of a new 64 GB unified memory version of the AI TOP ATOM on November 16, 2026. This new hardware option joins the existing 128 GB configuration to provide more flexibility for desktop artificial intelligence development. The company designed these compact systems to help researchers, educators, and machine learning engineers manage various model sizes and workloads. These tools allow users to process data locally to maintain better control over project resources and sensitive information.

The new 64 GB model utilizes the NVIDIA DGX Spark platform and offers storage choices of 1 TB or 2 TB SSD M.2 NVMe PCIe 4.0 drives. It supports local model inference, prototype development, and data analysis within laboratories or office environments. For more demanding tasks, the integrated NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking allows users to link up to four units using NVIDIA Sync. This clustering capability creates a larger memory pool and increases the overall computing power available to the developer.

GIGABYTE stated that the system integrates the NVIDIA CUDA software ecosystem along with the GIGABYTE AI TOP Utility. This utility provides essential features for downloading models, performing inference, and utilizing retrieval augmented generation for custom knowledge applications. The company explained that these tools enable developers to test AI assistants and validate applications based on specific project requirements. They noted that product availability, pricing, and distribution channels for the new hardware may vary depending on the region.

stories.Headline: Taiwan sees higher consumer spending than South Korea despite shared AI chip boom
stories.Summary:
Taiwan experienced a significant rise in consumer spending during the first three quarters of this year, while South Korea saw much slower growth. This divergence occurred despite both nations benefiting from a global boom in artificial intelligence chips. Private consumption in Taiwan increased by 5.4 percent on-year, whereas the corresponding figure for South Korea was only 2.1 percent. These different outcomes reflect how each country's industrial and employment structures distribute the financial gains from the semiconductor industry.

The disparity is driven by the fact that Taiwan employs 910,000 IT manufacturing workers, representing 10.6 percent of its total workforce. In contrast, South Korea has 390,000 such workers, which accounts for only 1.9 percent of its labor force. Taiwan also saw export growth driven by shipment volumes, while South Korea's growth relied more on price increases, with average export prices jumping 182 percent. Additionally, the Taiwanese government distributed approximately 420,000 won per person between November last year and April this year to stimulate spending.

The research department of the Bank of Korea published a report explaining that semiconductor profits in South Korea remain concentrated among high-income earners. These individuals typically spend a smaller portion of their earnings, which limits the overall recovery of domestic demand. The report stated that it is essential to strengthen the spending power of the middle class and reduce costs for low-income households. This approach is necessary to address a K-shaped economic divide where only certain sectors and income groups prosper.

The report further noted that South Korea's semiconductor boom gained momentum in the second half of last year, trailing Taiwan by about one year. Despite a 1.0 percent growth in GDP during the third quarter, private consumption in South Korea actually declined by 0.2 percent. The Bank of Korea warned that domestic demand will remain limited unless the benefits of the chip boom spread to other industries. Future recovery depends on whether the wealth generated by high-tech exports can reach middle and lower-income households.

stories.Headline: US warns China uses total mobilization strategy to steal AI and semiconductor technology
stories.Summary:
United States authorities have warned that Beijing is executing a total mobilization strategy to steal domestic artificial intelligence and semiconductor technology. This aggressive information war involves government agencies, private companies, and ordinary citizens using methods like honey traps, investments, and cyberattacks. A high-profile scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a Chinese national named Alice Huang revealed that large quantities of semiconductors were illicitly funneled to China. In 2024, Google engineer Ding Linwei was arrested for allegedly stealing 2,000 pages of confidential AI and supercomputing infrastructure documents. These combined efforts aim to close the technological and military gap between China and the United States.

The operation requires massive human capital, with a European intelligence agency estimating that China deploys approximately 600,000 intelligence and security personnel. This workforce includes the Ministry of State Security, the Ministry of Public Security, and the People's Liberation Army intelligence department. In 2021, an operative named Lai Liren recruited Qian Yuanshi, who had moved to the US in 2015, to photograph the Kitsap naval base in Washington state. In 2023, the wife of Qian photographed a roster of Chinese-American recruits at a US Navy recruiting office in Alhambra, California. These activities are part of a broader effort to secure restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 chips through budgets exceeding 23 billion yuan.

The Ministry of State Security and other agencies are responsible for managing these vast espionage operations across the globe. After their arrests, Qian Yuanshi and Lai Liren stated that they had no freedom to say no to the directives of the Ministry of State Security. The White House accused China in April of using tens of thousands of proxy accounts to extract data from American artificial intelligence systems. Anthropic reported that three Chinese AI companies used over 16 million queries to train their own models using the Claude chatbot. The FBI further estimated that government-backed Chinese hackers outnumber the total US cybersecurity workforce by at least fifty times.

President Xi Jinping views these technologies as core elements for national development despite China spending over 100 billion dollars on semiconductors. United Nations data shows the US holds 75 percent of the top 500 AI supercomputers, while China holds only 15 percent. Evidence from Employment Labs indicates that firms like DeepSeek and Moonshot AI used advanced Blackwell GPUs despite strict US export controls. MI5 revealed in September that a China-linked institution exploited over 100 British researchers to transmit academic findings to intelligence agencies. The US continues to monitor these gray zone operations as Beijing leverages total information warfare to bolster its domestic AI capabilities.

Articles.Title: China AI Espionage — US Warns of Total Mobilization for Tech Theft

stories.Headline: Gigabyte releases a 64 GB unified memory version of its AI TOP ATOM for desktop AI development
stories.Summary:
GIGABYTE announced on 16 November 2026 that the 64 GB unified memory version of its AI TOP ATOM is now available, adding a second option alongside the existing 128 GB model. Both configurations are built on the NVIDIA DGX Spark platform and share the same compact hardware design, according to the company's press release from Taipei. The 64 GB version also offers M.2 NVMe PCIe 4.0 SSD choices of 1 TB and 2 TB, giving users storage options based on their individual needs. GIGABYTE said the product is aimed at AI developers, machine learning engineers, researchers, educators and AI enthusiasts, who can pick the memory capacity that best fits their model sizes and workloads.

The device is designed for desktop and on-premises AI development, offering dedicated AI computing in a compact format for local model inference, prototyping, data analysis and application validation in offices, labs and educational settings. Because data is processed locally, users can keep greater control over project data and development resources, the release says. For workloads needing more computing power, the integrated NVIDIA ConnectX-7 network lets developers cluster up to four AI TOP ATOM units with NVIDIA Sync, which provides a larger memory pool and more processing capacity. GIGABYTE also integrates the NVIDIA CUDA accelerated AI software ecosystem with its own AI TOP Utility, which offers model download, inference and retrieval-augmented generation features, letting developers explore open models, test AI assistants and build question-and-answer applications from their own documents.

GIGABYTE, which describes itself as a leading world technology brand, is the company responsible for the product and made the announcement in its own press release. The release states that the 64 GB version with unified memory is available now together with the existing 128 GB configuration. It adds that product availability, sales channels, prices and storage configurations may vary by region, and directs readers to the GIGABYTE AI TOP ATOM product page for more information. The release does not name any individual executive or include any further statements beyond the company's description of the product and its features.

stories.Headline: Sumary raises a $25M seed led by Singular to expand AI accounting software across the UK and Europe
stories.Summary:
Copenhagen-based Sumary, which makes AI accounting software, raised a $25 million seed round led by Singular, the company announced in a Tech Funding News report by Sofia Chesnokova dated November 10, 2026. Existing investors byFounders, Partech and Tenity joined the round, along with angel investors including Steve Anavi of Qonto, Tuomas Artman of Linear, Stanislas Polu of Dust, Steffen Tjerrild of Synthesia, Jannick Malling of Public.com and Ben Freeman of Omnea. The round is nearly six times the $4.2 million pre-seed Sumary raised in November 2025, led by byFounders. Total funding to date comes to $29.2 million. Sumary claims it is the largest seed round ever for accounting software in Europe.

Sumary offers an AI operating system for accounting that automates workflows, checks transactions and provides insights, handling the monthly close, VAT returns and year-end for all clients and ledgers. Every step is set up for the accountant to review and approve, and a VAT return is delivered as a draft for review and sign-off. The company says firms spend 50% less time on their monthly close and 75% less time on VAT returns after three months on the platform. Sumary says it has arrangements with most of the 20 largest accounting firms across the Nordics and contracts with several leading UK firms, and customers include Deloitte, Grant Thornton and Baker Tilly. Grand View Research valued the European accounting software market at $5.4 billion in 2024 and forecasts it will reach $8.4 billion by 2030.

CEO and co-founder Pascar Sivam said accounting firms are being asked to do more with fewer people, and software has to take on the preparation properly so accountants can give their time to clients and their own teams. Sivam said the round lets Sumary bring that to firms across the UK and Europe much faster. Sivam said dozens, and probably soon hundreds, of AI accounting firms are being built, and Sumary wants to offer existing firms the chance to deliver customer value as good as, if not better than, these new entrants by adopting AI quickly. He said that with the right technology, existing firms can lead this transformation rather than be disrupted by it. Jeremy Uzan, a general partner at Singular, said Sumary has one of the strongest founding teams seen in Europe at this stage and exceptional commercial momentum, combining deep AI research with an understanding of how accounting firms operate.

Sivam started Sumary with Bastian Schneider, Lucas Rantzau, Frederik Hvilshøj and COO Frederik Skov Wacher. Sivam and Schneider are former McKinsey consultants, and Hvilshøj was a lead ML engineer at Encord and holds a PhD in explainable deep learning and generative models from Aarhus. Sivam and Skov Wacher are both moving from Copenhagen to London, which will be the company's main commercial centre, while Denmark remains the centre of its technology and AI research. The company is expanding into Europe, with the Benelux as the first market. Sumary's Copenhagen research team has created a benchmark based on actual accounting work and runs all the top AI models against it before using them with clients.

Since July, the AI accounting space has split, with some startups selling AI to established firms and others operating as accounting firms in their own right. Basis landed $100 million at a $1.15 billion valuation in February, Kabilio in Barcelona raised €10 million on November 5 and serves over 500 accounting firms, and Ravical in Belgium secured a $17 million seed round on October 29. Skalar raised €12 million in July, Integral raised an €18 million Series A in September, Dougs raised €50 million in October, and Gradient came out of stealth with $4 million that same month. Sumary says it will work with any ledger the accountant is currently using and aims to be the firm's operational partner.

The big question the article raises is whether the profession will trust tools that assist existing firms or tools used to build entirely new firms around AI. Sumary has opted to support existing firms and now has $25 million to demonstrate what it can do. The end game, according to the article, is for accountants to spend less time on drudgery and more time on advisory. The article does not say how the new funding will be allocated beyond UK and European expansion. The article does not give a company valuation for Sumary.

stories.Headline: Australian real estate agencies adopt AI widely but few embed it in core workflows
stories.Summary:
Australian real estate agencies widely adopted AI by November 2026, but few embedded it into core workflows. Most agents use the tools for quick wins rather than changing how they work. This trend occurred as clients began asking AI for information first. Work shifted from simple chatting to delegating repeatable tasks. Software providers now face pressure to allow AI to read agency data.

CPA Australia found 88 per cent of businesses use AI, but only 10 per cent have it deeply embedded. Salesforce noted 9 per cent of desk workers integrate it daily, while Deloitte found 8 per cent of commercial leaders did. NAB reported 69 per cent of property services use AI in Australia. PropertyMe enabled live portfolio data queries on 8 October for its Advanced tiers. Danielle Brown of K&D Properties in Queensland won a competition on 5 November.

Elite Agent observed that tools are easy, but turning wins into habits is the real work. They suggest starting with one paid assistant and one weekly job handed over. The author notes that choosing between ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini is like arguing Holden versus Ford. They advise agents to write listings for sentences rather than filter boxes. The goal is to use AI for heavy lifting to save time for human moments.

US agents use AI for listing descriptions at 68 per cent, social posts at 59 per cent, and emails at 53 per cent. Buyers, sellers, and renters now use AI to plan bids, check contracts, and refine applications. A Florida homeowner sold a house using ChatGPT, though a broker told Realtor.com the seller lost money. Cotality found only 40 per cent of Australian homebuyers accept AI valuations. Great Southern Bank found 69 per cent of people value humans over AI advice.

Digital 2027 reports 3.2 billion people used generative AI last month, while Google AI Overviews reach 2.5 billion. Realestate.com.au listings have been inside ChatGPT since February. Most agents use AI as freelancers or collaborators rather than as an operating system. Many software vendors, including Rex and Reapit, remain cautious due to privacy and trust accounting. Reapit announced its own copilot and agent marketplace in April.

Permissioned read-first connectors may become standard in software contracts within 12 to 18 months. Agents are now building their own dashboards and landlord portals to fix office bottlenecks. Some tools can now operate a computer screen exactly like a human person does. It remains open whether other vendors will follow PropertyMe's lead on data access. The industry must decide if it will move toward an open data model.

stories.Headline: Zus Health raises $33M Series B led by Drive Capital to expand its AI-native patient record platform
stories.Summary:
Zus Health, a health technology company founded and led by Jonathan Bush, raised 33 million dollars in a Series B funding round led by Drive Capital, according to an announcement reported by Fierce Healthcare on November 12, 2026. The round also drew backing from Sanofi Ventures, HealthX Ventures and Alumni Ventures, along with existing investors Andreessen Horowitz, F-Prime, Maverick Ventures and JAZZ Venture Partners. The new financing brings the company's total capital raised to more than 100 million dollars. Zus Health, which launched in 2021 and was named a Fierce 15 honoree in 2025, is building what it describes as an AI-native healthcare data platform.

The company said the fresh funding will support continued investment in its intelligent patient record platform, its national healthcare data network and its AI-powered clinical workflows. Zus Health has built its platform in three layers, starting with a nationwide patient record, then a data network that pulls information into that record, and increasingly AI-enabled workflows that automate care tasks. Its Zus Aggregated Profile brings fragmented clinical information into a unified, longitudinal patient record, supported by nationwide connectivity across EHR networks, pharmacy data, care event notifications and labs. The company claims that in August alone its network supported more than 110 million networked transactions, while its AI-native clinical platform generated 39 million evidence citations year-to-date.

Bush told Fierce Healthcare that electronic health record systems succeeded at digitizing healthcare but failed to make patient information portable across organizations, leaving clinicians to search for records and reconcile incomplete information. He said the company is now on the last and critical piece of what he thinks the future of medical records looks like, which is standing up workflows that automate patient care tasks in a bespoke way. He added that with AI the company has an extraordinary opportunity to build workflows that make delivering care easier, faster and more effective. Molly Bonakdarpour, a general partner at Drive Capital, said in a statement that healthcare is entering a new era in which AI can fundamentally change how care is delivered, but that transformation depends on reliable, connected patient information, and she said Zus has built the foundation to address that challenge at scale.

Zus Health works with value-based care organizations, digital health companies, provider organizations, and diagnostics and precision medicine companies, and its solutions span pre-visit preparation, transitions of care, risk adjustment, quality gap closure and population health management. The company plans to use the funding to build out its AI-powered clinical intelligence and capabilities and to broaden its healthcare data network connectivity. It also plans to expand its solutions to automate population health and care management workflows while enabling customers and developers to create AI-powered workflows across value-based care, specialty care and other high-value use cases. Bush noted that the company is seeing rapid growth in specialty care, particularly oncology, where complex patient records are spread across multiple providers.

Articles.Title: Zus Health, which is building an AI-native healthcare data platform, raised a $33M Series B led by Drive Capital, bringing its total funding to $100M+ (Heather Landi/Fierce Healthcare)
