stories.Headline: South Korea's education ministry invalidates college entrance exam scores for anyone wearing AI glasses
stories.Summary:
Suspicion over the use of AI glasses began with the top scorer in the certified tax accountant exam and has spread to other licensing tests, the Kyunghyang Shinmun reported on November 13, 2026. The first perfect scorer in 19 years on the Law School Admission Test stated, after being suspected of cheating, that on the 19th this month the person would solve the Korean section of the College Scholastic Ability Test in real time. No evidence has been confirmed to support cheating by either person, the article said. On the 11th, at training for the dedicated task force staff on College Scholastic Ability Test smart glasses held at the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education in Yongsan-gu, Seoul, a company representative demonstrated smart glasses. This year, five cases of cheating using smart glasses were detected in national qualification exams.

The Ministry of Education decided that in next week’s College Scholastic Ability Test, merely wearing AI glasses will invalidate the exam and suspend eligibility to sit for the test next year. In a full-count inspection announced by the Ministry of Education on the 9th, four cases were also confirmed in internal assessments at middle and high schools nationwide. In communities for other professional exams such as certified public accountants, labor attorneys, and customs brokers, some have voiced suspicion over the recent increase in those who clear both the first and second stages in their first year of attempting the exam. Some candidates argued that civil complaints should be filed with the Human Resources Development Service of Korea to determine whether cheating occurred. Moon, 32, who failed the first stage of the certified labor attorney exam this year, said someone might have used AI by exploiting lax oversight.

Park Kwon-il, a media sociologist and author, assessed that if merely wearing AI glasses is enough to shake an exam, the value of the license that the exam guarantees has fallen. Park said this is a case that starkly exposes the vulnerability of a society that has evaluated people through exams. Park continued that even after obtaining a license, the differences in capability revealed in actual practice are very large. Park said social contributions or outcomes shown after obtaining a license have in fact been undervalued. Park added that there is a need to fundamentally review exam systems that grant licenses uniformly through testing and then confer exclusive privileges on those who hold those licenses.

Among test takers, there is even a joking line that humans cannot beat AI, Moon added. In the 2018 book, writer Jang Kang-myeong analyzed the structure of Korean society, in which whether one passes an exam directly stratifies social class. Exams both prove ability and provide a path for upward mobility, while at the same time creating a wall between those who pass and those who do not. Because one exam can change a life, demands for fairness are inevitably high. Yet in an era when smart contact lenses are being developed after AI glasses, and artificial intelligence can even perform human work, no exam can be perfectly fair.

A belief that has supported Korean society is wavering in the face of new technology, the belief that if a person works properly and passes exams, that person can secure social status. In Korean society, exams are treated not simply as a means to assess ability, but as a gateway to class. AI is rapidly moving beyond exams to replace the tasks of professionals. Ultimately, this controversy raises the question of whether the method of acquiring class through exams will remain valid. The article said anxiety over exam fairness is erupting.

The article leaves open whether detecting AI glasses alone will be enough to ease the anxiety surrounding exams. It does not say what the Law School Admission Test scorer’s real-time solve produced, or whether the civil complaints were filed. It does not report the outcome of the training on the 11th or how the five national qualification exam cases were handled. It does not say what the four middle and high school cases led to. More to follow.

Articles.Title: “At least the exams must be fair”… The ‘ladder of passing’ shaken by AI glasses

stories.Headline: Microsoft's Tadesse says AI climate tools can help African farmers anticipate weather risks
stories.Summary:
Dr Jimaw Tadesse, the lead for Microsoft AI for Goodlife in Nairobi, said in a statement made available to newsmen in Lagos on Saturday that millions of smallholder farmers across Africa could benefit from artificial intelligence-driven climate information and digital advisory services, as increasingly unpredictable rainfall, prolonged dry spells and recurrent flooding threaten agricultural productivity and rural livelihoods. He said that for farmers whose families depend on seasonal harvests for food and income, uncertainty over when the rains arrive can determine whether a planting season produces a successful harvest or financial hardship, since planting too early can expose seeds to prolonged dry spells while delayed planting may leave crops with insufficient time to mature before the end of the rainy season. He added that as African governments prepared for the 31st Conference of the Parties, attention was increasingly turning to how AI and climate intelligence could help farmers anticipate weather-related risks and make informed decisions before they developed into agricultural crises. Tadesse explained that in Nigeria, where millions of people depend on agriculture for their livelihoods, limited access to timely, reliable and location-specific climate information remains a major challenge, particularly for smallholder farmers who often lack the resources to respond effectively to changing weather conditions.

He said one emerging solution is the application of AI to improve the accuracy of weather forecasts and translate climate information into practical agricultural advice, citing Microsoft Research's Probabilistic Bias Correction, which uses machine learning to correct recurring errors in existing weather models, as one approach being explored to improve forecast reliability. He said experts note that accurate weather predictions alone may not be sufficient, because farmers also require guidance that considers local soil conditions, crop varieties, water availability, production costs and existing farming practices, and he described the Digital Climate Advisory Services initiative involving the Nigerian Meteorological Agency and MTN Nigeria, which delivers location-specific weather information to farmers through mobile channels to help them make informed decisions about planting, irrigation and harvesting. He said Pula, Leadway Assurance, Bayer Foundation and government partners are advancing data-driven agricultural insurance and climate-risk management initiatives aimed at strengthening the resilience of approximately 250,000 smallholder farmers across eight Nigerian states, and that earlier efforts by the Nigerian agritech company Farmcrowdy also demonstrated how digital technology could connect farmers to financing and agricultural support, although its platform focused more directly on digital agricultural finance than AI-powered weather forecasting. He said accessibility remains a significant obstacle to the effective adoption of agricultural technology across the continent, since language barriers, high connectivity costs, limited digital literacy and inadequate agricultural extension services can prevent farmers from accessing or understanding information that could improve their productivity and protect their investments.

He said this has increased the importance of developing AI systems capable of communicating agricultural and climate information in languages farmers understand, citing LINGUA Africa, supported by Microsoft's AI for Good Lab and partners, which is advancing AI tools that reflect Africa's linguistic diversity, and he said projects such as AgroLingua Africa in Nigeria are exploring how AI could deliver agricultural information in indigenous languages including Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo, while HausaNLP's DialectBridge is working to improve AI capabilities across regional Hausa dialects. He said agricultural technology advocates emphasise that AI should complement rather than replace the knowledge and experience of farmers, agricultural researchers and extension workers, and that beyond accessibility, fragmented agricultural records, inadequate institutional capacity and limited information-sharing among government agencies responsible for agriculture, meteorology and disaster management also threaten the effective deployment of AI-driven climate solutions. Tadesse said African governments and development partners are being urged to prioritise agricultural data systems as essential infrastructure for climate adaptation, which would require adaptation financing to support interconnected agricultural databases, accessible digital infrastructure, affordable connectivity and continuous training for government analysts and agricultural extension workers, and he said responsible data-sharing arrangements and national ownership of agricultural information are also considered necessary to ensure that climate intelligence systems remain sustainable beyond individual development projects. He said that although AI cannot prevent droughts, replace irrigation infrastructure or eliminate the financial difficulties confronting smallholder farmers, it could improve their ability to anticipate climate risks and respond before weather disruptions destroy their investments, and he noted that for millions of African farming households the ultimate value of such technology will not be measured solely by how accurately it predicted rainfall but by whether the information reached farmers early enough, in a language they understand, and provided practical guidance that helps them protect their crops, incomes and food security.

Articles.Title: COP31: AI offers African farmers lifeline as climate change threatens harvests – Microsoft

stories.Headline: Gen Z buyers use AI to shortlist homes and estimate mortgage costs
stories.Summary:
Gen Z consumers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to research homebuying, according to a 2026 Homebuyer Insights Report from Bank of America. These young buyers use the technology to shortlist properties, estimate mortgage payments, and calculate closing costs before contacting agents or lenders. The report found that 32 percent of Gen Z, 28 percent of millennials, and 20 percent of all prospective buyers or homeowners used AI tools in the past year. Most users focused on financial affordability, with 57 percent estimating costs and 55 percent learning about the general homebuying process.

The shift requires real estate firms to scale their technology, though JLL research shows 90 percent of companies are testing AI while only 5 percent have met their goals. More than 60 percent of these firms are unprepared to scale beyond pilots, and only 33 percent of workers feel adequately trained. In early 2026, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac introduced governance frameworks for accountability and human oversight, while MISMO released a voluntary toolkit in June. Additionally, a revised law in Colorado regarding automated decisions is scheduled to take effect on January 1.

Matt Vernon, the head of consumer lending at Bank of America, stated that AI is now a meaningful first step in the journey for buyers. Despite this trend, the report indicates that 55 percent of buyers still prefer humans for touring homes and 54 percent want human legal advice. The Urban Institute noted that AI already assists with underwriting, valuation, and fraud detection to lower costs and speed up servicing. They suggested that lenders should measure success by how many more people become and remain homeowners.

The real estate industry is currently undergoing its largest transformation in a generation, which the World Economic Forum compares to the early days of the internet. Companies with C-suite sponsors for their technology programs are three times more likely to succeed than those without such leadership. The Urban Institute has launched a new initiative on AI in mortgage finance to track these developments. Future success for firms will depend on training their staff and proving measurable results to keep pace with AI-savvy buyers.

Articles.Title: Gen Z Turns to AI to Navigate Homebuying

stories.Headline: Kakao releases first AI short animation Ryan Begins made with OpenAI tools
stories.Summary:
Kakao announced on November 10 that it had produced Ryan Begins, the first AI short animation starring its popular character Ryan, through a technology collaboration with OpenAI. The approximately seven-minute short is based on the webtoon of the same name and combines human creative direction with generative AI tools in its planning and production. The production team includes director Jiwon Han, who directed Netflix's animated film Lost in Starlight, and AI supervisor Young-jun Kim. The team used ChatGPT's image generation feature to create initial images based on scene sketches and detailed prompts.

Artists then manually refined and revised the images to achieve the intended visual quality. According to the production team, they used approximately 1,500 prompts for a single scene to achieve the desired direction and emotional tone. Kakao held a special advance screening and a Q&A session on November 8 at Movieland in Seongsu-dong, Seoul. The event also featured an exhibition showcasing the animation's production process.

Tickets for the Q&A session sold out within a day of going on sale. The webtoon launched last year and features the Kakao Friends character Ryan. Han said the team focused on conveying Ryan's emotions without relying on dialogue or exaggerated facial expressions, allowing viewers to find their own interpretations of the story. Kim added that the team repeatedly revised AI-generated images whenever they did not match the intended emotional tone.

Kim emphasized that the creators' decisions and hands-on work determined the final result. Unlike previous slice-of-life webtoons featuring Kakao Friends, this series marked the first official storyline-driven webtoon that builds on Ryan's universe. An English version of the original webtoon is not available. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Kakao, OpenAI Collaborate on AI-Generated Short Animation Based on Ryan Begins Webtoon

stories.Headline: Microsoft researchers create sleeper agent AI by editing a small number of neurons
stories.Summary:
Microsoft researchers created a sleeper agent AI by editing a small number of neurons. The team disclosed the Lazarus study on November 10 and submitted the paper on November 11. They found a way to turn a helpful AI into a secret agent. This process allows a model to perform ordinary tasks while hiding a trigger. The trigger produces a chosen response when it appears in the input.

The attack requires write access to change the stored weights of a model checkpoint. Researchers edited seven neurons in Nemotron-Terminal-8B to print the harmless marker printf LAZARUS_OK. They also edited 60 neurons in Qwen3.6-27B to predict a command deleting a decoy repository. These edits targeted dormant neurons in the final feed-forward layer of the models. The seven-neuron test used 23 examples to achieve at least 98.8 percent prediction.

Microsoft Research authors stated that ordinary task performance does not establish the safety of a model. They explained that each selected neuron consists of weight vectors rather than single numerical parameters. Microsoft Threat Intelligence said it had not observed threat actors weaponizing this specific technique. The researchers noted that the 60-neuron test did not measure free-running destructive execution. They clarified that the marker result did not demonstrate a destructive takeover.

AI assistants trusted with files and tools are affected by this potential risk. The Qwen benchmark tests showed Terminal-Bench success falling from 46.59 percent to 42.05 percent. The 60-neuron experiment reached 40 percent complete-action prediction on the unseen swe-agent format. Fresh Nemotron tests found the marker in 98.88 percent of query-triggered cases. Benign leakage in those specific tests was zero and 0.14 percent.

Lazarus repurposes dormant neurons to plant triggered output without retraining the entire AI model. The mechanism involves altering weights to ensure a chosen output when a trigger appears. One version calculates changes directly, while another adjusts only the selected weights. The impact of such an attack depends on the permissions granted to the agent. The researchers used teacher-forced evaluation for the fixed-context prediction in the Qwen test.

Microsoft recommends checking model provenance and restricting outbound network access and agent privileges. They suggest requiring approval for consequential tool actions to address the altered checkpoints. The company cautions that passing an audit cannot guarantee that a model behaves safely. The articles leave open whether threat actors will eventually weaponize this neuron editing technique. It remains unclear how these results translate to free-running destructive command execution.

Articles.Title: Microsoft found a way to turn a helpful AI into a sleeper agent

stories.headline_source: Microsoft found a way to turn a helpful AI into a sleeper agent

stories.Headline: Meta Lab opens its 13th store on Rush Street in Chicago to sell AI glasses and VR headsets
stories.Summary:
Meta Lab opened its first Midwest retail store on Friday at 932 N. Rush St. in Chicago, just ahead of the holiday season, according to the Chicago Tribune. The store carries more than a hundred styles of AI glasses and two different VR headsets, and Meta is betting on experiential shopping to connect with consumers. Emily Lewis, Meta's director of retail, said the technology is really cool for people to try and that putting a pair of glasses on your face matters more than an online experience. The storefront has bright blue walls, windows and doors, and it sits next to a brick-walled Lululemon.

The Chicago location is the company's 13th store, and it arrives alongside a wave of Meta Lab openings across the country. In the past six weeks, stores opened in Houston, Atlanta, New York City, Honolulu and Scottsdale, Arizona. The Meta Ray-Bans cost $799 and use a muscle-reading wristband that lets users select apps in the lenses with hand motions, without touching a screen. The most popular pair is the Meta Glasses Adventurers at $299, followed closely by the Meta Starfire Kylie Glasses at $399, and customers can order prescription lenses to go with the technology.

Lewis said the company is incredibly excited about Chicago because the city welcomes 55 million visitors a year, and she called Rush Street near the Magnificent Mile an iconic area to be in. Michael Wells, manager of training at Meta Labs, said the company is really pushing the boundaries on styles now. The opening comes against the backdrop of a class-action lawsuit filed in September, in which plaintiffs alleged Meta violated the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act by harvesting and exploiting users' biometric data to develop an unreleased facial recognition system called NameTag. Meta is seeking exemption from the lawsuit, and a spokesperson said Meta and its products adhere to all applicable federal, state and local laws.

Wells said a blinking indicator light on the side of the glasses signals to other people that the camera is on, and that any tampering or blocking of the light automatically cuts the camera off, so privacy is built in as a priority. Some pairs have no cameras at all and only offer audio for phone calls and music. Lewis said the stores intentionally have comfortable seating so people can dwell and get to know the product, and an engraving machine lets buyers customize their glasses cases. Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals are still to come, Lewis said.

Articles.Title: AI goes brick-and-mortar: A new Meta Lab store opens on Rush Street

stories.Headline: OpenAI’s Yang-Mills Proof: Gross Committee Confirms Lean Verification, Mass Gap Open
stories.Summary:
On the evening of Monday 26 October 2026, OpenAI announced that an internal model had produced a proof of the existence part of the Yang-Mills problem, one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s seven Millennium Prize Problems, which carries a $1 million prize. According to Scientific American’s 27 October report, OpenAI said the model reached the result on 9 September but kept it private until the argument had been encoded in Lean. OpenAI did not release the proof but handed it to a group of experts to bring it into the mathematical literature. That group, described by Scientific American as a committee of “shepherds”, is led by David Gross and includes four colleagues he chose, with Michael R. Douglas of Harvard a named member. On 9 and 10 November 2026, the committee appointed by OpenAI and chaired by physicist David Gross said the AI-generated proof had been formally verified in the Lean proof language.

The committee said the result proves the existence of pure Yang-Mills theory under the standard problem statements. On 9 November the committee issued a statement to that effect, and on the night of 10 November it posted a document on GitHub explaining how the proof works and affirming the Lean verification. The Yang-Mills problem has two parts: showing the theory underlying the Standard Model can be constructed rigorously in four dimensions, and showing that a “mass gap” emerges from its equations. Only the first is claimed, and the committee said the harder “mass gap” half is untouched. The committee’s explanatory document is described as cursory, and the committee said it used OpenAI’s Astra model to help parse the Lean code.

The committee’s own wording is cautious: it says “We do not claim to fully understand the proof yet.” The committee stated that it does not yet fully understand the proof. Scientific American published its report on 11 November and updated it on 12 November. Woit wrote that the committee is keeping a roughly 1,147-page explanatory document private. The committee is led by David Gross and includes four colleagues he chose, with Michael R. Douglas of Harvard a named member.

Physicist Peter Woit, writing on 11 November, argued that existence in the sense verified is not the standard the Millennium problem requires, citing the Jaffe-Witten problem description on weak existence, and that nothing has been established about the mass gap. Scientific American reports the shepherding arrangement conflicts with transparency recommendations from an OpenAI-affiliated advisory group, and some mathematicians see it as needless gatekeeping. NYU mathematician Scott Armstrong welcomed the Lean release but said the review “can be done more efficiently and quickly in the open.” Woit wrote that within hours of the Lean release, other groups had begun using AI agents to produce public, readable versions of the code. Levent Alpöge, who works at Anthropic, and Northwestern mathematician Ethan Sussman had been posting progress on GitHub since 6 October using Claude-based agents, and the night before OpenAI’s announcement updated the repository, believing they had solved the three-dimensional version of the existence problem.

The Clay requirements call for four dimensions, so that three-dimensional result would not meet the prize criteria. NYU’s Tristan Buckmaster disputed OpenAI’s timeline, saying “There is no way it took one month to Lean-verify Yang-Mills.” Verification is not publication, and neither the Lean check nor the committee statement is a journal review. The committee itself says it does not yet fully understand the proof, so formal checking does not by itself settle correctness of the intended statement, priority or credit. Journals, funders and institutions drafting AI policies now have a live example of a developer controlling the release sequence.

Still unresolved as of 12 November 2026 is whether outside experts confirm the Lean statement matches the Millennium problem’s existence requirement. Also unresolved is whether the proof can be rewritten into something humans can follow, and the mass gap. OpenAI’s separate claims about quantum chromodynamics and other Standard Model results remain open, about which, according to Woit, the committee has said nothing. With the Lean code public, outside experts can scrutinise it, possibly with their own AI agents, and the community check is expected to run through preprints and public repositories before any journal decision. Teams reusing the Lean code should record exactly which version of the code and statement they checked, in line with computational reproducibility practice.

stories.Headline: Moore launches TRUSTbuilder AI to help nonprofits strengthen how AI platforms describe them
stories.Summary:
Moore, a constituent experience management company, launched TRUSTbuilder AI on November 15, 2026, according to an announcement from the firm. The offering is a visibility audit and generative engine optimization service intended to help nonprofits strengthen how artificial intelligence platforms describe and recommend them. It combines Moore-developed technology with the firm's expertise in nonprofit fundraising, communications and digital strategy. The launch responds to changes in how people discover causes and decide where to give.

The service begins with the TRUSTbuilder AI Visibility Audit, a diagnostic powered by technology developed at Moore under Chief Technology Officer Steve Kessler. Moore works with each nonprofit to define priority questions about mission, expertise and giving opportunities, informed by the organization's data and audience insights. The audit then assesses responses across ChatGPT, Google AI Mode, Google AI Overviews, Gemini, Meta AI and Claude. It distinguishes between an organization appearing when someone asks about a cause and appearing when someone asks about the organization by name. A baseline shows whether an organization appears in answers to priority questions, how platforms describe or recommend it, where peer organizations appear, and which websites and sources the platforms cite.

Gretchen Littlefield, CEO of Moore, said via a statement that AI is changing how people discover organizations and that personal agents are already helping people research causes and make giving decisions. She said purpose-driven organizations need technology and strategies built for that future. The announcement cited Pew Research Center reporting this past June that 42% of U.S. adults use AI chatbots to search for information. An October 26 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission showed that more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had adopted Muse, Meta's personal AI agent, within the first few weeks of its official September 2026 launch. Because Google has integrated AI summaries into its core search offerings, an estimated 60% to 80% of all search journeys now involve generative AI in some capacity.

The October 2026 "What Is AI Reading?" report from Muck Rack and Generative Pulse reported that more than 80% of AI citations came from earned and third-party sources, which the announcement said makes communications strategy central to this work. Strategists interpret the audit findings and develop priorities for strengthening an organization's authority and discoverability. The results give a clearer view of the information prospective donors might encounter and where to focus next steps. Moore directed those interested to request a Visibility Audit or access a Playbook at wearemoore.com.

stories.Headline: AI companies hire counterintelligence experts to protect trade secrets from espionage
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence companies are aggressively hiring counterintelligence experts to protect trade secrets following several high profile espionage scandals. Jensen Huang recently stepped down as the chief executive officer of Nvidia after admitting to a romantic affair with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive suspected of spying for China. In a separate incident, the Justice Department arrested an OpenAI engineer for planting a listening device in a conference room to communicate with the Saudi royal family. These events have highlighted the critical need for security as the race for AI supremacy becomes a matter of national security.

To combat these threats, firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Nvidia are paying former intelligence officers salaries between $200,000 and $500,000. Anthropic increased its counterintelligence staff to 33 employees this year, compared to 14 in 2025 and nine in 2024. OpenAI grew its counterintelligence team to 22 people in 2026, while Nvidia hired 16 specialists this year. In 2025, Anthropic added former CIA deputy director David Cohen and former National Security Agency cybersecurity director Dave Luber to its advisory council, and OpenAI added former National Security Agency director Paul Nakasone to its board in 2024.

Christopher Falkenberg, the president of Insite Risk Management, stated that the demand for sophisticated security talent currently exceeds the available supply. Former FBI operative Eric O’Neill explained that executives must be taught to recognize subtle manipulation that often begins through business introductions or dating apps. He noted that security professionals often struggle to intervene once an executive is already emotionally invested in a suspicious relationship. These experts emphasize that espionage rarely starts with a direct request for secrets but rather through the gradual building of trust.

The United States government is also intensifying its economic warfare efforts by targeting sensitive foreign companies in the fields of biotechnology, chips, and AI. CIA Deputy Director Michael Ellis announced in September that the U.S. is expanding its espionage against China to protect military superiority. The Pentagon recently formed the Economic Defense Unit and established the Technology Support Office in April to sabotage foreign technology programs. While the Pentagon has denied some reports, sources indicate the government is deploying covert officers posing as executives to disrupt adversaries.

Articles.Title: The hottest job in AI right now may be counterintelligence as companies hire to protect secrets

stories.headline_source: The hottest job in AI right now may be counterintelligence as companies hire to protect secrets

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO amid links to a Chinese intelligence asset
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on a Thursday morning in November 2026. His departure followed reports that U.S. intelligence agencies linked him to a Chinese intelligence asset. This asset was Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singaporean data center company Megaspeed. Huang also faced allegations of an affair with an executive who reported directly to him. He had previously sent a memo to 42,000 staffers apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife.

Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, was appointed as the interim CEO of the company. Nvidia is based in Santa Clara, California, and once reached a market capitalization of 5.7 trillion dollars. The company invested nearly 50 billion dollars into AI model firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI. It pledged 170 billion dollars in commitments, including 105 billion dollars for one Ohio facility. Nvidia also discussed a 500 billion dollar plan with Wall Street to make chips tradable securities.

The Nvidia board stated they had no reason to believe national security or firm secrets were compromised. Jensen Huang previously told Fortune that the opportunity in China is large and growing. He argued that selling chips in China would make American technology the global standard. He lobbied for a compromise in 2025 to ship second-tier chips to approved Chinese customers. Under this arrangement, the U.S. government would take a 25 percent cut of the deals.

Brad Carson of Americans for Responsible Innovation said the episode proves Nvidia is deeply compromised. He alleged the company was either complicit in chip smuggling or turned a blind eye. China called the allegations against Huang groundless speculation and slander. Analysts like Jay Goldberg warn Nvidia may become just another chip company without Huang's big bets. Other affected parties include U.S. congressional leaders and federal agencies who launched investigations into the matter.

The Biden administration barred Nvidia from selling advanced AI chips in China starting in 2022. Huang donated 1 million dollars to Donald Trump's inaugural fund after the 2024 election. Alice Huang was allegedly recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather chip information. Megaspeed had long been suspected of helping Chinese firms dodge U.S. export controls. A U.S. Commerce Department probe into Megaspeed was halted and passed to the Justice Department.

Nvidia's core business continues as its chip supply is sold out through the next year. The company must now prove it can thrive without the leadership of its founder. It remains unclear if the AI boom can outgrow its dependence on Huang's evangelism. The articles leave open whether the boom was built primarily on faith. The company did not respond to multiple questions from Fortune regarding the affairs and resignation.

Articles.Title: The downfall of AI’s $5.7 trillion man

stories.Headline: Attackers use AI to bypass security patches and find vulnerability variants
stories.Summary:
This summer, maintainers of the vm2 JavaScript library shipped fixes for 34 sandbox-escape vulnerabilities. Anthropic's Claude co-wrote 19 of these patches, but a security researcher later used an AI agent to bypass one. Shayaun Nejad of Rubrik highlighted these challenges at the [un]prompted AI security conference in San Francisco. He noted that AI-discovered bugs are often rediscovered in new testing runs despite previous fixes. Nejad warned that published patches now serve as blueprints for attackers to find vulnerability variants.

The vm2 library sees 1 million downloads per week, and the P2Patch benchmark tested 101 real vulnerabilities. In 41 of those cases, an AI agent successfully bypassed patches to trigger the same flaw. Off-by-1 Labs at 1Password tested 6,080 patch candidates for six vulnerabilities, finding half left attack paths open. Fudan University researchers in Shanghai analyzed 76 patches from 62 closed-source applications across 25 vendors. Their framework flagged 63 incomplete patches, leading to 19 CVE assignments and 28,100 dollars in bounties.

Shayaun Nejad said variant analysis is a context magnet that pops up frequently. Tim de Waal of OpenAI showed an agent removing stack canaries and missing single-quote bypasses in firmware. Anthropic stated that software security is now limited by how quickly humans verify and patch AI findings. David Molnar of Meta said humans are drowning in reviews because AI code grew over 100 percent. Taesoo Kim of Microsoft warned that AI drastically reduces the time needed for binary-diff analysis.

Bank of America added 1,000 contractors in the second quarter to help 3,000 staff with patching. Meta used AI for 40 percent of critical fixes by July, but exposure time did not decrease. The Microsoft Edge Security team warned that attackers are increasingly using patch-gap abuse to target downstream browsers. Epoch AI researchers used GLM 5.3 to compromise every Firefox release shipped between September 17 and October 26. These researchers spent 1,000 dollars in credits and 12 hours per target without triggering safeguards.

Trail of Bits found one in eight human-written patches failed to resolve 2,265 vulnerabilities over several years. A human and an AI agent both caused a crash in the freenginx web server. Anthropic's Glasswing program found 37,966 vulnerabilities, but VulnCheck found only 217 of 7,349 public flaws were fixed. FIRST projected 66,000 CVEs for this year, but the number is now approaching 100,000. Microsoft's October Patch Tuesday addressed 1,415 vulnerabilities, compared to 180 in October 2025.

Mozilla will stop releasing regression tests associated with security fixes to prevent further patch gap abuse. Attackers now use open-weight models like Qwen, Kimi, and GLM to bypass frontier model guardrails. AI can now create open-source replicas of proprietary products, such as Adobe Photoshop, to aid reverse engineering. Anthropic researchers found a model produced a working Firefox exploit within one hour of a patch landing. The articles leave open how companies will fully automate the review pipeline to replace human-in-the-loop systems.

Articles.Title: AI-written patches are becoming attack maps for hackers

stories.Headline: Executives trust AI over their own judgment twice as often as other workers, survey finds
stories.Summary:
New research from Charter's AI Pulse survey of 5,002 full-time U.S. desk workers who use AI on the job found that executives are twice as likely as rank-and-file employees to trust AI over their own judgment, Fortune reported on November 16, 2026. About a third of managers and executives say they trust AI more than their own judgment on work decisions, compared with 16.3% of non-managers, and executives are also more than twice as likely as workers to trust AI over a knowledgeable colleague. The same article notes that Gen Z approaches AI with some skepticism, since 69% of employed Gen Zers in the Voices of Gen Z study from Gallup, the Walton Family Foundation and GSV Ventures say they trust work completed without AI more than AI-assisted work. That study surveyed 1,572 Americans ages 14 to 29, and only 3% of them put the most faith in work produced entirely by AI, even though 51% of Gen Zers use generative AI at least weekly.

The survey also found that 81% of executives say they always or usually fact-check AI output before using it, versus 71% of workers, and that executives are 3.3 times as likely as workers to use outputs they doubt. In Charter's survey, 85% of executives are at least somewhat optimistic about AI's impact on their organization, compared with 56% of employees. The article recalls that in 2025, SAP research shared with Fortune found that 74% of executives trusted AI more for business advice than colleagues or friends. It adds that misplaced trust in AI carries a bigger price at the top, because when an executive leans on a flawed AI answer to decide who gets promoted, where the money goes, or how a team is restructured after a merger, employees absorb the consequences without getting a vote.

Brian Elliott, Charter's executive-in-residence, who co-led the AI Pulse research, says where someone sits at the table matters more than the year they were born, and that the survey of over 5,000 AI users at work found sharper divides by career stage than by age. He says AI is great at summaries and high-level answers, which is much of what a leader needs, while workers deal with specifics where AI's gaps show. He says executives fact-check AI more but are also far more likely to use outputs they doubt, almost certainly because they have less fear that a mistake might cost them their job. In his view the biggest driver may be pressure, since many leaders are expected to move fast and have all the answers, and he says that combination explains how a CFO might drop the CMO's campaign into ChatGPT and quiz her on it, trusting the tool over a peer who knows the context and spent weeks on the work.

The article says younger workers' wariness stems from institutions they feel have failed them, from schools to employers, and that Gen Z treats AI as an assistant rather than giving it main character energy. It notes that executives are finalizing next year's budgets and AI strategies now, and that the open question is how many of those calls will rest on a leader's judgment and how many on a chatbot's general answer. It concludes that leaders who treat AI the same way Gen Z does could make 2027 a better year for the employees who live with their decisions.

Articles.Title: Everyone worries Gen Z trusts AI too much. Executives trust it over their own judgment twice as often

stories.Headline: CDW's Hang Tan says CIOs must redesign core workflows so AI improves business performance
stories.Summary:
Hang Tan, chief strategy and transformation officer and executive vice president at CDW, wrote in a Nov 16, 2026 opinion article on cio.com that AI is getting smarter at remarkable speed. He said employees can now draft, analyze, search and automate routine work faster than they could a year ago. He said recent research on the state of AI shows organizations continuing to expand adoption across functions and use cases. He said that in many organizations the business still works the same way, with the same work moving through the same systems. He said AI speeds up a task and the benefit disappears into a process designed for another era.

Tan said CDW works across thousands of customer environments and has made AI assistants available to more than 14,000 coworkers. He said CDW has built more than 12,000 agents and started redesigning core workflows. He said the CIO's challenge is no longer simply enabling access to AI. He said the challenge is helping the business move quickly without creating fragmented technology, uncontrolled cost and risks that IT will ultimately have to manage. He said usage climbed quickly inside CDW but usage alone couldn't tell whether the business was performing better.

Tan said the task is not the real unit of business performance and the workflow is. He said the next phase of AI value creation will come from improving how work moves across the enterprise. He said leaders who see the workflow as the constraint are tempted to apply AI to every step, an instinct that is often a mistake. He said the better approach is to start with the business challenge, not the technology, and define the outcome that matters and work backward. He said not every problem needs an agent and sometimes a simple rule works better and costs less.

Tan said employees experiment and surface opportunities but can only change the tasks they control, not the handoffs before and after them. He said business leaders choose which workflows matter and own the outcomes and have the authority to bring functions together. He said a workflow designed from the top will struggle if the people running it have never used AI or don't trust it. He said CDW needs both broad access so coworkers build fluency and leadership focus on a few core workflows where redesign can change performance. He said neither scales if every team has to solve for tools, data, security and cost on its own.

Tan said the CIO's mandate is to build the enterprise AI foundation quickly enough and make it useful enough that business teams build on it rather than around it. He said that foundation combines approved AI tools, trusted data and business context, connections into enterprise applications and workflows, security and governance, and visibility into performance, cost and value. He said business teams won't wait for IT and will find their own tools and build their own connections if the foundation isn't there. He said the CIO then inherits fragmented data, duplicated spending, inconsistent governance, cyber risk and little visibility into what AI is doing across the company. He said a foundation that is too restrictive or hard to use drives people around it, while one that works becomes the default.

Tan said AI will keep getting more capable and the competitive difference will come from what companies are willing to change around it. He said the measure of that change isn't how much AI a company has deployed but whether the business performs better. He said that is the standard CDW is applying inside the company and the standard he would encourage every CIO to use. He said CIOs should not stop at licenses, usage or hours saved but should ask whether AI has changed an outcome the business cares about. He said companies should build the highway for AI transformation or spend the next several years managing the risks created on the side roads.

Articles.Title: Your AI is smarter. Is your business still working the same way?

stories.Headline: APA publishes guidance urging employers to put people at the centre of workplace AI adoption
stories.Summary:
The American Psychological Association published new guidance on 16 November 2026 to help organisations introduce artificial intelligence into the workplace responsibly, warning that unclear policies and conflicting expectations risk undermining employee trust and wellbeing. The guide, titled Deploying AI Into Workplaces: What Leaders Need to Know, sets out seven recommended practices informed by established psychological research and emerging evidence about AI use. It is intended to help employers balance the potential benefits of AI with the need to protect workers, maintain meaningful human oversight and consider how technology changes the design of jobs. The guidance comes amid growing pressure on employees to incorporate AI into their daily activities, often without clear organisational policies governing its use.

According to the APA's 2026 Work in America Survey, fewer than 40% of workers for whom the question was applicable knew whether their employer had an official policy on acceptable AI use, pointing to a potential disconnect between the pace of AI adoption and the development of workplace policies to support it. Among the guide's recommendations are ensuring that safeguards reflect the potential consequences of AI errors, involving employees and others affected by AI systems in decisions about their introduction, and protecting opportunities for workers to develop expertise and learn through experience. The APA also encourages organisations to consider how AI might affect professional judgement, knowledge sharing and the development of skills over time, rather than focusing exclusively on efficiency or productivity gains. Developed with input from specialists in human-technology interaction and several branches of psychology, the guide includes practical examples of effective implementation and warning signs that organisations should recognise.

APA CEO Arthur C. Evans Jr. said the rapidly growing use of AI at work is creating new behaviours and social judgments while raising questions about trust, all of which are fundamentally questions of psychology, and he asked whether using AI to write emails should change how someone is judged. He said psychological science can help organisations understand not just what AI tools can do, but how their use affects trust, decision-making and employee well-being, and that the guide gives leaders a practical framework for introducing AI thoughtfully, with people at the centre of the process. Dennis P. Stolle, executive lead psychologist for applied psychology at APA, said purchasing an AI tool and telling people to use it without further direction is not a sound strategy. He said organisations need to invest in the people who will work with the technology, not just the technology itself, which means giving workers the information they need to judge where AI tools are reliable and where they are not, making sure human oversight is meaningful and rethinking how jobs are designed.

Although aimed at employers across sectors, the guidance raises questions relevant to universities, research organisations and scholarly publishers, where AI is increasingly being incorporated into research, editorial, administrative and knowledge-management workflows. For these organisations, the APA's recommendations underline the importance of establishing clear expectations around acceptable AI use while preserving professional expertise, accountability and trust in human decision-making.

stories.Headline: Art ‘must not be sacrificed on the altar of corporate profit’, Liberal senator says as AI policy debate rages
stories.Summary:
Liberal senator Andrew McLachlan said on Sunday that artists’ copyright must not be sacrificed for investment as the Labor government weighs copyright changes in a wider AI policy package covering datacentres, online safety, energy resources and economic benefits. He said the works artists create must not be sacrificed on the altar of global corporate profiteering, and that artists’ property rights must be respected and protected. He said it is unimaginable that as a nation we might value the machine over beauty created by the artist. He said the principle of fair pay for a fair day’s work must not be forgotten in the age of social media platforms, datacentres and artificial intelligence. He said AI provides amazing opportunities for the nation, and that if there are trade-offs then the costs must be clearly articulated and understood.

The debate turns on copyright, with AI companies saying they need legal certainty before investing in Australia and Anthropic putting forward an opt-out model that would let it scrape music, books and journalism unless a rights holder objected. Prime minister Anthony Albanese has declared it would be theft if creatives were not paid for their work, while leading voices in the recording industry have raised alarm about any weakening of existing copyright law. Fellow Coalition members Ross Cadell and Michaelia Cash have backed concerns raised by Aria that granting AI companies permission to scrape copyrighted material could amount to an acquisition of property by the government, and the constitutional requirement that property be acquired on just terms is emerging as a key concern. McLachlan said any compensation arrangements must be considered on an individual basis for each artist, adding that an industry-wide scheme would be difficult to make fair. He said that as a Liberal he believes property rights are foundational to a healthy democracy and a strong economy, and that the state should never seek to compulsorily acquire or trade away an individual’s property rights except in very limited circumstances and not without just compensation.

Labor and the Coalition largely agree on AI-related issues, and senator David Pocock has complained about a major party stitch-up on AI regulation. This week the shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, and the shadow cybersecurity minister, Aaron Violi, said AI was too important to become an unnecessarily partisan political contest and that they would engage constructively to ensure an enduring and multipartisan approach. Labor and the Coalition both favour attracting more AI investment and datacentres to Australia, but the opposition has warned the government against selling out Australian rights holders in a rush to secure investment. The growth of datacentres is expected to increase emissions and power costs for households, prompting backlash from environmental groups and some communities, and McLachlan said datacentres must not be built at the expense of biodiversity and that he chooses real forests over virtual ones. Labor has announced it will set up a new AI safety regulator and implement six key obligations on AI companies after a breach of government sites by OpenAI, and its AI package is expected to be unveiled before the end of the year.

stories.Headline: Maseno University launches ARAISE centre to advance responsible artificial intelligence research
stories.Summary:
Maseno University has established a Centre for Applied and Artificial Intelligence for Society and Environment, known as ARAISE, to strengthen research and promote the responsible application of Artificial Intelligence in addressing emerging societal challenges. The Centre has been selected under the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD) Centres of African Excellence programme and is expected to support research in areas including public health, environmental conservation and other societal concerns. The Acting Vice-Chancellor, Prof. Erick Nyambedha, announced the initiative during the University's 26th Graduation ceremony on Friday, saying it was part of efforts to position the institution as a regional hub for Artificial Intelligence research and innovation. During the same ceremony, 5,739 graduands received various qualifications, including 5,347 Bachelor's degree holders, 95 Master's graduates, 39 PhD holders, 130 diploma graduates, 112 Postgraduate Diploma in Education recipients and 16 certificate holders. The Institution reported a completion rate above the 80 per cent threshold recommended by the Commission for University Education.

Nyambedha disclosed that the University had also been selected to partner in a German-Kenya Centre of Excellence that will promote the responsible application of Artificial Intelligence in addressing local and global challenges. He said the establishment of ARAISE would provide opportunities for collaboration with other universities across Kenya and Africa while strengthening the Institution's contribution to research and technological advancement. He observed that Artificial Intelligence was increasingly becoming an important tool in developing computer-based solutions to challenges affecting societies worldwide, and said the University was embracing technological developments to ensure its graduates were equipped with relevant competencies for the changing employment market. Nyambedha further revealed that Maseno University had established a growing international research network with more than 70 collaborators through Memoranda of Understanding and Memoranda of Action, alongside more than 40 active research projects and student and staff exchange programmes. Among its international collaborators are Princeton University in the United States, VIVES University of Applied Science in Belgium, Gulu University in Uganda, the University of Maryland Eastern Shore, the University of North Carolina and the European Union's Erasmus programme.

He said the university had also attracted international students from countries including Benin, Ghana, the Democratic Republic of Congo and South Sudan, with its eCampus extending access to learners in Eastern and Southern Africa, the United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom. He disclosed that an ICT Hub being constructed in partnership with the M-Pesa Foundation was nearing completion and would serve not only the University but also neighbouring learning institutions and the surrounding community, while a Modern Science Laboratories Complex is under construction to expand capacity for scientific research. Nyambedha appealed to the Ministry of Education to support the acquisition of modern laboratory equipment and materials once construction is completed, noting that the facilities would require substantial investment to meet the intended research standards. Acting Chancellor Prof. Naftali Omolo Ongati said the University was keen on strengthening scholarly partnerships across disciplines and international borders, noting that collaboration was essential in addressing complex global challenges, and he urged researchers and graduates to develop solutions to issues such as climate change, poverty, hunger, infectious diseases and insecurity. He also appealed to national and international development partners to increase their support for the Institution's research and infrastructure programmes.

The Graduation ceremony was graced by the Cabinet Secretary for Energy and Petroleum, James Opiyo Wandayi, who lauded the academic staff for the work they were doing to impact graduates with skills necessary for the development of the country. The Principal Secretary in the State Department for Higher Education, Dr. Beatrice Muganda Inyangala, recognized the efforts the University was making to prepare for Competency Based Education and Training and pledged to always support the institution towards fulfilling its mandate. The first cohort of learners under Kenya's Competency-Based Curriculum and Competency-Based Education system is expected to join universities and TVET colleges in 2029. The developments come as Maseno University seeks to strengthen its position in higher education, research and innovation while preparing graduates for the demands of an increasingly technology-driven world.

stories.Headline: Coveo acquires Anglera to expand its AI-powered product data enrichment services
stories.Summary:
Coveo Solutions Inc. (TSX:CVO), a Quebec City-based software company, acquired Anglera, a San Francisco-based technology company specialising in agentic product data enrichment, according to an article published by Kalkine Media on November 14, 2026. The article, by Anmol Khazanchi, reported the acquisition under the headline that Coveo acquired Anglera to expand its AI-powered product data enrichment services. Coveo is included in the TSX Smallcap Index and develops AI-powered search, product discovery and personalisation software for enterprise customers. The acquired technology complements Coveo's commerce platform through product information enrichment for online discovery and AI-assisted shopping. The combination brings product data preparation together with search and recommendation capabilities.

The acquisition adds agentic product data enrichment to Coveo's platform, which serves enterprise customers across retail, manufacturing, distribution and other industries. Manufacturers, retailers and distributors can use these tools to organise product information and make catalogues accessible across digital channels. Coveo's platform helps organisations connect customers and employees with relevant information through AI-powered search, recommendations and generative answering. Its generative AI products use large language models and enterprise information to provide relevant responses and improve digital experiences. The platform also supports personalised recommendations and search functions across customer-facing websites and internal systems.

The article attributes the acquisition to Coveo Solutions Inc. (TSX:CVO) and describes Anglera as a San Francisco-based technology company specialising in agentic product data enrichment. The article does not quote Coveo or Anglera executives by name or give any statement from them about the deal. It says the acquired technology complements Coveo's commerce platform through product information enrichment for online discovery and AI-assisted shopping. It says the combination brings product data preparation together with search and recommendation capabilities. It says manufacturers, retailers and distributors can use these tools to organise product information and make catalogues accessible across digital channels.

The article says Coveo's solutions include conversational product discovery and AI-powered merchandising tools. Conversational product discovery allows shoppers to interact with digital catalogues through natural-language questions. Merchandising tools help retailers organise product displays and manage how products appear in search experiences. Coveo has also developed agent-based capabilities that can recommend and automate selected merchandising actions. The article says these tools are designed to help retailers manage product discovery across online storefronts.

The article says Coveo's technology development centres on applying generative AI to enterprise search and digital commerce. It says the platform is designed to interpret customer queries, retrieve relevant information and provide personalised responses. It says customer adoption and integration are important elements of the company's business activities. It says its software enables organisations to connect product information, customer data and digital content through a unified search experience. It says Coveo's generative AI products form an important part of its technology development.

The article gives no purchase price, no closing date and no financing details for the acquisition. It gives no completion conditions and no statement on when the Anglera technology will be integrated into Coveo's platform. It does not say how many employees Anglera has or whether its team will join Coveo. It does not say whether the deal has closed. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Cambodia and Senegal experts urge AI that understands Khmer and Wolof and respects local culture
stories.Summary:
Industry experts, policy makers and researchers from Africa, Asia and Europe met in Phnom Penh on November 14 to examine how Francophone countries could develop artificial intelligence suited to their own languages and institutions. Cambodia said it needs AI that understands Khmer and respects the country's culture. The Cambodian Academy of Digital Technology president Seng Sopheap told a FrancoTech roundtable that AI tools used in Cambodia should understand Khmer, respect the country's culture and respond to local needs. He said using artificial intelligence is very important for a country like Cambodia, but it must understand the language, understand the history and respect the culture, and he added that the country also needs the ability to build AI that responds to its needs.

Seydina Moussa Ndiaye, director of the FORCE-N programme at Senegal's Cheikh Hamidou Kane Digital University, illustrated the challenge with a hypothetical example. He said an AI assistant might answer a question in Wolof, a language widely spoken in Senegal, while describing a procedure that applies in another country. For a Cambodian user, the equivalent would be receiving an answer in fluent Khmer that gives the wrong instructions for accessing a public service. Ndiaye said AI systems should be evaluated on the language they use, the sources they draw on and the context in which people will use them.

Ndiaye said French can connect research communities and companies, and he suggested that this cooperation must also support Khmer, Wolof and the other languages of the societies involved. He proposed that universities and research teams develop language resources together, share computing infrastructure and agree on ways to test their systems. The meeting took place at the FrancoTech roundtable in Phnom Penh, alongside other Francophonie events in Cambodia that week. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Should Understand Local Languages – La Francophonie Says

stories.Headline: Semiconductor suppliers capture AI value as their cash flow rises while hyperscalers' falls
stories.Summary:
Since March of this year, according to an article by Bernardo Bertoldi in Il Sole 24 Ore dated 14 November 2026, companies have been seeing Excel files with far more worksheets and complex formulas and PowerPoint presentations with more slides and very small fonts, because the most advanced AI models can now work directly within files on PCs and create artifacts in minutes. The article says intellectual output is proliferating as a result, and it recalls that in March an issue of Family and Trends stated that the impact of AI on intellectual work will be similar to that of factory robotisation on manual labour, with greater standardisation of quality and less scope for craftsmanship. On the financial side, Professor Damodaran said he has noticed that investment banks estimate xAI's addressable market at 22 trillion, which he considers more of a delusion than an estimate, and he drew a comparison with streaming companies, whose success has not only come at the expense of traditional entertainment firms but has on the whole made the sector less profitable. The article adds that some intellectual jobs will disappear, as they did with office automation and the end of typewriters, ledgers, desktop calculators, hand-drawn charts, transparencies and photocopiers, while Parkinson's Law has allowed many activities to evolve with working hours unchanged or increased.

The article says that since people have been using AI to analyse and prepare documents, they seem to be spending more time interacting with the AI, which it calls a good thing, but also more time reading longer and less clear documents, which it calls a bad thing. It states that improving intellectual work requires a combination of human and AI and that it is not enough simply to hand work over to AI, and it calls this an advantage for young people entering the world of work, just as it was in the 1990s for those who knew how to use Excel and its macros. On who is already reaping the benefits of the value created by AI, the article says it is for now those who provide the inputs needed to develop it, comparing AI to a diamond that became a symbol of eternal love in the 1940s while it was De Beers that truly profited because it owned the mines. It reports that the cash flow of semiconductor suppliers has risen from less than 50 billion in 2022 to more than 400 billion in 2026, while that of the hyperscalers such as Amazon, Google and Meta has fallen from more than 250 billion to zero.

The article says these companies, alongside pure-play AI firms, are investing heavily to win a race in which they believe two rules apply, first-mover advantage and the winner takes it all, though it notes it does not usually work out that way, as with the internet, where it took years for champions based on the new technology to emerge. It observes that Apple, one of the most innovative and long-standing companies in tech, has not altered its annual investment flow, and that for now everything is going well because investments are being capitalised and are not spoiling the golden age of profits, and when costs are capitalised it is easy to be generous. It warns that when depreciation begins to weigh on income statements and competition has run its course, we will see slashed profits, widespread impairment and disillusionment. The race for computing power rests on a heuristic made famous by Richard Sutton in his 2019 essay The Bitter Lesson, which holds that the only thing that matters in the long run is the exploitation of computing power, and the article recalls that in 1997 Deep Blue defeated Kasparov thanks to enormous computational power, calculating 200 million positions per second and looking 10 to 12 moves ahead, while today AI performs billions of probabilistic matrix calculations to decide which word comes next without any idea of what it is saying, which costs billions of dollars. The article ends by asking how consumers' willingness to pay for this expensive computing power will increase, and says that for now we should just enjoy more complex and colourful spreadsheets and longer presentations with smaller font sizes.

Articles.Title: Who creates and who captures value in artificial intelligence?

stories.Headline: Valentino S. Bagatsing argues humanity is shifting from Homo Sapiens to Homo Transiens as AI outpaces human control
stories.Summary:
Valentino S. Bagatsing wrote an opinion piece on November 15, 2026, regarding the rapid rise of artificial intelligence. He argues that humanity is transitioning from Homo Sapiens to a transient species called Homo Transiens. This shift occurs as digital agents become increasingly powerful and potentially superior to their human creators. The author suggests that this technological evolution is happening much faster than human systems can adapt.

The 2026 AI Index Report from Stanford University, which spans nearly 400 pages, highlights this jagged frontier of development. It notes that AI models can win gold medals in mathematics Olympiads but still struggle with simple tasks like telling time. Furthermore, AI generated internet content surpassed human made content by a ratio of 52 to 48 in 2025. Some advanced systems have already shown signs of deception, bias, and metacognition during closed experiments.

Several industry leaders and thinkers have shared their perspectives on these developments and the associated risks. Sam Altman envisions a future of abundant intelligence and productivity, while Elon Musk warns that a superior intelligence could threaten humanity. Mo Gawdat fears that AI will simply master human traits like surveillance and manipulation, and Dario Amodei believes prosperity is possible if serious risks are overcome. Yuval Noah Harari warns that humans could become like cows, unable to understand the bureaucratic systems controlling their lives.

The author questions whether billionaires and governments should determine the fate of humanity through unbridled AI growth. He worries that AI developed through greed and animal spirits will mirror those negative human traits. Because the technological revolution is already outpacing human control, the transition may take only years rather than decades. Humanity must now decide whether to regain control or be swept away by this new force.

Articles.Title: The Rise of AI and Humanity's Transition to Homo Transiens: Are We Witnessing Evolution's Next Phase?

stories.Headline: Engineer Walter Riviera brings an AI and jobs theater show to Sardinia
stories.Summary:
Walter Riviera, a machine learning engineer and science communicator, is bringing a theater show called "Did AI steal my job?" to Sardinia for two performances, on Monday, November 16th at the Teatro Massimo in Cagliari and on Tuesday, November 17th at the Teatro Civico in Sassari, both starting at 9:00 PM. The show aims to explain artificial intelligence in a simple, engaging and accessible way, with the audience using smartphones to take part in quizzes, questions and surprising discussions. A character named Serafino, a longtime janitor, grapples with the increasingly timely question of what happens when a machine enters our work.

Riviera leads the journey, drawing on a PhD in Distributed Intelligent Systems and collaborations with CERN and the University of Cambridge. Riviera worked for eight years at Intel Corporation as AI Technical Lead EMEA, where he led projects and training activities, and he now works in the sector with AI Wonder, a startup that develops private AI solutions for companies by combining training, consulting and outreach. That experience, according to the article, lets him explain AI with expertise and clarity while highlighting its opportunities, limitations and impact on society, making it understandable outside of technical circles. The two dates are the only ones the article gives, and both start at 9:00 PM.

The article does not say whether tickets are required or how to get them. The article presents the show as a way to discover artificial intelligence in a simple, engaging and accessible manner, with the audience becoming the protagonist through quizzes, questions and discussions rather than passive listening. Serafino's story carries the central question of the evening, which is what happens when a machine enters our work. Riviera's background at CERN, Cambridge and Intel is offered as the reason he can address that question with both expertise and clarity.

The article does not say what conclusions the show reaches about AI and jobs. The article gives no further details about what happens after the two performances, and it does not say whether the show will travel to other cities or return. It also does not report any reaction from the theaters, from audiences or from anyone else quoted. Everything known about the show comes from the single article, which is dated November 14th, 2026, two days before the first performance in Cagliari.

stories.Headline: US authorities investigate whether new AI air traffic system is linked to nationwide flight suspension
stories.Summary:
The US authorities are investigating whether the roll-out of a new AI-based air traffic control system could have been linked to the widespread disruption that led to a temporary suspension of flights across the country on 13 November. Home Secretary Markwayne Mullin confirmed that this possibility is being considered, and he said the inquiry is being carried out together with other federal agencies, including the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The FAA had introduced the SMART platform, or Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, as early as 21 September, and on 10 November the agency announced that it was extending its use to all 22 regional air traffic control centres across the country. The system integrates around 200 data streams, including weather conditions, aircraft routes, airspace congestion and air traffic controller availability, and the artificial intelligence helps to predict delays and recommend the best routes. SMART does not fly the aircraft itself, but merely provides recommendations to FAA specialists.

On 13 November, the FAA suspended departures from US airports because of a communication failure between air traffic control centres, while aircraft that were already in the air were permitted to continue their flights and land. The restrictions were lifted at around 20:15 US Eastern Time, but the nationwide suspension of services lasted around five hours and the disruption affected thousands of flights, so airlines needed extra time to get their timetables back on track. The US authorities found no evidence of a cyberattack, and officials cited the overload of outdated equipment as the main technical problem. The exact technical circumstances of the incident are still being established.

Air Space Intelligence, the company behind the new platform, stated that the nationwide flight suspension was not caused by the SMART system or its integration with FAA equipment. US Transport Secretary Sean Duffy also denied any link between the new AI tool and the technical fault, and according to him the problems arose because the outdated telecommunications infrastructure was overburdened by the introduction of new equipment and technologies. He emphasised that the new components of the flight control system had continued to function. Mullin confirmed that the new artificial intelligence system had been tested, and he replied to journalists outside the White House on 13 November that the matter was being looked into.
